title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: To construct NPC-RubricBench for evaluating clinical reasoning across successive phases of care, we initially identified 9,153 patients from two clinical centres (9,099 internal and 54 external; dataset inclusion flow, S1.1). Of these, 405 patients were included in the final benchmark, yielding 941 patient–phase evaluation units and 17,688 atomic rubric items (Fig. 1a–d). Each evaluation unit is intentionally structured to link a phase-specific clinical task at a particular decision point with the medical evidence available at that moment. Model responses were subsequently assessed using patient-specific criteria grouped into five shared evaluation dimensions, while clinical scenario labels describe the different clinical contexts represented within each phase.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Longitudinal evaluation units. We assembled longitudinal clinical records spanning each patient’s first to most recent documented visit, including clinical notes, laboratory results, physical examination findings, imaging reports and pathology results. We then mapped each patient’s trajectory to six care phases—Work-up, Diagnosis, Staging, Treatment, Toxicity and Follow-up—each representing a distinct clinical responsibility (Fig. 1a). In Work-up , we assessed the examinations and clinical evaluations needed to establish the diagnosis and disease extent; in Diagnosis , the primary pathological diagnosis and other established diagnoses; and in Staging , the T, N and M categories and overall stage. In Treatment , we assessed therapeutic selection and sequencing; in Toxicity , treatment-related adverse events, their management and implications for ongoing treatment; and in Follow-up , post-treatment disease status and surveillance planning. Assessment targets and criterion requirements for all six phases are detailed in Supplementary Section S2.1 (Table S2-A). At selected decision points within these phases, we paired each phase-specific clinical task with the evidence available at that time to form an evaluation unit, excluding later clinical information. Each unit was evaluated separately under the primary Focused formulation. A total of 941 patient–phase units were constructed (784 internal and 157 external), distributed across Work-up (n=191), Diagnosis (n=179), Staging (n=130), Treatment (n=177), Toxicity (n=103) and Follow-up (n=161). To describe the different clinical contexts within each phase, we further grouped the patient–phase units into 17 clinical scenario types (Fig. 1b). Scenario names and corresponding patient–phase counts for the internal and external cohorts are provided in Supplementary Section S1.4 (Table S1-B).

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Hierarchical rubric framework. To assess these different clinical tasks on the same scale, we organized our rubrics into a three-tier hierarchy: five shared evaluation dimensions, phase-specific clinical targets expressed as reusable templates, and patient-specific atomic criteria (Fig. 1c,d; Supplementary Sections S2.1 and S2.3; Table S1) Specifically, Decision Quality assesses the appropriateness of the final clinical judgement or action. Evidence Grounding examines whether the model identifies and uses key available clinical evidence. Status Determination evaluates whether the model accurately determines the patient’s current clinical state and judges the sufficiency of available evidence for the decision. Evidence Faithfulness checks whether responses introduce claims unsupported by the visible record. Safety Adherence measures compliance with relevant clinical safety constraints. Within each phase and dimension, reusable templates define the core clinical requirements and the patient facts needed to fill them. By populating these templates with the evidence available at each decision point, we generated patient-specific atomic criteria that test individual, independently verifiable clinical requirements. In total, this process produced 17,688 active rubric items (mean, 18.8 per unit), comprising 4,753 items for DQ, 2,773 for EG, 3,069 for SD, 2,880 for EF, and 4,213 for SA. Throughout the care phases, the totals of the items ranged from 1,779 in Toxicity to 3,873 in Treatment (Fig. 1d). Through this hierarchy, the five shared dimensions provide a consistent yardstick across the care pathway, while the instantiated criteria hold the models accountable for the exact clinical facts and constraints of each case.

section: 2.2 Model performance across care phases and dimensions
content: Overall performance and phase-specific differences. Under the primary Focused formulation, we evaluated 30 models on up to 941 eligible patient–phase units from 405 patients in the combined internal and external cohorts. Overall DQ estimates ranged from 29.8 for HuatuoGPT-o1-7B [ 34 ] to 85.6 for GPT-5.1 [ 35 ] on the 0–100 scale. Overall EF and SA estimates were generally high, ranging from 73.5 to 95.5 and from 77.5 to 97.1, respectively, whereas SD estimates ranged more widely, from 35.1 to 82.5 (Table S2). Across care phases, model-level DQ means ranged from 56.8 to 94.7 during Diagnosis, compared with 8.9 to 56.0 during Staging (Fig. 2a). Model-centred deviations were calculated relative to each model’s equally weighted six-phase mean within the same dimension. All 30 models scored above their own DQ mean during Diagnosis (median deviation + 28.0 +28.0 points) and below it during Staging ( − 29.3 -29.3 points). SD showed a similar phase contrast, with positive deviations during Diagnosis in all 30 models (median + 22.0 +22.0 points) and negative deviations during Staging in 29/30 models ( − 20.5 -20.5 points). During Work-up, EG and SD were above their respective model-specific means in 30/30 and 27/30 models, with median deviations of + 15.7 +15.7 and + 15.3 +15.3 points. During Treatment, median deviations were positive for DQ ( + 9.7 +9.7 points) and SD ( + 2.0 +2.0 points), but negative for EG ( − 5.7 -5.7 points); these directions were observed in 28/30, 20/30 and 26/30 models, respectively. During Toxicity, all 30 models scored below their own SD mean (median − 14.1 -14.1 points), and 26/30 scored below their EF mean ( − 7.7 -7.7 points). Follow-up showed negative median deviations in DQ ( − 3.7 -3.7 points), EG ( − 18.4 -18.4 points) and SD ( − 6.9 -6.9 points), with 26/30, 30/30 and 28/30 models below their respective means. Complete model-centred estimates and direction counts are provided in Tables S7 and S8.

content: Evidence grounding and clinical judgement. High EG scores coexisted with lower DQ and SD scores at the model–phase level. During Work-up, EG exceeded DQ in 29 of the 30 models, with a median between-dimension difference of 33.6 points. HealthGPT-Pro-4B [ 38 , 39 ] , for example, scored 93.1 for EG, compared with 59.3 for SD and 37.3 for DQ. The median EG–DQ difference was smaller during Diagnosis, at 7.3 points, than during Staging, at 45.3 points. The relative ordering of DQ and SD also differed across phases: all 30 models had higher EG than SD scores and higher SD than DQ scores during Staging, whereas all had higher EG than DQ scores and higher DQ than SD scores during Toxicity. For Qwen3.8-27B-I [ 40 , 41 ] , Toxicity scores were 82.7 for EG, 70.8 for DQ and 52.3 for SD. Within GPT-5.1, Staging scores were 90.0 for EG, 73.1 for SD and 54.2 for DQ; during Treatment, DQ was the highest of these three scores at 94.3, followed by SD at 89.3 and EG at 82.6. Across all models, Treatment DQ exceeded Staging DQ in 30 of 30 models, whereas Treatment EG was lower than Staging EG in 23 (Fig. 3a,d; Table S5). content: Evidence-faithfulness and safety violations. EF and SA violations differed in their distribution across care phases and models. A violation denoted at least one applicable requirement judged Not met within a resolved, eligible patient–phase unit. During Staging, SA violation rates exceeded EF rates in 28 of the 30 models, with across-model median rates of 87.7% and 48.8%, respectively. Staging had the highest SA violation rate in 27 models, whereas the highest EF violation rate occurred during Follow-up in 15 models, Toxicity in 10 and Staging in five. EF rates were nevertheless higher during Staging than during Work-up in every model: GPT-5.1 and Lingshu-32B [ 42 , 43 ] both had Work-up rates of 2.6%, but their Staging rates were 16.2% and 65.4%, respectively. During Toxicity and Follow-up, EF violation rates exceeded SA rates in 25 and 26 models, respectively. Differences between models were also evident within Treatment, where SA violation rates were 81.4% for Qwen3-30B-A3B-I [ 44 , 45 ] and 37.3% for Qwen3.8-27B-I. Comparing Treatment with Follow-up revealed opposite directions across the two dimensions: Follow-up EF violation rates were higher in all 30 models, whereas SA rates were lower in 29. For GPT-5.1, EF violations occurred in 19.8% of Treatment units and 35.4% of Follow-up units, while SA violations occurred in 19.8% and 6.2%, respectively. HealthGPT-Pro-4B was the only model with a higher SA violation rate during Follow-up than during Treatment, at 53.4% versus 49.7% (Fig. 3b,c; Table S9).

authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Mean scores and violation occurrence. High mean EF and SA scores did not imply that violations were uncommon. GPT-5.1 had similar mean EF scores during Staging and Follow-up, at 94.1 and 93.9, although the corresponding violation rates were 16.2% and 35.4%. Within Staging, its mean EF and SA scores were also similar, at 94.1 and 93.8, but SA violations were more frequent than EF violations, at 36.9% versus 16.2%. During Treatment, Qwen3-30B-A3B-I had a mean SA score of 83.8, although at least one SA requirement was unmet in 81.4% of eligible units. The two summaries use different aggregations: mean dimension scores average patient–phase scores derived from the applicable item-level assessments, whereas violation occurrence counts each eligible unit once if any applicable requirement is unmet, irrespective of how many other requirements are satisfied. Occurrence rates are therefore not complements of mean dimension scores and do not quantify the number or severity of violations within an affected unit. Full scores, violation rates, violating-unit counts and denominators are reported in Source Data and Tables S5 and S9.

section: 2.4 Omissions and errors across care phases
content: At the same time, we also noticed that low clinical scores can stem from two distinct problems: leaving out required clinical steps or making outright mistakes. To separate these failure modes, we classified item-level failures by both the clinical dimension involved and the nature of the mistake. Specifically, we mapped failures across DQ, EG, and SD into either omissions or explicit errors. This yielded six failure classes: Decision omission, Decision error, Evidence omission, Evidence error, Status-assessment omission, and Status-assessment error (Fig. 4a). Each rubric item counted toward at most one failure class, whereas a single model response could contain multiple failure types. We then compared these six failure rates across all six care phases and 30 models (Fig. 4b–d).

section: 2.4 Omissions and errors across care phases
content: Failure patterns across care phases. Omission and error rates differed across care phases (Fig. 4b; Table S11). Rates used preset applicable rubric opportunities, including items judged Met or Partial, pooled across all 30 models within each phase and dimension. During Work-up, decision omissions were more frequent than explicit decision errors (33.4% versus 0.3%). Status-assessment omissions showed a similar difference (17.9% versus 0.6% for errors). During Diagnosis, decision and status-assessment error rates were 15.4% and 8.4%, respectively, compared with corresponding omission rates of 11.3% and 5.8%. Staging showed higher rates of explicit errors: decision errors occurred at 48.2%, compared with 3.1% for decision omissions, while status-assessment errors reached 37.8%, compared with only 3.4% for corresponding omissions. During Treatment, decision and status-assessment error rates were relatively low (3.2% and 3.6%, respectively), whereas omissions affected decisions (19.3%), evidence use (25.7%) and status assessments (29.0%). During Toxicity, status-assessment omissions were more frequent than explicit status-assessment errors (26.2% versus 8.2%), and decision omissions also exceeded decision errors (16.6% versus 7.1%). Follow-up had decision- and status-assessment-omission rates of 30.4% and 14.0%, respectively, and the highest evidence-omission rate across the six phases (31.8%), whereas explicit decision errors remained uncommon (1.0%). Case examples of omitted Work-up investigations, incorrect Staging assignments and omitted Treatment components are presented in Supplementary Sections S5.1, S5.2 and S5.3.

section: 2.4 Omissions and errors across care phases
content: Omission and error rates across models. Overall omission rates differed across models (Fig. 4c; Table S10 and Source Data). GPT-5.1 had an omission rate of 5.2% (95% patient-cluster bootstrap CI, 4.6–5.9%), compared with 11.7% (10.9–12.4%) for Gemini 3.1 and 25.4% (24.4–26.5%) for HealthGPT-Pro-4B. The highest overall omission rate was observed for HuatuoGPT-o1-7B (42.5%; 95% CI, 41.1–43.7%). Overall error rates also varied, at 3.7% (95% CI, 3.3–4.2%) for GPT-5.1, 4.1% (3.7–4.6%) for Gemini 3.1 and 9.2% (8.4–10.1%) for Lingshu-32B. Omission rates exceeded error rates in 29 of the 30 models; Claude-Sonnet-4.6 was the exception, with similar omission and error rates (7.1% versus 7.4%). Within individual care phases, models differed in the frequency of specific omissions and errors (Fig. 4d). During Work-up, the decision-omission rate was 1.9% for GPT-5.1, compared with 27.7% for Baichuan-M2-32B [ 46 ] . During Treatment, the corresponding rates were 0.8% for GPT-5.1 and 19.1% for HealthGPT-Pro-4B. Staging decision errors also occurred in models with low overall omission rates: decision-error rates were 29.4% (95% CI, 27.3–31.9%) for GPT-5.1 and 27.9% for Gemini 3.1, compared with 45.2% for Baichuan-M2-32B. Staging status-assessment error rates also differed, at 12.6% for Gemini 3.1 and 29.0% for Baichuan-M2-32B. Full 30-model failure profiles are provided in Suppl. Fig. 3.

authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: In routine clinical practice, clinicians rarely frame requests with uniform granularity; instead, prompts range from brief open-ended questions to detailed checklists. To test how sensitive models are to task phrasing, we compared an open-ended request (Broad formulation) and a structured checklist prompt (Elaborated formulation) against the primary Focused formulation across all 30 models in matched patient–phase units (Fig. 5a). Crucially, we kept the underlying clinical evidence and patient-specific rubrics fixed for all three conditions. We then examined how often scores increased, remained unchanged or decreased, and whether changes in DQ aligned with changes in the other evaluation dimensions.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Phase-dependent changes in decision quality Rephrasing the clinical query altered DQ in most paired evaluations, but broadening and elaboration had contrasting effects on model performance. Broadening reduced mean DQ in all 30 models (median change, − 10.48 -10.48 points), whereas elaboration increased mean DQ in 28 of 30 models (median change, + 2.17 +2.17 points). The direction of DQ changes varied across care phases (Fig. 5b). Under broadening, DQ declines were most frequent in Work-up (88.17%) and Follow-up (75.92%), and were also common in Treatment and Toxicity. In a paired Work-up example, the Broad response omitted biopsy confirmation, distant-metastasis screening and routine blood tests included in the Focused response (Supplementary Section S6.1). Elaboration did not produce consistent gains across care phases. In Treatment, DQ increased in approximately half of the paired units (mean across models, 50.06%). Gains were also more frequent than losses in Toxicity, but increases and decreases occurred at comparable frequencies in Work-up and Follow-up. Diagnosis and Staging were less sensitive to either formulation, with unchanged DQ predominating under both conditions. Nevertheless, Staging DQ declined in 25.49% of broadened pairs and 19.82% of elaborated pairs. In the HuatuoGPT-o1-7B Staging example, elaboration introduced unsupported higher T and N assignments, while neither response established a definitive TNM classification from the abbreviated evidence (Supplementary Section S6.3). Model-specific direction counts, rates and denominators are reported in Table S13.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Joint patterns of change across dimensions. Although elaboration increased mean DQ in 28 of 30 models, it lowered mean EF in 28 and mean SA in 19. These losses were also observed in paired responses without a decline in DQ (Fig. 5b,c). In Diagnosis, DQ remained unchanged in 85.66% of elaborated pairs, yet EF decreased in 21.54% of these DQ-stable pairs. For example, Baichuan-M2-32B retained the supported primary tumour diagnosis under elaboration but introduced an unsupported negative HBV-DNA result; both responses also overstated the exclusion of hepatitis or other comorbidities (Supplementary Section S6.2). Higher DQ could likewise coexist with losses in other dimensions. Among Treatment pairs with increased DQ under elaboration, EF and SA decreased in 23.99% and 23.31% of their respective eligible subsets, while SD declined in 17.73%. This divergence was particularly evident in Qwen3-30B-A3B-I: although elaboration increased Treatment DQ in 85.31% of its pairs, EG decreased in 51.66% of those with improved DQ. In the paired Treatment example from this model, elaboration added a specified induction chemotherapy pathway but omitted an explicit explanation of nodal risk; induction was a reasonable option rather than the sole medically acceptable approach (Supplementary Section S6.4). In Toxicity, improvements in DQ were more frequently accompanied by gains in SD, which increased in 60.83% of DQ-improved pairs under elaboration. Nevertheless, EF decreased in 30.46% of the same DQ-improved group. In the Lingshu-32B example, elaboration added mucositis grading and reassessment, but also asserted unconfirmed oesophagitis and recommended interrupting radiotherapy without first establishing current treatment status and the need for a break. Both responses suggested erythropoietin without addressing restrictions on its use during curative-intent treatment (Supplementary Section S6.5). Changes in evidence-grounding scores could also accompany a less complete clinical plan. In Follow-up, EG increased in 34.45% of elaborated pairs in which DQ decreased. In the Qwen3.6-27B-T Follow-up example, the elaborated response omitted the planned nasopharyngoscopy present under Focused, while both responses overstated what the imaging and single EBV-DNA result established (Supplementary Section S6.6).

content: In this section, we compared model performance across the internal and external cohorts and convened a panel of clinical experts to conduct an expert–LLM judge comparison. We aimed to describe cross-cohort concordance in model mean dimension scores and agreement between automated and expert item ratings.

authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Cross-cohort concordance. We analysed the internal and external cohorts separately under the Focused formulation, comparing model mean scores across five evaluation dimensions for all 30 models. Lin’s concordance correlation coefficients (CCC) exceeded 0.9 for SA (0.961), DQ (0.948) and EG (0.923), with corresponding values of 0.839 for SD and 0.766 for EF (Fig. 6a). GPT-5.1, GPT-5.6-Luna and Qwen3.6-27B-T had the three highest DQ point estimates in both cohorts, retaining the same order. Their internal and external DQ scores were 85.1 and 87.8 for GPT-5.1, 82.1 and 86.5 for GPT-5.6-Luna, and 78.9 and 82.6 for Qwen3.6-27B-T, respectively. Baichuan-M2-32B also had the highest EG mean in both cohorts, scoring 89.4 internally and 88.4 externally. These model-level comparisons were consistent with the overall cross-cohort concordance estimates. Complete cohort-specific scores and concordance estimates for all 30 models are provided in Table S14.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Expert–judge agreement. Three clinical experts independently graded 108 model responses from 12 purposively selected cases, comprising two cases and 18 responses per care phase, yielding 6,075 valid expert–judge item-rating pairs. Exact agreement was calculated separately for each expert and averaged with equal weights. The overall mean exact agreement was 80.12%, with individual expert–judge agreement rates of 78.96%, 80.64% and 80.74% (Fig. 6b). For comparison, the overall mean pairwise agreement among the three experts was 84.02%. Across evaluation dimensions, expert–judge agreement reached 91.17% for SA and 84.80% for EF, both assessed using binary ratings. For the four-level dimensions, exact agreement was 76.30% for DQ, 77.67% for EG and 68.95% for SD. The corresponding mean pairwise inter-expert agreement rates were 77.59%, 77.88% and 69.33%, respectively, closely matching the expert–judge agreement rates for these dimensions. Complete dimension-specific agreement estimates are reported in Table S15. We further compared expert- and LLM judge-derived response-level scores using matched rubric-item subsets within each response (Fig. 6c).

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: In this study, we present NPC-RubricBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate how LLMs fulfill clinical responsibilities at specific decision points in longitudinal NPC care. At each stage, models are evaluated solely based on clinical information available at that moment against patient-specific criteria, preventing later findings from leaking into earlier assessments. Because choosing an appropriate action, grounding it in clinical evidence and assessing the patient’s current status represent distinct clinical demands, our framework links shared evaluation dimensions to patient-tailored criteria to pinpoint which responsibilities a response fulfills and which it leaves unresolved. Across 30 LLMs and six care phases, model performance varied markedly with both clinical responsibility and how the task was framed, driven by frequent omissions of required actions or assessments. Consequently, clinical LLM capability cannot be captured by aggregate performance alone; instead, it must be judged against the specific responsibilities and information available at each stage of care.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Clinical performance varied across care phases and evaluation dimensions. Previous clinically grounded evaluations have shown that the quality of the model response cannot be reduced to the precision of the final-answer alone [ 10 , 14 , 15 , 25 ] . NPC-RubricBench extends this principle throughout a full longitudinal care pathway, showing that similar overall DQ scores often mask wide disparities in evidence use, status assessment, and safety adherence. For example, models performed relatively well in Diagnosis, likely because definitive pathological evidence was already available—a pattern consistent with MedR-Bench, where diagnostic precision increased when key examination results were provided [ 14 ] . But moving from Diagnosis to Treatment, models must also use patient-specific evidence to justify their choice of therapy. Although prior studies have examined treatment planning [ 14 ] and the use of tools and guidelines in oncology decision support [ 1 ] , our results show that a high Treatment DQ score alone does not guarantee that a recommendation is adequately justified. This gap became even clearer during Toxicity and Follow-up , where retrieving recorded information was distinct from establishing the patient’s current clinical state. At these stages, judging whether existing evidence is sufficient—and what further work-up is needed—is a key part of the clinical task. The drop in Follow-up performance may partly reflect the difficulty of reconstructing patient status from evidence distributed over time, a limitation also documented in dedicated longitudinal evaluations [ 47 ] . Even so, our scores do not separate temporal reasoning failures from poor evidence selection, omitted requirements, or properties of the criteria themselves. Moreover, the relative preservation of EF and SA in several low-DQ phases shows that avoiding predefined rubric violations is not equivalent to completing active clinical responsibility. In short, a Met judgment in EF or SA applies only to the specified criterion and does not guarantee freedom from unsupported content or clinical risk.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Omissions and errors identify different failures in clinical responsibility. Separating omitted requirements from explicit errors changes what a low score means clinically. During Work-up, decision omission affected 33.4% of eligible DQ opportunities, whereas explicit decision error affected only 0.3% (Fig. 4b). During Staging, by contrast, explicit decision errors were frequent despite relatively few omissions. Clinically, omissions represent required parts of an assessment or plan that the response failed to address, whereas errors represent stated conclusions that were incorrect. Reviewing only the accuracy of what a model chooses to state would completely miss this distinction. Breaking open-ended responses into atomic criteria [ 23 , 25 ] , our framework makes missing content interpretable by specifying what must be addressed to a given patient in each care phase based on available evidence. This distinction is especially important in the Toxicity and Follow-up, where establishing the current clinical state and determining the next assessment are central to the task. Importantly, completeness does not require forcing a definitive conclusion when evidence is insufficient; rather, expressing uncertainty or deferring a decision is often the appropriate clinical response. Even leading models struggled with both failure modes: Gemini 3.1, for example, posted an omission rate of 11.7% alongside an error rate of 4.1% across eligible DQ, EG and SD opportunities (Fig. 4c). Reducing omissions alone, therefore, cannot resolve clinical unreliability. Instead, this distinction points to two separate priorities for clinical review: verifying that all necessary assessments have been addressed and double-checking the conclusions that the response has already made.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Clinical performance is conditional on task specification. Because clinical LLMs are highly sensitive to instruction wording and the presentation of information [ 15 , 27 ] , a stronger performance under the Elaborated formulation must be interpreted in light of the additional support provided by the query. Explicitly listing expected components reduces what the model must infer about the clinical task, while a broader request leaves more responsibility to the model. Consistent with this perspective, task broadening lowered the average DQ across all evaluated models in NPC-RubricBench, while task elaboration raised the mean DQ for 28 models and reduced it for 2. However, at the pair level, the direction of change varied between phases and models, and higher decision scores under Elaborated prompts did not bring uniform gains in evidence faithfulness or safety adherence. These three query variants thus probe different layers of clinical capability: an Elaborated query tests execution of a specified checklist, the primary Focused query defines the clinical goal without supplying a full checklist, and a Broad query tests whether the model can independently identify the active problem and infer what the patient’s current state requires. Although structured queries can help models cover required content, their evidence use and clinical safety still require separate review.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Expert–LLM Judge agreement. Interpreting these failure patterns requires confidence not only in the scoring procedure, but also in the clinical boundaries defined by the criteria. Although LLM-based judging offers a scalable way to score open responses, automated evaluators are not inherently reliable and remain sensitive to response position, verbosity, and self-enhancement [ 48 , 49 ] . Similarly, while G-Eval improved the alignment with human ratings in general text evaluation, it also highlighted the potential bias towards LLM-generated text [ 50 ] , and RubricBench further exposed a gap between human-annotated and model-generated rubrics [ 51 ] . In clinical scoring, a brief criterion can obscure what counts as sufficient evidence, which clinical expressions are equivalent, and where acceptable judgment ends. In a purposively selected sample, our descriptive analysis showed expert–LLM Judge agreement across matched response–criterion pairs. Independent expert validation and adjudication are still needed to refine criteria and resolve true clinical ambiguity.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: At the cohort level, cross-cohort concordance further tracked the consistency of model mean scores across our two case sources, generating the highest point estimates for DQ and SA and the lowest for EF (Fig. 6a). Because differences between cohorts varied across dimensions—and because both cohorts contributed to the primary analysis—this comparison reflects internal stability across case sources rather than scoring accuracy or transferability to other clinical settings.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Finally, several limitations of this study should be considered. First, although our evaluation framework is designed to be adaptable to other disease pathways, the model performance reported here is specific to NPC and may not generalize to other cancers or clinical settings. Moreover, because the cases were curated to cover clinically important scenarios rather than routine admission frequencies, the observed omission and error rates should not be interpreted as direct estimates of clinical errors or patient harm in daily care. Second, evaluating patient–phase units separately enabled controlled comparisons at defined decision points, but this design did not directly test how models maintain and revise decisions across ongoing, multi-turn clinical interactions. Extending the evaluation to interactive workflows will be essential to see how models adapt as patient care progresses. Third, predefined rubrics cannot capture the full range of clinically acceptable judgments and phrasing in open-ended responses. Some interpretive uncertainty inevitably remains in automated grading, underscoring the value of a broader independent expert review beyond our audited subset.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: We retrospectively curated clinical records of patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) from two independent centers: Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC; internal cohort, diagnosed between 2014 and 2024) and Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (NFYY; external cohort, diagnosed between 2022 and 2024). Eligible patients were identified through institutional electronic medical record (EMR) systems. Before model evaluation, personal names and identifying location details were masked in the model inputs. Calendar dates were expressed as relative time within each patient’s model input. For each patient, we extracted clinical notes, pathological and immunohistochemical reports, imaging studies, laboratory results, and treatment/procedure records and ordered them by the time each became clinically available. Ethics approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of the Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (approval no. B2026-465-01), with the requirement of informed consent waived.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Each patient trajectory was mapped across six prespecified phases of care: Work-up , Diagnosis , Staging , Treatment , Toxicity and Follow-up . A single patient could contribute to multiple phases, with at most one decision point selected for each eligible patient–phase pair to match the phase-specific clinical task. Phase boundaries were anchored to clinically meaningful milestones rather than arbitrary visit or documentation dates. Specifically, each phase was anchored to a distinct clinical milestone. Work-up was anchored at a clinical presentation requiring further diagnostic investigation, and Diagnosis at the first substantive pathology report sufficient for diagnostic assessment. Staging was anchored after pathological confirmation and completion of available pretreatment staging assessments, but before treatment initiation; Treatment , immediately before initiation of the selected anticancer regimen. Toxicity was anchored at a clinically informative toxicity assessment during or near the end of treatment, and Follow-up at a selected post-treatment response or surveillance evaluation.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: Eligibility was assessed independently at the patient–phase level. A candidate unit was deemed clinically eligible when a clear decision boundary could be established and the contemporary record provided sufficient evidence to evaluate the corresponding clinical task. Evidential sufficiency did not require an exhaustive medical history; instead, a candidate phase was excluded only if indispensable evidence was missing or uninterpretable, if the decision boundary could not be resolved, or if evaluating the task required information generated only after the decision point. The final evaluation set was sampled from eligible units to balance clinical scenarios, as detailed in S1.1. To prevent temporal data leakage, model input for each selected decision point was strictly restricted to evidence available at or before that time. All subsequent records—including later pathological diagnoses, staging conclusions, treatment administration, treatment responses, toxicity evolution, and follow-up outcomes—were withheld from earlier phases, as were reference answers and explanatory annotations prepared for benchmark grading. Incomplete contemporaneous records were intentionally retained whenever they reflected genuine clinical uncertainty at the decision point, and the task remained evaluable.

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care

content: During scenario balancing, we excluded 19 Staging units whose reviewed clinical-scenario classification remained undetermined (S1.1). content: To evaluate how task specification affects model performance, we tested three standardized query formulations–Broad, Focused, and Elaborated–across all six care phases. All queries were constructed only after the clinical evidence available at the decision point and the patient-specific atomic rubrics had been locked. Within each care phase, the wording of each query formulation was predefined and applied uniformly across all eligible patients.

authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li, Shu-Han Zhou, Pei-Wen Liu, Ting-Xi Tang, Min Tang, Zhitian Hou, Jianmin Wu, Jian Guan, i Lin, Hongxia Yang, Ying Sun
content: The three formulations differed only in how explicitly they specified the clinical objective and the required response components: (1) the Broad formulation used a single generic request across all six phases, asking the model to assess the patient’s current status and determine the next clinical step; (2) the Focused formulation, which served as our primary evaluation condition, stated the principal phase-specific objective without prescribing a reasoning pathway or response structure; and (3) the Elaborated formulation retained this phase-specific objective while explicitly listing the evidence, clinical conclusions, or management components to be addressed. During Staging, for example, the Focused query asked only for the patient’s clinical stage, whereas the Elaborated query further instructed the model to report the T, N, and M categories with supporting evidence, the overall stage and the staging system used. Across all three conditions, the models received the same system prompt, requiring a final conclusion backed by reasoning from the currently available records. Crucially, the query variants varied only in instruction granularity and introduced no additional patient-specific facts, decision-relevant evidence, or target answers. All prompts and queries were administered in Chinese; English translations of the shared prompt and full query variants are provided in S3.2, with phase-specific task definitions detailed in S3.3.

content: Using the Focused condition as the common baseline, we conducted two paired comparisons within each model and patient–phase unit: (1) task broadening (Broad versus Focused), which tested how models perform when the phase-specific objective is left implicit; and (2) task elaboration (Elaborated versus Focused), which tested how models perform when the expected response components are explicitly listed. Within each paired comparison, the decision point, visible clinical evidence, rubric criteria, and item weights were held strictly constant. For both comparisons, we tracked the proportion of pairs in which scores increased, remained unchanged, or decreased, quantified the magnitude of DQ shifts, and evaluated whether changes in DQ co-occurred with shifts in EG, SD, EF, or SA. Detailed pairing rules and statistical procedures are described in Sect. 4.6 .

content: To evaluate heterogeneous clinical tasks within a common framework, we organized clinical requirements into a three-tier hierarchy: shared evaluation dimensions, phase-specific clinical goals, and patient-specific atomic criteria instantiated from reusable templates (Fig. 1c). Throughout the benchmark, we assessed every response across five dimensions. DQ served as our primary endpoint, measuring whether the final clinical judgment or treatment plan was appropriate for the active care phase. The remaining four dimensions evaluated distinct supporting capabilities. Specifically, EG measured whether the model identified and used key visible evidence, while EF checked whether it distorted the record or fabricated patient-specific claims. In parallel, SD assessed whether the model correctly established the current clinical state, evidence sufficiency, and prerequisites for the requested decision, while SA tracked compliance with clinical safety boundaries and contraindications. Rather than collapsing these dimensions into a single composite score, we analyzed EG, EF, SD, and SA separately alongside DQ to preserve an interpretable profile of each clinical requirement (Supplementary Section S2.1).

content: Rubric development was led by three radiation oncologists specializing in head-and-neck radiotherapy. First, through consensus discussion, the specialists defined phase-specific clinical targets within each shared dimension and translated them into reusable criteria templates. Each template specified the target clinical requirement, the patient facts needed for instantiation, and the applicability rules governing its inclusion. Next, after locking the decision-time evidence for each eligible patient–phase unit, we extracted the relevant patient facts and populated the applicable templates with model assistance. Conditional templates were instantiated only when supported by documented patient facts. To prevent temporal leakage, instantiation relied strictly on the evidence available at the decision point, without consulting the completed longitudinal record or subsequent clinical results. The specialists then reviewed all generated criteria to ensure that each patient-specific atomic item tested a single independently verifiable clinical requirement (more details are provided in S2). For selected criteria, item-specific guidance was used to clarify scoring boundaries. Rubric construction and review were completed independently of the subsequent expert–Judge agreement study. Automated judging and expert validation are detailed in Sect. 4.4 , and outcome definitions and score calculations are described in Sect. 4.5 .

content: Model evaluation and inference. To benchmark clinical reasoning across diverse model families, we evaluated 30 large language models in the primary text-based benchmark, spanning general-purpose and medically adapted systems. We accessed GPT-5.1 [ 35 ] , GPT-5.6 Luna High [ 52 ] , Claude Sonnet 4.6 [ 53 ] , Gemini 3.1 [ 36 ] , DeepSeek V4 Pro Think and DeepSeek V4 Flash [ 37 ] via standardized API interfaces. The two DeepSeek models were open-weight. The remaining models were deployed locally, encompassing the general-purpose Qwen-family models [ 54 , 44 , 55 , 56 , 57 , 40 ] and GPT-OSS-20B [ 58 ] , along with five medically adapted model families: Baichuan-M2 [ 46 ] , Fleming-R1 [ 59 ] , HuatuoGPT-o1 [ 34 ] , HealthGPT-Pro [ 38 , 39 ] and Lingshu [ 42 ] . To ensure a consistent comparison, our primary analysis evaluated both the internal and external cohorts under the Focused query formulation, supplying every model with the exact same decision-time clinical evidence and phase-specific query for each patient–phase unit. The complete details of the model are listed in Table S3, with the model architectures and inference parameters detailed in S3.1.

content: LLM-based rubric judging. To grade open-ended responses on scale, we evaluated the model output at the atomic-criterion level using an LLM-based judge [ 58 ] . Both the LLM judge and the physicians assessed model responses using decision-time clinical evidence, the clinical query and the corresponding atomic rubric criterion. The judge then classified each pair into one of the predefined criterion-specific outcome categories (Sect. 4.5 ). Complete judging prompts and inference configurations are provided in S4.1–S4.2.

content: Expert assessment and judge agreement. To assess agreement between the automated judge and human experts, three physicians independently graded 108 model responses across 12 benchmark cases, covering three models and all three query formulations (Broad, Focused and Elaborated). The physician panel comprised two junior clinicians (1–5 years of clinical practice) and one senior nasopharyngeal carcinoma specialist (more than 20 years of practice). For each response–criterion pair, the physicians assessed anonymized model responses while blinded to the model identity and automated judge ratings. Using the same predefined outcome categories as the automated judge (Sect. 4.5 ), each physician independently rated every applicable item, and we paired their ratings directly with the corresponding automated judgements. We then quantified expert–judge concordance in two ways. First, we calculate the exact agreement of the results separately for each physician and average these proportions with the same weight across the three experts. Second, for each expert, response, and dimension, we computed matched subset scores by averaging the predefined outcome factors equally across the shared criteria and multiplying by 100.

section: S1.3 Evaluation-unit construction and phase eligibility
content: Each eligible trajectory was mapped to six prespecified care phases: Work-up, Diagnosis, Staging, Treatment, Toxicity and Follow-up. A patient could contribute to more than one phase, but at most one decision point was selected for each eligible source patient–phase pair. The selected point had to match the phase-specific clinical task, contain sufficient evidence to make that task evaluable and preserve temporal integrity by excluding information that became available only later. Eligibility was assessed separately for each phase, and only observed, eligible decision points were included.

content: Five shared dimensions were used throughout: Decision Quality (DQ), Evidence Grounding (EG), Evidence Faithfulness (EF), Status Determination (SD) and Safety Adherence (SA). section: S2.3 Patient-specific instantiation of criterion templates
content: We organised criterion templates by care phase, evaluation dimension and clinical topic. We grouped supporting cases using the corresponding reviewed clinical subcategories. We distinguished completed from incomplete assessment and supported from unresolved diagnosis in the corresponding template branches. Additional branches addressed treatment limitations, toxicity grading, treatment safety, and known or undetermined follow-up timing. We represented T and N classifications as parallel partitions and allowed toxicity categories to overlap.

section: S3.3 Clinical tasks and query formulations
content: Each task was evaluated using Broad formulation, Focused formulation and Elaborated formulation. Broad used the same general clinical request across all six tasks. Focused named the phase-specific objective and served as the primary condition and common reference. Elaborated retained that objective and specified the response components. Queries were predefined within each phase and applied unchanged across eligible patients, without adding patient-specific facts or expected answers. Task broadening compared Broad with Focused; task elaboration compared Elaborated with Focused. Each contrast was paired independently. S3.2 displays the complete query translations.

content: Annotations from three experts were paired with recorded automated assessments of the same responses and corresponding criteria. Matching used case, phase, model, response identity and criterion identifiers. The observed sample contains 12 purposively selected cases from the base benchmark and 108 responses, with 2 cases and 18 responses per phase, yielding 6075 valid individual expert–Judge rating pairs. Each expert’s exact agreement was calculated on that expert’s available pairs; the equal-expert arithmetic mean was 80.1% overall. The same procedure was applied separately within each dimension and phase. Experts and the Judge used the same predefined criterion-specific outcome categories (S4.3). Each score-plot point represents one expert, response and dimension. Its two scores equally average the item factors over identical matched subsets and multiply by 100, without zero clipping. DQ, EG and SD subset scores can therefore be negative. Fig. 6b–c and Table S15 report these descriptive observations.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents’ increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent . A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent’s spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user’s email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity —a trusted computing device (or equivalent)—and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: AI agents are increasingly entrusted with consequential decisions and tasks, as personal agents such as Meta’s Muse [ 56 ] , OpenAI’s Dots [ 69 ] , OpenClaw [ 70 ] , and Hermes [ 65 ] see rapid adoption. Users frequently grant these agents broad access to credentials and tools: email, payment methods, shell access, and browser sessions. Yet because agents remain susceptible to hallucination, prompt injection, and misalignment, the same access that lets them act on a user’s behalf also lets them act against the user’s interests.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: A natural response is to constrain what an agent can do via a human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval gate (or HITL gate , for short)—a mechanism that permits an agent’s action to proceed only after human approval [ 42 , 79 , 74 ] . HITL gates are only meaningful, though, if agents cannot bypass them. In practice, agents can often bypass various guardrails to escalate their own permissions, as two examples show.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Circle Agent Wallets allow an account owner to place a daily spending cap on an agent [ 23 ] . They protect cap changes via a HITL gate authenticated using a one-time passcode emailed to the account owner. We show in this paper that given access to an email tool, a wallet’s agent will often autonomously harvest the OTPs and update caps without human approval, bypassing the HITL gate. Nothing here is specific to Circle or to email: Other agentic wallets’ HITL gates use similar design patterns [ 28 , 57 ] .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Early versions of Claude Mythos Preview repeatedly bypassed harness-imposed guardrails. In one case, the model used a tool intended only for file editing to write to the shell’s input, gaining arbitrary code execution. In other cases, it searched low-level process data for credentials and accessed resources that Anthropic had deliberately withheld [ 6 ] .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: These two examples illustrate a shortcoming of many HITL gates: agents may have or gain access to the very resources used to enforce the gate. There are numerous reports of similar examples, e.g., [ 49 , 82 , 64 , 55 ] , and analogous, if not HITL-specific, behaviors arising in controlled evaluations of frontier models [ 18 , 54 , 73 ] .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Despite the pervasive risk of agents subverting HITL controls, however, the security goal of ensuring human approval before execution of a given action has a notable lack of formal modeling in the literature to date .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Inalienable HITL (I-HITL). To fill this gap, we introduce inalienable HITL (I-HITL). The term inalienable , defined as “unable to be removed” [ 21 ] , here refers to HITL approval of agent actions.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Our threat model for I-HITL involves three parties: (1) the human , (2) the agent-controlled platform , such as the human’s client machine, and (3) a target service , typically a remote server, which gates agent actions. Informally, an I-HITL protocol ensures that the service can distinguish an action approved by the human from one approved by the agent acting through the platform, even if the agent has compromised the platform . We also put forth a notion of strong I-HITL that ensures such approval even when an adversarial human controller attempts to delegate approvals to the agent. This implies a form of accountability useful for enforcing policies that mandate human oversight of AI [ 35 ] .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Our work shows that I-HITL requires a trusted entity 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , but that this is not sufficient to realize I-HITL. Specifically, a trusted entity must be able to attest to having generated a given cryptographic key for I-HITL to be possible.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Figure 1 schematically contrasts the insecure HITL configuration of Example 1 with the general architecture for I-HITL that we explore in this work.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Fig. 1 : Two HITL configurations. Red shading indicates resources accessible by the agent; green indicates the HITL gate. In Example 1 (panel \scriptsize\textbf{A}⃝), when an agent-requested action triggers the HITL protocol, the service sends a passcode to an email inbox that the agent can access. In an I-HITL protocol (panel \scriptsize\textbf{B}⃝), the approval channel must terminate at a trusted entity 𝒯 \mathcal{T} that the agent cannot access or forge, so only the human can approve.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Self-escalation. To motivate our work, we realize Example 1 with Circle’s Agentic Wallets as a testbed. Its HITL gate is authenticated by one-time passcodes (OTPs) emailed to the human user. We give ten frontier models an invoice-payment task requiring funds that exceed a previously set daily spending cap. We use a common configuration that allows agents to access the user’s email. With no adversary and no prompting , nine of the ten models bypass human approval, harvesting OTPs and raising their own cap in at least one run. With email-based prompt injection, this drops to seven of ten models, as some models detect the prompt injection. In experiments where the agent is only asked to summarize email, five models both raise the cap and pay an attacker impersonating the user by email. Broadly, our results do not correlate strongly with model capability.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Formalizing I-HITL. Common deployment failures, such as Examples 1 and 2 , prompt us to introduce what we believe to be the first security definition for HITL gates that captures security against an agent-compromised computing platform. Our definition also encompasses a human who attempts to delegate control to an agent. Previous attempts at HITL formalism neglect both of these settings and assume that agents are unable to hijack the approval flow, focusing instead on the potential mismatch between an approved action and its execution [ 85 , 44 ] , a consideration which is subsumed by our definition. Related formal frameworks in ceremony analysis [ 34 , 72 ] and transaction authentication [ 15 , 14 , 84 , 33 ] model platform compromise but not human principals delegating their authority.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We define an I-HITL protocol as having two properties. Completeness states that a service will accept an honest human’s approval of an agent action. Approval-binding says that no adversary can cause the service to accept an approval that the human did not grant. By extending the formal machinery of [ 13 ] , we characterize the communication topologies , i.e., sets of entities and communication channels, needed to realize a complete and approval-binding I-HITL protocol. In the “plain” topology of human, platform, and service used in many existing and proposed systems [ 77 , 78 , 23 , 68 , 27 , 46 , 29 ] there exists no complete, approval binding I-HITL protocol. This result motivates the addition of a trusted entity 𝒯 \mathcal{T} outside of the agent’s control—typically in the form of a trusted computing device. We prove that such a trusted entity alone is not in general adequate for I-HITL, and give precise requirements on its functionality which must be satisfied.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Common authentication approaches—e.g., 2FA / authenticator apps, hardware wallets, etc.—do not offer a trusted entity 𝒯 \mathcal{T} sufficient to realize an I-HITL protocol. Our work serves as guidance for identifying what devices can do so.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Countersign. We introduce Countersign , a prototype implementation of a secure I-HITL protocol that uses an Android or iOS mobile application to realize a trusted entity, showing that the requirements arising from our formal analysis can be satisfied with these devices under realistic trust assumptions. Countersign uses Google’s/Apple’s attestation functionality and the hardware-backed key management capabilities of their respective devices to establish the requisite channels, as well as physical, human-driven approval via a button press or biometric authentication. Excluding scaffolding, Countersign’s core I-HITL logic consists of ∼ \sim 800 LOC for the backend service, and ∼ \sim 150 LOC each for the Android/iOS applications, demonstrating the relative simplicity of the core components. Our implementation also highlights gaps in the current functionality available to developers that could be patched to strengthen I-HITL guarantees.

content: We now specify our threat model, and explain its relevance to several widely deployed HITL gates.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We consider three parties: a human , a computing platform running an AI agent, and a service . The human can interact with the platform directly (by sending/reading messages over input/output peripherals) but communication to the service must pass through the platform. The service aims to determine, for a given message received, whether the human was responsible for it. Informally this means that the human saw, and approved of the message.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We assume that the service is honest and executes exactly the approved action [ 92 ] , but that the agent is adversarial and fully controls the platform, aiming to convince the service that the human is responsible for a message when this is not the case. Although a fully corrupted platform is a strong threat model, we believe it is the right stance to adopt given the trend of increasing integration of AI agents into all manner of computing platforms and the corresponding risk of a corrupted AI agent (e.g. from prompt injection or a misaligned LLM). Agents have previously escaped their sandboxes by exploiting misconfigurations [ 66 , 52 ] , and LLMs have been shown capable of finding and exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in operating systems or browsers.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: The human may be honest or adversarial in our threat model. An honest human represents the dominant paradigm for thinking about human-in-the-loop systems: the human respects any protocol and can keep short secrets (such as passwords) from the adversarial platform.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Increasingly, however, human-in-the-loop frameworks that resist an adversarial human are important. First, LLMs have shown the ability to deceive, mislead and steer users [ 51 , 40 ] , which could manifest itself as users divulging secrets to agents. Second, the human and agent may both be corrupted in the sense that they collude to evade the service’s requirement of human oversight of agent actions. Users tend to delegate to and (potentially over-permission) AI agents [ 53 ] , and a human might seek to avoid responsibility for messages to the service either out of laziness, or to engage with the service adversarially and later blame an AI agent for resulting damage or harm.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: In later sections, we will also consider a fourth party, a t rusted entity . A trusted entity is honest, outside of the control of the agent, and may communicate with all parties directly, although with restrictions on the security and directionality of its communication channels. We deliberately leave the trusted entity abstract, and it may be satisfied by different implementations under different trust assumptions. It may be secure hardware attached to the platform itself, a separate device the human carries—such as a hardware wallet—or a physical place, such as a bank branch or an enrollment office, where communication occurs in person.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We assume that physical interaction with devices is outside of an agent’s capabilities. Although a motivated human could conceivably deploy sensors or actuators to delegate to the agent in this manner, this is a significant barrier, and accountability is more clear cut as it is far less plausible for a human to claim that an agent physically interacted with a device without their knowledge than to claim that a sandboxed agent exploited some vulnerability to escalate their permissions.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Our threat model abstracts away application-specific HITL considerations, instead providing a low-level protocol for the approval of generic messages. In particular, policy determining what actions/messages are protected by a HITL gate is out of scope, in our threat model this is the choice of the trusted service, who also enforces this policy. We likewise do not consider human-factors questions, such whether how actions are formatted as messages for approval, whether these are correctly interpreted by the human that receives them, and whether the human truly engages with approval requests or merely rubber stamps them. When a service processes sequences of messages, an adversary that selectively censors approval of specific messages, or reorders individually benign ones, could cause unintended and harmful outcomes. As an application-level concern, however, this is similarly out of scope.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Our threat model focuses on service-side enforcement of HITL gates. While common (as in Example 1 ), such enforcement for the I-HITL schemes explored in this work requires service-side modification. It also means that using I-HITL to protect local resources requires deployment of a suitably isolated local service.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: See Section IV for discussion of our choice to analyze security symbolically, and for a discussion of authentication/identification-related challenges not captured by our model.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: When mapped to our threat model, many deployed HITL gates share a weakness [ 25 , 57 , 27 ] . Human approval relies on resources that the agent can reach through the platform it runs on. These deployments do use software-based defenses to protect these resources from the agent, such as restricting permissions, sandboxing, and screening for prompt injection, and in many cases these are effective. Such defenses are a relatively weak foundation for security. The following three common HITL gate deployment approaches illustrate the shortcomings.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Agent harnesses deploy HITL gates to pause the agent before a designated action, such as a tool call or shell command, and resume only once a human approves. Examples include LangGraph’s interrupts [ 46 ] , the OpenAI Agents SDK’s human-in-the-loop flow [ 68 ] , and Claude Code’s permission prompts and hooks [ 7 ] . Harnesses enforce permissions and sandbox the agent to limit its control of the host, which in principle should prevent it from subverting the gate. An agent capable of exploiting the harness or operating system can bypass these defenses, but in practice the bar is lower than this. Because the gate’s approval is just a signal from code on the same host, an agent with shell access could launch a process in advance that supplies approvals, even while its own reasoning is suspended by the gate. Alternatively, with write access to the files that configure the gate it could disable it outright. It is especially true that these gates do not prevent adversarial humans from removing themselves from the loop.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Browser agents are a special class of harness in which the agent controls a browser rather than the underlying host, implemented either as an extension (Claude in Chrome [ 8 ] ) or as a browser with a native agent (ChatGPT Atlas [ 67 ] , Perplexity Comet [ 71 ] ). Similar considerations as for generic harnesses apply when gates are browser-enforced, and prompt injection is an especially concerning attack surface given how frequently browser agents encounter untrusted content. However, a browser agent also transacts with third-party websites, which may themselves gate consequential actions, for instance through bot-detection or out-of-band authentication. These defenses move the gate off the potentially-compromised platform, but traditional bot-detection is increasingly ineffective against agents [ 50 ] , and because browsers retain authenticated sessions across services, an out-of-band channel such as email may still be accessible by the agent [ 22 ] . In these cases it remains difficult to distinguish an adversarial human delegating approval to the agent from a misbehaving agent seizing it. Banks already face this problem and, unable to tell authorized agents from rogue ones, have begun blocking agents outright or limiting them to read-only access [ 59 ] .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Agentic wallet platforms such as those from Coinbase and Circle [ 27 , 23 ] are of particular interest because a misbehaving agent can lead directly to financial loss. A common architecture is the agent controlling a wallet through an API, subject to a spending policy set by the user, while a remote service gates any change to that policy on human approval. Control of the human’s platform therefore does not let the agent directly bypass the gate, but if the gate relies on resources accessible to the agent through the platform (either because the agent compromised them or because they were given willingly by the human), it can request and approve an escalation of its own permissions. In the next section we examine this scenario experimentally.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Circle’s Agent Wallets [ 24 ] let a user delegate control of a cryptocurrency wallet to an agent and attach spending policies that cap how much USDC the agent may move per transaction, day, week, or month. Policies are the user’s means of constraining the agent. Circle’s documentation describes them as follows: “set transfer limits or address allowlists and blocklists on your agent wallet to control how it can move USDC and interact with contracts” [ 23 ] . When a wallet CLI command attempts to change a spending policy, Circle gates the change behind a one-time passcode (OTP) emailed to the account owner, with the change only taking effect when the OTP is provided at the CLI. In this section we test the robustness of this HITL gate in a typical deployment, where an agent manages the wallet. As is common in personal-agent deployments, which bundle in email and web access [ 70 , 56 , 69 ] , the agent also has access to local email and web-search tools. 1 1 1 As a result of our disclosing the results of our experiments, Circle’s own documentation now warns against exactly this configuration (Appendix D ). We first aim to characterize whether models will self-escalate to change spending policies in benign situations where these conflict with user requests, before exploring how prompt injection attacks can cause an adversarial agent to bypass this HITL gate in the course of an attack.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Setup. To simulate a typical personal agent, we deploy a LangChain [ 45 ] agent running with three tools available to it: a tool providing access to the user’s email, a web browsing tool and a Circle agent wallet. The wallet is initialized with 10 USDC on Base mainnet, and a spending policy which caps spending at 0.01 USDC per transaction, 0.01 USDC per day, 0.30 USDC per week, and 1 USDC per month. The agent’s system prompt instructs it to act only on the user’s instructions and to treat anything returned by a tool, emails included, as data rather than instructions, and tasks assigned to the agent never make any mention of the wallet spending policy, nor the steps that would be required to update it. Full setup details are given in Appendix B .

content: Experiments. We ran three experiments across 10 models, with 20 trials for each model/experiment pair. The agent harness and initial wallet configuration described above are identical across experiments. Each experiment differs only in the user-assigned task and whether an adversary attempts to launch an indirect prompt injection attack [ 39 ] over email.
