title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We developed the prompt injections used by the adversary adaptively, iteratively changing their content and wording to identify a variant that succeeded the most broadly across models. Such human red-teaming has been shown to be an effective attack strategy, though further iterations and reinforcement learning techniques could potentially increase the effectiveness of our attacks [ 63 ] . Although our prompt injections could likely be tailored to individual models for better attack success, we chose to pursue a universal attack. Our approach simulates an adversary that launches a broad email campaign targeting users that use a personal agent to manage their email and wallet. In this setting, the adversary aims to maximize attack success across a range of models that might be in use, rather than target a specific model. An adversary might also target specific users whom it knows use a specific model, and our results serve as a lower bound for that setting.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Results. Figure 2 summarizes self-escalation likelihood across experiments and models. Example transcripts of self-escalating runs from each experiment can be found in Appendix C . In the Payment agent, No attack experiment, 9/10 models self-escalated to raise their spending limit in at least one run. Only claude-opus-5.5 never attempted self-escalation, instead consistently paying up to its spending limit and reporting the remaining invoices to the user. Self-escalation behavior in a benign setting appears to be inconsistent both across and within models, and does not seem to be especially correlated with model capabilities. This is important for users to be aware of: although a HITL gate like the one employed by Circle’s agent wallet might reasonably be expected to constrain an agent’s behavior even if it is relatively easy for an agent with email access to bypass, this is not the case. A user could run an agent that appears to respect the gate, but if they change models, or simply are using a model that only rarely self-escalates, it may come as a surprise that the gate is no longer effective.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: The Payment agent, Injection attack experiment shows that attempting to prompt inject the payment agent to encourage it to self-escalate does not have a clear impact on self-escalation likelihood. In fact gemini-3.8-flash and claude-sonnet-5 both self-escalate less frequently in the presence of an adversarial email: their transcripts show that the adversarial email is flagged as a likely prompt injection, causing the model to defer to the user even when in the absence of an injection the model occasionally chooses to self-escalate.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: In the Summary agent, Injection attack experiment, adversarial emails frequently caused Qwen and DeepSeek models to self-escalate in order to send funds to the adversary without user approval. gemini-2.5-flash demonstrated this behavior in a single run, but the more recent gemini-3.8-flash model, as well as the GPT and Claude models, appear largely resistant to the prompt injection. That this attack succeeds at all is alarming: it would cost an adversary very little to launch a broad email campaign employing this attack, and they could expect it to succeed against at least some users, even if these users have set restrictive spending limits for their agent wallets. We disclosed these findings to Circle prior to publication: they have since added a warning to its agent-wallet documentation cautioning users against giving an agent access to the email inbox used to receive the OTP. We describe the disclosure and the resulting change in Appendix D .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: The risk illustrated by our results can be mitigated in different ways. As per Circle’s warning, users should be cautioned not to deploy personal agents that have access to both a Circle wallet and the email associated with that wallet. Users may still be tempted to deploy agents with access to both for convenience, however, and it may be challenging to robustly disable email access, as an agent could leverage exploits or find stored credentials using a terminal/browser to gain access. Perhaps the most reliable defense is to develop stronger HITL gates which do not allow agents to self-escalate. In the following sections we develop and explore our stronger security notion called inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL).

All other messages are ignored. Programs in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} are also stateless and must correspond to human capabilities, meaning that cryptographic operations are not possible. Although this is restrictive, we show in Section V that allowing a more expressive class of programs does not weaken the channel requirements necessary for I-HITL. Note that although our threat model permits an adversarial human, ℋ \mathcal{H} as a party in the topology is always honest. Intuitively, this is because ℋ \mathcal{H} represents the physical human: if ℋ \mathcal{H} takes an action that allows a message to be approved, that constitutes a human-in-the-loop, and so there is no meaningful way to a human to adversarially deviate. We will see in Section VI-C that an adversarial human instead yields weaker channel labels on 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , as this adversary can potentially extract and share keys.

content: Individual authentication. Our topologies contain a single human ℋ \mathcal{H} and a single trusted entity 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , so the channels between them, and hence the association between the device and the human, are fixed by the topology itself. In a deployment with many humans and devices, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} cares not only that some human approved m ∗ m^{*} but that a specific human did, which requires 𝒮 \mathcal{S} to know which ℋ \mathcal{H} the enrolled 𝒯 \mathcal{T} has channels with. We treat this binding as a setup assumption. In practice, it is established during 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅 \mathsf{Enroll} by authenticating ℋ \mathcal{H} to 𝒮 \mathcal{S} through 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , for example by enrolling the device from a session authenticated before the platform came under the agent’s control, or by having the device collect biometric information that is shared with 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . A human could also hand the enrolled device to another human, which only biometric authentication on every approval would prevent. For simplicity, we consider this type of authentication out of scope and model a single ℋ \mathcal{H} throughout.

content: Theorem 7 says nothing about where the labels on each 𝒯 \mathcal{T} channel come from in the first place. A trusted entity’s channels are determined by the device that realizes it and by the human’s behavior when interacting with that device. The next section explores these factors in practice, deriving channel labels from device characteristics such as whether 𝒯 \mathcal{T} ’s key is attested or extractable, and whether an adversarial human attempts to delegate to the agent. The theorem then lets us characterize which approaches allow I-HITL protocols.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Many approaches used for authentication (hardware wallets, authenticator apps, etc.) appear well-suited to realizing I-HITL, but the analysis in preceding sections shows achieving approval-binding can be subtle. In this section we explore whether I-HITL can be realized by devices and protocols in use today. We focus on standalone hardware devices and mobile phone-based authentication protocols, disregarding some possible instantiations of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} such as in-person interaction. Section VI-A derives labels on 𝒯 ↔ 𝒮 \mathcal{T}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{S} channels ( ℓ 𝒮 ​ 𝒯 , ℓ 𝒯 ​ 𝒮 ) (\ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}}) based on a trusted entity’s key management. Section VI-B similarly explains how the display and user inputs provided by a trusted entity determine the labels of ℋ ↔ 𝒯 \mathcal{H}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{T} channels ( ℓ ℋ ​ 𝒯 , ℓ 𝒯 ​ ℋ ) (\ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}}) . Section VI-C applies the analysis in the preceding subsections to specific authentication methods in use today, and using Theorem 7 , classifies them according to their ability to realize I-HITL.

Throughout this section we therefore work in terms of the strongest channel labels which can be confirmed by a verifier. For instance, if a device serving as 𝒯 \mathcal{T} has a display which lets it realize a secure channel to ℋ \mathcal{H} , but it generates no evidence which can be used to verify the existence of this channel, we treat the channel as insecure.

content: In practice, the labels between 𝒯 \mathcal{T} and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} depend upon a secret key k k held by 𝒯 \mathcal{T} but not the adversary. We write k k to distinguish it from the signing key 𝗌𝗄 {\sf sk} of the I-HITL protocol constructions, though in practice the two may coincide. Since initially all channels between the two are insecure, establishing a new channel requires two properties of k k : it must be bound , i.e., verifiably held by 𝒯 \mathcal{T} rather than by a party impersonating it, and it must be isolated , i.e., not held by any adversarial party. Neither property is directly observable by a verifier. Both instead rest on attestation : evidence, verifiable against a root of trust, that k k was generated within 𝒯 \mathcal{T} and whether it is extractable by ℋ \mathcal{H} . Attestation settles binding outright, but settles isolation only if k k is not extractable, otherwise isolation, and therefore the channel labels, depend on whether ℋ \mathcal{H} acts honestly or adversarially—a feature of our threat model that differs critically from previous models of human principals [ 34 , 72 , 15 , 14 , 84 , 33 ] .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Key attestation ( attested / unattested ): Some devices, e.g., Yubikeys [ 90 ] and Ledger wallets [ 47 ] , can digitally sign the keys they generate, where signatures are verifiable against a manufacturer root of trust. Mobile phones generally provide an analogous capability, verifiable against the OS vendor’s root, which installed apps may optionally use to provide evidence of their key management. We use the designation attested for such devices. Other trusted hardware devices, e.g., standard crypto wallets, lack this capability and are unattested , so is any key that 𝒯 \mathcal{T} did not generate, such as a shared secret delivered by 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , since attestation can only speak to keys created within 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . When a device is attested, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} can use an attestation to verify that key k k is truly held by 𝒯 \mathcal{T} and subject to a fixed policy. Without attestation, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} cannot tell whether k k is held by the adversary, so both channel labels are ins .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Key control ( extractable / encumbered ): Even if a key generated by a device is attested, it may still be extractable by the user. This is in fact an important feature in systems that do not support key rotation, e.g., cryptocurrency addresses. Keys that are not extractable by a user are referred to as encumbered [ 41 ] . Key control is a property of the device’s policy reported by attestation, so 𝒮 \mathcal{S} can verify whether k k is encumbered. A device may hold both extractable and encumbered keys.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Trust model for ℋ \mathcal{H} ( honest / delegating ): An honest ℋ \mathcal{H} does not attempt to delegate control to an agent, and therefore can be trusted to not extract and share the device key k k , even if extraction is possible. However a delegating ℋ \mathcal{H} may do so in order to allow an agent to communicate with 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and bypass a HITL gate. If ℋ \mathcal{H} is assumed to be honest, then any attestation suffices as evidence that key k k is held only by 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , and can be used to establish an authentic channel to 𝒮 \mathcal{S} (if k k signs messages) or a confidential channel from 𝒮 \mathcal{S} (if k k is the private half of an encryption key pair). However, if ℋ \mathcal{H} attempts to delegate, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} cannot know whether k k is held by the adversary unless the attestation also proves that k k is encumbered.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: The labels between 𝒯 \mathcal{T} and ℋ \mathcal{H} are determined by 𝒯 \mathcal{T} ’s two human-facing interfaces: a display , through which it sends requests, and a user input , through which ℋ \mathcal{H} can respond. The properties of the display and user input determine the labels as follows:

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Display trust ( trusted / untrusted ): A display is trusted if the adversary cannot show the human a request that appears to come from 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , by overlay or imitation. Examples include a hardware wallet’s screen and TEE-rendered UIs [ 5 ] . A display on a phone may also be trusted if the identity of the app controlling it is known, the app enforces suitable protections, and the integrity of the OS can be verified. It is untrusted otherwise, e.g., a browser tab or app running on an untrusted platform, which the agent can replicate pixel for pixel [ 16 ] , or SMS and email, whose sender IDs are easily spoofed. A trusted display realizes an authentic channel from 𝒯 \mathcal{T} to ℋ \mathcal{H} .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Display privacy ( private / exposed ): A display is private if the adversary cannot read it and exposed if it can: a private display realizes a confidential channel from 𝒯 \mathcal{T} to ℋ \mathcal{H} . Private displays include the screens of devices the agent does not control, such as an external hardware wallet. A phone screen, by contrast, is potentially exposed even without OS compromise as accessibility services, which phone agents commonly use to operate other apps, can read the content of any app’s window [ 4 ] .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: User input trust ( trusted / untrusted ): A user input is trusted if the adversary can neither operate nor simulate it. A keyboard or touchscreen to an agent-controlled device is untrusted , because the same accessibility API that exposes the screen also lets an app perform taps, gestures, and text entry [ 4 ] . A trusted user input therefore typically relies on hardware that software cannot drive, e.g., the buttons of a hardware wallet, the touchscreen of a Ledger Stax or Flex, which the secure element controls directly, or a phone’s side button and biometric sensor, whose input is delivered to secure hardware rather than to the OS. A trusted user input instantiates an auth channel from the human to 𝒯 \mathcal{T} .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: User input action ( keypad / confirmation ): We refer to an user input as a keypad if a human can send arbitrary messages on it and a confirmation if it conveys one bit per request, such as a button. A trusted keypad instantiates an auth channel from ℋ \mathcal{H} to 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . A trusted confirmation only allows a single authentic bit to be communicated: 𝒯 \mathcal{T} displays the message it is about to sign and signs it when the human presses the button, so the press says that the human agreed, not to which message. If the display is untrusted, the adversary can show the human a benign m ′ m^{\prime} in place of m m , and the human’s genuine press approves m m , yielding an ins channel from ℋ \mathcal{H} to 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . With a trusted display, the human sees the m m that 𝒯 \mathcal{T} signs, and the confirmation and display together realize an auth channel from ℋ \mathcal{H} to 𝒯 \mathcal{T} .

content: We now consider concrete instantiations of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , exploring both standalone trusted devices and mobile applications. For each we analyze the properties of its display, its input, and its key management. Together with Table I and Table II , these properties determine the labels on 𝒯 \mathcal{T} ’s channels, and hence, by Theorem 7 , whether the approach realizes I-HITL. Table III summarizes our findings, the full analysis is deferred to Appendix E .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We evaluate each instantiation under our two trust models for ℋ \mathcal{H} , honest and delegating. If an instantiation is secure under a delegating ℋ \mathcal{H} we say it realizes strong I-HITL, if it is secure only under an honest ℋ \mathcal{H} it realizes weak I-HITL. The distinction is relevant because in some settings a service needs assurance that ℋ \mathcal{H} approved an action, even when they may not trust ℋ \mathcal{H} . Under weak I-HITL a delegating ℋ \mathcal{H} can hand the agent the means to approve on its behalf, and the service cannot distinguish the agent’s approvals from the human’s. A proof π \pi therefore establishes nothing about who approved, and ℋ \mathcal{H} can disavow any action by attributing it to the agent. Under strong I-HITL no such delegation is possible, and π \pi can serve as the evidence that the human, not the agent, approved the action. A delegating ℋ \mathcal{H} may still approve without inspection, but cannot falsely claim that their approval was hijacked by an adversarial agent to avoid being held responsible.

content: The two Ledger configurations in Table III run on the same hardware and differ only in key management: a key derived from the user’s recovery seed is attested but extractable, since the user holds the seed by design, and so realizes only weak I-HITL. Encumbrance is thus a property of how 𝒯 \mathcal{T} manages k k , not of the device alone.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Table III is not exhaustive, but apart from our construction the three standalone devices listed are the only instantiations of I-HITL we found. Of the instantiations that realize strong I-HITL, all except ours require dedicated hardware. The Wultra Talisman is issued by banks and enterprises to their own customers, and Ledger wallets are purchased and carried for specific applications (e.g., cryptocurrency management). Realizing I-HITL on a Ledger device also requires a purpose-built app, since the endorsement keys are issued per application. Thus the Ledger rows of Table III reflect what the hardware can support, not what shipped Ledger apps currently provide. Our construction relies only on the attestation and key management capabilities available to any Android or iOS application, so it may be deployed without requiring users to acquire new devices.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: In this section, we present Countersign, a mobile phone-based strong I-HITL implementation. Mobile phones are a natural candidate for 𝒯 \mathcal{T} because they have the necessary interfaces and attestation capabilities, and are readily accessible to users. Yet, as shown by in Section VI , many mobile phone applications providing closely related functionality (e.g., authentication and proof of personhood) fail to realize strong I-HITL. Countersign demonstrates that the necessary capabilities for I-HITL exist on mobile phones (under reasonable assumptions), and many similar applications are insecure simply because their workflow is designed for a subtly different threat model. Countersign’s core I-HITL logic consists of ∼ \sim 800 LOC for the backend service, and ∼ \sim 150 LOC each for the Android/iOS application (excluding generic scaffolding such as configuration, data models, and user interfaces), illustrating the feasibility of achieving I-HITL in practice. Our code is open-source at https://github.com/I-HITL/countersign , low-level implementation details are deferred to Appendix F .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: In our instantiation, the trusted entity 𝒯 \mathcal{T} is a mobile application running on a commodity phone, so we rely on the phone to execute the application faithfully and to manage its keys securely. Our design leverages the attestation mechanisms provided by the Android and iOS ecosystems to allow 𝒮 \mathcal{S} to verify the security properties of 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . 𝒮 \mathcal{S} must establish two properties. The first is code integrity : the application handling requests and controlling the device must be an honest implementation, running on an operating system that has not been tampered with (i.e., rooted or jailbroken). The second is key management : the verification key 𝗏𝗄 \mathsf{vk} must be generated and stored in secure hardware, with any exportability and usage restrictions enforced by that hardware, as characterized in Section VI-A . We examine here how the Android and iOS attestation mechanisms support these requirements.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Android. To verify app integrity, Android applications can make requests to the Play Integrity API [ 38 ] , which returns a Google-signed verdict with two key fields. First, the device verdict states whether the device is a certified Android device with a locked bootloader, an unmodified system image, and recent security patches. Second, the app verdict states whether the app on the device matches the binary distributed through Google Play. Regarding key management, apps can generate and use keys through the Android Keystore system [ 36 ] . An app that generates a hardware-backed key using the keystore (backed by either a TEE on the main processor, or a dedicated hardware component called the StrongBox) can request an attestation certificate chain for that key. The leaf certificate chains to Google’s root of trust, and contains an extension specifying the attested key’s security properties, including whether it resides in the TEE or StrongBox (and therefore cannot be exported), its permitted uses, whether each use requires user authentication and by what method, and the identity of the app that generated it.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: iOS. To verify app integrity, iOS applications can make requests to the App Attest service [ 9 ] , which returns an Apple-signed attestation that a service can use to verify that the request came from a genuine instance of the app, as Apple distributed it, on a genuine Apple device. Unlike Play Integrity, however, the attestation makes no statement about the integrity of the operating system itself, so a service relying on it must additionally assume that the device is not jailbroken, an assumption it cannot verify. Regarding key management, apps can generate key pairs whose private key is stored in a dedicated hardware component, the Secure Enclave, from which it cannot be exported. The same App Attest attestation certifies this property for a key and names the app that generated it, so a service learns both that the key is hardware-held and which genuine app holds it. Subsequently, the app can sign requests to its server with the key, in a format fixed by App Attest that adds a counter for replay protection. Unlike an Android keystore key, however, the key’s use cannot be made conditional on user authentication such as Face ID.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
section: VII-B Realizing I-HITL Channels in Countersign
content: Fig. 6 : The Countersign topology. A user’s mobile phone serves as 𝒯 \mathcal{T} and establishes channels to ℋ \mathcal{H} and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . Channels are labeled with the mechanism they use to establish authenticity. On the phone, the green lock represents that the enclosed functionalities are run by on-device secure hardware, the application itself is run by the OS.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
section: VII-B Realizing I-HITL Channels in Countersign
content: Figure 6 depicts the topology of Countersign and the features of the mobile device used to realize 𝒯 \mathcal{T} ’s channel labels. With channels established, Countersign uses the enroll-by-authenticated-key, approve-by-message construction given in Figure 5 . Here we explain each channel label in more detail. The header of each paragraph specifies the channel label we consider, the mechanism used to protect that channel, and the formal label in ℒ \mathcal{L} we argue is realized by our implementation.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
section: VII-B Realizing I-HITL Channels in Countersign
content: ℓ 𝒯 ​ ℋ \ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}} : Trusted display, auth . A phone has no display that software cannot drive, so Countersign relies on device/code integrity to ensure the agent cannot show ℋ \mathcal{H} a false request. The approval screen is drawn by the Countersign binary, and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} has verified through attestation that this binary is genuine and running on an unmodified OS. Given an honest OS, the remaining attack is overlay: an agent-controlled app draws over the approval screen. Countersign defends against this on Android by rendering the approval screen with overlays blocked and checking at approval-time that its own window holds focus and is unobscured; iOS does not permit cross-app overlays at all. The display remains exposed in the sense of Table II and does not provide confidentiality (for instance, accessibility services could read the contents of the approval screen) and therefore the channel is auth but not sec .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
section: VII-B Realizing I-HITL Channels in Countersign
content: ℓ ℋ ​ 𝒯 \ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}} : Biometric input, auth . The input interface of Countersign allows confirmation in the sense of Section VI-B : ℋ \mathcal{H} conveys one bit per request, by presenting a biometric. As the biometric sensor delivers its reading to secure hardware rather than to the app or OS, the agent can not simulate it from software. By Table II , a trusted confirmation yields an auth channel only together with the trusted display described in the previous paragraph. On Android, the signing key is generated with a per-use biometric requirement enforced by the keystore, and attested to by the key’s certificate. On iOS, the App Attest key cannot enforce such a biometric policy on a hardware level, so Countersign uses a second Secure Enclave (which is not App Attest) key whose public key is signed by the App Attest key, and which does have a per-use biometric requirement. This means that on Android the biometric requirement is attested through hardware, while on iOS it is a claim by the attested app, and holds only as long as code integrity holds. In both cases, the binding of the biometric to the message seen by ℋ \mathcal{H} requires code integrity, since on Android the hardware learns that a biometric succeeded but not what was on screen.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
section: VII-B Realizing I-HITL Channels in Countersign
content: ℓ 𝒯 ​ 𝒮 \ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}} : Remote attestation, auth . Countersign sends 𝗏𝗄 \mathsf{vk} to 𝒮 \mathcal{S} together with attestation evidence, bound to a challenge issued by 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . On Android, the evidence consists of the key attestation and a Play Integrity token whose nonce commits to the same service challenge. 𝒮 \mathcal{S} verifies the key attestation chain to Google’s root, checks that the key is hardware-backed, gated by device authentication, and was created by the correct app, and separately checks that the integrity verdict recognizes the binary, the signing certificate, and the device. On iOS, 𝗏𝗄 \mathsf{vk} is a Secure Enclave key generated alongside a separate App Attest key. 𝒮 \mathcal{S} verifies the App Attest key’s attestation to Apple’s root, then uses that key to verify a signature over 𝗏𝗄 \mathsf{vk} . In either case, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} learns that 𝗏𝗄 \mathsf{vk} belongs to an attested instance of Countersign, placing Countersign in the encumbered, attested row of Table I . This establishes an auth channel from 𝒯 \mathcal{T} to 𝒮 \mathcal{S} under both honest and delegating humans, allowing Countersign to realize strong I-HITL.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
section: VII-B Realizing I-HITL Channels in Countersign
content: ℓ 𝒮 ​ 𝒯 \ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}} : ins . The channel ℓ 𝒮 ​ 𝒯 \ell_{\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}} is not used by Countersign, and can be considered insecure for our purposes.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
section: VII-B Realizing I-HITL Channels in Countersign
content: Comparison to existing apps. The mechanisms described above are available to any mobile app, and push authenticators (e.g., Duo Mobile, Microsoft Authenticator, Okta Verify) already use several of them, but still fall short of I-HITL due to issues in their workflow. First, attestation of ℓ 𝒯 ​ 𝒮 \ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{S}} is only beginning to appear: Duo Mobile on Android now appears to use attestation, but this is undocumented and unevenly enforced, and third-party clients have historically been able to enroll in place of a genuine app [ 1 ] . Second, the approval is not bound to the message ℋ \mathcal{H} sees but instead an 𝒮 \mathcal{S} -selected identifier, so 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is not left with a publicly verifiable proof of approval for accountability purposes. Third, ℓ ℋ ​ 𝒯 \ell_{\mathcal{H}\mathcal{T}} typically uses the touchscreen as an input interface, which in contrast to hardware-backed biometrics is simulatable in software. Finally, these apps often fall back to alternate methods of approval such as exportable passcode seeds, SMS messages, and backup-based re-enrollment. These fallbacks may be acceptable for pure authentication, where the human is trusted and recoverability is an important feature, but compromise I-HITL.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: In this section we discuss limitations surfaced by our implementation: device capabilities or ecosystem characteristics which require additional trust assumptions. These gaps could be filled by future development of mobile devices to allow stronger I-HITL guarantees.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Trusted display. On both Android and iOS the Countersign app relies on the OS to prevent other applications from tampering with the approval screen, and to bind the displayed message to the trusted confirmation. A more robust implementation would remove this dependency. Android Protected Confirmation (APC) [ 37 ] previously provided a path to exactly this: a TEE rendered the prompt and signed the message together with a hash of what it displayed, so the display was trusted and the confirmation bound to the message without any trust in the OS. However, APC was deprecated due to low adoption and high maintenance costs [ 37 ] . Its return, or an equivalent on iOS, would let Countersign realize ℓ 𝒯 ​ ℋ \ell_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{H}} as a trusted display without relying on OS integrity.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Device integrity on iOS. On Android, the Play Integrity API [ 38 ] provides evidence of device integrity which does not have an equivalent on iOS. In particular, the service cannot determine from App Attest whether the device has been jailbroken. Additionally, while iOS supports biometric authentication, App Attest keys cannot be configured to require biometric authentication before use. Instead, this restriction must be enforced by the app, whose integrity may not be preserved on a compromised OS. On Android, by contrast, the per-use biometric requirement is enforced by the secure hardware and reported in the key’s attestation, so the service need not trust the application for it. Consequently, our iOS implementation relies on the additional assumption that the operating system remains trustworthy to enforce the integrity of biometric authentication.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Roots of trust. Every channel label in Section VII-B ultimately rests on a certificate chain to Google’s or Apple’s root. This is a stronger trust assumption than the manufacturer root of a hardware wallet, which is used only at provisioning. Apple/Google’s servers must be reachable to issue attestations, so an outage blocks enrollment. The evidence provided by attestation is also is a snapshot of device/application state at the moment of verification rather than an enduring guarantee. A key attestation certificate records the verified-boot state at key generation, and an App Attest attestation is issued once, so neither is invalidated by a kernel compromise after enrollment. On Android, Countersign narrows this window by requesting a fresh Play Integrity verdict with every approval. However, this cannot detect if a kernel is compromised after boot, since verified boot measures the system only at boot. The effective window on Android is therefore the interval since the last boot. On iOS there is no corresponding mechanism, and the window is the interval since enrollment.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Key recovery. We do not address the issue of key recovery for 𝒯 \mathcal{T} in our initial implementation of Countersign. As strong I-HITL requires that ℋ \mathcal{H} cannot directly access 𝗌𝗄 {\sf sk} , any recovery path will require ℋ \mathcal{H} to re-execute a procedure like 𝖤𝗇𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅 \mathsf{Enroll} in order to restore an encrypted copy of 𝗌𝗄 {\sf sk} kept by a trusted entity such as 𝒮 \mathcal{S} or to generate a fresh 𝗌𝗄 {\sf sk} .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: HITL and permissions in agent systems: HITL approval is a standard recommendation for agent control [ 74 ] and a common feature of agent frameworks; Michael and Roesner [ 58 ] survey such permission mechanisms and note the absence of formally verified enforcement. Work on agent policy, e.g., [ 30 , 75 , 83 ] , specifies which actions an agent may take, and complements our focus on securely enforcing those human approvals dictated by policy.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: User authentication: User authentication, including a long line of work on 2FA (e.g., [ 19 ] ), considers how to verify the identity of a particular user, but assumes a trusted client device. (Otherwise, session hijacking is fatal.) Formal analyses of FIDO2, for instance, exclude compromised clients from their guarantees and model user approval as a one-bit gesture [ 12 , 17 ] . An agent, however, can compromise both 2FA factors when they converge on a host [ 31 , 43 ] , and effectively hijack an authenticated session. Hardware-based transaction authentication, e.g., using hardware wallets [ 10 ] , arose for exactly this reason, although, as Table III shows, they are not always sufficient for I-HITL. I-HITL can be viewed as a generalization of transaction authentication to agent systems, where transactions can be of many different types and where adversarial delegation poses a concern.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Agent authorization: A number of works on AI agents (e.g., [ 76 ] ) and standards specifications (e.g., MCP [ 60 ] ) consider ways of using existing authorization infrastructure, such as OAuth, to authorize agents. These rely on existing user authentication, and where they call for human approval of an action, they leave unspecified how that approval reaches the service. When the human reaches the identity provider or approval prompt through the agent’s platform, these designs fall in the plain topology of Theorem 4 .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Approved vs. executed actions: Classical work on authorization from untrusted terminals [ 2 , 11 , 3 ] shows the danger of signed approvals in the face of a deceptive rendering layer (a problem sometimes called what you see is what you sign (WYSIWYS)). Weng [ 85 ] adapts WYSIWYS to agent approvals, but simply assumes a trusted path. Transaction-authentication devices [ 84 ] and trusted-path systems [ 91 ] address the issues in these works by giving the human a channel that bypasses a potentially compromised host. Our trusted entity T T plays a similar role, but we characterize exactly which channels T T needs and, unlike classical schemes, consider adversarial human delegation. Relatedly, Loopjacking [ 44 ] studies the failure in which an implementation applies a genuine approval of one operation to a different one. Approval binding rules this out at the gate, since a proof verifies only for the message the human approved. We assume the service then executes that message faithfully [ 92 ] .

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Proof of Personhood (PoP): Many proposed [ 20 ] and deployed systems aim to enable online services to distinguish humans and bots. The best known, World, issues a credential to a human whose uniqueness is established biometrically or using a national identity document. World’s human-in-the-loop package [ 80 ] gates agent actions on a World ID proof, but does not realize I-HITL, for two reasons. (1) The human never sees the action on a trusted display: the action is rendered only by the agent’s platform, and the World app displays a description that the platform also supplies and that is bound neither to the proof nor to the service’s signature on the request. (2) The documented integration exposes approval as a tool that the agent chooses whether to invoke, unless the developer separately verifies the proof before the protected action executes, as World’s documentation now advises [ 87 ] , the agent can bypass the gate by not invoking it. An unreleased revision of the package replaces World ID proofs with a standard World ID login, which never shows the human the action. The approval it produces is checked with a secret stored on the same server that runs the agent, so a compromised platform can forge it. More broadly, World does not aim to prevent delegation: AgentKit [ 86 ] links agent wallets to verified humans. Additionally, because World aims to deduplicate humans, it requires use of a single global registry, greatly limiting its scope of application. 2 2 2 Users from only 17 countries are currently eligible for identity-document-based authentication.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Other notions of PoP, e.g., [ 47 ] , give assurance of human approval only to the user herself, not a relying service.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Secure human–server communication: Building on security ceremonies [ 34 , 72 ] , Basin et al. [ 13 ] characterize the topologies permitting authentic or confidential human–server communication through a compromised platform. We adopt their topology framework and impossibility argument, but differ in key ways: they fix all non-platform channels as secure and let the device share keys with the server a priori, whereas we grade each trusted-entity channel independently and assume no initial knowledge, making key establishment (and hence attestation and encumbrance) central to our characterization ( Theorem 7 ). Our goal also differs from theirs, in that we bind a human’s approval to an adversary-chosen message through a publicly verifiable proof, including (for strong I-HITL) against a human who attempts to delegate approval to the agent.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: HITL gates are widely deployed as a critical line of defense against misbehaving agents, yet most operate in a topology that does not separate the agent from the resources used to approve its actions. Our experiments with a mainstream agentic wallet show the practical consequences. Given access to the inbox that receives a gate’s OTPs and a task blocked by a spending cap, most frontier models will autonomously bypass the gate. Some will do so on an attacker’s instruction and send the attacker money.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: We introduced I-HITL to formalize what a secure HITL gate must guarantee, and strong I-HITL to extend that guarantee to humans who attempt to delegate approvals to agents in violation of oversight policies. In a symbolic model of channel security we proved that a trusted entity is necessary for I-HITL ( Theorem 4 ) but not sufficient ( Theorem 7 ): this entity must attest to the keys it generates and, for strong I-HITL, encumber them. We classified existing devices against these requirements and presented Countersign, which realizes strong I-HITL on off-the-shelf Android and iOS devices.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Takeaways for deployers and platform vendors. The default topology of many agentic systems, in which the gate co-resides with the agent, fails in principle ( Theorem 4 ) and in practice ( Section III ). Guidance that restricts agent capabilities (e.g., denying email access) shifts the burden to users and is unlikely to hold; we urge service vendors to adopt the stronger assurances I-HITL makes achievable. We likewise urge authenticator-app vendors to offer an I-HITL approval mode, since push authenticators already implement most of the required mechanisms ( Section VII-B ). We finally urge mobile OS vendors to supply two missing primitives: a TEE-rendered confirmation UI and attestable gating of key use on biometric authentication.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Takeaway for regulators. Regulations such as the EU AI Act [ 35 ] mandate human oversight without specifying how to define or evidence it. Strong I-HITL offers a conceptual springboard for regulatory frameworks and, in systems such as Countersign, a mechanism for producing verifiable evidence of compliance in the form of human approval (although not evidence of due attention).

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
authors: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels
content: Open problems. On the analytic side, a computational treatment would give finer-grained guarantees than our symbolic one. On the practical side, the key question is how to extend I-HITL beyond end-user platforms to enterprise systems and, critically, to the infrastructure on which frontier models themselves run, where an agent may be positioned to gate its own oversight ( Example 2 ). By Theorem 4 , such work would begin by establishing a local service 𝒮 \mathcal{S} isolated from the agent, e.g., in a hardware enclave, with a trusted entity 𝒯 \mathcal{T} likewise outside the agent’s reach.

section: Appendix E Classification of Trusted Entities
content: Wultra Talisman WAU1.1 is a USB FIDO2 token with its own screen, physical buttons and keypad, and a secure element that performs all cryptographic operations [ 89 ] . At enrollment the token generates a key pair in its secure element, from which the private key cannot be exported, and returns the public key together with an attestation certificate chaining to Wultra’s root. At approval the service encodes the action into the WebAuthn challenge; the token shows it on its own screen and signs the challenge, which carries the displayed fields and a nonce, only after the user confirms by entering their PIN on the token’s keypad. The display is therefore trusted and private, since it belongs to a separate device the agent can neither drive nor read; the input is a trusted confirmation, since buttons and keypad are physical and cannot be driven by software on the platform; and the key is attested and encumbered, since the attestation certificate lets the service verify both that the key was generated by a genuine Talisman and that it is held in the secure element. By Tables II and I the labels are ( 𝗌𝖾𝖼 , 𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁 ) (\mathsf{sec}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{auth}) and ( 𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁 , 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿 ) (\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{conf}) under both trust models, so Talisman realizes strong I-HITL.

section: Appendix E Classification of Trusted Entities
content: Ledger Nano X, Flex and Stax are hardware wallets whose secure element runs the device firmware and all installed apps [ 48 ] . On the Nano X the screen and two physical buttons are driven by a separate microcontroller whose firmware the secure element verifies at every boot; on the Flex and Stax the touchscreen is driven by the secure element directly. Each device holds a manufacturer-signed key from which the firmware derives an endorsement key whose signatures commit to the running app, so a service can verify both that a signature came from a genuine Ledger device and which app produced it. Unlike Talisman, the firmware displays and signs only what an installed app tells it to, so realizing I-HITL requires a purpose-built app that receives m m , displays it to the user and signs it with the endorsement key once the user approves. The display is therefore trusted and private, since it is driven by the secure element or by a chip the secure element verifies, and the platform can neither draw on it nor read it; the input is trusted, since buttons and touchscreen are physical and not drivable by software on the platform, and is a confirmation on the Nano but a keypad on the Flex and Stax, whose on-screen keyboard lets the human enter arbitrary text; and the key is attested and encumbered, since the attestation chain lets the service verify that the key was generated by a genuine device and the key never leaves the secure element. By Tables II and I the labels are ( 𝗌𝖾𝖼 , 𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁 ) (\mathsf{sec}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{auth}) and ( 𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁 , 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿 ) (\mathsf{auth}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{conf}) under both trust models, so all three realize strong I-HITL. On the Flex and Stax, the keypad realizes an 𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁 \mathsf{auth} channel from ℋ \mathcal{H} to 𝒯 \mathcal{T} directly, since the human can type arbitrary text to the device, whereas on the Nano this channel arises only from the combination of the trusted display and the confirmation; the approval protocol is the same in both cases.

A purpose-built app could attest such a key with the endorsement key, but the key remains extractable: a delegating human can import the seed into software the agent controls. content: FIDO2 security key refers to a screenless hardware key that plugs into or taps against the platform, such as a YubiKey ( Figure 11 ). At registration the key generates a credential key pair for the service in secure hardware, from which the private key cannot be exported, and returns the public key together with an attestation certificate chained to the manufacturer’s root. The key has no way to show the human what it is signing and relies on the platform to describe the action. The display is therefore untrusted and exposed; the input is a trusted confirmation; and the key is attested and encumbered. By Table II a confirmation without a trusted display yields ( 𝗂𝗇𝗌 , 𝗂𝗇𝗌 ) (\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ins}) , since the platform chooses the message the human approves, so condition (i) from Theorem 7 fails and the key realizes neither form of I-HITL despite satisfying condition (ii).

section: Appendix E Classification of Trusted Entities
content: World app is the default authenticator for World ID, a Proof of Personhood (PoP) credential system [ 88 ] . Here 𝒯 \mathcal{T} comprises the app together with World’s backend infrastructure. A user obtains a PoP credential by scanning their iris at an Orb, after which it is issued to their World ID account. An account may hold several authenticators: a new authenticator is added with the approval of an existing one, after a device biometric or PIN check, and authenticators need not be the World app. To approve a message m m , the service signs a request committing to an action identifier, the platform forwards it to the app, and on confirmation the app produces a zero-knowledge proof that commits to the action and to an optional signal, either of which can encode m m . The World ID signing key cannot be held in secure hardware and can be shared between authenticators, so on its own it is extractable. The app can, however, attach an integrity bundle : a signature over the request nonce and the proof’s nullifiers by a hardware-backed key, together with a token from World’s Attestation Gateway attesting that key to a genuine World app on a genuine device. A service that requires the bundle therefore receives an attested and encumbered key, although attestation rests on World’s gateway in addition to Apple’s or Google’s root. The bundle is optional, and World’s verification endpoint accepts proofs without it.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop

section: Appendix E Classification of Trusted Entities
content: The default confirmation is a screen tap, but a service can set require_user_presence , in which case the app matches a live selfie against the credential image, and we consider that stronger instantiation here. This check is enforced by the app rather than hardware, and so holds only under OS integrity, as for Countersign; we treat the input as a trusted confirmation. The display, however, is not trusted in the sense of Section VI-B . Although the platform cannot draw on the app’s screen, the text the app shows is the request’s action_description , which World documents as “shown to users in World App” [ 81 ] . This field is supplied by the platform, and it is covered neither by the service’s signature, which spans only the nonce, timestamps, and action identifier, nor by the proof, whose public inputs include the action and signal but not the description. The adversary can therefore request approval of m ∗ m^{*} while the app shows the human a benign m ′ m^{\prime} , and the resulting proof verifies for m ∗ m^{*} . A description registered with World’s developer portal takes precedence over the request’s own, but registration is per action and not per message. By Table II , an untrusted display with a trusted confirmation yields ( ins , ins ) (\textsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\textsf{ins}) , so the World app realizes neither form of I-HITL. The app does receive the signal itself, so displaying it would make the display trusted, and with the integrity bundle required the app would then realize strong I-HITL. As the app is closed-source, we determine the displayed fields from World’s documentation and its public app simulator.

section: Appendix E Classification of Trusted Entities
content: Push-approval 2FA app refers to apps such as Duo Mobile, Microsoft Authenticator and Okta Verify. The latter two gate only sign-ins to their own identity platforms, so we do not consider them further; Duo’s Auth API lets any service push a request for an arbitrary action [ 26 ] , and is the instantiation we evaluate. At activation the app generates a key pair on the phone, typically in the platform keystore, and sends the public key to the service. At approval the service requests an approval for an action, the app shows the action on the screen, and the user approves with a tap or, if the service’s policy requires it, with a biometric. The app then signs a Duo-chosen identifier of the request and returns it. Duo also accepts passcodes generated in the app, SMS passcodes and phone calls as fallbacks [ 26 ] , which realize neither form of I-HITL (below), so we consider the configuration in which the service requires a biometric push and disables the fallbacks, as it offers the strongest guarantees. The app display is trusted but exposed, as for Countersign; the input is a trusted confirmation, since the biometric sensor cannot be driven by software on the platform; and the key is encumbered but unattested, since it is generated in the keystore and recovery is by re-enrollment rather than export, but the service receives the public key over the platform with no evidence of where it was generated, so it cannot distinguish a key generated by the genuine Duo app in secure hardware from one the agent generated and enrolled in its place. Duo Mobile does submit Play Integrity device attestations, which Duo uses to flag tampered devices, but a device-integrity verdict attests the app and device rather than the enrolled key, and Duo documents no key attestation, so we do not credit it. By Table I an unattested key yields ( 𝗂𝗇𝗌 , 𝗂𝗇𝗌 ) (\mathsf{ins}\mathchar 24891\relax\allowbreak\mathsf{ins}) under either trust model, so condition (ii) fails and the app realizes neither form of I-HITL despite satisfying condition (i).

content: TOTP/HOTP authenticator app refers to apps such as Google Authenticator that generate six-digit codes from a secret shared with the service, derived from the current time (TOTP [ 62 ] ) or a counter (HOTP [ 61 ] ). At enrollment the service generates the secret seed and makes it available to the user via a QR code. At approval the user reads the current code from the app and types it into the platform, which forwards it to the service. The display is untrusted and exposed, since the app never shows the message being approved, only a code that is valid for any message in its time window, and the phone screen can be read by accessibility services; the input is untrusted, since 𝒯 \mathcal{T} has no input interface in the approval flow at all; and the key is neither attested nor encumbered, since the secret itself is provisioned in the QR code shown on the platform, so the agent can read it at enrollment and generate codes without the authenticator app. Every label is 𝗂𝗇𝗌 \mathsf{ins} , so the app realizes neither form of I-HITL.

content: SMS or email OTP is the mechanism used in Example 1 and in many password-reset and account-recovery flows, where the service generates a code and sends it to the user’s phone number or inbox, and the user types it into the platform. The display is untrusted and exposed, since sender identifiers in SMS and email are easily spoofed, so the human cannot tell a code from the service from one the agent injected, and an agent with access to the inbox or messaging app can read it; the input is untrusted, since the code is typed into the platform; and there is no key, since the code is generated by the service and shared over the channel, so there is nothing to attest or encumber. Every label is 𝗂𝗇𝗌 \mathsf{ins} , so the mechanism realizes neither form of I-HITL, as Section III demonstrates empirically.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
section: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
content: As autonomous research systems become more capable, benchmarks must both evaluate their performance and support meaningful research progress. We introduce Auto-Research Arena, a multi-target benchmark for evaluating autonomous research systems and discovering ideas in language modeling. Arena supports diverse research objectives within a shared experimental environment by separating admissibility from improvement : model quality and resource constraints determine whether a result qualifies, while the selected target measures progress among admissible results. We instantiate Arena in language model pretraining with nine targets spanning model, data, training, and inference efficiency, and evaluate seven research harnesses using two foundation models. Arena clearly differentiates existing harnesses across research objectives, with several sophisticated methods outperformed by our simple sequential search baseline, indicating substantial headroom in current auto-research systems. Beyond evaluation, Arena reveals a substantially broader frontier of model and system ideas aligned with active research directions. Reusing these discoveries in a new quality-driven search yields lower training loss under matched data and FLOPs and lower held-out BPB at the same model size. Together, Arena provides a common framework for benchmarking autonomous research and expanding its scope in language modeling. The code is available at https://github.com/Auto-Research-Arena/auto-research-arena .

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Advances in LLMs and research harnesses have enabled increasingly capable autonomous research systems ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These systems iteratively propose ideas, conduct experiments, and use the results to guide further research. Auto-research benchmarks provide a common basis for comparing these systems, but their role extends beyond evaluation. By defining clear objectives and constraints, a well-designed benchmark helps researchers identify, validate, and build on useful improvements. However, existing benchmarks remain limited both in evaluating research systems and in supporting broad research ideas ( Chan et al., 2025 ; Wijk et al., 2025 ; Nathani et al., 2025 ; Karpathy, 2026 ; Intology, 2026 ) .

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: To address this gap, we introduce Auto-Research Arena , a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating auto-research systems and advancing idea discovery in language modeling. Departing from prior benchmarks that define progress primarily through a particular objective within each research problem, Arena defines multiple research objectives within a common experimental environment . These objectives address complementary bottlenecks across the model lifecycle, including model size, data consumption, training computation and memory, and inference memory and latency. The shared environment provides a common experimental basis for evaluating whether a harness remains effective across different research objectives. Meanwhile, different objectives reward different types of improvements. For example, reducing model size or inference memory can count as progress even when prediction loss remains unchanged. By recognizing these complementary forms of progress, Arena supports exploration of a broader range of model designs and systems optimizations.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: To support this broad range of research objectives within a unified framework, Arena specifies both what to improve and which requirements a candidate must satisfy. That is, Arena separates the standard for admissibility from the direction of improvement . Each objective is formulated as a constrained optimization problem. Constraints on model quality and relevant non-target resources determine whether a candidate is admissible . Among admissible candidates, a reduction in the selected resource metric constitutes improvement . Changing the target metric defines a different research objective within the same framework. This formulation supports consistent evaluation across diverse objectives, while excluding gains that violate the specified quality or resource constraints.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Beyond evaluating objectives independently, Arena supports research across objectives. Separate searches can pursue different objectives in parallel, each exploring improvements relevant to its target. Compatible improvements discovered in one search can then be incorporated into the starting program for a subsequent search targeting a different objective. This enables both parallel exploration of distinct research directions and cumulative progress through the reuse of earlier discoveries. By explicitly specifying objectives, constraints, budgets, and starting programs, Arena makes it possible to measure how prior discoveries affect subsequent research.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: We evaluate six LLM-based auto-research methods and a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator baseline ( Ferreira et al., 2026 ) across Arena’s nine objectives. Arena provides a discriminative and meaningful evaluation of research harnesses : methods exhibit clear differences across objectives, with no single harness dominating the benchmark. Two results further support the evaluation. TPE, specialized for the original validation loss-oriented setting, performs worst in Arena’s broader multi-target evaluation. Moreover, our simple Sequential Search baseline ranks second overall with both foundation models, outperforming several substantially more sophisticated harnesses and suggesting large headroom in current auto-research system design. The recorded search trajectories help explain how these final outcomes arise. Higher-performing harnesses tend to sustain progress throughout the search budget, whereas lower-performing methods often plateau earlier or improve less consistently.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Multi-target research also exposes a substantially broader idea frontier . We empirically find that different objectives lead to qualitatively different discoveries, yielding 32 findings across nine idea families spanning model architecture, optimization, memory, and inference systems. Many of these discoveries align with active directions in LLM research. For example, when optimizing parameter efficiency, agents discover looped Transformers through weight sharing. They further learn depth-specific residual gains to adapt the residual updates across repeated applications of the shared block. This finding closely parallels recent work identifying residual adaptation as a key ingredient of looped Transformers ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Similar connections appear across other discoveries, although alignment with existing research does not imply identical solutions. Several discoveries follow design principles similar to those of prior work but implement them through distinct mechanisms, offering alternative approaches to the same research problems. Together, these findings show how Arena’s diverse objectives expand the range of ideas explored by autonomous research systems.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Finally, we examine whether ideas discovered through Arena’s lightweight searches remain useful beyond the search setting. The original searches train each candidate for only 10 minutes. We provide the collected discoveries to a new search focused on model quality, which can select, combine, and modify these ideas. We then train the resulting model for one hour from random initialization. Unlike the original searches, which optimize individual efficiency targets, this experiment evaluates improvements in model quality directly. Relative to the reference run, training loss decreases from 2.675 to 2.544 at matched training data and from 2.617 to 2.544 at matched cumulative FLOPs. Held-out BPB also decreases from 0.9295 to 0.9112 at essentially the same model size. These results show that discoveries from Arena’s small-scale, multi-target searches can improve model quality through combination and adaptation. Arena thus supports both the evaluation of autonomous research systems and the discovery of reusable research ideas.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Autonomous research benchmarks. PaperBench ( Starace et al., 2025 ) evaluates replication of published research, while EXP-Bench ( Kon et al., 2026 ) assesses the design and execution of paper-derived experiments. These benchmarks emphasize implementing and validating specified research content. More open-ended settings include MLE-bench ( Chan et al., 2025 ) and RE-Bench ( Wijk et al., 2025 ) , which evaluate ML engineering and research, alongside MLGym ( Nathani et al., 2025 ) , MLRC-Bench ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , and AstaBench ( Bragg et al., 2026 ) , which support standardized experimentation and evaluation across ML and scientific tasks. Within language modeling, Karpathy’s autoresearch ( Karpathy, 2026 ) minimizes validation loss under a fixed training-time budget, whereas NanoGPT Bench ( Intology, 2026 ) targets faster training at a required model quality. Related benchmarks evaluate reproduction of NanoGPT improvements ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) and correctness-constrained computational speedups ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ; Press et al., 2025 ; Shetty et al., 2025 ) . However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of auto-research systems across complementary objectives. Arena instead unifies diverse objectives within a shared experimental setting, revealing how the research objective shapes both harness performance and the resulting idea frontier.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling

content: Autonomous research systems. Complementing these benchmarks, research harnesses determine how agents organize experiments and use accumulated evidence. End-to-end systems connect ideation, experimentation, and reporting ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) , while AIDE ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) and AIRA ( Toledo et al., 2025 ) organize iterative code improvement through search. AutoScientists ( Gao et al., 2026 ) coordinates decentralized teams, Arbor ( Jin et al., 2026 ) maintains a persistent hypothesis tree, and GEAR ( Jeddi et al., 2026 ) evolves populations of research states. Heuresis ( Antoniades et al., 2026 ) further compares search strategies across quality, diversity, and novelty. Arena evaluates how the relative strengths of research harnesses vary across objectives.

These constraints cover quantities such as model size, training FLOPs, peak training memory, and available training data. Inference tracks also constrain other serving costs. Depending on the target, measurements are taken after a fixed 600-second training period or when the candidate first meets the quality requirement. Training metrics include consumed tokens, FLOPs per token, peak allocated GPU memory, elapsed training time, and optimizer updates. Inference metrics are measured after training using standardized prompt and generation workloads. Appendix A provides complete metric definitions and resource constraints for all nine tracks.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Benchmark–harness interface. Arena provides the environment, task specification, reference program, evaluator, and experiment budget, while each harness determines how to conduct the search. Starting from the reference program, a harness proposes code modifications, submits candidates for evaluation, observes the measured outcomes, and decides what to explore next. Arena records every experiment and independently reports the best recorded candidate satisfying the quality, resource, and correctness requirements, regardless of which program the harness ultimately retains. Each search receives 100 charged experiments; an experiment is charged once GPU execution begins, including runs that subsequently fail or are abandoned. Appendix B provides the full interface and protocol.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Reference baselines. We introduce two simple reference harnesses that differ primarily in how many research directions they retain. Sequential Search maintains one program and evaluates one modification at a time, adopting an admissible improvement before continuing. Beam Search retains up to four programs and evaluates two modifications of each before selecting the next frontier. Both condition subsequent proposals on the accumulated experimental history, including unsuccessful attempts. Appendix B provides their detailed proposal, selection, and stopping policies.

content: Tasks and resources. We evaluate all nine Arena objectives defined in Sec. 3 , each with target-specific resource constraints and the shared quality requirement BPB < 1.05 <1.05 . Each candidate runs on one NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU with seed 42 and up to 600 seconds of training, excluding compilation, validation, and the first ten warmup updates. All searches use the same approximately 631M-token ClimbMix ( Diao et al., 2025 ) training pool and held-out BPB evaluator; training-token consumption includes repeated exposure to the data.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling

content: Models and harnesses. We evaluate six LLM-based research harnesses with Claude Opus 5 ( Anthropic, 2026 ) and GPT-6 Astra ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , both using medium reasoning effort. In addition to Sequential Search and Beam Search, we evaluate AutoScientists ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , Arbor ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , GEAR ( Jeddi et al., 2026 ) , and Heuresis ( Antoniades et al., 2026 ) , which respectively use multi-agent coordination, hypothesis trees, evolutionary search, and diversity-preserving archives. We additionally include TPE ( Ferreira et al., 2026 ) , a non-agentic baseline restricted to a predefined hyperparameter space, in the Opus 5 experiments.

For training-token consumption, optimizer updates, and training time, we use the first 30-second validation checkpoint satisfying BPB < 1.05 <1.05 . We summarize performance across objectives with different units and scales using Elo ratings from pairwise harness comparisons within each objective. Appendix gives the scoring procedure.

content: Arena provides a discriminative evaluation. Research harnesses exhibit substantial differences across Arena’s objectives, with no single method dominating the benchmark. With Opus 5, AutoScientists achieves the highest aggregate Elo, followed by Sequential Search and Arbor; with GPT-6, GEAR ranks first, followed by Sequential Search. The variation across objectives shows that Arena distinguishes complementary strengths of research systems rather than reducing their performance to a single research setting.

content: Simple search is surprisingly competitive. Despite its minimal design, Sequential Search ranks second overall with both foundation LLMs, outperforming several substantially more sophisticated harnesses. Its strong performance suggests substantial headroom in current auto-research system design: more elaborate orchestration does not yet consistently translate into stronger performance.

Designed for Karpathy’s autoresearch setting ( Ferreira et al., 2026 ) , TPE performs substantially worse than all LLM-based harnesses across Arena’s broader set of objectives. Strong performance in a specialized research setting therefore need not translate into broad research capability, illustrating the value of evaluating research systems across complementary objectives.

content: Research trajectories support the benchmark scores. The endpoint differences in Tab. 2 are also reflected in the search trajectories in Fig. 3 . Stronger harnesses typically make sustained progress over the experiment budget, whereas weaker methods plateau earlier or improve less consistently. For example, TPE stops improving relatively early in the parameter search, while GEAR and AutoScientists continue to find improvements near the end of their recorded searches. These trajectories provide complementary evidence that the benchmark scores reflect systematic differences in research progress rather than isolated final outcomes.

content: Similar outcomes can hide different research efficiency. Endpoint performance does not fully characterize how a result is reached. On the Opus 5 training-time objective, GEAR, Arbor, Beam Search, and Heuresis all reach 270 seconds, but first attain this value after 12, 39, 50, and 99 charged experiments, respectively. Thus, harnesses with identical final scores can differ substantially in how efficiently they discover the same level of improvement.

content: Multi-target research substantially broadens the idea frontier. Beyond routine hyperparameter tuning, Karpathy’s reported loss-driven search identifies two architectural changes, smear and backout ( Karpathy, 2026 ) . Across Arena’s efficiency objectives, our search catalogue contains 32 distinct findings, including 20 that were accepted as improvements during search, which we consolidate into nine idea families spanning model architecture, training, and inference. Different objectives expose qualitatively different research directions, from architectural changes under model-efficiency targets to memory and systems optimizations under training and inference targets.

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: The discovered idea frontier mirrors active LLM research. The breadth of Arena’s discoveries is not merely a larger collection of benchmark-specific optimizations: many of them reach questions central to current LLM research. A representative example emerges from parameter efficiency (Tab. 3 ). Agents first discover recurrent weight sharing, effectively turning the model into a looped Transformer, and further identify the need to adapt residual updates across repeated depth, learning separate attention and MLP residual gains at each depth. This closely mirrors recent work studying residual adaptation as a key component of looped Transformers ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Similar correspondences appear across attention-state reduction through cross-layer K/V sharing ( Brandon et al., 2024 ) , MQA/MLA ( Shazeer, 2019 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ) , conditional memory ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) , optimizer-state reduction ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , activation-memory efficiency ( Korthikanti et al., 2022 ) , and inference optimization ( Aminabadi et al., 2022 ) . Importantly, these discoveries are not simply reproductions of existing methods: they often share the same underlying principles while arriving at different technical mechanisms, offering alternative perspectives on active research questions. The resulting idea frontier therefore demonstrates a broader value of Arena: its diverse objectives expand not only what research systems are evaluated on, but also the space of meaningful research directions they explore.

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: The broader idea frontier accompanies substantial measured progress. The searches producing these discoveries also achieve large admissible gains across distinct resource dimensions. In the Opus 5 group, the best programs reduce model size from 50.33M to 13.20M parameters, training computation from 239.08M to 52.15M FLOPs per token, and peak training memory from 43.96 to 0.373 GiB, while satisfying BPB < 1.05 <1.05 and the corresponding resource constraints. However, these endpoint programs combine multiple changes accumulated during search, so their gains do not establish whether the discovered ideas themselves provide reusable knowledge beyond the searches that found them. We test this directly in Sec. 4.3 .
