section: 4.3 Validating Discoveries Beyond the Search Setting
content: Arena discovers mechanisms under specific objectives and short experimental budgets. To assess their usefulness beyond these conditions, we first test whether a library of discovered ideas can guide a new search for better model quality. We then ask a stricter question: can winning programs from the original Arena searches retain their advantages when retrained for longer without further search?

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
section: 4.3 Validating Discoveries Beyond the Search Setting
content: Combining discovered ideas improves model quality. We collect discoveries across Arena’s objectives and harnesses into an idea library to guide a quality-driven search. The agent can select, modify, and combine mechanisms from different research trajectories rather than continue from a single winning program. We extend the training time budget to 1 hour in this search.

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
section: 4.3 Validating Discoveries Beyond the Search Setting
content: The resulting design improves model quality under both matched-budget evaluations (Fig. 1 ). At matched training data, it reduces training loss from 2.675 to 2.544 (4.9%); at matched training FLOPs, it reduces training loss from 2.617 to 2.544 (2.8%). Final held-out BPB also decreases from 0.9295 to 0.9112 at the same model size (50.33M parameters). The resulting design selectively adapts and simplifies ideas rather than merely combining their original implementations. These results demonstrate that efficiency-targeted discoveries can serve as reusable model-design knowledge for improving quality. Appendix details how these ideas are selected and transformed.

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
section: 4.3 Validating Discoveries Beyond the Search Setting
content: Discovered programs can transfer far beyond the search horizon. We next ask a stricter question: can a program found under a short training budget be scaled directly, without further search? Arena normally evaluates candidate programs after 10 minutes of training. We select two programs from each of the training-time, token, and update objectives and retrain them from random initialization for 60 minutes alongside the reference program.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
section: 4.3 Validating Discoveries Beyond the Search Setting
content: Several discoveries retain their advantages far beyond the horizon at which they were found. A token-optimized GEAR program reaches 0.9593 BPB after 30 minutes using 1.004B tokens, while the reference requires approximately 47.6 minutes and 1.771B tokens to reach the same quality, corresponding to 43.3% fewer tokens. Its quality advantage persists until approximately 51 minutes, extending to five times the original search horizon. Similarly, a training-time program discovered by AutoScientists outperforms the reference over the 15–46-minute interval and reaches 0.9647 BPB after 30 minutes, a quality level that the reference reaches only after approximately 45.8 minutes, corresponding to 34.5% less training time (Figure 4 ; Table 5 ). Reference costs at matched quality are estimated by linear interpolation.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
section: 4.3 Validating Discoveries Beyond the Search Setting
content: The transfer is substantial but not indefinite. The GEAR program’s learning rate reaches its 2% floor around 27 minutes, while the AutoScientists schedule reaches zero around 24 minutes. Their early advantages consequently diminish as training continues; by 60 minutes, for example, the reference reaches 0.9295 BPB compared with 0.9478 for the GEAR program. Thus, short-horizon search can discover programs whose advantages persist for four to five times the original search horizon, while horizon-dependent training policies can ultimately limit direct extrapolation to longer training.

content: Arena also enables controlled study of what shapes the auto-research process. We examine quality constraints, budget allocation between evaluation depth and search breadth, and the role of research history in cross-target search.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Constraints shape the research space. We vary the BPB threshold across 1.02 1.02 , 1.05 1.05 , and 2.0 2.0 for parameter- and memory-efficiency searches with Sequential Search and Beam Search (Tab. 5 ). Relaxing the threshold from 1.05 1.05 to 2.0 2.0 allows Sequential Search to reduce parameters from 18.94M to 0.69M, while its separate peak-memory search reduces memory from 0.83 GiB to 0.035 GiB. The additional quality slack permits substantially more aggressive efficiency improvements. Conversely, tighter thresholds restrict which structural changes remain admissible. Quality constraints thus shape not only the final results, but also which regions of the design space can be developed.

content: Budget allocation creates a depth–breadth trade-off. For parameter minimization under BPB < 2.0 <2.0 , we vary candidate training time from 1,200 to 6,000 seconds under a shared 20 GPU-hour training budget, trading fewer, longer evaluations for more, shorter ones (Tab. ). The shortest setting evaluates 60 candidates and finds the smallest model; longer settings yield better BPB but more parameters. These outcomes illustrate the trade-off between evaluation depth and search breadth, with different allocations favoring different quality–efficiency balances.

content: Cross-target research builds on prior discoveries. We initialize searches under new objectives from programs discovered under earlier objectives, transferring code while reinitializing model weights (Tab. 6 ). Subsequent searches can accumulate compatible gains: parameter savings are fully preserved while training FLOPs decrease by a further 33.7%, and a FLOP-optimized program preserves its FLOP count while uncached decode latency decreases by 87.5%. Cross-target continuation can also introduce trade-offs: optimizing training time from the parameter-optimized program reduces time to quality by 21.1% but increases parameters by 24.6%. Prior discoveries therefore provide foundations for both cumulative gains and new trade-offs across objectives.

content: We introduced Auto-Research Arena, a multi-target benchmark for autonomous research across nine quality-constrained language-model efficiency objectives. Arena reveals complementary harness strengths and a broad frontier of architectural and systems ideas. Discoveries can seed searches under new objectives, while a program combining selected ideas can improve model quality. Controlled studies further show how constraints, budgets, and research history shape progress. Together, these results support evaluating autonomous research across complementary objectives and studying how useful discoveries accumulate.

For both the one-token and 1,536-token prefill settings, the maximum total-variation distance across all 513 scored positions must not exceed 0.05. The returned request-state object must own all retained KV data, including compressed representations or replacement token history, and these data must remain on the GPU throughout the request. Memory constraints use the same retained-allocation procedure as the KV-cache objective, with capacities of 513 and 2,048 for the short- and long-prompt settings, respectively.

section: Appendix B Harness Integration and Reference Baselines
content: This section specifies the integration interface and the two reference search policies used in Section 4 . Arena provides execution, measurement, and scoring; the baselines determine proposals and retention. Their selection rules are harness choices, not requirements imposed on other integrations.

content: Minimal interface. A harness must inspect the provided workspace and task definition, modify only the permitted program, submit experiments through Arena, read standardized results, and choose subsequent candidates. Arena defines the research problem and evaluation environment while leaving the research strategy open: an integration may retain an incumbent, beam, population, hypothesis tree, or another search state.

The terminal score is computed from measured admissible outcomes; the accompanying record supports audits and post-hoc trace analysis. Charged-experiment accounting follows Section B.4 , independently of harness-side bookkeeping.

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Sequential Search starts from one incumbent and proposes one candidate per round. Beam Search retains up to four programs and proposes two modifications per retained program in each generation. A full generation therefore contains eight candidate experiments; selection occurs after all outcomes are available.

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: A persistent controller coordinates an ideator, executor, and reviewer. The implementation calls the reviewer an evaluator , distinct from Arena’s evaluator. Agent sessions are fresh for each round or generation. Instructions, source code, task rules, and saved research history are supplied to each session, so continuation does not rely on conversational memory.

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: The ideator inspects the current code and prior experimental history, then records a proposal, rationale, timestamp, and position in that history. Edits may change architecture, attention, optimization, data processing, or training within the permitted boundary. A proposal can coordinate several edits implementing one mechanism; Sequential Search also requests follow-up experiments that could separate their contributions.

authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang

content: Arena checks the submitted source, protected files, available launch budget, and hardware, then runs training and task-specific evaluation. It records source, measurements, execution status, and logs. Successful execution alone does not establish admissibility.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Sequential Search uses one worker; Beam Search uses four. Parallel submission does not alter accounting: each candidate is one experiment. A full eight-candidate generation needs eight available slots and consumes eight launches if all reach chargeable GPU work, although at most four run simultaneously. Local CPU checks do not replace candidate training through Arena.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: The budget is 100 charged launches, including the reference evaluation. A recorded GPU-work-start marker determines charging. Once GPU work begins, crashes, out-of-memory errors, and task failures still consume budget. A resolved launch without the marker is not charged; an unresolved launch reserves a slot. A normally charged reference therefore leaves at most 99 candidate experiments. The harness reads Arena’s remaining budget rather than counting its own rounds or generations. Failed experiments remain recorded.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: The reviewer compares the proposal, parent and candidate code, measurements, and logs, then records feedback. Both baselines exclude failed or constraint-violating candidates from further development. Other harnesses may continue refining them, but only admissible results contribute to Arena’s score.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Unchanged-target attempts. An efficiency improvement may increase BPB while remaining below the quality threshold. Both baselines also permit limited attempts to improve quality without changing the target. Target equality means exact equality of recorded values, regardless of the proposal’s description. Such attempts consume the allowance even when rejected.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Sequential Search. An admissible candidate replaces the incumbent when it strictly improves the target. At exactly equal target value, it may replace the incumbent while the allowance remains if it improves either the task-defined tie-break metric or BPB. Otherwise the incumbent is retained. The allowance starts at four unchanged-target attempts and resets only after an accepted strict target improvement; accepting a quality improvement alone does not reset it.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Beam Search. Parents remain fixed throughout a generation. After every outcome is resolved, the reviewer pools parents and new candidates, removes exact program duplicates, and excludes failures, constraint violations, and missing required ranking measurements. Parents need not be replaced when their modifications fail.

title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
authors: Xi Chen, Chongjian Ge, Yiran Xu, Yiqun Mei, Henrik I. Christensen, Hao Tan, Ziwen Chen, Hanwen Jiang
content: Up to two unchanged-target attempts are permitted per generation only if the best retained target strictly improved during the preceding two completed generations. This allowance is determined before proposal generation. When permitted, a parent and modification with equal target are reduced to the admissible member with lower BPB. title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
content: Learning algorithms are usually analyzed under the assumption that informative gradients are continuously available. But this is not always true—learning signals in biological neural networks, for example, may be sparse, local, and only intermittently available at any given synapse. In this work, we show that if gradient information is noisy and only intermittently available, learning may be unstable. In particular, even if average learning dynamics converge to the correct optimum, variance in learning may be asymptotically infinite. We explore this point in a number of analytically tractable settings, including single-layer and multi-layer linear networks, and derive explicit conditions under which learning is stable. These conditions complement, but are conceptually distinct from, existing conditions related to the stability of stochastic gradient descent. Our work demonstrates that unbiased credit assignment is not enough for reliable learning; sufficiently frequent and informative feedback is also required, which yields an additional constraint on models of biologically plausible learning.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
content: The claim that the brain does not perform backpropagation ( Rumelhart et al., 1986 ) rests in part on the idea that gradient information may be difficult to communicate. In particular, the gradient of an objective function with respect to any given synaptic weight depends on the synaptic weights of a large number of downstream neurons, and it is not obvious in general how such non-local information could be reliably communicated ( Crick, 1989 ; Lillicrap et al., 2020 ) . This issue has motivated a substantial body of work seeking alternative and more biologically plausible learning rules ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ; Scellier and Bengio, 2017 ) , as well as schemes for approximately implementing backpropagation in specific contexts ( Sacramento et al., 2018 ; Whittington and Bogacz, 2019 ; Millidge et al., 2022 ) . It remains unknown if and how this information is communicated, but it is generally agreed that communicating it accurately would be difficult given locality constraints.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
content: In this paper, we consider a related but conceptually distinct issue. If gradient information can be communicated, it is not at all obvious that it can be communicated reliably . It is plausible that a scheme which delivers the correct updates on average only delivers them occasionally, to different neurons at different times, and perhaps somewhat noise-corrupted. How do learning dynamics change when gradients are noisy and only intermittently available? We argue that learning changes substantially, and in fact can become unstable if updates are not delivered sufficiently frequently.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
content: This idea is interesting for a few reasons. First, it implies that credit assignment which is correct on average is insufficient, since there remains the additional obstacle that weight updates cannot be too variable. Second, instability is not a generic consequence of noisy weight dynamics, but rather depends crucially on the multiplicative, sparse nature of the noise introduced by assuming intermittent gradient arrivals.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
content: We show that the severity of this issue can be reduced by a few obvious noise mitigation strategies, but that the presence of the issue (i.e., learning becoming unstable if feedback is sufficiently sparse) survives. This problem exists in both linear and nonlinear networks; in shallow and deep networks; and after averaging parameters or recent gradients. The details of the issue change, but the core finding remains: an informative signal must arrive sufficiently often for learning to remain stable.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
content: Learning is difficult, and in this work we have identified and analyzed yet another reason why. It is not enough to perform accurate credit assignment on average if the relevant learning signal is highly variable, since this high variance can produce unstable learning. The source of this variance, sparse gradient arrivals, is distinct from other types of noise relevant to learning (e.g., noise due to using stochastic rather than full-batch gradient descent), and its effects are apparently more insidious.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
content: Because any well-behaved network is approximately linear near a stable fixed point, one expects this issue to be generic rather than architecture-dependent. We considered three ways of addressing the problem— regularization , parameter-sharing , and gradient-averaging —and each reduces the severity of the issue but involves tradeoffs. Regularization and parameter-sharing reduce the (infinite) variance at the expense of bias; moreover, parameter-sharing may only be natural when there is specific (e.g., topographic) structure according to which spatial relationships correlate with relationships between synaptic weights. Gradient-averaging does not produce bias, but does slow down learning. It is plausible that all of these mechanisms, and perhaps others, are utilized by biological networks to avoid the kind of instability we study here.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
section: Connection to analyses of stochastic gradient descent.
content: Standard analyses of stochastic gradient descent ( Wu et al., 2018 ; Ahn et al., 2022 ) involve a mathematical idea similar to the one we study here, whose content is especially similar to the naive model we considered in Sec. 2 : if the learning rate or step size is taken to be too large, errors will accumulate and learning will become unstable. In other ways, the issue is qualitatively different. Our model is defined in continuous- rather than discrete-time, and moreover involves a nontrivial interaction between discrete and stochastic gradient arrivals on the one hand, and continuous relaxation (due to regularization) and accumulation (in the model considered in Sec. 7 ) on the other. Moreover, the biological interpretation of sparse arrivals—which can be viewed as related to error-communication difficulties rather than simply an overall learning rate—is conceptually distinct. Finally, average dynamics are unconditionally stable.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
section: Speculation regarding biological means of variance reduction.
content: If biological systems do indeed confront the problem of potential instability due to sparse gradient (or more generally, learning signal) arrivals, it is plausible that evolution has developed mechanisms to partially combat it. There is biological precedent for each of the three mechanisms—regularization, parameter-pooling, and gradient-averaging—we considered. It is known that the dendritic spines, which are sites of synaptic plasticity, turn over on relatively short time scales, e.g., on the order of one or two weeks in the hippocampus ( Attardo et al., 2015 ) . This continual ‘forgetting’ of synaptic weights can be modeled in the same way we have incorporated regularization. Our gradient-averaging model can be viewed as maintaining a kind of eligibility trace of learning-related information, and there is mounting evidence that such traces exist and play a major role in biological learning ( He et al., 2015 ; Gerstner et al., 2018 ) . Parameter-pooling has not been directly observed to our knowledge, but as we have mentioned, there are plausible means by which it could occur.

title: On the stability of learning
authors: John J. Vastola
content: For clarity and tractability, we have mainly analyzed simple linear models here. More interesting behavior may be possible in less linear regimes, e.g., away from a stable fixed point. Another major assumption we made is that sparse gradients arrive independently at each synapse according to a Poisson process. In reality, the delivery of gradient information to any given neuron is likely correlated with the delivery of gradients to other neurons (e.g., because the information is coming from roughly the same source). Although details associated with this issue likely differ for more general models, our observations suggest that it is worth further study. Putative methods of credit assignment must produce both good average performance and stable variance.

How- ever, existing research lacks a uniﬁed perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in state- ful workspaces and deliver veriﬁable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into ﬁve forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify ﬁve core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine ap- proaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a uniﬁed framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, veriﬁable, and practically valuable work outcomes. Keywords: Work Agents; Work Persistence and Openness; Agent Capabilities; Agent Optimization 1

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: 1 Introduction Advances in foundation models’ reasoning, planning, and tool-use capabilities are expanding the scope of work that agents can undertake [1]. Their responsibilities increasingly extend beyond short, narrowly scoped tasks to larger assignments that require them to maintain an overall objective, coordinate multiple stages, and carry the work through to completion. Furthermore, recursive self-improvement [2] explores how agents can improve their own models and runtime systems, bringing capability improvement itself into the range of work agents undertake. Humans are already delegating complex productivity tasks to agents across software engineering [3], office work [4, 5], web and computer use [6–8], enterprise operations [9], and scientific research [10]. Frontier agents such as Codex and Claude Code [11, 12] illustrate this shift by supporting multi-day, cross-session work with suitable orchestration and taking on parts of result assessment and feedback-driven revision previously handled by humans. Across these tasks, decisions often depend on evidence in related files, records, or applications and on states established by earlier actions. A work-centric perspective traces these dependencies from the initial request through execution to a verifiable outcome. From this perspective, we introduce the concept of a work agent, defined as a system that uses a foundation model as its decision-making core, relies on a runtime harness to organize environment observations and action execution, and carries out delegated tasks within a stateful digital workspace. The foundation model provides understanding, reasoning, and decision-making capabilities; the harness manages context construction, tool invocation, memory, skills, execution control, and error recovery; and the workspace contains interconnected objects such as files, applications, records, tasks, and other actors. A work agent aims to produce work outcomes that satisfy task requirements, with execution results verified through observable evidence. This perspective connects task objectives, model capabilities, system mechanisms, environment states, and verification, shifting the unit of analysis from isolated model outputs or tool calls to the complete process of accomplishing digital work. Work agents operate under different conditions depending on the tasks they undertake. To characterize these differences, we introduce two conceptually distinct yet complementary dimensions: ❶work persistence and ❷work openness. Work persistence concerns the conditions under which delegated responsibility can be considered complete, distinguishing work that concludes upon delivery from responsibilities that remain active across multiple stages, feedback cycles, or external events. Work openness describes the extent to which task-relevant objects, information, interfaces, and rules are specified before execution, or must instead be discovered and interpreted during execution. These working conditions impose different demands on an agent’s ability to understand its environment, manage task dependencies, maintain execution state, and verify outcomes. Based on the functional requirements that arise throughout the work process, we organize the core capabilities of work agents into five interrelated families: perception and understanding, reasoning and decision making, planning and coordination, execution and state management, and verification, recovery, and replanning. Together, these capabilities support the complete process of interpreting work requirements, organizing and executing actions, and verifying results, forming an iterative execution cycle driven by environmental feedback. The performance of work agents depends not only on their core capabilities but also on how foundation models and runtime harnesses work together. From an optimization perspective, some capabilities can be learned by models through training data, interaction experience, and feedback, while others can be supported by external mechanisms such as tool interfaces, memory management, and execution control. Improving work agents therefore requires considering model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. From an evaluation perspective, agent performance is reflected not only in the correctness of answers or individual actions but also in the quality of work artifacts, changes to environment states, workflow completion, and satisfaction of task requirements. Systematic evaluation across these dimensions provides a more comprehensive understanding of the practical performance and reliability of work agents. As agents move from executing bounded tasks toward sustained work delegation, their responsibilities increasingly extend across multiple stages and events. In this setting, agents must maintain continuity despite environmental changes, interruptions, and external feedback, while also leveraging experience accumulated 4

content: during execution to improve their capabilities without disrupting ongoing responsibilities. Work execution and capability improvement thus form two interacting loops, raising new research challenges for the long-term development of work agents. Personal work agents, human digital twins, and organizational work systems provide research settings for sustaining goals between requests, representing a particular person’s judgment, and coordinating responsibilities across roles. Future research must address reliability, environmental adaptation, and outcome verification during sustained execution, while also considering the practical value of work outcomes and the human and computational resources required to produce them. These challenges will shape the transition from completing individual tasks to undertaking more persistent, complex, and valuable digital work. Based on this perspective, the main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: • A unified, work-centric framework for agent systems. We present a unified perspective centered on digital work, characterizing the structure and execution of work agents through six elements: task, model, harness, workspace, work outcome, and verification. We further describe the scope, organization, and execution conditions of digital work through five work forms and two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness. • A systematic account of core capabilities and optimization for reliable work. We identify five core capability families required by work agents and examine their roles under different working conditions. We further examine training environments, data and reward design, model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization, highlighting how model learning and external system support contribute to reliable work execution. • An outcome-oriented perspective on agent evaluation. We systematically analyze existing benchmarks, evaluation metrics, judging methods, and execution environments, examining how they assess work artifact quality, environment-state changes, task completion, and constraint satisfaction. This provides a structured perspective for understanding the practical performance and reliability of work agents. • Future research directions toward sustained work delegation. We explore emerging applications, including personal work agents, human digital twins, and organizational work systems, and discuss key challenges involving persistent responsibility, memory and adaptation, outcome verification, and the value of work in open environments. We further examine the interaction between work execution and capability improvement to outline research directions for next-generation work agents. This paper focuses on digital knowledge work across office productivity, professional services, enterprise operations, software engineering, and scientific research. Section 2 introduces the foundations of work agents, including their system components, working conditions, and core capabilities. Section 3 examines five forms of digital work undertaken by agents. Section 4 examines training environments, model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. Section 5 covers evaluation benchmarks, methodologies, metrics, and execution environments. Section 6 discusses future applications, technical frontiers, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. Section 7 concludes the paper. 2 Foundation of Work Agents Section 1 argued that the performance of a system that carries out digital work depends not only on its model but also on its interfaces, the information available to it, the organization of its state, and the verification of its results. Studying such systems therefore requires a common account of what the system consists of, the conditions under which it works, what it must be able to do, and how it differs from related lines of agent research. This section develops this account in four steps. Section 2.1 identifies the elements involved when digital work is delegated to an agent and defines a work agent. Section 2.2 introduces two dimensions of working conditions, work persistence and work openness, which describe when a responsibility may close and how much the agent must find out before and while it acts. Section 2.3 identifies five core capabilities that the work process requires and examines how the two dimensions raise their demands. Section 2.4 compares work agents with long-horizon, computer-use, and office agents. 5

The model and harness form the work agent within the dashed boundary. The task specifies the objective, constraints, resources, permissions, and completion conditions. The harness supplies context to the model, carries out proposed actions in the stateful workspace, and receives observations. Outcomes include answers, artifacts, state changes, and process outcomes. For ongoing responsibilities, they also include maintained conditions and event responses over an agreed interval. Verification assesses evidence from these outcomes, workspace states, and execution records against task requirements. Programs, humans, or model-based judges apply task-specific criteria. Verification may occur during execution, with feedback informing subsequent decisions, or afterwards to assess the work. 2.1 Definition of Work Agents We begin with the system itself. By digital work we mean work carried out on digital objects such as files, applications, and records, for example updating a report or handling a service request. When a person or an organization hands such work to an agent, three things happen: the requester states what should be done, the agent acts on these objects to do it, and the result is checked against what was asked. We call such work delegated: the agent carries it out on the requester’s behalf and is accountable for the result. We first describe the six elements involved in this process, as shown in Figure 1, then define a work agent in terms of them, and finally describe how the elements interact during execution. Task (T) specifies the objective, the relevant constraints, the available resources, the permissions, and the conditions for valid completion. For an ongoing responsibility, it also specifies the conditions to maintain, the agreed interval, and the criteria for closure or renewal. Model (M) serves as the system’s decision-making core. Given context supplied by the harness, it interprets the available information, weighs possible courses of action, and proposes responses or actions [13, 14]. Harness (H) organizes context construction, tool use, memory, skills, execution control, feedback handling, and recovery, mediating between the model and the workspace [14]. Workspace (E) is the stateful environment in which work takes place. It contains files, applications, records, messages, tasks, and other actors. These are linked to one another, and the agent accesses them through interfaces within its permissions. Both the agent’s actions and external events change its state as work proceeds. Work Outcome (O) is the task-relevant result that the agent produces. Outcomes include answers, such as analyses, plans, and executable specifications; artifacts such as documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and code; state changes in applications or business records, such as updated records and sent messages; process outcomes, such as a completed process or the stages, approvals, and handoffs finished so far; and maintained 6

content: conditions and event responses over an agreed interval. One assignment may combine several outcomes, such as an updated workbook, a report, and the corresponding changes to business records, and require them to remain consistent across related artifacts, records, and applications. Verification (V ) assesses work against task requirements. It inspects evidence from answers, workspace states, artifacts, and workflow records (Section 5.2.1). Programs, humans, or model-based judges [15] assess this evidence against task-specific criteria, which may be organized as rules, rubrics, or checklists (Section 5.2.2). The checks cover task completion, correctness, completeness, quality, constraint satisfaction, and intended effects. For example, SWE-bench [16] executes tests against a modified repository, whereas PresentBench [17] applies task-specific checklist items through a model judge. Verification may be performed by the agent during execution (Section 2.3.5) or after execution by the requester or a benchmark (Section 5); its judgments support completion decisions, quality measures, and diagnostic feedback for subsequent work. With these elements, we define a work agent as a system that uses a foundation model as its decision-making core and a harness to organize observations and actions in a stateful workspace. It pursues a delegated work objective under specified constraints, resources, and permissions, and its outcomes are assessed against task requirements through observable evidence. The agent itself consists of the model and the harness, shown as the dashed box in Figure 1; the task, workspace, outcome, and verification define the work for which it is accountable. The definition covers a wide range of tasks. In the minimal case, a question-answering system counts as a work agent when answering is delegated to it and its answers are checked against task requirements. Its harness only assembles the question and the supplied material into context and returns the model’s answer, and its workspace is that material, which the agent reads but does not change. A system that edits workbooks or carries business processes to completion uses the same elements with a fuller harness and a workspace that its actions change (Section 3). The six elements interact in a loop during execution. The harness constructs context from the task, workspace observations, and retained execution information and passes it to the model. The model proposes responses or actions; the harness carries out the actions, receives observations, and uses them with verification feedback to update the context for the next decision. At an assessment point t, execution and verification have distinct roles: (T, E0) M,H −−−−−−−−−−−−−→ closed-loop execution (τ0:t, Et, Ot), (1) St = V (T, E0, τ0:t, Et, Ot). (2) Equation (1) summarizes execution by the model–harness system; Equation (2) defines an assessment of its evidence against the task requirements. Here, E0 is the initial workspace state, τ0:t is the observable sequence of actions and feedback up to t, Et is the workspace state at t, and Ot is the outcome produced so far. The assessment St records how the inspected evidence meets the task requirements. Assessment can mark completion or occur during an ongoing responsibility. All work-agent settings share these elements and this loop; what differs is the conditions under which the loop runs, which Section 2.2 examines. 2.2 Working Conditions Across tasks, these conditions differ in two respects: whether the work ends once the agent delivers its result, and how much the agent must find out before and while it acts. We capture these two differences as ❶work persistence and ❷work openness. Section 2.2.1 defines work persistence and traces it through existing research, Section 2.2.2 does the same for work openness, and Section 2.2.3 shows that the two dimensions are conceptually distinct, illustrates their four combinations, and relates them to the forms of work examined in Section 3. 2.2.1 Work Persistence The first difference concerns when the agent may consider delegated work finished. In some tasks, the work is finished once the agent delivers its result, such as an answer, a confirmed change, or a tested patch. In others, the agent’s delivery alone does not finish the work: other participants must still assess, approve, or contribute, 7

authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: or later events require earlier results to be revisited. Work persistence thus ranges from responsibility that closes at delivery to responsibility that remains open across stages and events. As persistence increases, the agent must carry state across waiting periods and events and must determine at each point which parts of its responsibility are still open. Existing research covers both sides of this range. Responsibility closes at delivery when closure depends only on what the agent itself delivers. In early work on reading comprehension and question answering over text, tables, documents, and charts [18–23], responsibility closes once an answer is returned. Tool-use research, from Toolformer [24] and API-Bank [25] to Gorilla [26], extends the output from text to tool invocation. When an action changes the workspace, the work also requires a confirmed effect: in AndroidWorld [27], a messaging task counts as complete only when the intended message is recorded in the phone’s SMS database. Responsibility can also close at delivery after a sequence of dependent actions. In SWE-bench [16], producing a patch involves localization, editing, and testing; in MINT [28], tool outputs and language feedback across turns guide subsequent actions. On the other side, closure depends on more than the agent’s own delivery: on other participants or on later events. When it depends on other participants, responsibility cannot close until they provide the confirmation or contribution the task requires: τ-bench [29] withholds specified database updates until the user confirms them, τ 2-bench [30] requires the agent to coordinate with a simulated user who carries out part of the work, and TheAgentCompany [31] includes tasks that cannot proceed without information from simulated coworkers. When it depends on later events, earlier results or completed stages may need to be revisited: in OSWorld 2.0 [32], revised budget and vendor constraints arrive through a team chat and require the agent to reconsider affected entries in a purchase-order form. When the task defines an obligation over an agreed interval, the agent remains responsible for responding to such events throughout that interval: E-Commerce Bench [33] spans a simulated year of operational decisions, and VibeLifeBench [34] evaluates proactive and persistent assistance as events change the environment over simulated weeks. Dividing the examples by what closure depends on also separates persistence from task difficulty and execution length. Answering a question can demand harder reasoning than submitting a form for approval, yet responsibility for the answer closes at delivery, whereas the workflow remains open until approval is received. The same holds for execution length, a central concern of long-horizon research (Section 2.4.1). A long run may pass through many dependent steps, yet its responsibility still closes when the result is submitted; an obligation to keep a service within its operating constraints may require only a short run each week, yet its responsibility remains open for a quarter. The two examples sit on opposite sides of the boundary: the first closes once its run delivers a result, whereas the second stays open across many runs until the agreed interval ends. 2.2.2 Work Openness The two examples at the end of Section 2.2.1 illustrate when responsibility may close, but do not specify how much the agent must find out before and while it acts. The long run may operate on a repository whose relevant files are named in the request, or on one whose relevant files it must first locate; the weekly run may read the same fixed metrics each time, or have to trace which components a new incident affects. In some tasks, the task world, that is, the objects, interfaces, rules, and actors relevant to the task, is specified with the request. In others, the agent must establish during execution which objects are relevant and how they are represented and related. It may also need to find out where the relevant state is held, how other actors have changed it, and which actions it is authorized to take. Work openness thus ranges from a predefined task world to one discovered during execution. As openness increases, completing the work depends more on the agent’s ability to build and update its understanding of the task world while acting in it. As with persistence, existing research spans this range, and the examples below are ordered by how much the agent must establish during execution. Early research largely studied predefined task worlds. Reading- comprehension and question-answering tasks supply the passage, table, document, or chart to be analyzed [18– 23], and tool-use studies such as API-Bank [25], Gorilla [26], and BFCL [35] expose an explicit set of tools and interfaces. The agent reasons or acts within a space that has already been defined, and the difficulty lies in using the supplied material and tools correctly rather than in finding them. 8

authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: Finding them becomes part of the task in web and computer-use environments. In WebArena [6], the information needed for a task must be obtained by navigating and interacting with functional websites rather than read from the prompt. OSWorld [7] extends the setting to real computer environments, where the agent works across applications and heterogeneous digital objects. In Workspace-Bench [36], the agent must also identify which files are relevant and how they depend on one another, so locating material across a workspace becomes the core of the work. Beyond objects, other environments make the state of the task world, the actions of other actors, and authority part of what must be established. AppWorld [37] spreads the information a task needs across multiple applications, so the agent must determine which applications and records hold it before acting. In τ 2-bench [30], a simulated user acts on parts of the shared environment that the agent cannot operate, so the agent must find out from the user what has changed. Authority must be established when the request does not state who may do what. In EntCollabBench [38], instructions describe business goals rather than workflows, and each agent may use only its own department’s tools, so the agent must infer which role is responsible for each step and delegate to it. Applicable permissions may likewise have to be discovered during execution: in a card-unlocking task in τ-Knowledge’s τ-Banking domain [39], the agent must retrieve the relevant policy and inspect the card’s status to determine that a security hold prevents it from unlocking the card and requires it to offer escalation to the security team. 2.2.3 Combining Persistence and Openness Having defined both dimensions, we now consider how they combine. The two dimensions answer different questions, as the two examples at the start of Section 2.2.2 already suggest: openness concerns what the agent must find out, whereas persistence concerns when it may stop. The same workspace change can involve both dimensions: discovering which objects it affects concerns openness, while responsibility that remains open as further changes arrive concerns persistence. The two dimensions are thus conceptually distinct: a setting can be high on one and low on the other. As shown in Figure 2, all four combinations appear in existing research. Question answering (bottom left) combines a predefined task world with responsibility that closes at delivery: the system answers from given material, as in SQuAD [18] and DocVQA [22]. Information seeking (bottom right) asks the agent to discover the relevant material during execution, yet responsibility still closes at delivery, as in GAIA [40], whose questions require finding a source on the web, and Workspace-Bench [36]. Service workflows (top left) keep the task world predefined, yet responsibility remains open while the requested updates await user confirmation, as in τ-bench [29], where the tools, domain policy, and database are specified in advance. Ongoing work under changing conditions (top right) combines a task world discovered during execution with responsibility that remains open as later events arrive: revised constraints arriving mid-task in OSWorld 2.0 [32] require the agent to find the affected entries, and in VibeLifeBench [34], some changes come without notification, so the agent must re-inspect the environment to discover them. These combinations describe the conditions of work rather than its form. Section 3 distinguishes five work forms by the scope and organization of delegated work, from work at the Conversation Level, which answers questions over supplied material, to work at the Workspace Level, which operates across related objects in a workspace. Persistence and openness characterize the conditions under which each form is carried out: work at the Workflow Level, for example, can run in the predefined task world of τ-bench [29] or require the agent to track a shared state that a simulated user also changes, as in τ 2-bench [30]. Because both dimensions change what the agent must find out and keep track of, they also determine how demanding its core capabilities become, which Section 2.3 examines. 2.3 Core Capabilities of Work Agents Whatever the working conditions of Section 2.2, carrying out the work process of Section 2.1 raises five questions, each answered by one capability that recurs across office applications [4, 5], software repositories [3, 16], enterprise services [9, 29], and professional workspaces [31, 36]: (1) what the work involves: Perception and Understanding interprets the objects and their relationships; (2) what to do next: Reasoning and Decision Making weighs goals, constraints, and evidence to decide how to proceed; (3) how dependent steps and 9

The following subsections examine the five capabilities in turn, using one task throughout: updating a business report, together with its source workbook and associated slides, when new data arrive. Each subsection describes what the capability does and what it passes on, examines representative work, and states what it provides. To show how the two dimensions raise the demands listed in Table 1, each subsection then considers an extended version of the task: the agent is responsible for keeping the report up to date until it is approved, a data revision arrives during assessment in an upstream workbook that feeds the source workbook, and the request names neither that workbook nor the owner of the revised data. 2.3.1 Perception and Understanding Before acting, an agent must know what the task refers to. Perception and Understanding interprets objects and relationships: it identifies the objects involved in a task, interprets the content and structure of each object, and traces its links to other objects. It produces evidence whose meaning and source can be traced, including where each target of an edit is located, for use by Reasoning and Decision Making. In the report task, a value in the workbook becomes usable evidence only once its header, unit, and reporting period are known, and an edit can be applied only once its target cells or slide element are located. Existing work studies both the structure within an object and the links between objects. The structure within an object tells what a value means and where an edit applies. For meaning, SpreadsheetAgent [41] extracts hierarchical headers and layout cues from local spreadsheet regions, and PPTAgent [5] analyzes the functional types and content structures of reference slides. For location, SpreadsheetLLM [42] uses structural anchors, cell-address mappings, and format aggregation to locate relevant spreadsheet regions, and AutoCodeRover [43] searches program structure to locate issue-relevant classes and methods. The links between objects tell what else a task involves: RepoBench [44] evaluates the retrieval of relevant code across 11

Perception and Understanding thus provides an actionable account of the task’s objects and the links between them. In the report task, it links a reported value to its source cells and to the chart or slide that uses it, so that later checks can follow these links. When the revision arrives during assessment, perception must determine which values already cited in the report are affected; to do so, it must locate the upstream workbook that the revision changes. 2.3.2 Reasoning and Decision Making Located evidence does not by itself determine what to do next. Reasoning and Decision Making weighs goals, constraints, and evidence to decide how to proceed among the available alternatives. Goals determine the desired result, and constraints limit acceptable actions; goals and some constraints are supplied with the task, while further constraints may need to be established during execution. Evidence establishes the current situation and accumulates as the work proceeds, and domain knowledge, learned by the model or retrieved, determines how it should be interpreted. The result is a chosen approach, which Planning and Coordination arranges into a plan. In the report task, such reasoning determines whether two figures are comparable, which calculation is appropriate, and whether more information is needed before an edit is made. Existing work studies both domain-guided decisions and the use of evidence gathered during work. For domain-guided decisions, FinQA [21] requires domain knowledge to reason numerically over financial reports, and τ-bench [29] makes domain policies and user requirements constrain tool-use decisions. For evidence gathered during the work, ReAct [13] interleaves reasoning with actions and observations, SheetAgent [45] queries relevant spreadsheet subviews for its planner and uses code-execution results to inform subsequent operations, and CodeAct [46] expresses actions as executable code and feeds interpreter outputs and error messages into subsequent decisions. Reasoning and Decision Making thus provides decisions that can be checked later. To make this possible, the harness records each decision in the shared work context, together with the goal it serves, the constraints that applied, and references to the supporting evidence. Later steps can then tell whether it worked and whether its basis still holds. In the report task, the record of a decision to recompute a growth rate shows which figures were compared and why they were judged comparable. The revision reopens decisions like this one, and the agent must decide whether it can act on the revision directly or must first gather more information. 2.3.3 Planning and Coordination When delegated work involves several dependent actions or contributions from other participants, each decision must be connected to the work that follows. Planning and Coordination arranges the dependencies and handoffs among these actions and contributions. Planning specifies subgoals, required inputs, and the order in which results become available [47–49]; coordination obtains and routes the information, authorization, or artifacts supplied by other participants [50]. The result is a plan, which Execution and State Management 12

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: carries out. In the report task, the analysis must be completed before the dependent charts are revised, and any information needed from collaborators must be obtained in time. Representative work emphasizes different aspects of planning and coordination. Planning methods make dependencies explicit and revise them as results arrive: Data Interpreter [51] represents workflows as hierarchical dependency graphs, records task results and status, and adjusts affected tasks as execution develops, and Agent S2 [52] updates the remaining subgoals from the original task and new observations after each subgoal concludes. Coordination frameworks make one participant’s output available as another’s input: AutoGen [53] organizes role-based exchanges among agents, tools, and human input, and MetaGPT [54] passes structured artifacts such as requirements and designs through a shared message pool and a subscription mechanism. Planning and Coordination thus provides a plan that records the result each step produces, the inputs needed to produce it, and the steps or participants that will use it, including dependencies that are still pending. In the report task, the record leads from a revised data source directly to the analysis, charts, and slides that must be redone. Because responsibility lasts until approval, the plan must span the assessment period and take in the revision when it arrives, and the owner of the revised data must be identified during execution. 2.3.4 Execution and State Management Plans take effect only when they are applied to the workspace. Execution and State Management takes actions on workspace files, applications, and records through tools and interfaces, receives observations of their state, and records progress. Execution performs operations through code, tool interfaces, or graphical interfaces within the task’s authorized scope; state management tracks the objects and versions involved, completed operations, returned results, and pending items. The two are connected because operations can change workspace state or reveal information that affects the next decision. The results are the artifacts produced and the records kept, which Verification, Recovery, and Replanning checks; in the report task, these are the revised workbook and the list of calculations and dependent edits already completed. To retain the effects and observations on which later decisions depend, existing systems maintain action and state records during execution. SheetCopilot [4] executes spreadsheet operations through an observe– propose–revise–act state machine and updates its action and state records after each successful execution. InfiAgent [55] extends this practice beyond a single run: it stores plans, intermediate artifacts, and tool outputs in a task directory and updates progress markers, so that an interrupted task can be resumed from the record. Execution and State Management thus provides a record that tells which effects can be relied on. The record distinguishes an attempted action, an accepted call, a committed effect, and a verified effect: an attempted action has been issued; an accepted call has been acknowledged by the interface; a committed effect is reflected in the target state; and a verified effect has additionally been checked against the relevant requirement. These states need not coincide, so acceptance of a call alone does not establish task success. An operation whose effect is known to be committed becomes the starting point for the next one, whereas an operation with an uncertain effect remains pending until its state is inspected. In the report task, the saved workbook and its current version are the basis for the next edit, whereas a chart update that may not have been applied stays pending until the slide is checked. Because the work resumes when the revision arrives during assessment, the record must be kept across sessions so that resumed work does not repeat edits already made; before reading the upstream workbook, the agent must also establish that it is permitted to access it. 2.3.5 Verification, Recovery, and Replanning Recorded changes show what has happened but not whether it satisfies the task. Verification, Recovery, and Replanning confirms outcomes and guides correction. Its three functions proceed from assessment to corrective action: verification checks results against task requirements and completion criteria, recovery repairs the objects or operations responsible for a problem, and replanning revises the remaining steps when feedback shows that a prerequisite or condition has changed. We examine representative work for each function in turn. Verification relates each requirement to evidence that can establish whether it has been met. The appropriate evidence depends on the property being checked, whether a benchmark defines the check or the agent runs 13

content: it itself. Behavior is checked by execution: SWE-bench [16] runs tests against the modified repository, and SpreadsheetBench [56] applies a spreadsheet transformation to several workbook inputs. Claims are checked against external information: CRITIC [57] uses external tools to obtain evidence for critiquing and correcting its own outputs. Presentation is checked on the rendered artifact: DeepPresenter [58] inspects rendered slides to identify issues such as overlap and overflow. The report task needs all three: executing its calculations, checking its claims against their sources, and inspecting its rendered slides. When verification detects a problem, recovery repairs it. Self-Refine [59] revises the current output from generated feedback, whereas Reflexion [60] retains reflections on task feedback to improve the next attempt. In a workspace, a repair must also target the object or operation responsible, such as a wrong formula or an overflowing slide. When the effect of an earlier operation is uncertain, the agent must first inspect the current state to decide whether to retain, repair, or retry it; this matters most for operations, such as sending a message, that produce an additional effect when repeated. Some problems cannot be repaired locally because a prerequisite or condition has changed. Replanning then revises the remaining course of work: it uses the dependencies recorded in the plan (Section 2.3.3) to identify the steps the change affects and draws on Planning and Coordination to rebuild them. LATS [61] searches over alternative reasoning and action paths, using environmental feedback and reflection to choose among them. Verification, Recovery, and Replanning thus provides confirmed outcomes and corrections matched to the scope of each problem: a local defect receives a local repair and recheck, whereas a changed prerequisite leads to a revised plan and a check of its downstream results. After the revision, affected results already checked must be re-verified, and the agent must first establish which source counts as evidence for the revised figures. With it, the cycle in Figure 3 closes: a confirmed result is delivered or becomes the basis for further work, and a remaining problem is directed to the capability it concerns, with missing evidence going back to Perception and Understanding, a questionable decision to Reasoning and Decision Making, a changed prerequisite to Planning and Coordination, and an execution error to Execution and State Management. Section 2.4 relates this framework to existing agent paradigms. 2.4 Work Agents and Related Agent Paradigms Relative to this framework, three established lines of agent research each focus on one facet of the work: long-horizon agents on sustaining execution over many steps, computer-use agents on the action interface, and office agents on the type of artifact produced. A work agent is instead defined by its delegated objective and by outcomes assessed against task requirements, regardless of how long it runs, which interface it uses, or what artifacts it produces. Sections 2.4.1 to 2.4.3 summarize the research focus of each paradigm and state what the work-agent view adds, and Section 2.4.4 shows how the perspectives combine on one shared task. 2.4.1 Long-Horizon Agents The first paradigm concerns sustaining execution over many steps. Long-horizon agents study how to maintain task progress, context, and state over extended execution and how to handle dependencies whose consequences emerge in later stages. A recent synthesis organizes this research into three levels [62]: the intra-context level covers coupled reasoning steps, the cross-context level covers state continuity beyond a single context window, and the cross-task level covers experience accumulation across tasks. Evaluations quantify this ability: the METR time-horizon analysis [63] measures task length by the time human experts take to complete the task and estimates the length at which an agent reaches a given success rate, while RE-Bench [64] compares research-engineering performance under different time budgets. To sustain such work, representative methods keep information available beyond a single context window. InfiAgent [55] constructs its reasoning context from a snapshot of its stored task state and a fixed window of recent actions. On the evaluation side, LongMemEval [65] tests memory through timestamped user–assistant histories, including information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, and updates to user information, and LoCoMo [66] evaluates very long-term conversational memory. 14

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: These methods and measures concern continuity of execution and retained information. Work persistence asks a different question: when responsibility may close (Section 2.2.1). Persistent delegation requires tracking open obligations, responding to other participants and later events, and re-verifying earlier results against the current workspace. 2.4.2 Computer-Use Agents The second paradigm concerns the interface through which actions are taken. Computer-use agents study how to complete tasks through software interfaces in browsers, desktop applications, and operating systems. A central problem is to ground task intent in operations executable in the current interface: identifying relevant controls, locating action targets, and deciding what to do next from the resulting interface state [67–71]. SeeClick [72] studies the visual-grounding part of this process by locating screen elements from screenshots and instructions, and uses GUI-grounding pre-training to improve downstream task performance. Grounding individual operations is not enough; the operations must also add up to the task outcome. Bench- marks in this line, such as WebVoyager [73], therefore evaluate whole sequences of operations. WebArena [6] checks, depending on the task, whether an answer, page location, or website state satisfies the intended goal, and OSWorld [7] uses task-specific scripts to check the resulting files and application states. The work-agent view places these interface operations within the delegated task as a whole. Computer use is one interface through which the harness acts on the workspace [74]. Beyond the interface, this view also asks when responsibility closes and which permissions and dependencies the agent must discover during execution, including dependencies on objects that the interface does not show. Relating interface operations to these questions shows what each operation contributes to the task. 2.4.3 Office Agents The third paradigm concerns the type of artifact produced. Office agents, such as SheetCopilot, PPTAgent, and Huawei Cloud OfficeAce [4, 5, 75], create and modify common work artifacts such as documents, spreadsheets, and presentations. Task requirements concern both content and the structure and use of the objects that carry it: spreadsheet operations must act on the correct data and cells, while presentation production must balance content, layout, and overall coherence. The quality of the resulting artifact depends both on how individual objects are manipulated and on how the task is organized. Representative studies address these two aspects. For object manipulation, SheetCopilot [4] controls spread- sheets through a set of atomic actions, and PPTAgent [5] generates slides from reference presentations through code-based editing and evaluates content, design, and coherence. For task organization, OfficeBench [76] provides single- and multi-application tasks involving documents, spreadsheets, calendars, and email; its cross-application tasks require information obtained earlier to be used in later operations, and their results are verified through matching rules or execution-based checks. Office agents thus take office objects and the workflows around them as their main setting. The work-agent view offers a framework for analyzing such work alongside software, service, and organizational work: it describes office outcomes in the same terms as other work outcomes (Section 2.1), so that an updated workbook, the corresponding changes to business records, and the approval required before publication can be analyzed as parts of one delegated task. 2.4.4 Relationships among Paradigms Having examined each paradigm separately, we now compare them on the same task. Table 2 uses the report task from Section 2.3, updating a business report when new data arrive; as its column “What is tracked” shows, the three related paradigms each track a different part of this task. A single system may need all three, as when an office agent completes a long reporting task through desktop applications and must maintain state over many steps. The work-agent view places these concerns within one work process, from task requirements through execution in the workspace to verified outcomes. This allows the paper to relate research across paradigms, identify which parts of the work each supports, and determine which capabilities must still be combined for a given delegated task. 15

authors: Zishan Xu, Enjun Du, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yang, Junhao Shen, Zirong Chen, Zhiyuan Yao, Yifu Guo, Yuquan Lu, Jinyang Huang, Zhengxi Lu, Siyi Liu, Ziyu Zheng, Yongqi Zhang, Difan Zou, Weiwen Liu
content: 3 Work Forms: What Work Do Agents Undertake? Section 2 describes the system elements, working conditions, and core capabilities of work agents. Together, these provide a foundation for explaining how an agent interprets a task, organizes its actions, and checks their effects. The demands on these capabilities depend on the work delegated to the system. We examine that work through three questions: what outcome must the agent produce, which objects and dependencies fall within its responsibility, and what conditions determine completion? The five work forms below describe how these responsibilities are organized. Because a workflow can contain informational responses and local actions, Figure 4 assigns each representative task setting to the broadest form it requires. At the Conversation Level, the agent produces an informational result, whereas at the Atomic Action Level, it executes a local operation on a work object. Moving to the Multi-step Level, the agent combines such dependent actions to achieve a complete objective. This responsibility broadens at the Workflow Level, where the process also becomes part of the delegated work and the agent advances it through stages governed by procedural requirements and interactions with other participants. It extends further at the Workspace Level, where the request no longer specifies every object involved and the agent must establish which files, records, and applications bear on the work and how they are related. As the scope expands, the agent must manage more of the dependencies surrounding an outcome, from intermediate results to stage transitions and relationships among work objects. Table 3 summarizes the resulting work requirements. 3.1 Conversation Level Work at the Conversation Level produces an informational result from a request and its associated evidence, such as an answer, analysis, classification, or judgment. The agent interprets the relevant material and applies the knowledge or computation needed to produce that result. Completion is assessed on the returned information and does not require modifying the source artifacts, external work objects, or their states. 3.1.1 Producing Informational Outcomes In these tasks, the delegated deliverable is information that answers the requester’s question or supports a judgment. It may range from a short factual answer to an assessment, explanation, or detailed proposal. SQuAD asks for an answer extracted from a supplied passage [18], FinQA requires a numerical answer derived from financial text and tables [21], and MMTU includes classifications and judgments about whether a statement is supported [77]. Professional requests extend these demands: AAAR-1.0 asks for equation checks and critiques of research papers [78]; FinLFQA requests financial analyses grounded in sources and calculations [79]; PRBench asks for justified legal and financial advice [80]; and MMLongBench includes summarization of supplied PDF documents [81]. Responses can also take the form of plans or executable specifications. In Idea2Plan’s direct-prompting setting, models develop a supplied research idea into a plan that includes experimental design, while TravelPlanner’s sole-planning setting asks for a feasible itinerary based on supplied travel information [82, 83]. WorfBench asks for a workflow graph of proposed subtasks and dependencies [84]. Program outputs specify how an object can be constructed: BlenderLLM’s CADBench asks for Blender scripts from modeling instructions, while the CADBench reconstruction benchmark asks for editable CAD programs from supplied images or meshes [85, 86]. 3.1.2 Interpreting Evidence and Deriving Responses The complexity of a response task depends on both the source material to be understood and the reasoning needed to process it. Prose presents facts in linguistic context, while tables relate values through rows and columns [87, 88]. Document images carry information in page layout [89], while charts encode values and relationships visually [23]. Extracting a value or comparing entries therefore depends on interpreting these structures [21, 22, 90]. In GDP.pdf, a footnote changes which employers belong in a chronological ranking [91]. Repository code and structured data also appear as supplied evidence in LongBench v2’s multiple-choice comprehension tasks [92]. 17
