content: Strict metrics and core vs. detail. Core checks are harder than detail checks for every system (Astra 97.0 vs. 97.8%; Gemini 3.8 Flash 79.4 vs. 86.7%). The share of tasks with no failed check of any kind (no video counts as failure) ranges from 73.6% (Opus) and 72.1% (Astra) to 23.8% (Gemini 3.8 Flash), close to strict success (76.3, 74.5 and 26.6%): most tasks that fail strict success fail a core check, not only detail checks. What keeps a task from strict success differs by system: for Opus, Astra, Sonnet and DeepSeek it is almost always a failed core check, whereas 19–25% of the runs of Gemini 4 Argon, GLM and Gemini 3.8 Flash fail it by delivering no playable video.

content: Tab. E.2 reports each panel separately. The panels differ in leniency but largely agree on the order: the top four are the same in every panel (Astra, Opus, DeepSeek, Sonnet), followed by Kimi and GPT-5.6 Sol. Their disagreements are between near-ties: J1 and J3 put Astra first (3.946 vs. 3.915; 4.285 vs. 4.172) and J2 puts Opus first (4.137 vs. 4.095); at the bottom J1 ranks GLM above Gemini 3.8 Flash (2.529 vs. 2.478), while J2 and J3 rank Flash above GLM. J3, whose vision judge sees sampled frames, leaves far more checks unknown (5.4–7.0% of delivered checks, against 0.6–1.7% for J1 and 0.2–0.6% for J2), which is why the “all core” rate of Tab. E.2 , where an unknown counts against the task, is much lower under J3 and why strict success counts only failures. Even so, the panels differ widely in strictness (Opus: 83.7, 93.3 and 51.9% strict success under J1–J3), so only the three-panel mean is comparable across systems (App. D ).

content: Tab. E.3 gives bootstrap intervals for the headline score and compares each system with the next one. Adjacent pairs show how delivery and quality interact. Astra leads Opus ( P = 0.91 P{=}0.91 ; 127 vs. 89 head-to-head wins), and both are clearly ahead of DeepSeek ( P = 1.00 P{=}1.00 ). DeepSeek is ahead of Sonnet on the mean only through delivery (Sonnet wins 121 of the head-to-heads, DeepSeek 89; P = 0.70 P{=}0.70 ), and Gemini 4 Argon wins 142 of 239 head-to-heads against GPT-5.6 Sol yet ranks below it, because its 23% non-delivery contributes zeros. Gemini 3.8 Flash and GLM are statistically tied ( P = 0.50 P{=}0.50 ). Delivered-only per-run means (95% CI) are Astra 4.126 [4.090, 4.163], Opus 4.074 [4.039, 4.109], Sonnet 3.995 [3.940, 4.052], Argon 3.988 [3.950, 4.022], DeepSeek 3.957 [3.901, 4.010], Kimi 3.861 [3.800, 3.923], GLM 3.733 [3.636, 3.829], GPT-5.6 Sol 3.734 [3.678, 3.789] and Flash 3.466 [3.365, 3.553].

VA is the highest dimension for most systems and TM the lowest for all but Gemini 4 Argon. By category (Fig. E.1 b, Tab. E.4 ; mean over the nine systems, no video = 0 =0 ), Building & process is hardest (3.07) and spreads the systems most (best minus worst 2.66), because it demands long, stateful assembly; Visual art & form is next (3.15). Classroom lessons score highest (4.19) and spread least (0.88); every system averages at least 3.59 on them. Astra or Opus is best in 10 of the 12 categories, Sonnet on lessons and papers.

content: Among the 1,628 playable deliveries on the core tasks the most frequent program-check failure is duration (34), followed by a missing source project (20), frame rate (15; e.g . , 24 instead of 30 fps, or drift such as 30.01), exact frame count (10), silent or absent audio where audio is required (10) and resolution (6). On the 34 lessons and papers, the rule-based checks (decodable MP4, resolution, frame rate, duration, audible audio, narration coverage by VAD, narration language by Whisper language ID, black or frozen stretches) fail in only 14 of 306 runs, 6 of them Gemini 4 Argon’s; nearly all are runs without a playable video. Program checks thus certify the container reliably, but defects of that kind are rare in delivered videos, and their effect on the ranking overlaps almost entirely with delivery itself.

content: Strong systems finish with time to spare. Opus and Astra usually end well before the hour, while GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM often run into the deadline; Sol has usually saved a playable video by then, GLM often has not. Within every system longer runs score lower: long runs are runs in trouble. The harnesses shape how agents work: Claude Code and Codex agents act almost entirely through the shell, Gemini, Kimi and GLM rely more on dedicated file tools, and Gemini 3.8 Flash spends much of its time waiting on background tasks. Sub-agents and web search are rarely used; installing packages is common.

content: The pipeline is always “code → \rightarrow frames → \rightarrow ffmpeg”, and each system has a house style (Tab. F.2 ): the Claude agents and Gemini 4 Argon draw vectors with cairo, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi and GLM rasterize frames with PIL/numpy, and Astra, DeepSeek and Gemini 3.8 Flash capture browser canvases and three.js scenes. Off-the-shelf video frameworks such as Manim or MoviePy are almost never chosen. Vector and 2D-canvas pipelines deliver most often and score highest; 3D scenes, rendered with software WebGL, are the slowest and score lowest. Since renderer and system are coupled, this is an association.

content: Almost every run looks at its own rendered frames, but how much it looks does not predict delivered quality across systems: Astra looks least and scores best. Within systems, looking more goes with better videos for some (Sonnet, Kimi, GLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash) and not for others. Final reports often claim verification that does not hold: for videos that fail spec compliance, the report still says the video was “verified” in most of Astra’s cases and in a minority of the others’.

content: Cost buys little quality. The mean list-price API cost per task spans 49 × 49\times across systems, from $0.32 (GLM) to $15.38 (Opus), but its rank correlation with the headline score is not significant ( ρ = 0.55 \rho{=}0.55 , permutation p = 0.13 p{=}0.13 , n = 9 n{=}9 ; 0.43 with the delivered-only score). DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reaches 95% of Astra’s score at 5.8% of its cost, and DeepSeek and GLM obtain 8.3–8.8 points of overall per dollar, about seven times the next system (Fig. 5 ). Spending is not effort either: Astra produces the fewest output tokens (61k per task, against 77k–289k for the others). The Pareto frontier (lowest cost, highest overall) is GLM → \rightarrow DeepSeek → \rightarrow Astra.

content: Protocol. Annotators compare two videos made by two systems for the same task. Both videos are playable and judged by all three panels, so the study measures the quality of delivered videos, not delivery. System pairs are balanced across tasks and the sides are randomized; annotators are blind to system identity and judge scores. The interface shows the full prompt and two synchronized players with a choice of audio track, and offers A better , B better , tie and both bad ; the instruction is “which better matches the prompt and is better overall”. We fit Bradley–Terry strengths on decisive votes (MM algorithm with a weak prior; Elo scale with geometric mean 1000), with 2,000-sample bootstrap CIs over decisive pairs and Wilson intervals for win rates.

content: We took 30 delivered videos, re-encoded each one cleanly and built ten defective versions with ffmpeg: five picture defects in the window from 35% to 65% of the runtime (black frames, a grey box over the center, heavy blur, a frozen picture) or over the whole video (left–right mirror), two sound defects (a silent window, another task’s soundtrack), audio delayed by 0.5 or 1.5 s, and the two halves swapped. Apart from the black window, every defective version passes all program checks, so only a judge can notice it. J1 judged each video in its clean version and in five of the defects (15 videos per defect, 180 judgments) with the unchanged prompt and rubric, and was not told that anything was injected.

title: Do vision models know that three is three?
authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Arnas Uselis, Seong Joon Oh
section: Do vision models know that three is three?
content: Do vision models encode the transition 2 → 3 2{\to}3 the same way whether it appears in handwritten digits or in hand gestures, and do they “understand” that clean → {\to} dirty is the same transformation regardless of whether it is applied to a kitchen or a carpet? The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) answers this for language models: concept changes correspond to directions in (language) embedding space. In vision, the same concept can manifest in visually unrelated regimes that rarely co-occur: images of digits and hands do not share much in common in pixel space. To understand whether vision models still encode the underlying abstract concepts, we study 46 46 vision encoders across architectures, training objectives, and scales, on 10 10 concept families including numerosity, age, object identity, and MIT-States attributes. Within each regime, we find statistically significant concept directions near-universally across our tested models. However, two distinct regimes do not always share the same concept direction. Several models learn multiple linear structures for the same concept transition, split across regimes. We call this phenomenon fragmented linearity : strong local linearity coexisting with near-absent global linearity. Fragmentation is, however, not fixed: models with stronger local linearity progressively escape it (local-global linearity correlated with τ ∈ [ 0.38 , 0.89 ] \tau\in[0.38,0.89] across all concepts), and where global linearity does emerge, concept directions can transfer as linear probes across regimes.

title: Do vision models know that three is three?
authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Arnas Uselis, Seong Joon Oh
content: The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) [ 1 , 2 ] claims that the embedding spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain linear directions corresponding to high-level concept changes, enabling interpretability and algebraic interventions in representation space. Yet as vision encoders increasingly serve as the perceptual backbone of multimodal systems [ 3 , 4 ] , understanding whether the same linear structure holds in vision is essential to completing the picture.

title: Do vision models know that three is three?
authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Arnas Uselis, Seong Joon Oh
content: Vision is fundamentally different from language in that the same concept often manifests in visually drastically different ways. For instance, the concept of “3” can be represented using handwritten digits [ 5 ] , the number of objects in an image [ 6 ] or hand gestures [ 7 ] . While these different groups ( regimes ) of images do not share much in common in pixel space, a human would understand that the same underlying concept is being manipulated; do vision embedding spaces encode the same abstractions? A linear representation in embedding space would hint that they do.

title: Do vision models know that three is three?
authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Arnas Uselis, Seong Joon Oh
content: Linear structure ( linearity ) in the embedding space is indeed often an assumption (implicit or otherwise) in prior works that attempt to interpret vision embeddings [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Prior work has also studied linearity of vision embeddings after projection onto a tangent space [ 11 ] , with respect to ordinal attributes [ 12 ] , and its emergence as a consequence of data diversity [ 13 ] . While these findings hint toward the presence of linear structure in vision embeddings, a more rigorous study exploring whether it survives across drastically unrelated visual regimes remains missing.

title: Do vision models know that three is three?
authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Arnas Uselis, Seong Joon Oh
content: To address this gap, we study 46 vision encoders varying in architecture, training objective, model size and pretraining data, using the concepts of numerosity, age, and object identity, as well as 7 7 attributes curated from MIT-States [ 14 ] . We show that within a given regime, concepts are almost universally encoded linearly to an extent that is statistically distinguishable from a random baseline. However, this applies only partially to cross-regime transfer ( Figure 1 ). This finding motivates our definitions of local (within-regime), global (cross-regime) and fragmented (only within-regime without cross-regime) linearity.

title: Do vision models know that three is three?

content: While local linearity is present even in supervised models with complete fragmentation across regimes (supervised models), models with stronger local linearity (CLIP-like models) also tend to exhibit stronger global linearity. This suggests a gradual convergence of regime-specific representations into abstract regime-invariant ones.

content: Global linearity does hold almost universally for object identity and age , with (99.3%) and (94.6%) of all statistical significance tests passing respectively. title: Do vision models know that three is three?
authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Arnas Uselis, Seong Joon Oh
content: Almost all vision models encode “three”, but not all of them know it is “three”. While vision embeddings are locally linear to the extent of statistical significance almost without exception, many of them learn the same concept several times, once per regime, reflected in the phenomenon we characterize as fragmentation. As locally linear structure gets stronger, cross-regime alignment increases and global linearity emerges, producing semantically meaningful concept directions that can act as effective linear probes. Given our characterization of vision embedding geometry, the overarching question as to whether regime-specific skills are also converging into abstract ones (and whether they are related to geometry) remains open to future work.

content: Although we cover a broad range of concepts exhibiting varying degrees of difficulty, our conclusions are limited in scope to the investigated concept types. Our counterfactual pairs are approximate: matched by embedding space distance. While these limitations are unavoidable in the current scope, we argue that our statistical tests and downstream capability (probing) results together establish sufficient evidence to validate our main claims.

content: Linear directions in embedding space can potentially be exploited to steer representations toward harmful outputs; our work characterizes this geometry but does not introduce new attack surfaces beyond what already exists in existing models. On the other hand, our work contributes to the literature on interpretability, which strives to make AI systems fair and transparent.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
section: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
content: 4D novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to render dynamic scenes across viewpoints and timestamps, which requires jointly inferring 3D structure and temporal dynamics. Existing monocular feed-forward methods often rely on explicit 4D Gaussian representations, which are prone to temporal inconsistency and severe rendering artifacts. We present FL4N , the first feed-forward latent 4D NVS model. Instead of relying on explicit 4D primitives, FL4N encodes a 4D scene prior into a unified latent representation across space and time. Our core insight is that learning temporal dynamics as residuals on top of a pretrained static latent prior enables effective 4D modeling with limited dynamic training data. To this end, we introduce a lightweight dynamic encoder that leverages static scene features to disentangle object motion from camera-induced parallax. Trained solely with an image synthesis objective, FL4N achieves state-of-the-art 4D NVS quality while rendering in real time. Its learned latent representation generalizes to real-world videos and disentangles viewpoint from time.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
section: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
content: Figure 1: Teaser. FL4N is the first feed-forward latent 4D novel view synthesis model. It models dynamics in a latent space to render temporally coherent frames, whereas Gaussian-based methods such as 4DGT ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , MoVieS ( Lin et al., 2026a ) , NeoVerse ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and C4G ( Kim et al., 2026c ) suffer from temporal ghosting, artifacts, holes, or blur.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: 4D novel view synthesis (NVS) is a cornerstone of understanding and simulating our ever-changing physical world, enabling broad applications, e. g . , immersive graphics ( Li et al., 2025 ) , world models ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , robotics ( Kim et al., 2026b ) , autonomous driving ( Song et al., 2025 ) , and 4D-aware vision-language models ( Cho et al., 2026 ) . Unlike static NVS ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Hong et al., 2025 ) , 4D NVS requires capturing both persistent 3D structure and temporal dynamics. While slow optimization-based methods ( Pumarola et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) and multi-view methods ( Xu et al., 2024b ; Balice et al., 2026 ) are impractical in the wild, monocular feed-forward approaches offer a practical, real-time solution by inferring a 4D scene from a casual video.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: However, monocular feed-forward 4D NVS is highly ill-posed, as it must jointly infer entangled 3D structure and object motion from monocular observations alone ( Wang et al., 2025b ) . This requires the model to learn a strong 4D prior. To make this tractable, existing methods ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026 ) rely on the explicit 3D inductive bias of 3D Gaussians ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) with added 3D motion and dense geometry and motion supervision. However, this reliance on explicit 3D primitives often bottlenecks 4D rendering quality. Inaccurate prediction of Gaussian attributes across timestamps often yields rendering artifacts, e. g . , temporal ghosting, floaters, and holes ( Kim et al., 2026c ; An et al., 2026 ) , as in Fig. 1 . Moreover, time-varying effects ( e. g . , shadows and illumination changes) must be encoded in per-primitive attributes ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and regions with insufficient primitive coverage tend to be over-smoothed ( Li et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2026c ) .

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: In recent static NVS literature, latent-based methods ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Szymanowicz et al., 2026 ; Mitchel et al., 2025 ) avoid these limitations by learning view synthesis end-to-end with transformers, mapping input views directly to target views conditioned on a target camera, without an explicit 3D representation. With minimal 3D inductive biases and large-scale training, these latent models outperform 3D-Gaussian-based methods in visual fidelity ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026a ) . However, directly extending the latent approach to dynamic scenes faces a fundamental challenge. Without explicit 3D priors, learning to disentangle 3D structure and temporal dynamics purely from data would require massive multi-view dynamic scene datasets ( Van Hoorick et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) , which are much scarcer than static datasets ( Watson et al., 2025 ) .

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: To resolve this challenge, we propose FL4N , a F eed-forward L atent-based 4 D N VS model, which augments a frozen pretrained static latent NVS model with a trainable dynamic encoder. Our key insight is that a 4D latent model does not need to learn dynamic scene representation from scratch: pretrained static latent NVS models already possess a strong, generalizable 3D prior, allowing the dynamic encoder to exclusively focus on modeling temporal changes ( e. g . , object motion or appearance variation). Consequently, our method can be trained with a small amount of dynamic data while fully inheriting the pretrained model’s ability to synthesize coherent novel views.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: Concretely, we attach the lightweight trainable dynamic encoder alongside the frozen static encoder, similar to ControlNet ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) . The dynamic encoder takes the same input views with a learnable per-view time token and cross-attends to frozen static encoder features to isolate true scene dynamics from camera-induced motion. A lightweight time module then modulates the residual latent for the queried timestamp, which is residually added to the static latent ( He et al., 2016 ) and decoded by the frozen renderer at the target camera pose. Multi-view videos naturally disentangle viewpoint and temporal variation through same-time views and fixed views across time. Sampling unseen view–time pairs, FL4N learns this disentanglement through image synthesis with binary dynamic mask supervision, without dense geometry or motion supervision.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: We evaluate our approach on synthetic and real datasets under a systematic protocol. To effectively demonstrate the performance of 4D novel view synthesis and the capability of view-time disentanglement, we separate the setting with novel view synthesis, cross-time view synthesis, and novel time synthesis. FL4N achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance across datasets in the pose-free setting without test-time pose optimization, while optionally incorporating context camera poses further enables state-of-the-art performance across all three settings.

authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: Feed-forward Gaussian splatting for 4D novel view synthesis. Explicit feed-forward 4D methods typically represent scenes with 3D Gaussians extended with temporal dynamics, such as velocity ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) or deformation fields ( Lin et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2026b ) . However, independently modeling motion per Gaussian often disrupts object rigidity and temporal consistency due to incoherent motion among nearby Gaussians ( Kim et al., 2026c ) , yielding artifacts such as temporal ghosting. Anchoring Gaussian prediction to each target timestamp ( Liang et al., 2025 ) can sidestep the issue but is susceptible to view bias by primarily relying on nearby frames while underutilizing observation from distant frames. Query-based Gaussian representation ( Kim et al., 2026c ) alleviates this via dense motion supervision, yet its limited number of queries constrains rendering quality due to insufficient Gaussian coverage, particularly for large outdoor scenes. Multi-view approaches ( Balice et al., 2026 ) can exploit observations from multiple time-synchronized static cameras, but the setup is far more restrictive than a monocular moving camera. We introduce a feed-forward latent-based method with minimal geometric inductive bias in a practical but more challenging monocular camera setup.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: Latent-based novel view synthesis. Latent-based NVS models synthesize novel views with transformers conditioned on the target pose ( Sajjadi et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Szymanowicz et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026a ) or latent pose variable ( Mitchel et al., 2025 ) , bypassing explicit 3D representations. Although RayDer ( Prestel et al., 2026 ) trains on dynamic videos, it still targets static NVS while suppressing object motion via per-view nuisance token that is dropped at inference. Despite their strong generalization, these methods either assume static scenes or treat dynamic content as variation to be ignored rather than modeled. Toward dynamic latent representations, DyST ( Seitzer et al., 2024 ) extends RUST ( Sajjadi et al., 2023 ) with a dynamics estimator, yet keeps its scene latent time-invariant. Temporal variation is decoded via control codes extracted from target-pose and target-time frames, which limits explicit view and time control and risks appearance leakage from these frames. In contrast, our model constructs a time-conditioned scene latent that is rendered from arbitrary target cameras, enabling synthesis at novel views and novel timestamps.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: Generative novel view synthesis. NVS becomes inherently ambiguous when target views extend into regions unseen in the input views. Deterministic methods maintain strong cross-view consistency on observed content but tend to blur unobserved regions ( Prestel et al., 2026 ; Szymanowicz et al., 2026 ) . Generative approaches ( Van Hoorick et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) can extrapolate plausible content beyond the observed regions, yet their stochastic sampling often compromises cross-view consistency and scene faithfulness ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026c ) . Although generative refinement can post-process rendered views from Gaussian representations ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026c ) or serve as a diffusion decoder for latent-based model ( Szymanowicz et al., 2026 ) , our work focuses on deterministic NVS and remains orthogonal to such generative refinement directions.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim

To learn to disentangle dynamic motion from static scene structure in monocular videos, we freeze the pretrained static encoder ℰ st \mathcal{E}_{\text{st}} and renderer ℛ \mathcal{R} , and introduce a lightweight dynamic encoder ℰ dyn \mathcal{E}_{\text{dyn}} . The static encoder ℰ st \mathcal{E}_{\text{st}} already captures time-invariant content and camera-induced viewpoint changes from its static-scene training. During our dynamic-scene training, the frozen static encoder and renderer allow the dynamic encoder ℰ dyn \mathcal{E}_{\text{dyn}} to learn temporal variations as residuals to the pretrained static representation. Freezing the renderer ℛ \mathcal{R} fixes latent-to-image mapping, forcing the residual feature to the pretrained latent space. This encourages them to complement the static representation rather than learn a new feature space from limited dynamic data.

Having no target-time input, the static latent 𝐳 st \mathbf{z}_{\text{st}} compresses the video sequence into a single time-invariant prediction; moving content is thus discarded or frozen at observed frames with the input pose entangled, as in Fig. 3 . content: Training dataset. To effectively disentangle camera and object motion, we train our model using synchronized multi-view video datasets such as Kubric4D ( Van Hoorick et al., 2024 ) and CamxTime ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , captured by V V cameras with fixed poses with T T frames. Unlike costly, explicit 3D annotation ( e. g . , dense depth or 3D motion) that is commonly used for 3D-Gaussian-based approaches, the multi-view datasets provide cost-effective indirect 4D supervision from 2D images. Furthermore, our residual formulation specifically makes this RGB-only supervision directly tractable, with requiring relatively small amount as well.

content: Evaluation setting. We evaluate three settings, novel view synthesis (NVS), cross-time view synthesis (CTVS), and novel time synthesis (NTS), illustrated in Fig. 6 . NVS evaluates held-out viewpoints at input timestamps, CTVS evaluates unseen viewpoints-timestamps combinations from a monocular video, and NTS evaluates intermediate timestamps from temporally strided inputs. NVS and CTVS use multi-view datasets from fixed cameras: NVIDIA ( Yoon et al., 2020 ) , N3DV ( Li et al., 2022 ) , Kubric4D, CamxTime, and Charge ( Nazarczuk et al., 2026 ) . NTS is evaluated on monocular videos captured by moving cameras: DyCheck ( Gao et al., 2022 ) , ADT ( Pan et al., 2023 ) , and TUM ( Sturm et al., 2012 ) . Kubric4D and CamxTime are evaluated on held-out test scenes from our training distribution, whereas the other datasets evaluate zero-shot generalization. Detailed evaluation protocol is provided in Appendix B .

content: Quantitative results. Tables 1 , 2 , and 3 report the three protocols. Here, † denotes 2,000-step test-time pose alignment with target frames, and Pose (✓/✗) indicates context pose input. FL4N achieves state-of-the-art performance among all pose-free baselines, even without test-time alignment, except for SSIM on NVS of two real-world datasets. On real-world datasets, whose camera poses are noisy estimates, C4G benefits from test-time pose alignment while our model is forced to estimate slight inaccurate pose relation, resulting in a slight misalignment of pixels. An optional incorporation of context camera poses further improves the accuracy by exploiting the explicit context-to-target pose relation achieving state-of-the-art performance across all benchmarks on all protocols. These results demonstrate the substantial strength of our proposed latent representation: strong 4D prior, generalization to novel view and time, and decouplement of view and time, all successfully learned in the latent space. Additional rendering quality evaluation on dynamic region and discussion on test-time pose alignment are provided in Appendices D.1 and F .

Freezing the renderer is crucial (variant (ii)); unfreezing it disrupts dynamic branch training by destabilizing the established latent-to-image mapping in the renderer. The dynamic mask loss (variant (iii)) modestly improves the accuracy by helping the model resolve depth ambiguity and localize dynamic regions during training. Without it, the model tends to collapse as training progresses. Static feature anchoring to the residual encoder (variant (iv)) further improves the overall accuracy, helping the residual branch to effectively isolate temporal variation from injected intermediate features from the static encoder.

content: Video depth estimation. Although the model receives no explicit geometric supervision, its latent representations can encode scene geometry information. We probe this by attaching DPT depth predictors on the static and dynamic latent and training them Kubric ( Greff et al., 2022 ) . Table 7 reports the video depth accuracy. This suggests that dynamic latent largely preserves geometry-aware information encoded by the static latent while incorporating additional cues from temporal dynamics.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: In this work, we introduced FL4N, a feed-forward latent model that renders dynamic scenes from a monocular video at novel views and timestamps. By learning a temporal residual on top of a frozen static latent model, FL4N acquires a 4D representation from limited dynamic data, supervised only by images and binary dynamic masks. Across eight benchmarks and three evaluation protocols, FL4N outperforms prior feed-forward Gaussian-based methods and generalizes to real-world videos, while its latent space successfully disentangles view from time and preserves scene geometry. Our work demonstrates the potential of latent representations for feed-forward 4D novel view synthesis, opening new directions for latent-based 4D scene understanding and modeling more complex dynamics.

content: Static encoder and renderer. The static prior used is a pretrained feed-forward novel view synthesizer whose encoder is a 24 24 -layer transformer alternating frame-wise and global attention, followed by a 12 12 -layer transformer renderer. Both use a hidden size of 768 768 with 12 12 heads on 8 × 8 8\times 8 patches, and remain frozen during our training.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: Dynamic encoder. The dynamic encoder adopts the same core architecture as the static encoder, augmented with cross-attention, but uses one-third of its depth, with 8 8 layers. It is initialized with weights uniformly sampled from the pretrained static encoder. Each layer additionally cross-attends to the last layer of static features, allowing the residual branch to access camera-pose-aware representations throughout encoding. This provides a spatial anchor for learning motion residuals, complementing the static features rather than relearning scene structure. A DPT decoder ( Ranftl et al., 2021 ) attached to the dynamic encoder predicts the binary dynamic mask.

title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
authors: Eunbeen Hong, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jooho Son, Hyunah Ko, Soowon Son, Chaehyun Kim, Jahyeok Koo, Jisoo Kim, Junhwa Hur, Seungryong Kim
content: Temporal conditioning. We use a single learnable time token 𝝉 ∈ ℝ C \bm{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} with C = 1024 C=1024 , and attach a copy of it to each input view by concatenating it with that view’s tokens. Each copy becomes view-specific ( 𝝉 ^ k \hat{\bm{\tau}}_{k} ) through attention with its own view, allowing the same token to handle an arbitrary number and ordering of context frames. The resulting time representation is processed by a time module consisting of two transformer blocks with adaptive layer normalization conditioned on the target-time token, followed by a zero-initialized linear residual gate.

content: Training setup. We train with AdamW at a learning rate of 3.5 × 10 − 5 3.5\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 0.05 0.05 , and 3 3 k warmup steps, while keeping the static encoder and renderer frozen for whole training. FL4N is trained on four NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada Generation GPUs with a batch size of 8 for total of 32k steps. Each training sample contains 8 conditioning views and 12 target views at a resolution of 336 × 512 336\times 512 .

To disentangle camera and object motion, we train the model to reconstruct target frames at view–time pairs not included in the input set.

content: Loss. We use an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} photometric loss ℒ 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{2}} , LPIPS losses ℒ perc \mathcal{L}_{\text{perc}} and ℒ perc dyn \mathcal{L}_{\text{perc}}^{\text{dyn}} , and an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} image-gradient loss ℒ grad dyn \mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}}^{\text{dyn}} . The dynamic-region losses are computed using the dynamic mask M k M_{k} to select moving pixels, on 128 × 128 128\times 128 crops centered on the moving content. For the image loss term, the dynamic and static regions are averaged over their respective areas and weighted equally. Dynamic mask loss is only comptued for context frames. We set λ perc = 0.5 \lambda_{\text{perc}}=0.5 , λ perc dyn = 2.0 \lambda_{\text{perc}}^{\text{dyn}}=2.0 , λ grad dyn = 1.0 \lambda_{\text{grad}}^{\text{dyn}}=1.0 , and λ mask = 1.0 \lambda_{\text{mask}}=1.0 .

content: Pseudo dynamic mask generation. We generate pseudo dynamic masks by thresholding the magnitude of optical flow estimated by an off-the-shelf flow estimator ( Wang and Deng, 2026 ) . Since the flow is computed between frames captured by the same static camera, camera-induced motion and parallax are absent, making the remaining flow primarily reflect object motion. This leverages the static-camera multi-view configuration of our training data to identify dynamic regions with binary pseudo labels. The mask generation can also be easily replaced with off-the-shelf segmentation models, such as SAM3 ( Carion et al., 2025 ) , without changing the training framework.

content: Table C extends Table 4 to more variants and temporal strides { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \{1,2,4,8\} . We first compare against the static NVS backbone and its fine-tuned variant. While both provide a strong static-scene prior, fine-tuning alone does not effectively capture scene dynamics. We further ablate architectural choices. Unfreezing the renderer degrades performance, suggesting that preserving the pretrained latent-to-image mapping is beneficial. The single-branch encoder, removal of the dynamic mask loss, and sinusoidal time embeddings all underperform our full model. Removing static feature anchoring also reduces performance overall, highlighting the benefit of conditioning dynamic features on the static representation. Finally, we vary the dynamic encoder depth and initialization. Our 8-layer encoder achieves the best overall performance among the tested configurations. Random initialization also yields competitive results, although initializing from the static encoder weights consistently improves performance across temporal strides.

section: Appendix F Test-time pose alignment for latent models
content: Evaluating models that do not receive conditioning poses can introduce scale misalignment with the ground truth, resulting in poor rendering metrics even when the predicted scene is geometrically accurate. Since the input images do not determine an absolute scale, a pose-free model may reconstruct the scene at an arbitrary scale. Pose-free methods therefore perform test-time pose alignment before evaluation and report rendering metrics using the aligned poses ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026c ) . This alignment only brings the prediction into the coordinate frame and scale of the ground truth without modifying the underlying scene content.

section: Appendix F Test-time pose alignment for latent models
content: The pose-free Gaussian baselines in our quantitative comparisons are evaluated with 2,000 step pose-alignment steps, whereas FL4N is reported without pose alignment in the main tables. However, FL4N is also pose-free and therefore suffers from the same scale ambiguity that motivates this evaluation procedure. We thus additionally evaluate FL4N with the same 2,000 step pose alignment to provide a consistent comparison.

section: Appendix F Test-time pose alignment for latent models
content: For Gaussian models, Gaussians are predicted once from the conditioning images and kept fixed throughout the alignment process. Differentiable rasterization allows the rendering loss to be backpropagated to the camera pose, so each alignment step re-rasterizes the same frozen Gaussians under an updated pose, without modifying the network or scene representation.

section: Appendix F Test-time pose alignment for latent models
content: The analogous procedure can be done to our latent renderer. The scene latent is predicted solely from the conditioning images and is independent of the rendering process. We therefore compute the latent once and keep it fixed throughout the alignment process, with the renderer serving the role of rasterization by re-rendering the cached latent under an updated target pose at each step. For both Gaussian and latent models, we optimize a rotation and translation offset for each target pose ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , initialized at zero such that the initial rendering exactly matches the feed-forward prediction. We use the same objective as the Gaussian baselines, with 2,000 Adam steps using pixel and perceptual losses. Table G reports the effect of this alignment under the NTS protocol on ADT and TUM. Alignment is worth 5.94 5.94 dB to C4G on ADT and 5.13 5.13 dB on TUM, against 3.59 3.59 dB and 2.55 2.55 dB for our model, so a large part of the published margin of C4G on these cells comes from fitting the pose to the image it is then scored on. How much alignment recovers therefore measures how much error the supplied cameras carry rather than the quality of the reconstruction, and our model without any alignment remains ahead of both aligned baselines on every metric.

authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: Physical intelligence [ 1 , 2 ] , including autonomous driving [ 3 ] and embodied control [ 4 ] , holds the promise of freeing human workers from physical tasks that are dangerous, laborious, or tedious. A general-purpose physical agent should not only act from visual observations, but also anticipate the physical consequences of their actions. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, including those standard models [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] and specialized end-to-end ones [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , typically predict actions directly without explicitly modeling the future evolution of the environment. This has motivated a shift toward World Action Models (WAMs) [ 4 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] for physical AI, which build on pretrained video generative models [ 14 , 15 ] to jointly predict future visual states and their corresponding actions.

content: However, WAMs follow the imagine-then-execute paradigm [ 16 , 12 ] and incur prohibitive inference latency, rendering them impractical for latency-critical applications such as autonomous driving. Borrowing few-step techniques from image and video generation, some methods apply step distillation [ 17 ] to reduce this latency, but often at the expense of a substantial drop in control accuracy, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . To address this issue, efforts [ 4 , 11 ] propose to switch from the imagine-then-execute paradigm to direct-policy WAMs. These methods retain video prediction as a training-time objective that shapes physically grounded representations, without synthesizing future observations at test time. This direct-policy formulation is more than 3 × 3\times faster than the imagine-then-execute paradigm.

authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: Despite this speedup, efficiently generating high-quality actions remains a key challenge for direct-policy WAMs. They require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, resulting in latency that remains too high for real-time applications such as autonomous driving. This bottleneck cannot be resolved by reducing the number of denoising steps. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 2 , the performance degrades as the step count decreases, dropping by 20 % 20\% on NAVSIM (autonomous driving) and 40 % 40\% on RoboTwin (embodied control) in the one-step setting. We attribute this to the lack of action structure in random noise: multiple denoising steps can gradually impose temporal and physical consistency, whereas one-step generation must recover a coherent action sequence in a single update. Existing few-step accelerations, such as step distillation [ 17 ] and trajectory rectification [ 18 ] , still start from Gaussian noise and, therefore, do not supply the missing action prior. This motivates introducing structured action priors at initialization, providing an informed starting point for high-quality action generation in a single denoising step.

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: In addition, direct-policy WAMs [ 4 , 11 ] remain limited in their ability to exploit future dynamics for effective control. They use a consistent first-frame-only interface during training and inference, relying on video co-training to encode future dynamics into the current representation. However, compressing all future information into a single first-frame representation may provide insufficient temporal context for effective future-aware control. To address this limitation, subsequent methods reintroduce future features at inference and mitigate the associated rollout cost through caching, sparse interaction [ 19 ] , or compact latent representations [ 20 ] . Despite these efforts to reduce rollout cost, generating and incorporating future features at test time still incurs additional inference overhead.

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: To address the aforementioned issues, we propose OSWAM , a world action model with one-step action generation for more effective physical control. Our key observation is that previous one-step action generation methods fail mainly because the action diffusion processing is initialized from unstructured Gaussian noise. To supply the missing action structure, we learn a compact set of imagination tokens from the video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) and use them as structured start points for action denoising. These tokens are far fewer than video first-frame tokens and are obtained in a single forward pass, so they add negligible computation, yet they interact with visual features to accumulate physically grounded, action-relevant context. We then noise the imagination tokens to an intermediate timestep and decode them with the action DiT in one step, replacing the long denoising trajectory required by random initialization. To enhance future-aware control, we train these imagination tokens with privileged-information distillation. A teacher attends to visual tokens over the full future horizon, while the student imagination tokens, at test time, attend only to the first frame. By distilling the teacher’s privileged representations into the imagination tokens and subsequently into the action DiT, OSWAM transfers long-horizon context without reintroducing future-dependent features at inference. This design preserves the first-frame-only interface of direct-policy WAMs, while enabling high-quality action generation in a single denoising step.

section: 2.1 World Action Models for Autonomous Driving
content: Autonomous driving has recently shifted from modular pipelines with separate perception [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] and planning [ 25 ] modules toward end-to-end frameworks [ 26 ] . To further integrate future dynamics modeling, world models [ 14 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] for autonomous driving have recently been extended into world action models (WAMs). Existing methods fall into two categories: bird’s-eye view (BEV)-based and video-generation-based world models. BEV-based approaches [ 10 , 30 , 31 ] forecast occupancy evolution and ego motion, predict future latent scene features, or infer future BEV layouts for online trajectory evaluation. They are computationally efficient but do not exploit large-scale video generative priors. A complementary line of research leverages pretrained video generators and predicts the future in the image domain. These methods [ 32 , 13 , 33 ] transfer such priors to driving, but jointly rolling out video features at test time remains inefficient. SimWAM [ 11 ] follows the direct-policy design of Fast-WAM [ 4 ] to avoid test-time video rollout, yet the remaining multi-step denoising is still impractical for onboard driving. In contrast, our proposed OSWAM inherits large-scale video generative priors without test-time video rollout, and reduces action generation to a single denoising step.

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
section: 2.2 World Action Models for Embodied Control
content: Unlike autonomous driving, where compact BEV representations naturally encode road topology and traffic interactions, embodied control needs to model fine-grained object interactions and appearance changes in close-range scenes. As these phenomena are naturally captured in video, embodied WAMs are predominantly built on pretrained video generators for image-domain future modeling in two ways: explicit future imagination and direct-policy inference. Explicit-imagination methods [ 12 , 16 ] generate future visual representations at test time to guide action prediction, incurring substantial rollout latency. Direct-policy WAMs [ 4 ] retain video prediction as a training signal but generate actions directly from current observations, avoiding test-time visual rollout; however, its iterative action denoising remains a bottleneck for high-frequency closed-loop control. In contrast, OSWAM preserves large-scale video-generative priors without test-time visual rollout and reduces action generation to a single denoising step.

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: The main deployment bottleneck for WAMs lies in the high computational cost of diffusion-based video and action generators, whose test-time latency is prohibitive for onboard driving and closed-loop manipulation. Drawing one-step distillation from video generation, Flash-WAM [ 17 ] compresses joint video-action diffusion to a single denoising step per modality, but still synthesizes future video at inference. Fast-WAM [ 4 ] removes test-time video rollout by predicting actions from current observations only, yet retains iterative action denoising. Light-WAM [ 34 ] further replaces the generative action expert with a lightweight fusion head for single-pass action prediction, but underperforms on challenging benchmarks such as RoboTwin. SimWAM [ 11 ] follows Fast-WAM to drop test-time video rollout, but its multi-step action denoising keeps inference latency well above the budget required for onboard deployment. Building on this video-rollout-free direct-policy formulation, OSWAM addresses the remaining action-generation bottleneck through one-step action denoising.

content: An overview of OSWAM is shown in Fig. 3 . As in previous works [ 4 , 11 ] , we consider predicting an action chunk 𝐚 1 : H \mathbf{a}_{1:H} from the current frame f 0 f_{0} and an optional task instruction l l , with ego-state information additionally provided for driving tasks. We follow Fast-WAM in the world model backbone configuration and direct-policy setting. Specifically, the Video DiT uses the Wan2.2-5B backbone [ 14 ] , accompanied by its pretrained T5 text encoder and video VAE. The Action DiT is initialized by interpolating and downsampling the pretrained Video DiT weights. For autonomous driving, we add an ego encoder to encode the ego state and the driving command. The task languages and ego states are both provided to all tokens through cross-attention. The full model is organized as a Mixture-of-Transformer (MoT) architecture with shared attention between the video and action blocks. We also follow the direct-policy protocol: video modeling is used only as a training signal, and future video is not rolled out at inference.

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: Unlike prior direct-policy methods, which use the Video DiT at inference solely to encode the first-frame visual feature for Action DiT through shared MoT attention, OSWAM additionally introduces two groups of imagination tokens into the Video DiT: Action Imagination Tokens (AIT) and Scene Imagination Tokens (SIT). As shown in Fig. 3 , both AIT and SIT are initialized from noise in the Video DiT and interact with the first-frame visual features. The resulting AIT representation then replaces the unstructured Gaussian initialization of the Action DiT, providing a compact, structured start point for action denoising. SIT provides additional latent slots that aggregate scene context for AIT; they are updated indirectly through privileged distillation and the auxiliary action loss on AIT. Together, AIT and SIT comprise far fewer tokens than the first-frame visual input and therefore introduce only a small computational overhead during inference. To strengthen future-aware control under this first-frame-only interface, we introduce privileged-information distillation. The privileged teacher comprises a Video DiT with AIT that attends to visual tokens over the full clip, while the AIT in OSWAM attends only first-frame visual context. By aligning OSWAM’s intermediate imagination token features with those of the teacher, we transfer this privileged information to improve action generation, while OSWAM remains first-frame-only at inference.

content: Autonomous Driving. For autonomous driving, we evaluate OSWAM on the NAVSIM [ 43 ] , which provides real-world driving data sampled at 2Hz, with eight cameras covering a 360-degree field of view and LiDAR observations. The dataset comprises 1192 scenarios for training and 136 scenarios for testing. NAVSIM introduces practical and reliable metrics that effectively bridge open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. Specifically, NAVSIM evaluates model performance using the Predictive Driver Model Score (PDMS), which is calculated based on five factors: No At-Fault Collision (NC), Drivable Area Compliance (DAC), Time-to-Collision (TTC), Comfort (Comf.), and Ego Progress (EP). We report PDMS, which is calculated as PDMS = NC × DAC × ( 5 × EP + 5 × TTC + 2 × C ) / 12 . \mathrm{PDMS}=\mathrm{NC}\times\mathrm{DAC}\times({5\times\mathrm{EP}+5\times\mathrm{TTC}+2\times\mathrm{C}})/{12}.

content: Embodied Control. For embodied control, we evaluate OSWAM on RoboTwin 2.0 [ 44 ] , which is a challenging bimanual manipulation benchmark featuring more than 50 tasks that require coordinated dual-arm control. We adopt the multi-task setting of Fast-WAM, using data from over 50 tasks. The training data consist of 2,500 demonstrations from clean scenes and 25,000 demonstrations collected with heavy scene randomization. Performance is evaluated by the average success rate over 100 trials per task under both clean and randomized conditions.

For NAVSIM, we follow [ 11 ] to use a single front camera at 384 × 672 384\times 672 resolution and predict eight waypoints over four seconds at 2Hz. We use the current frame and eight future frames in training. For RoboTwin, we concatenate the head and two wrist views into a 384 × 320 384\times 320 image and use an action horizon of 32, with nine video frames sampled at a temporal stride of 4. For temporal RoPE, we set s a = 1 s_{a}=1 and d t = 4 d_{t}=4 on both benchmarks, with s v = 1 s_{v}=1 for NAVSIM and s v = 4 s_{v}=4 for RoboTwin. AIT and SIT therefore use t n = n / 4 t_{n}=n/4 , ( n = 1 , … , 8 n=1,\ldots,8 ) on NAVSIM and t n = n / 16 t_{n}=n/16 , ( n = 1 , … , 32 n=1,\ldots,32 ) on RoboTwin; video latents use temporal coordinates { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} in training.

content: NAVSIM . Table 1 compares OSWAM with state-of-the-art planners on NAVSIM. OSWAM achieves a competitive PDMS of 90.3 90.3 with a latency of 136 136 ms. Compared with SimWAM, OSWAM matches its PDMS while reducing action denoising from ten steps to one, yielding a 3.01 × 3.01\times speedup. OSWAM also outperforms Metis by 1.2 1.2 PDMS with a 3.24 × 3.24\times speedup. Compared with DriveVA, OSWAM achieves a 4.36 × 4.36\times speedup with only a 0.2 0.2 lower PDMS. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of structured initialization in enabling efficient one-step action generation while maintaining competitive planning performance.

content: RoboTwin 2.0 . Table 2 reports success rates across 50 tasks under Clean and Randomized settings. OSWAM achieves an average success rate of 90.00 % 90.00\% with a latency of 142 142 ms. Compared with Fast-WAM, OSWAM reduces action denoising from ten steps to one and achieves a 2.80 × 2.80\times speedup, with only 1.83 % 1.83\% decrease in average success rate. Compared with the one-step Flash-WAM variant, OSWAM improves average success by 8.59 % 8.59\% and achieves a 4.29 × 4.29\times speedup. While Light-WAM achieves lower latency, OSWAM substantially improves the average success at the cost of only 35 35 ms additional latency. Overall, OSWAM is competitive with multi-step direct-policy WAMs while substantially accelerating inference on embodied control tasks.

content: Inference Efficiency . Table 3 compares inference efficiency with cached language context under the same environment. On RoboTwin 2.0, OSWAM reduces action GPU time from 67.61 67.61 to 6.78 6.78 ms compared with Fast-WAM, while imagination tokens increase visual GPU time by 5.48 5.48 ms. This yields a 3.39 × 3.39\times overall speedup, reducing latency from 323.67 323.67 to 95.35 95.35 ms with nearly unchanged peak memory. On NAVSIM, OSWAM similarly achieves a 3.32 × 3.32\times speedup over SimWAM, reducing overall latency to 99.70 99.70 ms. With compiled inference using torch.compile and CUDA Graph optimization, OSWAM achieves latencies of 40.81 40.81 ms on RoboTwin 2.0 and 52.64 52.64 ms on NAVSIM, supporting inference rates above 10 10 Hz and facilitating deployment in latency-critical applications such as autonomous driving. These results show that the reduction in action denoising cost outweighs the additional computation introduced by imagination tokens.

content: Effectiveness of Each Component. To more clearly illustrate the effectiveness of the different components in OSWAM, we conduct experiments by adding each of them to a baseline, which is set to one-step Fast-WAM. As shown in Table 5 , AIT substantially improves performance across both benchmarks, raising NAVSIM PDMS from 71.04 71.04 to 89.81 89.81 , and increasing RoboTwin success rates from 57.38 % 57.38\% to 87.42 % 87.42\% under Clean settings and from 55.80 % 55.80\% to 88.16 % 88.16\% under Randomized settings. The gains demonstrate the importance of structured start points for one-step action generation. Besides, privileged-information distillation further improves PDMS to 89.96 89.96 and RoboTwin success rates to 89.42 % 89.42\% and 89.62 % 89.62\% , without increasing inference latency. Finally, incorporating SIT yields the best performance on both benchmarks, demonstrating the complementary benefit of aggregating scene context for learning effective action priors.

content: Action Initialization. To evaluate different strategies for utilizing the structured action prior, we compare rectified-flow refinement [ 18 ] with re-noising at different noise levels. As shown in Table 7 , all re-noising variants outperform rectified-flow refinement, achieving higher PDMS and lower ADE. Increasing τ r \tau_{r} from 400 to 500 improves PDMS without affecting ADE, whereas a further increase to 600 slightly degrades both metrics. Uniformly sampling τ r \tau_{r} from 400 to 600 also underperforms the fixed setting of 500. These results suggest that a fixed intermediate noise level provides a favorable trade-off between preserving the structured prior and allowing sufficient action refinement; we therefore set τ r = 500 \tau_{r}=500 by default.

content: We further evaluate OSWAM on a PiPER robotic arm using two real-world tabletop manipulation tasks: placing a packaged bread into a bowl and placing a board eraser into an open drawer. Both tasks require coordinated grasping, transport, and accurate placement, while the drawer task additionally imposes clearance constraints from the drawer opening and surrounding cabinet. We use 50 training demonstrations for bread and eraser placement, respectively. Each method is evaluated over 20 trials per task. A trial is successful if the object is released into the target container and remains inside at the end of the execution.

content: As shown in Table 8 , OSWAM achieves success rates of 85% on bread placement and 80% on eraser placement, compared with 80% and 75% for Fast-WAM, respectively. These results indicate that OSWAM’s structured action initialization followed by a single Action DiT denoising step supports effective physical manipulation, with higher observed success rates than Fast-WAM on both evaluated tasks. Among successful episodes, OSWAM reduces the mean video-estimated task completion time by 34.2% for bread placement and 21.8% for eraser placement compared with Fast-WAM. Figure 5 presents representative successful rollouts, showing the progression from grasping and transport to final placement. OSWAM places the bread inside the bowl and releases the board eraser into the target drawer. Together, the quantitative results and execution examples complement our simulation evaluation and demonstrate the applicability of OSWAM to real-world manipulation. Additional execution videos are available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM .

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: In this paper, we presented OSWAM, an efficient world-action model for one-step action generation. To address the reliance of direct-policy WAMs on iterative action denoising, we introduced Action Imagination Tokens to learn a structured initialization, supported by Scene Imagination Tokens that aggregate complementary scene context. We further developed privileged-information distillation to transfer full future context into the Action Imagination Tokens. Together, these designs enable action generation with a single Video DiT pass and one Action DiT denoising step. Experiments on NAVSIM and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrated the competitive planning and manipulation performance of OSWAM and its substantial latency reductions over direct-policy baselines. OSWAM offers a practical approach to efficient world-action modeling for latency-critical control.

content: Limitations. Our study is focused on learning action DiT structured initialization. Although SIT and privileged-information distillation support this objective, their potential to directly enhance the Action DiT remains unexplored. Extending scene-context conditioning and privileged supervision to the action expert is a promising direction for future work.

content: nuScene. We also evaluate OSWAM on the nuScenes [ 47 ] dataset for autonomous driving. nuScenes comprises 1,000 real-world driving scenes, with keyframes annotated at 2 Hz. The scene images are captured by 6 cameras covering 360 degree FOV horizontally. The dataset is split into 700 scenes for training, 150 for validation, and 150 for testing. Following previous works [ 41 , 48 ] , L 2 L_{2} Displacement Error (DE) and Collision Rate (CR) are adopted to comprehensively evaluate the planning performance.

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: For nuScenes, we use a single front camera at 384 × 672 384\times 672 resolution. Each training sample contains the current frame and eight future frames sampled at 2Hz. We use eight action steps to match the four-second video horizon, with supervision and evaluation limited to the first three seconds. Each action is represented as ( x , y , θ ) (x,y,\theta) in the current LiDAR coordinate frame, with padded and unsupervised positions excluded from the action loss. For Role-aware 3D RoPE, we set s a = s v = 1 s_{a}=s_{v}=1 and d t = 4 d_{t}=4 , giving AIT and SIT temporal coordinates t n = n / 4 t_{n}=n/4 for ( n = 1 , … , 8 ) (n=1,\ldots,8) . Video latents use temporal coordinates { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} during training.

title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
authors: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang
content: We train for 10,000 steps with a global batch size of 128 using AdamW, a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay of 0.01 0.01 , and cosine decay with 5% linear warmup. For distillation, the frozen teacher uses a video timestep of 200, and feature alignment is applied after Video DiT blocks [ 8 , 16 , 24 , 30 ] [8,16,24,30] . We set λ dist = 10 \lambda_{\mathrm{dist}}=10 . Distillation starts after 500 steps, with its weight increased linearly over the next 500 steps. We set the AIT diffusion timestep to t max = 1000 t_{\max}=1000 and the re-noising timestep for Action DiT initialization to τ r = 500 \tau_{r}=500 ( σ r = 0.5 \sigma_{r}=0.5 ).

authors: Chenglong Ma, Yuanfeng Ji, Junzhi Ning, Jiyao Liu, Yujie Wei, Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Wenjie Li, Wenhao Tang, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Shujian Gao, Yujie Zhang, Ying Chen, Zilong Li, Zongyuan Ge, Diping Song, Jin Ye, Ming Hu, Junjun He, Hongming Shan
section: MedVTok: A General-Purpose Medical Visual Tokenizer
content: Multimodal medical AI requires a common visual interface for encoding heterogeneous imaging evidence for patient condition modeling. However, existing medical visual tokenizers are often tied to a specific dimension and imaging modality, forcing multimodal systems to rely on fragmented and poorly reusable representations. We introduce MedVTok, a general-purpose visual tokenizer that maps 2D images and 3D volumes from diverse imaging modalities into a unified token space. Building such a tokenizer poses two key challenges: preserving anatomical structure across dimensions and capturing clinical semantics across modalities. To this end, MedVTok introduces ( i ) slice differential regularization, which explicitly models inter-slice anatomical coherence missing in previous per-pixel/per-voxel supervision, and ( ii ) multi-expert representation alignment, which integrates knowledge from multiple medical expert encoders while retaining modality-specific complementary knowledge. Trained on 28M images and 70K volumes across 9 imaging modalities, MedVTok supports classification, retrieval, segmentation, synthesis, visual question answering, and medical report generation through a single tokenizer. Across 24 benchmarks, MedVTok achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating a scalable token interface that unifies medical image dimension, modality, and task usage. content: Multimodal medical AI aims to integrate heterogeneous patient evidence, including laboratory measurements, longitudinal records, and medical images, to form a holistic understanding of a patient’s condition. As the field shifts from isolated task-specific models toward generalist multimodal systems [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , a central requirement is a shared interface through which diverse clinical evidence can be encoded, transferred, and reused across tasks . Among these evidence sources, medical images are particularly rich and high-dimensional, capturing anatomical structures, pathological findings, and disease progression. Visual tokenization therefore serves as a critical front end that converts raw imaging data into compact visual tokens compatible with multimodal models.

content: However, medical imaging data are highly heterogeneous across both modality and dimension, including 2D images such as dermoscopic images, color fundus photographs (CFP) and histopathology patches, as well as 3D volumes such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). These data differ in acquisition protocol, anatomical coverage, and diagnostic content. Existing medical visual tokenizers are often tied to a specific modality and dimension, producing fragmented representations that are difficult to reuse in a multimodal system. Consequently, downstream models must absorb much of the burden of modality adaptation and cross-modality representation learning [ 4 ] . A general-purpose medical visual tokenizer should instead provide a single token interface across modalities while natively supporting both 2D images and 3D volumes.

authors: Chenglong Ma, Yuanfeng Ji, Junzhi Ning, Jiyao Liu, Yujie Wei, Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Wenjie Li, Wenhao Tang, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Shujian Gao, Yujie Zhang, Ying Chen, Zilong Li, Zongyuan Ge, Diping Song, Jin Ye, Ming Hu, Junjun He, Hongming Shan
content: Building such a tokenizer poses two key challenges. (i) Preserving structural fidelity across dimensions. Unlike 2D images, 3D scans present volumetric continuity, where organs, vessels, lesions, and tissue boundaries extend across adjacent slices. Existing tokenizers often specialize in either 2D or 3D settings [ 5 , 6 ] , or are optimized for local appearance fidelity or per-pixel/per-voxel reconstruction [ 7 , 8 ] , failing to encode inter-slice structure. (ii) Capturing multimodal semantics across modalities. Different modalities may describe related clinical concepts while exposing distinct evidence, e.g. , histopathology reveals cellular and tissue-level morphology, whereas CT and MRI capture organ-level anatomy. Existing semantic alignment strategies typically learn representations of different imaging modalities from a single pretrained semantic encoder [ 9 , 10 , 6 , 11 ] , which may underrepresent modality-specific semantics outside that encoder’s representation space.

title: MedVTok: A General-Purpose Medical Visual Tokenizer

content: In this paper, we introduce MedVTok, a general-purpose medical visual tokenizer that maps heterogeneous 2D images and 3D volumes from diverse imaging modalities into a unified token space. To preserve structural fidelity across dimensions, MedVTok introduces Slice Differential Regularization (SliDR) in addition to per-pixel/per-voxel supervision, which explicitly models inter-slice volumetric continuity. To capture clinical semantics across modalities, MedVTok proposes Multi-Expert Representation Alignment (MERA), which builds a shared representation space integrating knowledge from multiple modality-specialized experts instead of a single one, while retaining complementary semantics in each expert’s representation space. Together, they enable MedVTok to produce visual tokens that preserve structural fidelity and encode multimodal clinical semantics.

content: Contributions. Our main contributions are as follows. (i) We introduce MedVTok, a general-purpose medical visual tokenizer that provides a shared token interface across diverse imaging modalities and natively supports both 2D images and 3D volumes. (ii) We propose a multi-level supervision strategy that combines slice differential regularization for inter-slice continuity with multi-expert representation alignment for cross-modality clinical semantics. (iii) We curate a large-scale medical imaging corpus and conduct comprehensive evaluations across 24 benchmarks, demonstrating the broad utility of MedVTok across classification, segmentation, retrieval, synthesis, visual question answering, and medical report generation.

content: Visual tokenizers convert images into compact tokens while preserving structural fidelity [ 12 , 7 ] . Recent tokenizers [ 13 , 9 ] further explore how a single tokenizer can handle heterogeneous visual formats such as images and videos. In medical imaging, however, tokenizers are commonly tied to specific input dimensionalities [ 5 , 6 ] . A few works have explored adaptation to different dimensionalities by pooling 3D weights into 2D [ 8 ] or by duplicating 2D images to fit a 3D model [ 14 ] . While these approaches can handle 2D and 3D inputs simultaneously, they do not consider the respective properties of each dimensionality, e.g. , through-plane anatomical continuity in volumes, and thus cannot fully preserve structural fidelity across input forms. In contrast, MedVTok introduces Slice Differential Regularization to explicitly preserve anatomical continuity in volumetric data, and provides a unified 2D–3D token interface via dimension-agnostic patchification.

section: Semantic representation across medical imaging modalities.
content: Medical image representation learning has produced both broad biomedical encoders and modality-specialized expert models. General medical encoders [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] learn transferable representations from large-scale biomedical data, offering broad coverage across medical domains but potentially missing specialty-specific cues. Meanwhile, specialized encoders capture finer clinical semantics within individual imaging modalities or specialties [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 14 , 25 , 26 ] , yet remain isolated in different representation spaces. Existing tokenizers [ 5 , 6 ] have only partially captured these different semantics, e.g. , MedITok [ 6 ] aligns its representations with those of a single semantic encoder [ 15 ] , thereby inheriting the single-expert bias and limiting the learning of complementary knowledge across modalities. MedVTok instead uses Multi-Expert Representation Alignment to integrate knowledge from multiple medical experts into a single token space, while retaining modality-specific semantics.

content: Apart from structural fidelity, a unified medical visual tokenizer should also encode high-level clinical semantics. Achieving this across the full breadth of medical imaging is challenging as different modalities embed distinct knowledge. Aligning to a single expert [ 15 , 6 ] constrains the tokenizer to inherit a single semantic geometry, which may underrepresent modalities outside the expert’s training distribution. We therefore propose Multi-Expert Representation Alignment (MERA), which uses a panel of pretrained modality-specific encoders as semantic experts . MERA involves two objectives: (i) shared-space contrastive alignment, which jointly aligns representations from multiple modality experts into a shared space, and (ii) expert-space complementary alignment, which preserves complementary information in each modality expert’s representation space.

content: We assess token fidelity by how well the tokenizer reconstructs input data from its encoded tokens, reporting PSNR and SSIM between the input and the reconstructed data. Table 1 reports 2D reconstruction quality. MedVTok ranks first on all nine modalities in both PSNR and SSIM. The improvement is most notable in challenging domains such as pathology, where other tokenizers suffer from limited training diversity. Medical-domain tokenizers (MedITok, MedVAE) and general-domain ones (TokenFlow, UniTok, MingTok) lag significantly behind, confirming that medical images benefit from specialized architectures and large-scale multimodal training. Fig. 3 visualizes the reconstruction error maps of the competing methods and the reconstructed images produced by MedVTok. The last two columns of Table 1 report native 3D reconstruction. MedVTok achieves the best PSNR and SSIM on both MRI and CT volumes by a large margin over PUMIT and MedVAE. The strong 3D performance suggests that our unified 2D–3D training paradigm effectively transfers learned representations to volumetric data. Please see § C.2 for qualitative comparisons.

content: To directly measure the representation quality for image classification, we adopt a k k -nearest neighbor protocol. Each test sample is classified based on its k k nearest training neighbors with k ∈ { 10 , 20 , 100 , 200 } k\in\{10,20,100,200\} , and we report the highest accuracy among k k values for each tokenizer. For retrieval, the training split serves as the gallery, and the test split provides the queries. Gallery images are ranked by cosine similarity, and we report Recall@1 performance.

content: We follow Siméoni et al. [ 55 ] and adopt a linear segmentation protocol to evaluate the representation quality for image segmentation. Specifically, a single linear segmentation head is trained with a cross-entropy loss on top of the frozen patch tokens produced by each tokenizer, with learning rates searched over { 10 − 2 , 10 − 3 , 10 − 4 } \{10^{-2},10^{-3},10^{-4}\} . For each tokenizer, the best-performing head on the validation set is selected for evaluation. Results are presented in Table 3 . MedVTok achieves the best average Dice score, outperforming all baselines including semantic encoders. This task reveals a clear hierarchy: although general autoencoding tokenizers ( e.g. , SDVAE, PUMIT) can embed rich low-level details into the latent space, their high-level semantics are not activated, resulting in low segmentation performance. Semantic encoders provide explicit visual semantics and significantly outperform the autoencoding tokenizers. Unified tokenizers (MedITok, MedVTok) encode both fine-grained spatial information and high-level semantics, enjoying the benefits of both and improving dense prediction. Please see § C.2 for qualitative comparisons.

content: We evaluate how the tokenizer influences text-conditioned medical image synthesis within a latent diffusion [ 29 ] framework. A UNet denoising backbone is trained from scratch in each tokenizer’s latent space while keeping both the tokenizer and the text encoder frozen. This design isolates the effect of the tokenizer: the architecture, noise scheduler, optimizer, and training data are held constant across experiments. Training uses 70K image–text pairs spanning seven imaging modalities. We report the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [ 56 , 57 ] in Table 4 ; lower FID indicates higher fidelity. MedVTok achieves the highest image synthesis quality with the best average FID, outperforming both specialized tokenizers (PUMIT, MedVAE) and the previous unified tokenizer (MedITok), as shown in Fig. 4 . PUMIT and MedVAE consistently underperform, confirming that synthesis quality depends not only on reconstruction fidelity but also on a well-structured, semantically meaningful latent space that facilitates the diffusion model’s learning.

content: We evaluate each tokenizer as a frozen visual backbone within the LLaVA-Med [ 58 ] framework, training only the LLaVA-Med connector and the LLM, and evaluating the resulting models on VQA benchmarks [ 6 ] . We report accuracy assessed via LLM-as-judge grading. As shown in Table 5 , MedVTok achieves the best average accuracy among the competing tokenizers. Notably, MedVTok does not use image–text pairs for training, yet still outperforms MedITok, which relies on millions of textual captions for representation learning.
