title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are a family of machine learning models inspired by the organization of biological nervous systems. The architecture of an ANN, defined by the arrangement of its neurons and connections, plays a central role in determining its representational capacity, generalization performance, and computational efficiency [ 17 ] . Identifying effective architectures, however, remains a challenging optimization problem due to the enormous number of possible network topologies.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: To address this challenge, neural architecture search (NAS) methods have been developed to automate the design of ANN architectures [ 7 ] . Among these approaches, evolutionary algorithms (EAs) provide a particularly attractive framework because they naturally support the exploration of large, discrete, and non-differentiable search spaces. In neuroevolution, evolutionary principles such as mutation, recombination, and selection are applied directly to neural networks, enabling the optimization of network parameters, architectures, or both simultaneously [ 26 , 8 ] . Approaches such as NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies (NEAT) demonstrated that evolutionary search can successfully discover increasingly complex neural architectures while maintaining architectural diversity through mechanisms such as speciation [ 26 ] .

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Despite these successes, neuroevolution still faces important challenges. Small syntactic modifications to an encoded neural network may produce disproportionately large functional changes in the resulting architecture. As a consequence, mutation and recombination frequently disrupt useful organizational structures, limiting the efficiency of evolutionary search. This problem becomes increasingly severe as network complexity increases and represents a longstanding challenge for evolutionary representations of neural systems.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Biological evolution provides an intriguing source of inspiration for addressing this limitation. In living organisms, complex networked phenotypes emerge from genetic information that has remained evolvable over hundreds of millions of years of evolution. However, directly emulating the genetic encoding of biological nervous systems is difficult because the mapping between DNA sequence and mature neural circuitry involves multiple intermediate processes, including gene regulation, development, cellular differentiation, and environmental interactions.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: An alternative perspective is to focus on biological networks whose organization is more directly related to their genetic encoding. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks represent one such example. Proteins are the primary functional products of genes, and their interactions depend largely on sequence-derived structural features. Consequently, the relationship between genotype and network organization is substantially more direct than for large-scale nervous systems.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Moreover, PPI networks frequently exhibit modular and hierarchical organization, properties that have long been proposed to contribute to robustness, functional specialization, and evolvability in biological systems [ 12 , 2 , 31 ] . Experimental and computational studies have shown that cellular functions are often organized into semi-independent modules whose components interact more strongly within modules than between them, facilitating the reuse and adaptation of functional units across different biological contexts [ 12 , 24 ] .

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Importantly, large collections of experimentally characterized PPI networks are now available across diverse organisms. Advances in high-throughput experimental techniques, together with extensive curation efforts, have led to the reconstruction of protein interaction maps containing thousands of proteins and interactions in organisms ranging from yeast to humans [ 28 , 22 , 20 ] . These resources can be viewed as biological interaction architectures that have persisted under evolutionary pressures and therefore represent a rich source of naturally occurring connectivity patterns. While it remains unclear which specific properties contribute to their evolutionary persistence, the reuse of such structures may provide useful architectural priors for evolutionary search. Rather than initializing neuroevolution from random topologies, biologically derived interaction motifs may bias the search process toward more coherent regions of the architectural landscape and reduce the disruptive effects of mutation and recombination.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: In this study, we propose TRON, a neuroevolution framework that incorporates experimentally characterized PPI networks as architectural substrates for artificial neural network evolution. Rather than searching exclusively from randomly generated topologies, TRON reuses biologically derived interaction patterns as candidate building blocks for ANN architectures. We hypothesize that these structures may provide a more evolvable substrate for neuroevolution by promoting the preservation of functional organization during mutation and recombination. To evaluate this hypothesis, we compare TRON against established evolutionary and neuroevolutionary approaches across a collection of classification and regression benchmarks and assess its impact on both predictive performance and evolutionary robustness.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Gradient-based optimisation is highly effective for training the weights of a fixed network, but it is poorly suited to searching over architectures themselves, leaving design decisions such as depth, width and connectivity to be chosen manually. Differentiable NAS methods such as DARTS [ 19 ] avoid this by relaxing the architecture choice into a continuous mixture of candidate operations. This makes the search efficient, but it confines it to predefined cell-based search spaces and makes it prone to collapse towards degenerate architectures [ 33 ] . However, the resulting topologies are stacks of repeated, hand-designed cells. They carry no information about which structures stay functional when modified, a property that biological networks have acquired under long-term evolutionary pressure. Where biological networks have entered deep learning, they appear either as input data, as in graph convolutional networks [ 15 ] , whose architectures remain hand-designed and suffer from over-smoothing [ 18 ] , or as fixed wiring, as in knowledge-primed models such as P-NET [ 6 ] and KPNNs [ 9 ] , whose topologies are imposed rather than searched. Neither treats biological interaction patterns as reusable, evolvable building blocks.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Population-based metaheuristics offer a natural alternative. They require no gradients, and because they maintain a population of candidates rather than a single solution, they can explore several regions of the search space in parallel. Among these optimisers, Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) [ 14 ] is one of the earliest and most widely adopted. PSO is a swarm-intelligence metaheuristic algorithm inspired by collective cooperative behavior in social organisms, such as birds, fish and insects. In PSO, a swarm of particles is initialized as a set of candidate solutions to an objective function. At every iteration, each particle’s current position is updated according to its previous best position, as well as the global best position found by the swarm. Due to its relatively simple implementation and gradient-free nature, PSO has been applied to a number of optimization problems ranging from image processing to electrical power systems optimization. However, it is known to be susceptible to premature convergence due to insufficient population diversity, particularly when solving highly complex and multi-modal optimization problems, as well as suboptimal particle velocity tuning which can lead to stagnation around an optimal solution. Fundamentally, PSO steers its search by a few elite positions instead of using the information held in the population as a whole.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Differential Evolution (DE) [ 29 ] removes this dependence on elite attractors by deriving search directions from the population itself. DE begins by randomly initializing a set of candidate solutions represented as real-valued vectors. At each iteration, new candidate solutions, referred to as trial vectors, are generated through mutation strategies that typically involve the weighted difference of randomly selected population members. The resulting donor vectors undergo recombination with existing solutions, creating trial vectors that are evaluated according to the corresponding objective function. Solutions are then selected based on their fitness, guiding the population toward the global optimum. Despite its robustness and applicability to high-dimensional optimization problems, DE remains sensitive to noisy objective functions as well as parameter tuning, particularly regarding the mutation factor, crossover rate and population size, leading to issues such as premature convergence or inefficient search space exploration.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: The Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) [ 11 ] addresses this limitation by explicitly handling the dependencies between variables, which makes it one of the most robust metaheuristics for handling ill-conditioned and multimodal problems. CMA-ES optimizes a given objective function by iteratively adapting a multivariate normal mutation distribution. Initially, the mutation is modelled as a normal distribution with zero mean, characterized by a covariance matrix. At each iteration, candidate solutions are sampled from the current distribution and are evaluated according to the objective function. The mean, step size and covariance matrix of the distribution are subsequently updated according to the solutions with the highest fitness. This strategy allows the algorithm to progressively adapt its search distribution to the local geometry of the optimization landscape. Despite its strong local adaptation capabilities, CMA-ES remains vulnerable to converging to local optima on multimodal landscapes, a weakness that has been reduced by restart schemes with increasing population size, such as IPOP-CMA-ES [ 1 ] . Even so, CMA-ES shares a limitation with PSO and DE: all three operate on a fixed-length real-valued vector. They can optimise the weights or hyperparameters of a given network, but the topology must still be manually optimized.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Architecture search requires an encoding whose size can change during evolution. NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies (NEAT) [ 26 ] introduced dynamic direct genetic encodings that allow the optimization of both neural network parameters and topology. Built on principles of complexifying evolution, NEAT initializes a population of relatively simple artificial neural networks (ANNs) and progressively increases their structural complexity through mutation and crossover. Each network is encoded as a flexible genome comprising node and connection genes, enabling the emergence of new graph components while maintaining direct genotype-phenotype mapping. Historical markings are assigned to structural mutations, providing a consistent record of their evolutionary origin and allowing corresponding genes to be aligned during crossover. This framework enables architecture search and weight optimization within a dynamically expanding search space, allowing increasingly complex topologies to evolve in response to fitness-driven selection.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Because NEAT involves direct mapping of a network’s elements to a genetic encoding, it is impractical for scaling to complex problems and modern deep architectures, such as convolutional neural networks. Indirect encodings address this limitation by evolving a compact rule that generates the network rather than the network itself. HyperNEAT [ 25 ] uses NEAT to evolve a Compositional Pattern-Producing Network (CPPN) [ 27 ] , which computes each connection weight from the spatial coordinates of the two neurons it joins. Because a single function generates the entire connectivity, structural motifs are reused across the network allowing large architectures to emerge from small genomes. This reuse, however, comes with a bias towards regularity, and HyperNEAT’s advantage diminishes on problems that require irregular connectivity [ 4 ] .

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Existing NAS methods either optimize within predefined architectural search spaces, evolve network structures without explicitly incorporating biologically derived organizational patterns, or integrate biological knowledge as fixed architectural constraints. To address these limitations, we propose TRON, a neuroevolutionary framework that incorporates experimentally characterized PPI networks as architectural building blocks for artificial neural networks. TRON leverages biologically derived structural priors during ANN initialization, introducing connectivity patterns shaped by millions of years of biological evolution into the evolutionary search process. These architectures are subsequently optimized through mutation and fitness-based selection, allowing their connectivity to evolve in response to task-specific objectives. By combining the architectural flexibility of neuroevolution with the modular and hierarchical organization observed in biological networks, TRON investigates whether evolutionarily shaped connectivity patterns can provide a more robust substrate for neural architecture optimization. We evaluate this hypothesis by comparing TRON with established optimization and neuroevolutionary approaches across classification and regression benchmarks, assessing both predictive performance and evolutionary robustness.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: The primary objective of this study is not to optimize performance for a specific application domain, but rather to evaluate whether biologically derived architectural priors improve the effectiveness and robustness of neuroevolutionary search. Consequently, the experimental evaluation was designed to assess the generality of the proposed framework across multiple machine learning problems with different statistical properties. To this end, TRON was evaluated on a collection of widely used benchmark datasets comprising both classification and regression tasks.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Because TRON is intended to improve the evolutionary search process itself, rather than exploit task-specific biological information, benchmarks were intentionally selected from unrelated domains. This design minimizes the possibility that any performance improvements arise from a direct correspondence between the source biological pathways and the target prediction task. Furthermore, the selected tasks were intentionally unrelated to the biological origin of the PPI networks. Consequently, any observed improvements are more likely to reflect general properties of the evolutionary search process rather than domain-specific biological knowledge.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: For classification, we selected the CORA, CITESEER, and PUBMED datasets. These citation-network benchmarks have been extensively used for the evaluation of machine learning, graph mining, and graph neural network methods, making them among the most widely adopted benchmark datasets for node classification tasks [ 23 , 32 , 15 ] . CORA contains scientific publications categorized into seven research topics, CITESEER comprises six classes and exhibits greater sparsity and class overlap, whereas PUBMED represents a larger biomedical citation network consisting of three classes. Together, these datasets provide classification problems of increasing scale and complexity and enable the evaluation of evolved neural architectures under different topological and statistical conditions.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: For regression, we selected the DIABETES, FRIEDMAN, and CALIFORNIA datasets. These benchmarks are commonly employed for evaluating regression algorithms due to their diversity in sample size, dimensionality, noise characteristics, and underlying functional relationships [ 5 , 10 , 21 ] . The DIABETES dataset represents a real-world biomedical prediction problem involving physiological measurements, whereas the FRIEDMAN dataset is a synthetic benchmark specifically designed to assess the ability of machine learning models to capture nonlinear interactions in the presence of irrelevant variables. The CALIFORNIA housing dataset constitutes a larger real-world regression problem characterized by heterogeneous demographic and geographic predictors. Collectively, these benchmarks enable the assessment of evolved architectures across a broad range of continuous prediction scenarios.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: The selected benchmarks collectively provide a broad evaluation framework spanning graph-base node classification, tabular classification, synthetic nonlinear regression, and real-world regression problems. This diversity is particularly important in the context of neuroevolution because the central hypothesis being tested concerns the evolvability of the architectural substrate itself rather than task-specific inductive biases. If protein-derived network topologies indeed provide a more favorable substrate for evolutionary optimization, performance improvements should emerge across multiple problem domains rather than being restricted to a single dataset type.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao

content: Since its introduction, NEAT has become one of the most influential neuroevolutionary frameworks by demonstrating that network topology and connection weights can be evolved simultaneously while preserving innovation through speciation [ 26 ] . The central insight of NEAT is that architectural innovation must be protected from direct competition with already established solutions. TRON adopts this principle but extends it in two important directions. First, the search process begins from biologically derived topologies rather than minimal or randomly generated architectures. Second, the introduction of species quarantine provides an additional mechanism through which newly generated topological innovations can undergo a period of maturation before entering the broader competitive population.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: From this perspective, TRON differs conceptually from most existing neuroevolution approaches. Traditional methods primarily seek improved exploration through modifications of evolutionary operators, fitness functions, diversity maintenance procedures, or encoding schemes. By contrast, TRON focuses on the nature of the structures being evolved. Rather than asking how evolution can more effectively search arbitrary architectural spaces, TRON asks whether the space itself can be made more evolvable by seeding it with organizational motifs that have already been optimized through natural evolution. This distinction is closely related to the concept of evolvability, defined as the capacity of a system to generate heritable phenotypic variation that can subsequently be refined through selection [ 16 ] . In biological systems, evolvability is frequently associated with properties such as modularity, robustness, reuse of functional components, and hierarchical organization. Protein interaction networks exhibit many of these characteristics, having emerged through extensive evolutionary refinement. Consequently, rather than constructing candidate neural architectures from random topologies, TRON begins from connectivity motifs that have already persisted throughout biological evolution.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution

content: To determine whether these biologically derived architectural priors provide an advantage during evolutionary search, we evaluated TRON on a diverse collection of classification and regression benchmarks and compared its performance against several established evolutionary and neuroevolutionary approaches. Because the selected tasks are unrelated to the biological origin of the protein networks, any observed improvements are more likely to reflect general properties of the evolutionary search process rather than domain-specific biological knowledge.

content: Classification experiments were conducted using the CORA, CITESEER, and PUBMED datasets. Across all three benchmarks, TRON consistently achieved the highest predictive performance among the evaluated evolutionary approaches (Tables 4 , 5 , and 6 ). The improvement was particularly pronounced for CORA and PUBMED, where TRON outperformed both classical evolutionary optimizers, including PSO, DE, and CMA-ES, and dedicated neuroevolutionary approaches such as NEAT. Similar advantages were observed for CITESEER despite the greater difficulty associated with the dataset.

authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: These results suggest that biologically derived connectivity patterns can substantially improve the efficiency with which evolution explores the neural architecture search space. Rather than constructing architectures entirely through random variation, TRON begins from topological organizations that already exhibit coherent interaction patterns.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Although the specific mechanisms responsible for these improvements remain to be fully characterized, the results are consistent with the hypothesis that naturally evolved network organizations represent a more favorable substrate for evolutionary optimization than randomly generated topologies.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: An additional and particularly noteworthy observation concerns the consistency of the evolutionary process. Across all classification datasets, TRON exhibited substantially lower variability across independent runs than competing approaches. Standard deviations were often several-fold lower than those observed for alternative methods, indicating that evolutionary trajectories converged toward high-performing solutions more reliably and reproducibly. This reduction in variability may be as important as the observed gains in average predictive performance. Many optimization algorithms can occasionally discover highly effective solutions through favorable stochastic trajectories. In contrast, consistently converging toward high-quality solutions across independent runs is substantially more difficult.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: The results therefore suggest that the biological architectural priors employed by TRON constrain the search process toward more coherent regions of the architectural landscape, reducing sensitivity to random initialization and stochastic evolutionary events. More broadly, these observations support the idea that protein interaction networks may contribute not only useful initial topologies but also organizational properties that influence how effectively evolutionary operators act upon those topologies. Randomly generated architectures may be particularly vulnerable to the disruptive effects of mutation and recombination. In contrast, naturally evolved interaction networks may contain forms of modularity, robustness, or redundancy that allow beneficial structural features to persist across generations. This interpretation is consistent with previous work linking modularity and robustness to improved evolutionary adaptation. Modular systems tend to localize the effects of perturbations, thereby allowing innovations to accumulate without disrupting existing functionality [ 30 ] . Studies in evolutionary computation have similarly suggested that preserving functional building blocks can facilitate long-term adaptation by reducing the destructive effects of genetic variation. The protein interaction networks used in TRON may naturally provide such building blocks, allowing evolution to exploit organizational principles that have already demonstrated their effectiveness in living systems.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: On the DIABETES dataset, TRON achieved a substantial improvement over all competing methods (Table 7 ), exceeding the strongest baseline by approximately 36%. This result demonstrates that the advantages associated with biologically derived architectural priors are not restricted to discrete classification tasks and can generalize effectively to continuous prediction problems. As observed for the classification benchmarks, the performance gain was accompanied by remarkably low variability across runs, reinforcing the view that TRON promotes stable evolutionary optimization.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: The framework also achieved the highest predictive performance on the synthetic FRIEDMAN benchmark (Table 8 ). Because FRIEDMAN was specifically designed to evaluate the ability of machine learning models to capture nonlinear interactions in complex search spaces, this result suggests that the benefits of protein-derived architectures are not limited to biological datasets. Instead, it indicates that the organizational principles embedded in naturally evolved interaction networks may provide generally useful inductive biases for evolutionary architecture search.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: The CALIFORNIA housing benchmark produced a more nuanced outcome (Table 9 ). Although TRON remained among the highest-performing approaches, its advantage over the strongest competitors was considerably smaller than that observed on the previous datasets. This observation provides an important counterbalance to the otherwise consistent performance gains observed throughout the study. Rather than suggesting a fundamental limitation of the framework, it indicates that the utility of biological architectural priors is likely context dependent. Certain predictive problems may align more naturally with the organizational principles embodied within protein interaction networks, whereas others may derive more modest benefits from such structures.

content: Taken together, the regression experiments reveal a pattern similar to that observed for classification. Across datasets with distinct statistical characteristics, sample sizes, and underlying functional relationships, TRON either matched or exceeded the performance of all evaluated evolutionary competitors while maintaining superior robustness and reproducibility.

authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: A central hypothesis motivating this work is that protein interaction networks may represent architectural building blocks that are inherently more evolvable than randomly generated topologies. The results obtained across both classification and regression tasks are broadly consistent with this hypothesis.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Traditional neuroevolution methods primarily focus on improving the evolutionary process itself through modifications of mutation operators, crossover mechanisms, selection strategies, or diversity-preservation techniques. In contrast, TRON focuses on the substrate upon which these mechanisms operate. Rather than asking how evolution can more effectively search arbitrary architectural spaces, TRON asks whether the architectural space itself can be enriched with structures that have already undergone extensive evolutionary refinement. From this perspective, the superior performance and reduced variability exhibited by TRON may arise because protein interaction networks encode organizational properties that promote robustness to evolutionary perturbation. If useful functional structures are more likely to survive mutation and recombination, evolutionary adaptation can proceed more efficiently because beneficial modifications accumulate rather than being repeatedly disrupted. The markedly lower variance across independent runs is particularly consistent with this interpretation. It is important to note, however, that the present results do not fully disentangle the individual contributions of biological priors, speciation, and quarantine. Consequently, the observed improvements should not be attributed exclusively to any single component of the framework.

content: The improvements in predictive performance and evolutionary stability were associated with increased computational requirements. As shown in Figures 3 and 4 , TRON generally requires greater memory consumption than most of the competing approaches. This increase is expected because biologically derived interaction networks have larger memory requirements in general since they retain information about the proteins that have been assigned to the respective neurons. Furthermore, the quarantine mechanism introduces additional evaluations that increase the computational burden of the evolutionary process. On the other hand, regarding time complexity, TRON is amongst the top performers, especially when tested on large datasets like Pubmed and California. At the same time, TRON requires significantly fewer runs to verify its results, courtesy of its high SNR. From an engineering perspective, this trade-off reflects a deliberate design choice. The primary goal of TRON is to improve evolvability and search robustness rather than minimize computational cost. Consequently, the framework sacrifices some degree of efficiency in exchange for a richer architectural substrate and a more stable evolutionary search process.

content: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the present study focused exclusively on protein interaction networks and did not evaluate alternative biological network classes such as gene regulatory networks, signaling pathways, metabolic networks, or developmental programs. Second, the current experiments do not fully disentangle the contributions of biological priors, speciation, and quarantine. Third, although the results are consistent with the hypothesis that biological architectures improve evolvability, the specific structural properties responsible for this effect remain unknown.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Despite these limitations, the findings provide encouraging evidence that naturally evolved biological networks can serve as useful architectural priors for neuroevolution. In particular, the observed improvements in robustness and reproducibility suggest that biological organization may offer advantages extending beyond predictive performance alone.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Finally, the current implementation of TRON relies exclusively on experimentally characterized protein interaction networks. Recent advances in protein structure and interaction prediction, particularly through AlphaFold and related approaches, suggest the possibility of moving beyond known interaction maps toward predicted interaction landscapes derived directly from sequence information. Future generations of TRON may therefore exploit not only experimentally validated protein networks but also vast numbers of biologically plausible interactions inferred computationally. Under this perspective, genomes themselves become repositories of potential computational architectures, enabling neuroevolution to explore a substantially larger design space derived from the products of natural evolution.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: More broadly, these findings support the possibility that real biological networks may serve as reusable computational substrates for artificial intelligence and provide a foundation for progressively transferring increasingly complex forms of biological organization into artificial systems.

title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: The present implementation of TRON relies on experimentally derived protein interaction networks to define the architectural substrate upon which neuroevolution operates. While this strategy already enables the direct reuse of connectivity patterns shaped through natural selection, it likely represents only a small fraction of the architectural information accessible from biological systems.

authors: Konstantinos Zacharopoulos, Alexandra Bekou, Jose M Serradell, Foteini Paraskevopoulou, Apostolos Fournaris, Ioannis Arapakis, Oscar Lao
content: Recent advances in protein structure prediction have dramatically expanded our ability to infer molecular interactions directly from sequence information. In particular, AlphaFold and its multimer extensions have demonstrated the ability not only to predict protein structures with near-experimental accuracy, but also to identify and model protein–protein interactions from sequence alone [ 13 , 3 ] . Rather than restricting TRON to currently known protein interaction networks, future implementations may therefore generate architectural priors from predicted interaction landscapes derived directly from genomic sequences.

Instead of reusing only experimentally characterized pathways, artificial neural architectures could be generated from millions of potential molecular interactions spanning diverse organisms, evolutionary lineages, and even synthetic sequences. In this scenario, evolution would no longer be limited to selecting among known biological networks, but could instead explore a vastly richer space of biologically plausible organizational motifs inferred computationally.

Under this perspective, genomes become encodings of network organization from which artificial systems can derive architectural priors without requiring prior biological annotation. As protein structure and interaction prediction continue to improve, the boundary between biological sequence information and computational architecture design may progressively diminish, opening new opportunities for transferring the products of natural evolution into artificial intelligence systems.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
section: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
content: LLMs now prove hard theorems in Lean. Can they also design algorithms and prove their correctness and efficiency? LLM-guided design of optimisation heuristics (such as AlphaEvolve) is purely empirical. Automated theorem provers with LLMs prove given statements. So far, there has been little evidence that LLMs can do both: design an algorithm and guarantee its efficiency by a mathematical proof. We present a staged pipeline modelled after research methodology in design and analysis of evolutionary algorithms. The agent proposes black-box optimisation algorithms, and Lean guards filter out flawed designs. The agent then defines a potential function and proves drift bounds that guarantee an expected runtime improvement over the baseline algorithm. At no point in the pipeline are the algorithms compared empirically. The agent generates a black-box optimisation algorithm with expected runtime O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) on a CycleUncover problem, where the classical (1+1) EA needs runtime e Ω ⁡ ( n ) e^{\Omega(n)} . The pipeline also designs and analyses a black-box optimisation algorithm for integer-valued submodular minimisation with expected runtime O ⁡ ( n 2 + 2 ​ c ) O(n^{2+2c}) , and it matches the optimal order O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) on LeadingOnes . Across 8 problem classes, 12 of 15 runs with frontier models complete the pipeline with a machine-checked expected-runtime bound. In 9 of them the bound is polynomial without relying on offline computation, which the black-box model does not charge. An ablation study shows that removing the staging and asking the agent to zero-shot an algorithmic design with a runtime guarantee leads to a copy of the seeded baseline algorithm (random search) or to incomplete proofs. Open-weight models (Goedel-Prover-V2-32B and Gemma 4) did not complete the pipeline. Our study suggests that machine-checked specifications in Lean can replace empirical evaluation in open-ended algorithm discovery. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of an automated pipeline that designs efficient black-box optimisation algorithms with machine-checked runtime bounds in Lean.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: From the perspective of theoretical computer science, algorithm design must produce two artefacts: First, the algorithm itself, a finite sequence of instructions that when executed in a computational model transforms within a finite number of steps any problem instance (the input) into an output (the solution) ( Knuth, 1997 ) . Secondly, the analysis of the algorithm, a mathematical proof that the algorithm produces the correct output on every problem instance, and a guarantee for the amount of computational resources required by the algorithm to produce that output (its complexity). In the context of machine learning, analysis also involves guaranteeing additional algorithmic properties, such as convergence rates, and regret and/or generalisation bounds. Inventing new and better algorithms involves an iterative developmental process between the two artefacts: a new candidate design drives the analysis in a certain direction, and obstacles in completion of the analysis can lead to insights into problem structure which motivate alterations to the algorithm design. The high cost and deep expertise needed for traditional algorithmic design have motivated research into automated design of heuristics. Recent LLM-based heuristic design approaches evaluate a candidate pool of heuristics on benchmark functions, and well-performing heuristics are varied through LLM-prompts to produce better ones. While this has been successful in many domains, the methodology is highly empirical and does not lead to any guarantees on the correctness or performance of the heuristics produced.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: It is a significant open problem whether AI agents can carry out algorithmic design as seen from theoretical computer science. It has been argued that automated theorem proving (ATP) is challenging for AI, because proofs are either correct or incorrect, not in-between. Furthermore, the space of proofs is infinitely large ( Buzzard, 2024 ) . Formal algorithmic design goes beyond ATP, because it requires both navigating a space of algorithmic designs and automatically proving properties about these. Yet, the improvement in mathematical capability of frontier AI models over the last years has been remarkable. Long-standing conjectures have been closed using publicly available reasoning models with Lean-checked proof certificates ( Sothanaphan, 2026 ) . The time and cost needed to rigorously prove non-trivial mathematical statements have fallen significantly.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: We take inspiration from the field of runtime analysis of evolutionary algorithms which has a well-defined approach to design and analysis. The field requires that algorithms fit in a black-box optimisation framework ( Droste et al., 2006 ) (more often called the query model in TCS) where optimisation is formulated as an interaction between an oracle which knows the function to be optimised, and an algorithm which queries the oracle for fitness values. The field has developed a small number of highly generic mathematical tools that aid in the analysis. In particular, we build on drift analysis ( Hajek, 1982 ; He & Yao, 2001 ) which measures the progress of the algorithm with a potential function. The potential function, which is introduced for the purpose of the analysis and is not part of the algorithm itself, maps the state of the algorithm into a potential value. Bounds on the runtime can be obtained from properties of the distribution of the drift (change in potential per oracle query). The black-box model allows for an enormous variety of algorithms, most of which are useless. To constrain algorithm search, we use Lean guards to filter out provably flawed designs. We only allow algorithms that are able to visit all parts of the search space, that use randomness, and that take into account fitness responses from the oracle. The full staged pipeline is shown in Figure 2 . The pipeline is seeded with a problem card that provides the definition of the problem, its problem instances, and basic properties. Additionally, the pipeline is seeded with an initial algorithmic design with a stated runtime bound. In all the experiments described here, we use uniform random search as the initial algorithm, with expected runtime O ⁡ ( 2 n ) O(2^{n}) . The staged pipeline consists of some informal stages where an informal model produces one or more prose descriptions of designs. There are also formal stages where the agent needs to synthesise a definition or a proof that is then verified by Lean. In case Lean reports a failure, the formal stage is repeated, until it backtracks (determined by a Luby sequence ( Luby et al., 1993 ) ), or the formal stage passes. Some formal stages are gates to filter out flawed designs, others collect definitions that are used later, e.g., the definition of the algorithm or the potential. If a run reaches the end of the pipeline, it obtains an algorithm A i + 1 A^{i+1} with a guaranteed improved runtime compared to algorithm A i A^{i} . The pipeline can be looped, e.g., producing an algorithm A i + 2 A^{i+2} which beats A i + 1 A^{i+1} , and so on. In most of the experiments described here, we make one iteration of the loop; two runs iterate it for three and five generations.

content: Research on automating the design and analysis of algorithms can be classified according to the level of automation in the design and the level of automation and rigour in the analysis (see Table 1 ). Firstly , there are efforts to formalise existing (informal) mathematical analyses of algorithms manually in proof assistants such as Lean, Coq or Isabelle/HOL. These contributions have the same strong benefits as formalising any other type of informal mathematics in Lean, including enabling machine-checked proofs, curation of a digital library of mathematical results, and providing a foundation for machine-generated mathematics ( Buzzard, 2024 ) . Recent efforts in this direction include Li et al. (2024) who focused on first-order convex optimisation methods, with Lean proofs of convergence rates for some function classes. They considered deterministic algorithms, and the proofs therefore avoid technical challenges arising from stochasticity. In contrast, there are also Isabelle/HOL formalisations of complexity analysis of randomised tree data structures ( Eberl et al., 2020 ) . Kaminski et al. (2017) introduced a calculus for formally deriving the expected runtime of probabilistic programs, such as the coupon collector process. Recent formalisations in machine learning also consider stochastic effects ( Vajjha et al., 2021 ) . Schäffeler & Abdulaziz (2025) analysed convergence of value and policy iteration for finite-state Markov decision processes. Other work considers properties of neural networks, e.g., formalising a classic result about the expressive power of depth in neural networks ( Cohen et al., 2016 ; Bentkamp et al., 2019 ) . In contrast to our work, these works consider pre-existing algorithms and proofs, and proofs are human-designed. Secondly , the area of LLM-assisted automated theorem proving in Lean has gained significant momentum recently, with breakthrough results announced during Summer/Autumn 2026. There are recent examples of semi-automatic algorithm design and proof generation where humans with assistance from frontier models design new algorithms with Lean proofs. Thirdly , there is a large body of research where algorithm design is automated via LLMs, but where evaluation of candidate algorithms lacks machine-checked proofs and is entirely empirical ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Systems such as AlphaEvolve ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) , ShinkaEvolve ( Lange et al., 2025 ) , LLaMEA ( van Stein & Bäck, 2025 ) , and EoH ( Liu et al., 2024 ) formulate algorithm design as a search problem where candidate algorithms are evaluated empirically on a set of benchmark functions, and an LLM is used to generate algorithm variants. These systems do not provide any machine-checked guarantees. Related approaches in highly restricted problem domains where correctness can be checked without formal proofs include AlphaTensor, which optimises matrix multiplication algorithms via reinforcement learning ( Fawzi et al., 2022 ) .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Apart from automation of algorithmic design and analysis, there are other relevant works. An orthogonal task to algorithm design is problem formulation and modelling. Robbins et al. (2026) proposed FLARE to certify in Lean the correctness of mixed integer linear program (MILP) reformulations of combinatorial optimisation problems. Another related area is automated software verification. Here, the goal is to synthesise proofs (e.g., in Lean) that a piece of software satisfies a specification (pre-condition and post-condition) ( Li et al., 2026 ) . More ambitiously, vericoding studies AI systems that take formal specifications as inputs and produce software along with proofs that the software satisfies the specification ( Bursuc et al., 2025 ) .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: To formally define a design space of optimisation algorithms, we will adopt the so-called black-box scenario from theory of discrete evolutionary algorithms ( Droste et al., 2006 ) , also called query (or decision tree) complexity in theoretical computer science ( Buhrman & de Wolf, 2002 ) . This scenario describes a broad class of algorithms by defining the goal of the algorithm, what information is available to an algorithm, what actions the algorithm can take, and how its runtime is measured. The algorithm is given a class of real-valued fitness functions F F over a search space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . An adversary picks a function f ∈ F , f : 𝒳 → ℝ f\in F,f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} , and the goal of the algorithm is to find an optimal search point x ∗ x^{*} such that f ⁡ ( x ) ≤ f ⁡ ( x ∗ ) f(x)\leq f(x^{*}) for all x x (i.e., maximisation of f f ). In each iteration t t , the algorithm queries a search point x t x_{t} based on its previous history, and obtains from the oracle the function value f ⁡ ( x t ) f(x_{t}) . The search point x t x_{t} along with its fitness f ⁡ ( x t ) f(x_{t}) is added to the history, and the process repeats until an optimum is found. The running time of the algorithm is defined as the number of times the algorithm queries the oracle until the algorithm queries an optimal search point for the first time. This definition is based on the assumption that the evaluation of the fitness function is the most time-consuming part of the algorithm. Following the literature on runtime analysis of evolutionary algorithms, the algorithm does not specify a termination criterion. A termination criterion could be specified, but it would not impact the runtime of the algorithm as defined below. The entire interaction between the oracle and the optimisation algorithm is given in Algorithm 1 . Within the black-box scenario, the algorithm design is fully specified by a tuple A = ( 𝒴 , 𝚒𝚗𝚒𝚝 , 𝚚𝚞𝚎𝚛𝚢 , 𝚜𝚝𝚎𝚙 ) A=(\mathcal{Y},\mathtt{init},\mathtt{query},\mathtt{step}) , which will be described below. Executing an algorithm A A involves executing Algorithm 1 with the given tuple A A .

Yet, due to the free choice of 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} and 𝚒𝚗𝚒𝚝 \mathtt{init} , 𝚚𝚞𝚎𝚛𝚢 \mathtt{query} , 𝚜𝚝𝚎𝚙 \mathtt{step} , the framework is highly general and can express most commonly used black-box optimisation algorithms, such as simulated annealing, population-based evolutionary algorithms, and estimation of distribution algorithms.

content: Drift analysis ( Hajek, 1982 ; He & Yao, 2001 ) is the main technique used to derive bounds on the runtime T A T_{A} , and it is incorporated into our pipeline. Most evolutionary algorithms are Markov processes over their state space 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} : the state y t ∈ 𝒴 y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y} of the algorithm at iteration t t completely determines the distribution of the state y t + 1 y_{t+1} in the next iteration. In principle, Markov chain theory could be applied to estimate the hitting time of the process from its state transition matrix. However, the state spaces induced by the algorithms are often so large that this approach becomes impractical. Instead, one can introduce a potential function Φ : 𝒴 → ℝ \Phi:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} which given the current state of the algorithm measures how far the algorithm is from reaching its goal, i.e. Z t = Φ ⁡ ( y t ) Z_{t}=\Phi(y_{t}) . Note that the potential function is not part of the design of the algorithm, but is only used for the drift analysis. Designing a good potential function is often the most challenging part of the analysis of the algorithm. Given information about the distribution of the change in potential per time step, i.e., the drift Z t + 1 − Z t Z_{t+1}-Z_{t} of the process, drift theorems provide statements about the long term properties of the process. Informally, the additive drift theorem states that if the expected drift is at least ε \varepsilon , then the expected time to reach distance zero is Z 0 / ε Z_{0}/\varepsilon . The proof of the theorem (see Corus et al., 2018 ) uses standard arguments from martingale theory; the precise statement is Theorem B.1 in Appendix B . A Lean formalisation of the general additive drift theorem will be published in a separate manuscript. It is proved in the Lean library on which the pipeline builds, not assumed: for every run in which we printed the axioms (rows 2–5 and 15 of Table 2 ), the final runtime theorem depends only on Lean’s standard axioms propext , Classical.choice and Quot.sound .

content: We now describe the motivation and details of the staged pipeline shown in Figure 2 . The task of zero-shotting an algorithmic design along with its runtime analysis is challenging. We therefore break down this task into multiple stages according to how a human researcher in theory of evolutionary algorithms would solve the problem. Starting from an initial algorithmic design we want to improve, we make some informal design proposals. We describe the best algorithm formally in pseudo-code, then design a potential function which measures its progress, and finally apply a drift theorem. The most challenging aspects of this process are to design the algorithm and choose the potential function. The space of algorithmic designs allowed by our framework is vast. We therefore propose a staged pipeline where candidate designs are filtered through formal proof obligations via proof guards. The formal guards are designed to filter out flawed designs. The implementation, with its two backends (CLI and vLLM) and the Kimina Lean server, and the structure of the stage prompts are described in Appendix C .

authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: We now describe the stages in the pipeline informally. The pipeline has informal stages where the agent proposes in English an informal design (either of an algorithm or potential function), and formal stages that are either definitions or formal guards. Formal statements are stated fully in Table 3 in Appendix A .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Stages 0–8 produce an algorithmic design along with proofs about its properties. Stage 0 ( DesignLock ): We ask the agent to provide an informal algorithm design along with justification why it would complete the full pipeline. When using frontier models (rows 1–15 in Table 2 ), the agent is asked to sketch at least one alternative design before committing to one design in a single response. With the open-weight models (rows 19–21 in Table 2 ), the informal model generates eight proposals sequentially. Each proposal is prompted with all previous ones and asked to differ from them. A winning proposal is then selected through a knockout tournament. The proposals were compared in pairs by the informal model, and the winners advance until one design remains. Stages 9a and 10a use the same procedure in these runs. Stage 1 ( ConstructAlgorithmComponents ): We ask the agent to formalise in Lean the algorithm as a tuple A = ( 𝒴 , 𝚒𝚗𝚒𝚝 , 𝚜𝚝𝚎𝚙 , 𝚚𝚞𝚎𝚛𝚢 ) A=(\mathcal{Y},\mathtt{init},\mathtt{step},\mathtt{query}) . Stage 1c ( StepMeasurability ): We require that the step function is a measurable function. This condition will be required for the drift analysis later in the pipeline. Stage 2 ( Completeness1 ): We require that the algorithm must be able to query any search point in every iteration. More precisely, for every search point x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} , and for every reachable state y ∈ 𝒴 y\in\mathcal{Y} , there exists a random input z ∈ 𝒵 z\in\mathcal{Z} and fitness value f ∈ ℝ f\in\mathbb{R} , such that if the algorithm receives fitness f f for the query associated with state y y , it will transition on random input z z to a state where x x is queried. This condition is satisfied by almost all evolutionary algorithms, e.g., those that involve bit-wise mutation. Note that the completeness condition can be trivially satisfied for an arbitrary algorithm by querying a uniform search point with some non-zero (but perhaps very small probability) in every step. The completeness condition is not always necessary for an efficient algorithmic design. However, the condition makes it straightforward to prove that the algorithm eventually queries the optimal search point (i.e., the algorithm is correct), and that for finite search spaces, the algorithm has a finite expected hitting time which is required by our formulation of the drift theorem. The extra assumption that y y is a reachable state and not an arbitrary state was included to avoid imposing the condition on inconsistent states that the algorithm never visits. For example, the state of the UMDA algorithm is a probability vector p ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] n p\in[0,1]^{n} where p i , i ∈ [ n ] , p_{i},i\in[n], is the probability of sampling a 1-bit in position i i . The algorithm maintains the invariant p i ∈ [ 1 / n , 1 − 1 / n ] p_{i}\in[1/n,1-1/n] in order not to get stuck in a particular bit-position. Stage 3 ( NonAbsorbing ): We require that the algorithm uses the random input. More precisely, for every reachable state y ∈ 𝒴 , y\in\mathcal{Y}, and any oracle response f ∈ ℝ f\in\mathbb{R} , there exist two random inputs z 1 , z 2 ∈ 𝒵 z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathcal{Z} such that the algorithm in the next iteration makes different queries on random input z 1 z_{1} and z 2 z_{2} . This condition is not necessary to have an efficient algorithm. However, the condition filters out many poor algorithms, such as those that only return a constant value. Stage 4 ( NotRandomSearch ): We require that the algorithm can reach a state where the query distribution is different from the uniform distribution (random search). Random search has expected running time 2 Ω ⁡ ( n ) 2^{\Omega(n)} , and any efficient algorithm must have a different query distribution than random search. We observed that weaker models applied to the pipeline with random search seeded as algorithm 0 tended to produce designs that were essentially random search. In an early version of the pipeline, we did not include the reachable state assumption in the condition. We discovered that this would allow the model to cheat by devising a state space with unreachable witness states 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} which could serve as witnesses for the NotRandomSearch and other properties. Stage 5 ( Adaptiveness ): We require that the state update of the algorithm depends on the fitness responses from the oracle. Clearly, no algorithm which completely ignores the oracle can be an effective optimiser on even simple problem classes such as OneMax . Stage 6 ( QueryNonInjectivity ): We require that there exist two different states which lead to the same query, i.e., the function 𝚚𝚞𝚎𝚛𝚢 \mathtt{query} is not injective. This condition ensures that the state carries information beyond the current query, such as the best search point or fitness seen so far, or a learned parameter, and filters out designs whose state is just the current search point. The remaining algorithm construction stages (Stages 7–8) are designed to package all the definitions into a Lean structure. This will allow the later proof infrastructure to process the algorithmic design as one mathematical object. These stages also include measurability requirements, e.g., that all the components of the algorithm are measurable functions. The next main part is the drift analysis. We would like the agent to prove that the three conditions of Corollary 3.1 are satisfied, where X t X_{t} corresponds to the potential of the algorithm at iteration t t . The pipeline asks the agent to, for every state y y , define three subsets of random inputs Good ⁡ ( y ) , Worsen ⁡ ( y ) , BigWorsen ⁡ ( y ) \mathrm{Good}(y),\mathrm{Worsen}(y),\mathrm{BigWorsen}(y) corresponding to the three conditions respectively, drift parameters ε \varepsilon and p p , and a jump probability lower bound p jump p_{\text{jump}} .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Stages 9a–9f produce a potential function used to measure the progress of the algorithm. Stages 9a–9b ( PotentialDesign and DefinePotential ): In the informal Stage 9a, the agent produces several candidate potential functions together with the parameters above and an informal “drift story” explaining why the potential function applied to the algorithm has drift towards the optimum. For experiments with frontier models (Rows 1–15 in Table 2 ), the agent proposes three candidates one after another, each critiquing the earlier ones, and ends its response with a ranking. The top-ranked candidate is then formalised in Stage 9b. We require that the value of the potential is always in the interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Although not required for drift analysis, this requirement which is not difficult to satisfy through normalisation simplifies the formal drift analysis machinery later in the pipeline. Stage 9c ( PotentialOpt ): We require that the potential of a state y y is 0 if and only if the algorithm queries an optimal search point in state y y . This is a necessary condition for the drift theorem to give a meaningful statement about the runtime of the algorithm. Stage 9d ( PotentialFineGrained ): The seeded design uses a potential function with only the values 0 and 1, where 0 corresponds to optimal states and 1 all other states. This is sufficient to prove runtime bound for random search, however it will be insufficient to capture the gradual progress of an efficient algorithm. Experiments with weaker models often reproduced the two-valued potential function. We therefore added the formal guard that the potential function must contain a value between 0 and 1. Stage 9e ( PotentialMeasurability ): We require that the potential function is measurable. This property is needed for the later drift analysis. The remaining guards in this part of the pipeline involve proving measurability properties of the potential function, and packaging into a Lean structure for easy handling later (Stage 9f, ConstructPotentialStructure ).

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Stages 10a–10j prove drift conditions for the potential and obtain a final runtime bound by applying a drift theorem. Stage 10f ( PositiveDrift ): We require that for any reachable, non-optimal state y y , if the algorithm receives a random input z ∈ Good ⁡ ( y ) z\in\mathrm{Good}(y) , then the potential decreases by at least ε \varepsilon in the next iteration. Stage 10g ( NegativeDriftAndJump ): We require that for any non-optimal reachable state y y and any random input z ∈ 𝒵 z\in\mathcal{Z} , if the potential increases in the next iteration, then z z belongs to Worsen ⁡ ( y ) \mathrm{Worsen}(y) , and if it increases by more than ε \varepsilon , then z z belongs to BigWorsen ⁡ ( y ) \mathrm{BigWorsen}(y) . Furthermore, for any reachable state y y , if the algorithm receives input z ∈ Jump ⁡ ( y ) z\in\mathrm{Jump}(y) , then the potential in the next iteration is 0. In other words, the algorithm jumps directly to an optimal search point whenever it receives a random input in Jump ⁡ ( y ) \mathrm{Jump}(y) . Stage 10h ( DriftSetMass ): We require that, for every reachable, non-optimal state y y , the probabilities that the random input lies in Good ⁡ ( y ) \mathrm{Good}(y) , Worsen ⁡ ( y ) \mathrm{Worsen}(y) and BigWorsen ⁡ ( y ) \mathrm{BigWorsen}(y) satisfy conditions (1)–(3) of Corollary 3.1 ( Figure 1 ). Stage 10i ( JumpMass ): We require that from all states y y , p jump ≤ Pr ⁡ ( z ∈ Jump ⁡ ( y ) ) p_{\text{jump}}\leq\Pr\left(z\in\mathrm{Jump}(y)\right) . When satisfied, this condition implies that the runtime of the algorithm is stochastically dominated by a geometrically distributed random variable with success probability p jump p_{\text{jump}} . The expected runtime is therefore finite, which implies one of the conditions of the additive drift theorem. The only requirement on p jump p_{\text{jump}} is that it is positive. Stage 10j ( RuntimeBound ): The final stage is an application of a runtime bound 𝔼 ⁡ [ T A ] ≤ 4 / ( ε ​ p ) \mathds{E}\left[T_{A}\right]\leq 4/(\varepsilon p) that follows immediately from the previously collected proof certificates.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: Runtime analysis of new evolutionary algorithms is often initiated on simple theoretical benchmark functions which have a clear structure. Here, we consider the three most common functions, OneMax , LeadingOnes , and Jump k , which are defined in Appendix D .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: The OneMax value of a bitstring is the number of positions in which it differs from some hidden bitstring z z . Standard evolutionary algorithms have expected runtime O ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n\log n) , which can be seen via a multiplicative drift argument ( Doerr et al., 2012 ) : The probability that a random bit-flip in the current bitstring improves the fitness is proportional to the number of bits it has in common with z z . The optimal algorithm runs in Θ ⁡ ( n / log ⁡ n ) \Theta(n/\log n) queries by querying the fitness of Θ ⁡ ( n / log ⁡ n ) \Theta(n/\log n) uniformly sampled bitstrings from which the hidden bitstring z z , and the optimum, can be determined with high probability. One generation of the staged pipeline rediscovers a variant of the (1+1) EA with mutation rate 1 / ( n + 1 ) 1/(n+1) rather than the standard 1 / n 1/n . The true expected runtime of this algorithm is O ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n\log n) , however the agent obtains the weaker (but still mathematically correct) upper bound O ⁡ ( n 3 ) O(n^{3}) . As potential function, the agent uses essentially the normalised Hamming-distance to the optimum. The weak runtime bound is partly due to the pipeline which forces the agent to use Corollary 3.1 which does not allow for multiplicative drift.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: The LeadingOnes value of a bitstring is the number of consecutive bits it has in common with some hidden bitstring z z , when the bit positions are ordered by a hidden permutation σ \sigma . Typical evolutionary algorithms have runtime O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) which can be seen by an additive drift argument: a random bit-flip in a selected bitstring improves its fitness with probability Θ ⁡ ( 1 / n ) \Theta(1/n) , and Θ ⁡ ( n ) \Theta(n) improvements are needed to reach the optimum. One generation of the staged pipeline discovers a variant of (1+1) EA, but where the mutation rate is chosen as 1 / ( f ⁡ ( x ) + 2 ) 1/(f(x)+2) where f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) is the fitness of x x . This fitness-adaptive mutation rate is nearly identical to the optimal adaptive mutation rate of 1 / ( f ⁡ ( x ) + 1 ) 1/(f(x)+1) ( Böttcher et al., 2010 ) . For this algorithm, the agent obtains a sub-optimal runtime of 4 ​ ( n + 1 ) ​ ( n + 2 ) 2 = O ⁡ ( n 3 ) 4(n+1)(n+2)^{2}=O(n^{3}) , while the true runtime for this algorithm is ( e / 4 ) ​ n 2 ​ ( 1 + o ⁡ ( 1 ) ) (e/4)n^{2}(1+o(1)) (Theorem 5 in ( Böttcher et al., 2010 ) ). When inspecting the drift analysis of the agent, we observed that the missing factor n n comes from the weak lower bound 1 / n ≤ ( 1 − 1 / r ) n − 1 1/n\leq(1-1/r)^{n-1} . We therefore created another problem card which provided the inequality 1 − 1 / r ≥ exp ( − 1 / ( r − 1 ) ) 1-1/r\geq\exp(-1/(r-1)) . The agent now produced a (1+1) EA-type algorithm with the same fitness-dependent mutation rate and runtime 4 ​ e ​ ( n + 1 ) ​ ( n + 2 ) = O ⁡ ( n 2 ) 4e(n+1)(n+2)=O(n^{2}) .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: The Jump k \text{{\sc Jump}}_{k} function takes the value k + OneMax k+\text{{\sc OneMax}} , except for non-optimal search points at Hamming distance d < k d<k from the optimum which take the value n − OneMax n-\text{{\sc OneMax}} . The problem therefore has a fitness gap (a local optimum) at distance k k from the optimum. Typical evolutionary algorithms have runtime O ⁡ ( n k ) O(n^{k}) because they need to flip k k bits simultaneously to jump from the local optimum to the global optimum. By using more sophisticated diversity and variation operators, it is possible to reduce the runtime further. One generation of the staged pipeline discovered a variant of (1+1) EA with fixed mutation rate 1 / ( n + 1 ) 1/(n+1) . The agent proved a runtime bound of O ⁡ ( n k + 2 ) O(n^{k+2}) which is a factor of n 2 n^{2} weaker than the true runtime for this algorithm which is O ⁡ ( n k ) O(n^{k}) . A factor n n was lost due to using a weak lower bound p k ​ ( 1 − p ) n ≥ p k + 1 p^{k}(1-p)^{n}\geq p^{k+1} for p = 1 / ( n + 1 ) p=1/(n+1) . In a second set of experiments, we ran the pipeline for three generations and added the inequality 1 − 1 / r ≥ exp ( − 1 / ( r − 1 ) ) 1-1/r\geq\exp(-1/(r-1)) to the problem card. This produced an algorithm with machine-checked runtime O ⁡ ( n k + 1 ) O(n^{k+1}) .

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: The runtime analyses of evolutionary algorithms on OneMax , LeadingOnes , and Jump k are widely known. It is likely that the LLMs used in this study have seen many of these during their pre-training (although their Lean formalisations are as far as we know not available at the time of writing). To rule out the possibility that the agent simply restates Lean formalisations of well-known algorithms and analyses, we would like to test the agent on a new problem not previously discussed in the literature. We therefore designed CycleUncover (defined in Figure 3 ), which is a problem solvable in polynomial time, but not by a typical evolutionary algorithm. The problem is independent set on a cycle graph, where the length of the cycle is even by construction. The fitness function is defined such that infeasible solutions lead to a deceptive trap at large Hamming distance from the optimum. Given the hidden permutation σ \sigma , a solution is simply to choose every second vertex along the permutation cycle.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: The agent produced an algorithm for CycleUncover with a machine-checked expected runtime of O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) (row 6 of Table 2 ). The algorithm works differently from an evolutionary algorithm: it builds up a two-colouring of the graph, and then queries the optimum. The two-colouring is obtained by keeping a current vertex u u which is coloured, and then by repeatedly sampling uniformly at random a vertex v v until v v is both uncoloured and adjacent to u u . This newly found vertex is coloured oppositely to u u and becomes the new current vertex. To determine whether two vertices u u and v v are adjacent in the graph, the algorithm queries the fitness of the bitstring where only u u and v v are selected. As shown in Figure 3 , the fitness is 2 if and only if u u and v v are connected. After the first step, u u has at most one uncoloured neighbour, and the probability of sampling one is Ω ⁡ ( 1 / n ) \Omega(1/n) . The algorithm therefore needs O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) queries in expectation to obtain the next vertex v v . Repeating this procedure O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) times, the algorithm obtains a two-colouring after O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) queries in expectation. From the complete two-colouring, the algorithm can queries the optimum by choosing only vertices with the same colour. Since the cycle has even length, vertices of either colour class is optimal. This result suggests that, even for a problem that to our knowledge has not been studied in this form, the pipeline can identify the problem structure and provide a tailored and efficient algorithm.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
authors: Per Kristian Lehre
content: We now turn to instance classes of the NP-hard minimum VertexCover problem. Given an undirected graph G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) , the minimum vertex cover problem asks for the smallest subset V ′ ⊆ V V^{\prime}\subseteq V of the vertices such that for each edge { u , v } ∈ E \{u,v\}\in E , at least one of the vertices u u and v v belong to V ′ V^{\prime} . This problem is NP-hard, but a simple greedy algorithm returns a 2-approximate solution in polynomial time. We do not attempt to design approximation algorithms here, we focus on finding a globally optimal vertex cover. We adopt the conventional pseudo-Boolean representation of VertexCover instances. Given a graph with n n vertices V = { 1 , 2 , … , n } V=\{1,2,\ldots,n\} , we encode a subset of the vertices V ′ V^{\prime} by a bitstring x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n x\in\{0,1\}^{n} , where x i = 1 x_{i}=1 if and only if vertex i ∈ V ′ i\in V^{\prime} . We adapt the multi-objective formulation from ( Kratsch & Neumann, 2013 ) into a single-objective fitness function which counts the number of chosen vertices (first term), and the number of uncovered edges (second term).
