title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
section: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
content: Besides domination-based algorithms such as the NSGA-II, the decomposition-based MOEA/D is one of the most popular and successful optimization heuristic for multi-objective problems. It decomposes the problem into several, single-objective subproblems. By solving these in a co-evolutionary manner and archiving non-dominated solutions, it approximates or computes the Pareto front. Interestingly, so far no advantages from the co-evolutionary communication of subproblem solutions were proven. In this first mathematical runtime analysis addressing this research question, we investigate how the mutation-based MOEA/D solves the classic OMM benchmark when solutions are exchanged among subproblems in different distances r r . We show, for the first time, that the MOEA/D profits from an exchange of solutions, and that already very small communication radii r r are sufficient to maximally profit from this feature of the algorithm. More precisely, for all values r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 we prove a tight runtime guarantee of Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) , where n n is the problem size. This is asymptotically faster than the known bound of O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{2}\log n) guarantee for r = 0 r=0 , which we complement with a matching bound of Ω ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) \Omega(n^{2}\log n) .

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Many real-world problems require the optimization of multiple competing objectives. This naturally leads to various, mutually incomparable, optimal trade-offs, known as Pareto optima , where improving one objective necessarily reduces the quality of another objective. Thus, the overall optimization goal is to quickly find as many Pareto optima as possible. To this end, multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) are widely and very successfully applied [ ZQL+11 , CLvV07 ] . Their population-based approach of maintaining a set of currently best-so-far solutions lends itself well to the multi-objective setting, and their general-purpose nature allows for great flexibility.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: State-of-the-art MOEAs can be classified into two main approaches. Using Pareto dominance as main selection criterion and then a secondary criterion ensuring a balanced coverage of the Pareto front is the strategy of the NSGA-II [ DPAM02 ] —the most popular MOEA, with over 60,000 60{,}000 citations on Google Scholar. Other popular MOEAs using this general strategy include the NSGA-III [ DJ14 ] , SMS-EMOA [ BNE07 ] , and SPEA2 [ ZLT01 ] . All these algorithms are intensively used in practice. Since more recently, they are also subject to intensive theoretical research, see [ ZD23 , WD23 , BZLQ23 , RBLQ24 ] and follow-up works.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: An alternative and more recent strategy is to consider a decomposition of the objective function f f into several less complex subproblems, and obtain a good set of solutions for f f by optimizing these. The most popular MOEA making use of this approach is the decomposition-based MOEA (MOEA/D) [ ZL07 ] , which decomposes f f into a user-specified number of single-objective subproblems. The MOEA/D proceeds by optimizing these subproblems instead of f f directly. However, the best-so-far solutions of each subproblem are stored in a shared archive that stores all non-dominated solutions according to the original objective function f f , thus ensuring that high-quality solutions for f f are obtained. The subproblems themselves are optimized in a co-evolutionary fashion, where each subproblem exchanges its best-so-far solution with all subproblems of a user-specified communication radius r r . The intention of r r is to benefit from potential positive correlations among the different subproblems.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: The MOEA/D has been subject to rigorous mathematical investigation for considerably longer than dominance-based MOEAs [ LZZZ16 ] , however, the theoretical understanding of this algorithm seems less developed (see Section 2 for a more detailed discussion). In particular, we have to this day no theoretical results on the necessity of or benefits from the co-evolutionary solution exchange in the MOEA/D. All theoretical results so far conduct their analysis as if there was no exchange of solutions. Hence this central aspect of the MOEA/D, distinguishing it from a simple parallel optimization of the subproblems, is not at all understood via theoretical means by now.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: We prove tight bounds for how the expected runtime of the MOEA/D depends on the choice of its communication radius r r . As our main result, we show that already a radius r = 1 r=1 leads to asymptotic speed-ups when compared to a trivial communication radius of r = 0 r=0 . In particular, as we discuss at the end of Section 2 , the guarantees that we obtain with non-trivial communication are better than that of various state-of-the-art MOEAs based on non-dominated sorting, when using a comparable parametrization. Interestingly, we obtain the same runtime guarantees for all r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 , that is, increasing r r further does not lead to further speed-ups when waiting for the entire Pareto front to be witnessed. However, for achieving partial progress, we show that the runtime scales linearly in 1 r \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} , the details of which we discuss at the beginning of Section 4 .

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: In more detail, we study how the mutation-only MOEA/D optimizes the bi-objective OneMinMax ( OMM ) benchmark of size n n , when using the Chebyshev decomposition into n + 1 n+1 subproblems with uniform weights. Hence, each Pareto optimum is represented by the optimum of exactly one subproblem. We further assume that the reference point is initially set to the ideal value of ( n , n ) (n,n) . This is a standard setting for runtime results for the MOEA/D.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: In our main result ( Theorem 1 ), we show that if the MOEA/D uses a communication radius of r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 , it exhibits an expected runtime of Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) function evaluations until its archive witnesses the entire Pareto front of OMM for the first time. This result improves the previously best known bound of O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{2}\log n) [ LZZZ16 ] by a factor of O ⁡ ( log ⁡ n ) O(\log n) , and our bound is asymptotically tight. Our result follows from a careful analysis of the exchange of solutions among subproblems. We show that an extremal subproblem propagates its solution quickly to sufficiently many other subproblems. In turn, this increases the probability to pick a suitable subproblem for finding an improving solution. The amount of how many subproblems can actually benefit from such an exchange is limited by the structure of OMM , which is why the expected runtime is the same for all communication radii greater or equal to 1 1 . However, the benefit of larger search radii is observable to some extent, before this capping occurs.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: We prove Theorem 1 for both a uniform and cyclical way of selecting which subproblem to choose next in an iteration. This shows that the exact choice in which communication occurs is not relevant. Moreover, we note that we prove the upper and lower quadratic bound separately (in Theorems 2 and 6 ), for more general types of mutation, of which standard bitwise mutation—the most widely applied type of mutation—is a special case ( Lemma 7 ).

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: We complement our quadratic bound in Corollary 8 with a bound of Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) \Theta(n^{2}\log n) for a trivial communication radius of r = 0 r=0 . This result follows directly by combining known results in the literature for similar processes. It shows that the speed-up for r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 is, indeed, a result of the communication radius, since all other parameters remain the same as in the setting for r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 .

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: We discuss related work in Section 2 . In Section 3 , we introduce our mathematical notation and terminology, and we present the MOEA/D. In Section 4 , we discuss and prove our tight Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) runtime bound for non-trivial communication radii. We complement this result in Section 5 with a Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) \Theta(n^{2}\log n) runtime bound for trivial radii. Last, we conclude our paper in Section 6 .

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: The MOEA/D has been studied mathematically from several angles so far. However, none of these results studied the impact of the communication radius on the runtime. In fact, none of the papers take the communication among subproblems into account when conducting a runtime analysis.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: The first runtime analysis of the MOEA/D was conducted by Li et al. [ LZZZ16 ] . Besides other results, the authors prove an O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{2}\log n) bound for the expected runtime on the OMM benchmark 1 1 1 The authors erroneously refer to this benchmark as COCZ in their paper. in the same setting as in this article.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Huang and Zhou [ HZ20 ] study the MOEA/D with contiguous hypermutation, which is a non-standard mutation operator from artificial immune systems that performs larger changes more frequently than standard operators. The authors study a general decomposition of the objective functions into N N subproblems, where N N is a user-specified value. Important for the comparison to our work, Huang and Zhou [ HZ20 ] prove that the MOEA/D with contiguous hypermutation optimizes the OMM benchmark in O ⁡ ( N ​ n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(Nn^{2}\log n) expected time. Hence, even for a minimal value of N = 2 N=2 , their upper bound only matches the upper bound of Li et al. [ LZZZ16 ] for the classic MOEA/D.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Huang et al. [ HZC+21 ] consider the MOEA/D with standard bitwise mutation and with the slightly problem-specific one-point crossover, also in the setting of a general decomposition into N N subproblems. Relevant to our article, the authors prove an O ⁡ ( N ​ n ​ log ⁡ n ) O(Nn\log n) bound for the OMM benchmark. For the minimal choice of N = 2 N=2 , this results in an O ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n\log n) bound, which is faster than the traditional O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{2}\log n) by Li et al. [ LZZZ16 ] by a factor of O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) . The reason for this speed-up is that the crossover operator allows to easily find all Pareto optima once the extremal solutions of the Pareto front have been found. While impressive, this work highlights the benefit of crossover, and it does not focus on communication among the solutions.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Similar to the result by Huang et al. [ HZC+21 ] , Doerr, Krejca, and Weeks [ DKW24 ] also study the MOEA/D with a general decomposition into N + 1 N+1 subproblems, studying only the OMM benchmark. The authors analyze the impact of mutation, studying both standard bitwise mutation and fast mutation, the latter of which performs changes following a power law with exponent β > 1 \beta>1 . They prove for the version with bitwise mutation an expected O ⁡ ( n ​ N ​ log ⁡ n + n n / ( 2 ​ N ) ​ N ​ log ⁡ n ) O(nN\log n+n^{n/(2N)}N\log n) runtime 2 2 2 The authors complement a specific part of this runtime with a loose lower bound that is also exponential in n / N n/N . and for the version with fast mutation an O ⁡ ( n ​ N ​ log ⁡ n + n β ​ log ⁡ n ) O(nN\log n+n^{\beta}\log n) expected runtime. As with the previous results, this result highlights how different operators can lead to a far higher tolerance with respect to the number of problem decompositions, in particular making the setting N = 1 N=1 feasible. Nonetheless, the communication radius is not discussed.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Huang et al. [ HZLL21 ] study the mutation-only MOEA/D for problems with m ≥ 2 m\geq 2 objectives. They are interested in the first time that the algorithm finds any optimal solution, which is very different from the standard setting of witnessing the entire Pareto front at once. The authors consider three different decompositions, into m m subproblems each, studying the performance of the MOEA/D on the m m LOTZ and m m COCZ benchmarks. The main result of the paper is that the weighted-sum decomposition performs drastically outperforms the other two decomposition methods. This paper explicitly sets the communication radius to the lowest-possible value.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Zhang et al. [ ZZZD26 ] also consider the mutation-only MOEA/D for a flexible number N N of subproblems. Similar to Huang et al. [ HZLL21 ] , the authors study the impact of the decomposition type, but they consider the standard runtime definition, which is the time until the archive witnesses the entire Pareto front. Most important to our work, Zhang et al. [ ZZZD26 ] show that with a logarithmic number of subproblems, the MOEA/D with the weighted-sum decomposition has an expected runtime of O ⁡ ( n ​ log 2 ​ n ) O(n\log^{2}n) on the OMM benchmark, which is considerably faster than the typical O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{2}\log n) bound. Again, this highlights the importance of the decomposition choice, but the communication radius is not studied. The latest work studying the MOEA/D on classic benchmarks [ DKW26 ] proves that a self-adjusting way to adapt the decomposition can lead to drastic runtime gains for unevenly scaled Pareto fronts.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: In the only work on a classic optimization problem, Do et al. [ DNNS23 ] study how the MOEA/D solves multi-objective minimum-weight-base problems. The authors introduce a special decomposition for their problem and prove that it finds the entire Pareto front in an expected time that is fixed-parameter tractable.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Besides the MOEA/D, other MOEAs have been theoretically studied. Most relevant to our work, Doerr and Qu [ DQ23 ] showed that the NSGA-II has a lower bound of Ω ⁡ ( N ​ n ​ log ⁡ n ) \Omega(Nn\log n) on OMM , where N ≥ 4 ​ ( n + 1 ) N\geq 4(n+1) denotes the population size of the algorithm. Thus, for an optimal choice of N N , the algorithm has an Ω ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) \Omega(n^{2}\log n) lower bound, which is tight [ ZLD22 ] . The same bound of Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) \Theta(n^{2}\log n) also holds for the global SEMO, another MOEA that is commonly studied theoretically [ BS24 ] . We note that while for other algorithms based on non-dominated sorting, when relying solely on mutation, only a comparable O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{2}\log n) for best-possible parameter values is known [ WD24a , WD24b , ZLD22 , RBLQ24 , WD23 , ZD24 ] , even for variants that are more robust in their parameter settings [ DIK25 , DKS26 ] , there is little reason to believe that these algorithms can optimize OMM faster than Ω ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) \Omega(n^{2}\log n) when only using mutation.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Outside the theory domain, some suggestions on the optimal size of communication radius exists, but due to their experimental nature, they are less clear than a typical theoretical result. In the work [ ZL07 ] proposing the MOEA/D, generally the MOEA/D was perceived as not very sensitive to the size of the neighborhood used for the exchange of solutions. However, the authors observed that for a knapsack instance, a large radius was detrimental, whereas for the ZDT1 benchmark, a large radius was preferable. A more detailed study on the influence of the communication radius [ IAN13 ] finds that it depends on the number of objectives, but that generally a small constant fraction of the population size such as 10 10 to 20 20 percent gives good results. We are not aware of more detailed results, in particular, we have found none that discuss whether the coevolutionary solution exchange is advantageous at all.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Let ℕ \mathbb{N} denote the set of natural numbers, including 0 0 , and let ℝ \mathbb{R} be the set of reals. authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
section: 5 A Super-Quadratic Lower Bound for Trivial Communication Radius
content: Corollary 8 follows directly from well-known results. The upper bound is given by Li et al. [ LZZZ16 , Proposition 4 4 ] , following from an n n -times application of the coupon collector problem. The lower bound follows from noting that solving subproblem 0 0 takes Ω ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) \Omega(n\log n) function evaluations if only considering function evaluations spent on this subproblem. This is a special case of the fact that the ( 1 + 1 ) (1+1) evolutionary algorithm (EA) takes Ω ⁡ ( n ​ log ⁡ n ) \Omega(n\log n) function evaluations on each objective function with a unique optimum [ DJW98 , Theorem 1 1 ] . Since the MOEA/D with communication radius 0 0 runs an independent ( 1 + 1 ) {(1+1)} EA for each subproblem, this result translated directly to subproblem 0 0 . The overall lower bound follows by noticing that, on average, we require n + 1 n+1 function evaluations in order to perform 1 1 function evaluation for subproblem 0 0 .

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: We derived tight runtime guarantees for the MOEA/D ( Algorithm 1 ) when optimizing the classic OMM benchmark of size n n . Theorem 1 shows that for any communication radius r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 , the expected runtime is Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Theta(n^{2}) function evaluations, which improves the previously best bound of O ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{2}\log n) [ LZZZ16 ] . Our improvement is a result of studying the process more carefully, showing that currently best-so-far individuals are propagated to sufficiently many subproblems quickly. This results in a higher chance of selecting a useful subproblem for finding new Pareto-optima. However, as our lower bound shows, the exact size of r r , once at least 1 1 , is irrelevant, as the number of subproblems that share the same sub-optimal individuals is limited by the problem structure of OMM .

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: We contrast Theorem 1 with Corollary 8 , showing that if r = 0 r=0 , the expected runtime is Θ ⁡ ( n 2 ​ log ⁡ n ) \Theta(n^{2}\log n) . Hence, the speed-up for r ≥ 1 r\geq 1 is, indeed, due to the exchange of individuals among subproblems.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: As usual in the mathematical runtime analysis of randomized search heuristics [ NW10 , AD11 , Jan13 , ZYQ19 , DN20 ] , we were able to analyze rigorously only one particular but commonly studied situation, and for arbitrary value of the parameter r r and for a broader class of mutation operators. From the working principles of our proofs, we are optimistic that the co-evolutionary solution exchange is advantageous also in other settings. This is clear when crossover is used with some constant probability p c < 1 p_{c}<1 , simply because our proof is monotonic in the sense that the creation of other individuals at most slows down the proven progress by the time spent on these other individuals. Similarly, when using the PBI decomposition with weight θ > 1 \theta>1 , we obtain the same set of subproblems, and hence the same process. The weighted-sum decomposition leads to a particular behavior on the OMM benchmark that is most likely not representative for a typical use of the MOEA/D [ ZZZD26 ] . For the number of subproblems N N different from the size n + 1 n+1 of the Pareto front, it is somewhat clear that N > n + 1 N>n+1 simply implies that some points of the Pareto front are targeted by more than one subproblem. This should give a similar behavior as shown in our work except for that all numbers of individuals are scaled up appropriately. When N < n + 1 N<n+1 , for any value of the communication radius, there is the risk that points of the Pareto front are skipped and then are hard to find. Apart from this, the co-evolutionary solution exchange should work as in our setting, that is, the outermost solution is communicated to a large number of subproblems, which then in parallel search for more outermost solutions.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: What is less clear from our work, and an interesting next step is to study, is for which other benchmarks such a speed-up exists and whether the runtime differs for different non-trivial communication radii. A natural next benchmark is LOTZ , for which, different to OMM , only very few individuals are on the Pareto front. Deriving in such a setting a central lemma like Lemma 3 , which succinctly summarizes when a subproblem updates its best-so-far individual, seems to be a logical next step.

authors: Benjamin Doerr, Moaad Elmoutassim, Martin S. Krejca, Guy Mushiata Kibulu
content: Another natural question is to study an additional positive effect of crossover. In this setting, since r r also determines which subproblems are chosen for the crossover, the exact value of r r may play a more important role. In particular, it could be that a small value of r r leads to a more suitable parent selection than a uniform parent selection as often used in domination-based MOEAs.

content: Last, we currently lack mathematical guarantees for the importance of the communication radius for problems with at least three objectives. So far, there is only a single work studying such a setting for the MOEA/D, and it does not consider Pareto front coverage [ HZLL21 ] .

content: Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

content: Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

title: A Dynamic Decomposition Strategy for the MOEA/D With Proven Performance Guarantees
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Martin S. Krejca, Noé Weeks
section: A Dynamic Decomposition Strategy for the MOEA/D With Proven Performance Guarantees
content: The MOEA/D is one of the most successful multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. It operates by decomposing the optimization problem into single-objective subproblems, which are then solved in a co-evolutionary manner. The performance of the MOEA/D depends critically on this decomposition. In this work, we propose a novel way to adjust this decomposition on the fly, for the case of discrete bi-objective optimization. Different from all previous works in this direction, we support our new algorithm with a proven performance guarantee. This is the first work that rigorously proves the runtime of a dynamic multi-objective evolutionary algorithm. For monotonic distortions of the simple LOTZ benchmark, it is known that classic decompositions leave large holes in the Pareto front, making it very hard for the MOEA/D to cover the entire Pareto front. In contrast, we prove that our self-adjusting MOEA/D solves all these LOTZ problems in an expected number of O ⁡ ( n 4 ) O(n^{4}) function evaluations. This relatively low runtime as well as the details of our mathematical proof show that the dynamic decomposition strategy indeed evolves a decomposition adjusted to each of these problem instances.

content: Many real-world optimization problems feature several conflicting objectives. Such multi-objective optimization problems (MOOPs) usually do not possess a single optimal solution. Thus, a common approach is to compute a diverse set of Pareto optima (incomparable optimal trade-offs) and let a human decision maker pick one of these, based on their broader understanding of the problem.

content: There are two general approaches to the design of multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). The classic one works with a population of individuals and employs diversity mechanisms to ensure that this population approaches the full Pareto front. This concept is found in the algorithms SPEA2 [ ZLT01 ] , NSGA -II [ DPAM02 ] , SMS-EMOA [ BNE07 ] , and NSGA-III [ DJ14 ] .

title: A Dynamic Decomposition Strategy for the MOEA/D With Proven Performance Guarantees

content: More recently, decomposition-based approaches were proposed. Here the idea is to decompose the MOOP into scalar subproblems and solve these in a co-evolutionary manner, that is, they are optimized in parallel and exchange solutions. The hope is that the co-evolutionary approach helps solve similar subproblems efficiently, but also that the evolutionary process finds Pareto optima that are not the optimum of one of the designated subproblems. We refer to a recent survey [ XXM20 ] on decomposition-based MOEAs and note that the by far most prominent such algorithm is the MOEA/D developed by Zhang and Li [ ZL07 ] . The survey reports that the MOEA/D with a static decomposition oftentimes leads to a worse spread of the final solutions in terms of objective values when compared to a dynamic choice. This behavior shows repeatedly for continuous and for discrete combinatorial problems, and in the presence of crossover, oftentimes reported for the common Chebyshev decomposition [ HJH19 , ISMN17 , LL11 , LY20 , QML+14 ] .

content: Our contribution: We propose a simple dynamic decomposition for the bi-objective MOEA/D on discrete search spaces and analyze the performance of the resulting self-adjusting MOEA/D (sMOEA/D; Algorithm 2 ). In our dynamic decomposition scheme, some ideas present in other works can be found again, but overall we view it as a new development. In particular, since we aim at computing the full Pareto front of a discrete problem, we have to adjust the number of subproblems, whereas most previous schemes work with a static number of subproblems. Furthermore, our sMOEA/D makes use of a particularly good choice for new subproblems (see line 2 in Algorithm 2 and eq. 2 ) that allows to find new useful subproblems quickly (see Lemma 7 ).

In order to estimate the expected waiting time until sufficiently many improvements occurred, we sum the expected times for each improvement. As each trial for an improvement is independent of the other trials, the probability for an improvement follows a geometric law. Bounding the improvement probability of such a law from below results in an upper bound of its expected waiting time, allowing us to bound the overall waiting time from above.

Moreover, we ran experiments for 0 0 / 1 1 - Knapsack instances, which we report in Section B.1 . In these experiments, we compare the sMOEA/D to the classic MOEA/D with tuned parameters, finding that the former is at least as good if not better than the latter while requiring almost no parameter tuning. Natural next steps, in order of increasing need for new ideas, are (1) the use of our algorithm for discrete problems on search spaces other than bit strings, (2) the extension of our algorithm to more than two objectives (this in particular needs the definition of a suitable way to insert new subproblems), and (3) possibly an extension to continuous problems, which usually operate with a fixed number of subproblems.

content: We complement our theoretical results from Section 4 by experiments that analyze the sMOEA/D in aspects not present in the theoretical analysis. To this end, we follow the experimental setup of Zhang and Li [ ZL07 ] and consider random instances of the NP-hard bi-objective 0 0 / 1 1 - Knapsack problem. Zhang and Li [ ZL07 ] used this setup when introducing the classic MOEA/D, and they showed that it empirically outperforms another common multi-objective search heuristic known as GSEMO.

title: A Dynamic Decomposition Strategy for the MOEA/D With Proven Performance Guarantees
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Martin S. Krejca, Noé Weeks
content: In total, we compare the performance of the sMOEA/D to that of the classic MOEA/D, and we analyze the number of subproblems of the former during the run. Our results show that the archive of the sMOEA/D is superior to that of the classic MOEA/D. Moreover, the number of the subproblems of the sMOEA/D grows over time, suggesting that less time is spent on improving bad solutions, and more time is spent on exploring the Pareto front. We detail our experimental setup in Section B.1.1 , and we discuss our results in Section B.1.2 .

content: We also conducted experiments for the sMOEA/D and the classic MOEA/D on random LOTZ u,v instances, but we detail this analysis only in Section B.2 . Our results support our claims from Section 4 . That is, they suggest that the sMOEA/D optimizes LOTZ u,v in reasonable time by finding new elements of the Pareto front one by one. The classic MOEA/D gets to the Pareto front quickly but does not find all Pareto optima within reasonable time.

content: Table 1 reports on the average of the 5 5 independent runs per instance and per value of n n . In terms of the set coverage measure C C , that is, the relative number of individuals in one archive weakly dominating that of the other, we see that the archive of the sMOEA/D always weakly dominates far more points of the archive of the classic MOEA/D than the other way around. This difference is statistically significant for a p p -value of 0.01 0.01 for all three values of n n . This suggests that the sMOEA/D generally finds better solutions in terms of weak domination.

content: Moreover, the table reports on the average size of the final archive per instance. Here, we see that the classic MOEA/D has a slightly larger archive on average than the sMOEA/D, but the sizes are often comparable between both algorithms. The difference is most likely a result of the random creation of the offspring, as the differences are within one standard deviation of the data (reported in Table 2 ). In combination with the set coverage above, these results suggest that the sMOEA/D outperforms the classic MOEA/D in parts of the search space that they both explore.

title: A Dynamic Decomposition Strategy for the MOEA/D With Proven Performance Guarantees
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Martin S. Krejca, Noé Weeks
content: Figure 2 shows how the number of subproblems of the sMOEA/D evolves over time. Although the figure only shows two examples, we note that the figures for all instances follow the same qualitative trend. Initially, the sMOEA/D operates with not so many subproblems. This means that many solutions weakly dominate each other, not requiring more subproblems. This strategy works well until it gets harder to find improving solutions, most likely because the Pareto fron (or local optima) are found. From this point on, the number of subproblems grows until progress is hard to make and the algorithm runs out of budget of FEs.

title: A Dynamic Decomposition Strategy for the MOEA/D With Proven Performance Guarantees
authors: Benjamin Doerr, Martin S. Krejca, Noé Weeks
content: This behavior is good as it allows the algorithm to only use up few FEs early on and to use most of its budget once it gets closer to the Pareto front. This allows it to explore the Pareto front more thoroughly, which is potentially why we see in Table 1 that the archive of the sMOEA/D dominates that of the classic MOEA/D to a large degree. In contrast, the classic MOEA/D uses the same larger number of subproblems, namely N = 200 N=200 , in each iteration, providing it with fewer opportunities to explore the Pareto front once it gets there.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
section: Reva : Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
content: A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered in the software lifecycle. As coding agents now generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a stronger first line of defense that screens each new function in real time, as it is generated. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long to keep pace with code generation. Faster AI-based detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are considerably less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM’s generated verdict has proven unreliable in prior work even when some of that context is given.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
section: Reva : Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
content: We present Reva (REal-time Vulnerability Analysis), an AI vulnerability detector that brings the security context and code understanding components behind agentic detectors into a single forward pass of an LLM. For each new function, Reva provides the LLM with a pre-computed threat model of its module, along with lightweight static analysis findings and call-graph information. Rather than asking the LLM for a verdict, Reva lets a trained probe read the LLM’s internal representations of the function in this context. On PrimeVul’s held-out test set, Reva on GLM-5.3-Flash reaches 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function. This matches VulTriage (59.2%), the state-of-the-art agentic function-level detector in the literature, run on the same LLM, while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. On the same prompt, the probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM’s own direct verdict. Across three open LLMs, Reva is at least as accurate as VulTriage, and about 10% more accurate on two of them. These results suggest that an LLM’s internal representations already encode much of what agentic detectors obtain through reasoning.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: The cost of remediating a vulnerability grows the later it is discovered in the software lifecycle [ 1 ] . Vulnerabilities are therefore cheapest to fix when they are detected as the code is written. Coding agents now generate code faster than developers can review it, which calls for a first line of defense that screens each new function in real time, as it is generated.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Static analyzers run in real time, but at the scale of agent-generated code, they produce more reports than developers can review, many of them false positives [ 2 , 3 ] . LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities [ 4 , 5 ] by combining such tools with their own analysis of the code, and agentic detectors bring this approach to function-level detection. VulTriage [ 6 ] , the state of the art in the function-level detection literature, and VulAgent [ 7 ] enrich the prompt with retrieved vulnerability knowledge and program facts, and VulTrial [ 8 ] lets several agents debate a verdict. This reasoning, however, spans several model calls, which amounts to minutes per function. Faster AI-based detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, reduce this latency but are considerably less accurate [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] .

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Fig. 1: Overview of Reva on a vulnerable function from LibRaw (CVE-2020-35530). ① The prompt combines the function with its security context. ② The LLM processes the prompt in one forward pass, up to the deepest of four probed layers. ③ The hidden states of the code tokens are kept at each probed layer. ④ An attention probe pools them into a risk score.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Reva is designed to close this gap between speed and improved accuracy. Instead of letting the LLM gather context through multiple rounds of tool calls, Reva assembles it in the prompt, including a threat model of the function’s module, its static analysis findings, its call graph and its file. Instead of reasoning towards a verdict, the LLM then processes this prompt in a single forward pass without generating text, and a small probe trained on labeled functions maps its internal representations of the code tokens to a risk score. This second choice builds on evidence that LLMs encode knowledge that their answers do not express, for example about the truth of a statement [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] or the correctness of their own answers [ 15 , 16 ] , and that chain-of-thought explanations are not always faithful to the underlying computation [ 17 ] .

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: We evaluate Reva on PrimeVul [ 9 ] , a high-quality dataset of vulnerable C and C++ functions paired with benign versions of the same functions, which spans 651 projects and 121 vulnerability types (CWEs). On its held-out test set, Reva on GLM-5.3-Flash [ 18 ] is on par with VulTriage and more accurate than VulAgent run on the same LLM, in about one second per function, over 250 times faster than VulTriage. On two other open LLMs, it is 9% to 13% more accurate than both agentic detectors.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: This paper makes three contributions: (i) we propose Reva , a vulnerability detector that combines targeted security context with a probe on an LLM’s internal representations, in a single forward pass per function; (ii) we compare it with state-of-the-art agentic function-level detectors run on the same three LLMs, on PrimeVul’s held-out test set, in terms of accuracy, cost and robustness; and (iii) we outline a research agenda towards detectors that screen every function as coding agents generate it and escalate likely vulnerabilities to more capable agents that construct a proof of vulnerability.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: LLM-based vulnerability detection. LLMs in non-agentic settings typically struggle to tell a vulnerable function from its benign counterpart: on PrimeVul [ 9 ] , GPT-4 with chain-of-thought labels both versions correctly in only 12.9% of the pairs, and LLMs asked for a verdict in non-agentic settings, often reason inconsistently about security [ 19 , 20 ] . Reva instead reads the LLM’s internal representations rather than its answer or reasoning.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Agentic detectors. Recent detectors improve accuracy by adding knowledge and reasoning steps. VulTriage retrieves CWE descriptions and verbalizes control- and data-flow facts [ 6 ] , VulAgent lets specialized agents propose and validate hypotheses against the project’s code [ 7 ] , and VulTrial stages a debate between agents [ 8 ] . Their cost grows with each call, and their context can exceed the LLM’s context window. Reva instead pre-loads the key parts of this context into the prompt and replaces the multi-step reasoning with a single probed forward pass.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Probing LLM internal representations. Probes are small classifiers trained on a model’s hidden states [ 21 ] . For code, linear probes indicates some capability to separate secure from insecure code on toy datasets [ 22 , 23 ] , and predict whether generated code will be insecure or incorrect [ 24 , 25 ] . These probes read the code alone, whereas Reva probes real-world functions read with targeted security context.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Pitfalls of vulnerability benchmarks. Detectors can exploit spurious features of their datasets, such as code metrics or semantics unrelated to the vulnerability [ 26 , 27 ] . Such a detector tends to classify a vulnerable function and its benign counterpart with the same label, which share these features. We therefore score each function independently, then check whether the two versions of each pair receive their correct labels.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: In Reva , an LLM reads a new function with its security context in one forward pass, and a probe maps the hidden states of the code tokens to a risk score (Fig. 1 ).

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: ①Prompt with security context. The prompt contains the new function and the context around it, in labeled sections (Fig. 1 ). A threat model, built once per project by a workflow of LLM agents over the entire software, describes the project (summary, attacker-controlled inputs, trust boundaries) and the module that contains the function (role, inputs that reach it, typical sinks and guards). The prompt adds the Semgrep [ 28 ] findings for the function, its call sites and the signatures of the helpers it calls, and the includes, types, macros and sibling functions of its file, extracted with tree-sitter from the repository. It is available for 84% of the training functions; otherwise the prompt has the function and its Semgrep findings only. The median prompt has 3,840 tokens, 601 of them code.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: ②One forward pass. The LLM processes the prompt in one forward pass that stops after the deepest of four probed layers, so the remaining layers are never run and it generates no output token. We probe intermediate layers, which probing studies often find most informative [ 21 ] : four evenly spaced layers from 38% to 85% of the depth of the LLM, selected by cross-validation.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: ③Code-token states. At each probed layer, Reva keeps only the hidden states of the function’s tokens. Each state is normalized and projected to 1,024 dimensions, and the four layers are concatenated.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: ④Attention probe. A probe with 8 attention heads pools the token states into one risk score. It has 0.57 M parameters and is trained on PrimeVul’s training functions. Its loss combines a per-function classification term with a term that ranks each vulnerable function above its benign counterpart. These pairs serve only in training: Reva scores each function on its own.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Use in practice. The LLM and Semgrep’s rules are loaded once at startup, so they don’t have to be booted for each new analysis, and each project’s threat model is built ahead of time. For each new function, Reva extracts its context, runs Semgrep, builds the prompt, runs the pass and applies the probe. With Muse-Glimmer-30B on one H200 GPU, this takes 0.93 s per function, 0.46 s of which is context extraction.

content: On GLM-5.3-Flash, Reva reaches 60.0% accuracy (95% CI [57.8, 62.2]), against 59.2% for VulTriage and 52.8% for VulAgent run on the same LLM (Table I ). Over all test functions, Reva is 0.8 points above VulTriage (CI [ − - 2.1, +3.8]) and 7.2 points above VulAgent (CI [+4.4, +10.3]). On Qwen3.8-27B and Muse-Glimmer-30B, Reva is 5.1 to 6.7 points more accurate than both agentic detectors, and all four confidence intervals exclude zero.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Beyond accuracy, Reva also compares favorably with VulTriage, the state-of-the-art function-level agentic detector, when both run on the same LLM. On all three LLMs, Reva has a lower false positive rate (FPR) and inverts the labels of fewer pairs ( P-R ), and on two of them it labels more pairs entirely correctly ( P-C ). Reva thus not only matches or exceeds VulTriage in accuracy, but also separates vulnerable from benign functions more reliably, which suggests that the probe captures the vulnerability itself rather than surface features that a vulnerable function shares with its secured counterpart.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Fig. 2 summarizes this trade-off. On each LLM, Reva is at least as accurate as both agentic detectors while being 100 to 6,000 times faster. Its accuracy also varies little across LLMs, by 1.1 points against 5.6 for VulTriage, so that Reva on Muse-Glimmer-30B matches VulTriage on GLM-5.3-Flash, the LLM on which VulTriage performs best. The signal read by the probe is therefore present in all three LLMs, whereas the accuracy of the agentic detectors depends on how well each LLM reasons about the code. VulTriage on GPT-4o reports a higher accuracy (63.6%), but we were unable to replicate these results.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: End to end, Reva takes 0.88 s to 1.33 s per function, against 108 s to 5,614 s for the agentic detectors on the same LLMs. Although these times, measured under parallel load, overstate single-request latency, the token counts confirm the gap. Reva reads about 3,100 to 3,400 tokens per function and generates none, whereas the agentic detectors process 3 to 70 times more tokens, many of them generated. As Reva needs the LLM’s hidden states, it cannot run behind an API. On a rented H200 GPU, it screens 1,000 functions for $0.9 to $1.3, against $9 to $61 for VulTriage and $63 to $307 for VulAgent at the public API rates of the same LLMs.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: We ablate each component of Reva on the Muse-Glimmer-30B validation set (Fig. 3 ). Asking the same LLM for a Yes/No verdict on the same prompt, instead of probing it, reduces accuracy to chance. On the test set, it stays 7.4 to 8.7 points below the probe, and Semgrep, Cppcheck and Flawfinder alone are also at chance (50.8% to 51.3%). The LLM’s internal representations thus carry information that neither its verdict nor the static-analysis findings provide alone. Within the probe, replacing attention pooling by a plain average of the token states lowers accuracy by 4.2 points, which suggests that the evidence of a vulnerability lies in a few tokens. Using a single layer, omitting the standardization or dropping the ranking term lowers accuracy by 0.4 to 1.5 points, and removing the repository context or keeping only the function by 1.0 and 1.9 points, none of which is significant. On PrimeVul’s short functions, the function alone thus carries most of the signal; we expect the context to matter more for interprocedural vulnerabilities.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Leakage and selection on the evaluation data can inflate probing results [ 21 , 31 ] . When no project appears in both training and evaluation folds, cross-validation accuracy drops by only 1.3 to 2.7 points, so most of what the probe learns transfers to unseen projects. Likewise, choosing the four probed layers on the training folds only, instead of on all development data, changes accuracy by less than half a point, so the layer choice does not inflate the results. Accuracy is, however, 6 points lower on the test set than in cross-validation (60.0% against 66.2% for GLM-5.3-Flash). As PrimeVul splits its data chronologically, this gap likely reflects the shift towards newer code, which cross-validation does not capture.

authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Step 1: Complete the comparison. We will run both agentic detectors and Reva on larger open LLMs. We will also test whether reading the internal representations after a short self-generated analysis adds information. Success criterion: Reva matches or exceeds them on the same LLM at every scale.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Step 2: Calibrated screening in coding agents. We will learn a project- and function-dependent threshold, and integrate Reva into a coding-agent loop that escalates only high-risk functions to an agentic detector or a proof-of-vulnerability check [ 32 ] . Success criterion: for a given budget of escalations, the loop finds more vulnerabilities than the agentic detector alone.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Step 3: Generalization beyond PrimeVul. We will evaluate on other datasets [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] , on interprocedural vulnerabilities [ 36 , 32 ] and on vulnerabilities disclosed after each LLM’s training cutoff, and study fine-tuning the LLM with the same objective. Success criterion: Reva keeps its accuracy on vulnerabilities the LLM cannot have seen.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
authors: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini
content: Reva detects vulnerabilities by probing an LLM’s internal representations of a function and its security context in a single forward pass. On PrimeVul’s held-out test set, it matches or exceeds agentic detectors run on the same LLM, with fewer false positives, in about one second per function and at a small fraction of their cost. An LLM’s internal representations thus carry more information about vulnerabilities than its verdicts, and reading them enables real-time screening of every function as it is written.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: Abstract Cybersecurity governance, risk management, compliance, and security architecture rely on numerous concepts, including security properties, domains, controls, risks, implementation measures, capabilities, and compliance requirements. Although these concepts are widely used, they are often represented through heterogeneous abstractions and vocabularies, making relationships among them difficult to express consistently and leaving much of the associated reasoning dependent on expert knowledge. This paper introduces the concepts of Security Concerns and Atomic Security Concerns (ASCs) and explores the hypothesis that cybersecurity knowledge may be represented through a finite set of foundational concerns. Inspired by the role of atoms in chemistry, the proposed approach views cybersecurity concepts as compositions of more fundamental concerns rather than as independent abstractions. Hence, Atomic Security Concerns could be viewed as a common abstraction layer for the representation of cybersecurity concepts, independently of their domain, nature, or level of granularity. Building upon this perspective, the paper explores how Atomic Security Concerns may provide the vocabulary of a cybersecurity language and how cybersecurity concepts may be represented as concern sets supporting explicit relationships among concepts. The contribution of this work is intentionally conceptual: it introduces a framework and research hypothesis for investigating the foundations of a common language for cybersecurity knowledge representation, reasoning, and future formalization. Keywords: Atomic Security Concerns, Security Concerns, Cybersecurity Language, Cybersecurity Knowledge Representation, Cybersecurity Governance, Risk Management, Compliance, Security Architecture, Security Reasoning.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: 1 Introduction Cybersecurity governance, risk management, compliance, and security architecture rely on a diverse set of cybersecurity concepts, including security properties, security domains, security controls, security requirements, security risks, and security architectures. These concepts are extensively employed across standards, regulatory frameworks, risk assessment methodologies, and architectural practices. Despite their widespread adoption, they are generally defined through distinct vocabularies, conceptual structures, and levels of abstraction, making it difficult to establish explicit, consistent, and traceable relationships among them. In practice, cybersecurity professionals routinely reason about relationships between security risks and security controls, security controls and security domains, security requirements and technical implementations, or organizational capabilities and security objectives. However, such relationships are rarely represented through a unified conceptual framework. Instead, they often depend on tacit knowledge acquired through experience, organizational practices, and familiarity with multiple standards and frameworks. Consequently, cybersecurity reasoning remains difficult to formalize, communicate, automate, and systematically reproduce across organizational and technological contexts. This observation raises a fundamental research question: does cybersecurity possess a foundational language capable of representing its knowledge structures through a common and coherent conceptual model? Many mature scientific disciplines rely on a finite set of foundational elements from which increasingly complex structures can be constructed. Natural languages are built upon alphabets that enable the construction of words, sentences, and documents. Similarly, chemistry relies on atoms as foundational elements from which molecules and more complex forms of matter are derived. In both cases, a relatively small set of foundational elements provides the expressive capacity required to represent a substantially larger body of knowledge. This paper investigates whether a similar principle may exist within cybersecurity. More specifically, it explores the hypothesis that cybersecurity knowledge can be represented through a limited set of Atomic Security Concerns (ASCs) that serve as candidate foundational elements of a cybersecurity language. Under this hypothesis, cybersecurity concepts such as security properties, security domains, security controls, security requirements, security risks, and security architectures are viewed not as independent abstractions, but as compositions of more fundamental security concerns. The objective of this work is not to establish an exhaustive catalog of Atomic Security Concerns. Rather, it seeks to introduce a conceptual framework for investigating the existence of a cybersecurity language founded upon a finite set of foundational elements. More specifically, this work seeks to characterize the properties that such foundational elements should possess. It is proposed that Atomic Security Concerns satisfy two

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: essential properties. First, they should exhibit irreducibility, meaning that they cannot be decomposed into more fundamental security concerns without loss of security semantics. Second, they should exhibit expressiveness, meaning that a sufficiently complete set of concerns should provide the representational capacity required to describe the principal cybersecurity concepts encountered within cybersecurity governance, risk management, compliance, and security architecture. Based on these principles, this paper makes five primary contributions: 1. It introduces the hypothesis that Atomic Security Concerns may serve as foundational elements of a cybersecurity language. 2. It proposes irreducibility and expressiveness as the defining properties of Atomic Security Concerns. 3. It presents an initial illustrative taxonomy of candidate Atomic Security Concerns. 4. It demonstrates how common cybersecurity concepts can be represented as compositions of Atomic Security Concerns. 5. It discusses the implications of this perspective for cybersecurity knowledge representation, traceability, reasoning, and future automation. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work and discusses existing approaches to cybersecurity knowledge representation. Section 3 introduces the concept of Atomic Security Concerns and presents their definition, atomicity principles, and identification criteria. Section 4 presents an initial taxonomy of Atomic Security Concerns. Section 5 introduces the proposed composition model and demonstrates how Atomic Security Concerns can be used to represent security properties, security capabilities, security functions, security domains, and security controls. Section 6 provides illustrative examples and validation scenarios. Finally, Sections 7 through 9 discuss implications and limitations of the proposed approach, identify future research directions, and present the conclusions of this work. 2 Related Work Cybersecurity knowledge has traditionally been structured through multiple complementary perspectives, including security properties, security controls, cybersecurity ontologies, and framework mapping initiatives. These approaches provide mechanisms for describing, implementing, organizing, and relating cybersecurity concepts. However, they generally do not address whether such concepts can be reduced to a common set of foundational elements from which broader cybersecurity knowledge structures may be derived. 2.1 Security Properties Security properties constitute one of the most established approaches to describing cybersecurity objectives. The Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) model remains a widely adopted conceptual framework for expressing fundamental security

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: objectives. Additional properties, including authenticity, accountability, non-repudiation, privacy, and resilience, have subsequently been introduced to address broader cybersecurity concerns. Although security properties provide a high-level description of desired security outcomes, they do not provide a mechanism for representing the relationships among security properties, security controls, security domains, security requirements, security risks, and security architectures. Consequently, they are generally treated as objectives or characteristics of secure systems rather than as foundational elements of a cybersecurity representation model. 2.2 Control-Based Frameworks Security standards and frameworks frequently organize cybersecurity knowledge through collections of security controls. Frameworks such as NIST Special Publication 800-53 [2], ISO/IEC 27001 [1,3], and CIS Controls classify controls into categories intended to address specific security objectives and risks. This approach provides practical guidance for governance, risk management, compliance, and security implementation activities. However, control frameworks primarily define security measures rather than the conceptual structures from which such measures originate. Multiple controls may contribute to the same security objective, while a single control may support several objectives simultaneously. As a result, control frameworks provide limited support for explaining the underlying conceptual relationships among security controls, security risks, security requirements, security properties, and security architectures. 2.3 Cybersecurity Ontologies Cybersecurity ontologies have been proposed to improve the formal representation, integration, and interoperability of cybersecurity knowledge. Existing work has modeled concepts such as assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, incidents, and compliance requirements, together with the relationships connecting these concepts. Examples include security ontology surveys by Souag et al. [5] and ontology engineering efforts such as the cybersecurity ontology proposed by Oltramari et al. [6], which seek to provide formal semantic structures for cybersecurity knowledge. More recently, ontology-based approaches have been extended to support the integration of heterogeneous cybersecurity knowledge sources. Examples include the Unified Cybersecurity Ontology (UCO) and more recent work integrating MITRE ATT&CK [9], D3FEND [10], CWE, and CVE [4] within common semantic frameworks. These approaches aim to improve interoperability, semantic consistency, automated reasoning, and knowledge sharing across cybersecurity repositories.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: Ontology-based approaches [5,6,7,8] focus on defining concepts and formalizing relationships among those concepts. Their primary objective is therefore the representation and integration of cybersecurity knowledge within coherent semantic structures. However, cybersecurity ontologies generally assume the existence of the cybersecurity concepts being represented. They describe how concepts relate to one another but do not typically investigate whether those concepts can themselves be decomposed into more fundamental semantic elements. The research question addressed in this work differs from that of ontology engineering. Rather than focusing on the representation of cybersecurity concepts and their relationships, it investigates whether a finite set of irreducible security concerns may exist beneath those concepts. Under this perspective, concepts commonly represented in cybersecurity ontologies may themselves be expressible as compositions of more fundamental concerns. Consequently, Atomic Security Concerns should not be viewed as an alternative to cybersecurity ontologies but rather as a potentially complementary abstraction layer. If such concerns can be identified and validated, they may provide foundational semantic elements upon which future cybersecurity ontologies can be constructed. 2.4 Cross-Framework Mapping and Interoperability A complementary line of research focuses on establishing correspondences among cybersecurity standards, regulations, frameworks, and methodologies. Crosswalks, mappings, and harmonization initiatives seek to improve consistency, interoperability, and traceability by establishing relationships among controls, requirements, and concepts defined by different frameworks. These approaches recognize that many cybersecurity frameworks address similar concerns through different organizational structures and vocabularies. While framework mappings facilitate alignment and interoperability, they remain dependent on the concepts defined within the frameworks being mapped. Consequently, they do not generally address the existence of more fundamental semantic elements that may underlie those concepts. 2.5 Research Gap and Positioning of This Work The reviewed approaches demonstrate that cybersecurity knowledge can be organized according to multiple perspectives, including security properties, security controls, ontology models, and framework mappings. These approaches contribute to the description, implementation, representation, integration, and interoperability of cybersecurity knowledge. However, they generally address cybersecurity concepts as predefined entities. Security properties define objectives, control frameworks prescribe measures, ontologies formalize

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: concepts and relationships, and mapping initiatives establish correspondences among existing frameworks. Comparatively little attention has been devoted to identifying whether such concepts originate from a smaller set of irreducible security concerns. More specifically, existing ontology-based approaches focus on defining concepts, establishing semantic relationships, and enabling interoperability among heterogeneous knowledge sources. Similarly, taxonomy and framework mapping initiatives seek to classify, organize, or align existing cybersecurity concepts. In contrast, relatively little research has investigated whether cybersecurity concepts themselves can be decomposed into a finite set of more fundamental concerns. This observation motivates the following research question: “Can cybersecurity concepts be represented as compositions of a finite set of irreducible and expressive security concerns?” To address this question, this work investigates the hypothesis that cybersecurity concepts may be decomposed into Atomic Security Concerns (ASCs). Unlike security properties, which define objectives, control frameworks, which prescribe measures, ontology models, which define and relate concepts, or framework mappings, which align existing conceptual structures, the proposed approach focuses on identifying candidate foundational elements from which cybersecurity concepts may be constructed. The objective is not to replace existing cybersecurity standards, frameworks, taxonomies, or ontologies. Instead, it is to explore whether a finite set of irreducible and expressive security concerns can provide a common foundation for representing higher-level cybersecurity concepts. Under this hypothesis, concepts such as security properties, security capabilities, security functions, security domains, and security controls may be represented as compositions of Atomic Security Concerns, supporting the construction of a formal language capable of expressing cybersecurity knowledge in a consistent and traceable manner. 3 Atomic Security Concerns The hypothesis proposed in this paper is that cybersecurity knowledge may be represented through a finite set of foundational elements referred to as Atomic Security Concerns (ASCs). Hence, Atomic Security Concerns (ASCs) are proposed as a common abstraction layer for the representation of cybersecurity concepts, independently of their domain, nature, or level of granularity. Before defining Atomic Security Concerns, it is first necessary to establish the broader notion of a Security Concern, as Atomic Security Concerns represent a specific category of Security Concerns characterized by the property of atomicity.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: 3.1 Security Concerns Cybersecurity knowledge is commonly expressed through concepts such as security properties, security controls, security requirements, security risks, security capabilities, security functions, and security architectures. Although these concepts differ in purpose, scope, and level of abstraction, they frequently address underlying security-related matters that motivate cybersecurity decisions, objectives, and activities. In this work, a Security Concern is defined as a security-related matter, objective, condition, capability, property, or expectation that stakeholders seek to establish, preserve, verify, enforce, or protect within a cybersecurity context. Security Concerns are independent of specific technologies, implementation mechanisms, standards, frameworks, or organizational structures. Instead, they represent the underlying security considerations that recur across different cybersecurity concepts and contexts. For example, Authentication may be analyzed as a composite Security Concern. In order to authenticate an entity, a system must first establish the Identity being claimed and then verify the Authenticity of that claim. Under this interpretation, Authentication can be represented as the combination of the concerns Identity and Authenticity. Similarly, Confidentiality may be viewed as a composite concern. Confidentiality requires information to remain secret from unauthorized parties while ensuring that access to the information is restricted to authorized entities. Under this interpretation, Confidentiality can be represented as the combination of the concerns Secret and Access. Non-Repudiation provides a third example. Demonstrating that an action cannot later be denied generally requires the ability to associate the action with an Identity, to maintain Traceability of the action, and to preserve Evidence supporting that association. Under this interpretation, non-repudiation can be represented as the combination of Identity, Traceability, and Evidence. These examples suggest that some Security Concerns may themselves be composed of other concerns. Consequently, not every Security Concern should be assumed to be fundamental. This observation motivates the introduction of Atomic Security Concerns. Table 1 provides illustrative examples of Security Concerns and potential decompositions into more fundamental concerns.
