The validity of such decompositions and the atomic status of the underlying concerns are examined through the principles and criteria introduced later in this paper. 3.2 Atomic Security Concerns

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: An Atomic Security Concern (ASC) is a Security Concern that cannot be further decomposed into more fundamental Security Concerns without loss of security semantics. The notion of atomicity adopted in this work is semantic rather than technical. A concern is not considered atomic because it is simple, widely used, or represented at a lower level of abstraction. Instead, a concern is considered atomic when no decomposition into more fundamental Security Concerns can preserve its cybersecurity meaning. For illustrative purposes, consider the concept of Authentication. Authentication is a meaningful cybersecurity concept and therefore constitutes a Security Concern. However, if authentication can be systematically represented as the combination of Identity and Authenticity, then Authentication should be regarded as a composite Security Concern rather than an Atomic Security Concern. Similarly, if Confidentiality can be represented as the combination of Secret and Access, then Confidentiality is better understood as a higher-level Security Concern derived from more fundamental concerns. Likewise, if Non-Repudiation can be represented through the concerns Identity, Traceability, and Evidence, it should also be regarded as a composite Security Concern.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: By contrast, concerns such as Identity, Authenticity, Secret, Traceability, Evidence, Privilege, or Trust may be considered candidate Atomic Security Concerns if they cannot be decomposed into more fundamental Security Concerns without loss of security semantics. Whether these concerns are truly atomic remains an open question and requires evaluation through the identification criteria proposed in this work. The proposed model assumes the following relationship: 1. Every Atomic Security Concern is a Security Concern. 2. A Security Concern may be either atomic or composite. 3. A composite Security Concern can be represented as a composition of one or more Atomic Security Concerns. Under this model, Authentication, Confidentiality, and Non-Repudiation are treated as composite Security Concerns because they can be represented through combinations of more fundamental concerns. In contrast, Identity, Authenticity, Secret, Traceability, and Evidence are treated as candidate Atomic Security Concerns pending evaluation against the atomicity principles introduced in the following section. The relationship can therefore be summarized as: Atomic Security Concerns ⊂ Security Concerns All Atomic Security Concerns are Security Concerns, but not all Security Concerns are Atomic Security Concerns. The distinction between Security Concerns and Atomic Security Concerns is analogous to the distinction between molecules and atoms in chemistry. A molecule may be decomposed into more fundamental elements while preserving its scientific interpretation. Atoms, by contrast, represent the smallest units considered fundamental within the model. Similarly, composite Security Concerns may be represented as combinations of more fundamental concerns, while Atomic Security Concerns represent candidate foundational elements from which cybersecurity concepts may be derived. Under the hypothesis proposed in this paper, Atomic Security Concerns constitute the basic vocabulary of a cybersecurity language. Higher-level concepts such as security properties, security capabilities, security functions, security domains, and security controls may therefore be represented as compositions of one or more Atomic Security Concerns. The following sections introduce the principles of atomicity and the criteria used to identify candidate Atomic Security Concerns. 3.3 Atomicity Principles The identification of Atomic Security Concerns requires a definition of atomicity that can be applied consistently across cybersecurity concepts. Without such principles, the distinction between composite Security Concerns and Atomic Security Concerns would remain subjective and dependent on individual interpretation.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: In this work, atomicity is evaluated from a semantic perspective rather than a technical, organizational, or implementation perspective. A Security Concern is not considered atomic because it is frequently used, because it appears at a low level of abstraction, or because it is associated with a specific technology or control. Instead, atomicity depends on whether the concern can be meaningfully represented through more fundamental Security Concerns without loss of cybersecurity semantics. Three principles are proposed to evaluate the atomicity of a Security Concern. 3.3.1 Principle 1: Decomposability A Security Concern should not be considered atomic if it can be consistently represented as a composition of other Security Concerns. Example: Authentication Authentication may be represented as: Authentication = Identity + Authenticity Authentication therefore represents a composite Security Concern because its meaning can be expressed through more fundamental concerns. Example: Non-Repudiation Non-Repudiation may be represented as: Non-Repudiation = Identity + Traceability + Evidence The concern can therefore be decomposed into constituent concerns while preserving its cybersecurity meaning.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: If a concern can be represented through a meaningful combination of other Security Concerns, it should be regarded as a composite Security Concern rather than an Atomic Security Concern. 3.3.2 Principle 2: Preservation of Security Semantics A decomposition is only valid if the resulting concerns preserve the original cybersecurity meaning of the concept being decomposed. Example: Valid Decomposition Authentication may be decomposed into: Identity + Authenticity The resulting concerns collectively preserve the essential meaning of authentication because authentication requires both an asserted identity and verification that the identity claim is genuine. Example: Invalid Decomposition

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: Authentication cannot reasonably be decomposed into: Identity + Access Although access control frequently follows authentication, the notion of access does not capture the semantic meaning of verifying the authenticity of an identity claim. Similarly, Confidentiality cannot be reduced to: Secret because confidentiality also requires restrictions on access to information. Hence, a decomposition is acceptable only when the resulting concerns preserve the complete cybersecurity meaning of the original concern. Decompositions that omit essential semantics should be rejected. 3.3.3 Principle 3: Reusability Across Concepts A candidate Atomic Security Concern should appear repeatedly across multiple cybersecurity concepts and contexts. Example: Identity Identity appears in several concepts: • Authentication • Identity Governance • Federated Identity Management • Digital Signatures • Non-Repudiation • Privileged Access Management The repeated occurrence of Identity across multiple concepts suggests that it captures a fundamental aspect of cybersecurity knowledge. Example : Traceability Traceability appears in: • Auditing • Monitoring • Logging • Forensics • Non-Repudiation • Incident Investigation Again, the concern is reusable across multiple domains and use cases. The more broadly a concern is reused across cybersecurity concepts, the more likely it is to represent a foundational semantic element rather than a contextual concept.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: 3.3.4 Atomicity Evaluation Based on the preceding principles, a Security Concern may be considered a candidate Atomic Security Concern when: 1. It cannot be consistently decomposed into more fundamental Security Concerns. 2. Any attempted decomposition results in loss of security semantics. 3. The concern is reusable across multiple cybersecurity concepts and contexts. Conversely, a Security Concern should be regarded as composite when it can be represented as a meaningful combination of more fundamental concerns while preserving its cybersecurity semantics. The following examples illustrate the application of these principles. Example: Authentication Authentication= Identity + Authenticity Composite Security Concern because it satisfies Principle 1. Example: Confidentiality Confidentiality = Secret + Access Composite Security Concern because a valid decomposition exists. Example: Identity No decomposition has been identified that preserves the complete cybersecurity meaning of Identity. Furthermore, Identity appears in numerous cybersecurity concepts. So, Identity can be a Candidate Atomic Security Concern subject to further validation. Example: Traceability No accepted decomposition has been identified while maintaining the meaning of Traceability. Traceability is also reused across auditing, monitoring, forensics, investigation, and accountability-related concepts. So, Traceability can be a Candidate Atomic Security Concern subject to further validation. These principles do not guarantee that a particular concern is atomic. Rather, they provide a systematic basis for evaluating candidate Atomic Security Concerns and distinguishing them from higher-level composite concerns. In this work, atomicity is therefore treated as a research hypothesis rather than an established property. Formal validation methods, composition rules, and mathematical foundations remain subjects for future research.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: The next section applies these principles to develop an initial taxonomy of candidate Atomic Security Concerns. 4 Taxonomy of Atomic Security Concerns Having introduced the notions of Security Concern and Atomic Security Concern, the next step is to explore what candidate Atomic Security Concerns might constitute a foundational cybersecurity vocabulary. The objective of this section is not to establish a definitive or exhaustive taxonomy of Atomic Security Concerns. Rather, it proposes an initial set of candidate concerns intended to illustrate the Atomic Security Concern hypothesis and demonstrate how a broad range of cybersecurity concepts may be represented through compositions of more fundamental concerns. The candidate concerns presented in this section were identified through the examination of recurring concepts appearing across cybersecurity properties, controls, risks, requirements, capabilities, functions, and architectural patterns. Particular attention was given to concerns that appear repeatedly across different cybersecurity contexts and that appear difficult to decompose without significant loss of security semantics. The resulting taxonomy should therefore be viewed as illustrative rather than normative. Future research may refine, expand, merge, or redefine individual concerns based on further theoretical and empirical investigation. 4.1 Candidate Atomic Security Concerns Table 1 presents the candidate Atomic Security Concerns proposed in this work. Candidate Atomic Security Concern Description Identity The concern that entities can be uniquely distinguished, represented, and referenced within a cybersecurity context. Authenticity The concern that a claimed identity, source, origin, or assertion is genuine and can be verified. Access The concern that interactions with resources are permitted, restricted, or denied according to defined conditions. Privilege The concern that permissions, authorities, or capabilities are assigned to an entity. Secret The concern that information remains unknown or undisclosed to unauthorized entities.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: Integrity The concern that information, systems, processes, or states remain accurate, complete, and unaltered except through authorized actions. Trust The concern that sufficient confidence exists regarding the expected behavior of an entity, system, process, assertion, or relationship. Traceability The concern that actions, events, decisions, and state changes can be followed and associated with their origins over time. Evidence The concern that information exists to support, validate, or demonstrate a claim, action, event, or conclusion. Availability The concern that systems, services, functions, or information remain usable when required. Recovery The concern that systems, services, data, or operations can be restored following disruption, failure, or compromise. Table 1. Candidate Atomic Security Concerns The concerns listed above should be interpreted as candidate Atomic Security Concerns rather than validated atomic elements. Their inclusion reflects the hypothesis explored in this paper and serves as a basis for investigating how cybersecurity concepts may be represented through composition. Several observations emerge from the proposed taxonomy. First, the candidate concerns are intentionally independent of specific technologies, standards, frameworks, or implementation mechanisms. For example, the concern Identity remains applicable regardless of whether identities are managed through directories, certificates, federation protocols, or decentralized identity systems. Second, the proposed concerns are intended to capture cybersecurity semantics rather than cybersecurity mechanisms. Technologies such as encryption, multifactor authentication, logging systems, certificate authorities, or backup platforms are not considered Atomic Security Concerns because they constitute mechanisms that protect, support, enforce, or operationalize underlying concerns. Third, the candidate concerns appear repeatedly across multiple cybersecurity domains. For example, Identity appears in authentication, identity governance, privileged access management, digital signatures, and non-repudiation. Similarly, Traceability appears across auditing, monitoring, incident response, and forensic investigations. Finally, the proposed taxonomy should be viewed as a starting point for discussion rather than a finalized classification scheme. Additional concerns may emerge, some concerns

content: may ultimately prove to be composite, and alternative decompositions may arise as the Atomic Security Concern hypothesis is further investigated. 4.2 Illustrative Compositions Across Cybersecurity Concepts The relevance of the proposed taxonomy lies not only in the candidate concerns themselves but also in their potential ability to represent diverse cybersecurity concepts through composition. Security Properties The first category considered is security properties. Security properties represent desired security outcomes and are commonly used to define protection objectives. The examples below illustrate how such properties may be expressed through combinations of candidate Atomic Security Concerns. Security Property Illustrative ASC Composition Authentication Identity + Authenticity Confidentiality Secret + Access Non-Repudiation Identity + Traceability + Evidence Authorization Identity + Privilege + Access Accountability Identity + Traceability + Evidence Table 2. Illustrative Security Properties Security Risks Security risks provide a different perspective. Rather than representing desired outcomes, they describe situations in which one or more concerns may be threatened, compromised, or not adequately preserved. The following examples illustrate how risks can be associated with underlying concerns. Security Risk Threat against Illustrative ASC Composition Account Takeover Identity + Authenticity Unauthorized Data Disclosure Secret + Access Privilege Escalation Privilege + Access Log Tampering Traceability + Evidence Service Outage Availability Data Corruption Integrity

The examples below illustrate how controls can be viewed as operational implementations addressing one or more candidate concerns. title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: Many cybersecurity functions and capabilities encompass broader operational activities than individual controls or technologies. Nevertheless, they can still be interpreted as compositions of candidate concerns. The following examples illustrate this perspective. Security Function / Capability Illustrative ASC Composition Identity and Access Management (IAM) Identity + Authenticity + Privilege + Access Privileged Access Management (PAM) Identity + Privilege + Access + Traceability Security Monitoring Traceability + Evidence + Integrity Incident Response Traceability + Evidence + Recovery Key Management Secret + Trust + Integrity Business Continuity Management Availability + Recovery Table 6. Illustrative Security Functions and Capabilities Organizational Teams and Specialized Capabilities The abstraction is not limited to technical concepts. Organizational teams and specialized capabilities can also be interpreted through the concerns they are responsible for managing, operating, or preserving. The examples below illustrate this possibility. Team / Organizational Capability Illustrative ASC Composition Identity and Access Management Team Identity + Authenticity + Privilege + Access Security Operations Center (SOC) Traceability + Evidence + Integrity Incident Response Team Traceability + Evidence + Recovery Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Team Authenticity + Trust + Secret Disaster Recovery Team Availability + Recovery Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) Capability Traceability + Evidence + Accountability Table 7. Illustrative Organizational Capabilities Several observations emerge from the preceding examples. First, the same candidate Atomic Security Concerns appear across multiple categories of cybersecurity concepts. For example, Identity and Authenticity are present in security properties such as Authentication, security risks such as Account Takeover, security controls such as Multi-Factor Authentication, and organizational capabilities such as Identity and Access Management.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: Second, security controls, technologies, implementation measures, and organizational capabilities do not necessarily introduce additional foundational concerns. Instead, they appear to protect, support, operationalize, or enforce one or more underlying concerns. Third, security risks can be interpreted as threats directed toward specific concerns, while security controls and technical measures can be interpreted as mechanisms intended to preserve those same concerns. These observations support the central hypothesis of this work: a relatively small set of Atomic Security Concerns may provide a common vocabulary capable of representing a broad spectrum of cybersecurity concepts, including properties, risks, controls, technologies, functions, and organizational capabilities. 5 Atomic Security Concern as a Foundation of a Cybersecurity Language The Atomic Security Concern hypothesis extends beyond the identification of candidate foundational concerns. Its broader implication is the possibility that cybersecurity knowledge may be represented through a common language built upon a finite set of foundational concerns. The objective of this section is not to define a formal cybersecurity language. Rather, it explores how Atomic Security Concerns may provide the vocabulary of such a language and how cybersecurity concepts may emerge through combinations of those concerns. 5.1 Atomic Security Concerns as a Cybersecurity Vocabulary A language requires a vocabulary from which more complex expressions can be constructed. Natural languages rely on words. Chemistry relies on atoms and molecules. Similarly, the Atomic Security Concern hypothesis proposes that cybersecurity knowledge may be expressed through a finite vocabulary of foundational concerns. Under this perspective, candidate Atomic Security Concerns such as Identity, Authenticity, Access, Privilege, Secret, Integrity, Trust, Traceability, Evidence, Availability, and Recovery do not represent complete cybersecurity concepts. Instead, they provide the elementary cybersecurity vocabulary from which more complex concepts may be expressed. For example, concepts such as Authentication, Confidentiality, Non-Repudiation, Privileged Access Management, Multi-Factor Authentication, and Digital Signatures can be viewed as different expressions composed from a common vocabulary of concerns.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: The significance of this perspective is that cybersecurity knowledge may be described through a relatively small set of recurring concerns rather than through an ever-growing collection of independent concepts. 5.2 From Vocabulary to Expressions If Atomic Security Concerns constitute the vocabulary of a cybersecurity language, then higher-level cybersecurity concepts may be viewed as expressions constructed from that vocabulary. For example: Authentication= Identity + Authenticity And, Confidentiality = Secret + Access And, Non-Repudiation = Identity + Traceability + Evidence Under this view, cybersecurity concepts are not treated as isolated entities. Instead, they represent different combinations of recurring concerns. This perspective provides a possible explanation for the observation that many cybersecurity concepts share common foundations despite belonging to different domains, standards, technologies, or organizational practices. The examples presented in Section 4 suggest that the same vocabulary may be used to represent security properties, security risks, security controls, security measures, organizational capabilities, and specialized security teams. Consequently, concepts that are traditionally described through separate models may be interpreted as different expressions generated from the same underlying vocabulary. 5.3 Toward Security Reasoning One potential implication of representing cybersecurity concepts through Atomic Security Concerns is the ability to reason about relationships among concepts using their constituent concerns. For example, two cybersecurity artifacts may share one or more concerns. Such common concerns may indicate conceptual overlap, shared objectives, or complementary relationships between the artifacts.

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: Consider the following examples: Authentication = Identity + Authenticity And, Multi-Factor Authentication = Identity + Authenticity Both concepts share the concerns Identity and Authenticity. This observation explains why Multi-Factor Authentication contributes directly to strengthening Authentication. Similarly: Unauthorized Data Disclosure = Threat against Secret + Access And, Encryption= Protection of Secret Both concepts are related through the concern Secret, suggesting a direct conceptual relationship between the risk and the measure intended to mitigate it. More generally, concepts represented through Atomic Security Concerns may be compared according to: 5.3.1 Shared Concerns Two concepts may share common concerns. Illustratively: Authentication = Identity + Authenticity And, Identity Governance = Identity + Privilege + Traceability Both concepts share the concern: Identity which suggests a semantic relationship between them. 5.3.2 Aggregated Concerns Multiple concepts may collectively contribute to a broader set of concerns.

authors: Hanane Houmani
content: For example: Encryption = Secret And, Access Control = Access Together they contribute to: Secret + Access which corresponds to the concerns represented by Confidentiality. 5.3.3 Inclusion Relationship Some concepts may encompass all concerns represented by another concept. For example: Authentication = Identity + Authenticity And, Identity and Access Management = Identity + Authenticity + Privilege + Access The concerns associated with Authentication are entirely contained within those associated with Identity and Access Management, suggesting that Authentication forms part of the broader IAM capability. These examples illustrate how cybersecurity concepts may potentially be analyzed through their underlying concerns rather than exclusively through framework-specific terminology. Although this work does not introduce a formal reasoning model, the proposed perspective suggests that concern-based representations may support more explicit and traceable relationships among cybersecurity concepts. 6 Future Work This work introduces the Atomic Security Concern hypothesis as a conceptual foundation for investigating whether cybersecurity knowledge can be expressed through a finite set of foundational concerns. Several directions for future research emerge from this initial exploration. A first direction consists of refining and validating the proposed taxonomy of candidate Atomic Security Concerns. This includes evaluating the completeness of the taxonomy, investigating alternative decompositions, and assessing whether additional concerns are

title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
authors: Hanane Houmani
content: required to represent cybersecurity concepts across different domains, architectures, and frameworks. A second direction involves the formalization of the proposed concepts and their relationships. Future work will investigate formal definitions of Atomic Security Concerns, composition mechanisms, and concern-based reasoning using mathematical foundations. Such formalization may enable the development of a rigorous conceptual model in which cybersecurity concepts can be represented, analyzed, and compared through well-defined operations. A third direction consists of exploring the construction of a formal cybersecurity language founded on Atomic Security Concerns. In such a language, Atomic Security Concerns would constitute the vocabulary, composition rules would define the syntax, and the meaning associated with concerns and their compositions would provide the semantics. This may ultimately support formal reasoning, knowledge representation, ontology development, automated analysis, and AI-assisted cybersecurity decision-making. 7 Conclusion This paper introduced the concepts of Security Concerns and Atomic Security Concerns (ASCs) and explored the hypothesis that cybersecurity knowledge may be represented through a finite set of foundational concerns. An initial taxonomy of candidate Atomic Security Concerns was proposed, together with illustrative examples demonstrating how cybersecurity properties, risks, controls, measures, capabilities, and organizational functions may be represented as compositions of recurring concerns. The proposed perspective suggests that Atomic Security Concerns may provide a common vocabulary capable of describing cybersecurity concepts that are traditionally represented through different abstraction models and frameworks. By focusing on underlying concerns rather than framework-specific constructs, the approach offers a potential foundation for a more consistent, traceable, and interoperable representation of cybersecurity knowledge. The contribution of this work is primarily conceptual. Rather than formally proving the existence or atomicity of individual concerns, it introduces a research hypothesis and an initial framework for investigating the foundations of a cybersecurity language. If further validated and formalized, Atomic Security Concerns may ultimately serve as the vocabulary of a formal cybersecurity language, with composition mechanisms providing its syntax and concern semantics providing its meaning. Such a language could offer a unified basis for representing, reasoning about, and communicating cybersecurity knowledge across domains, frameworks, and organizational contexts.

content: A Category-Selective Encryption Framework for Privacy Protection of UAV Images 1st Ting Yan Dartmouth College Hanover, NH 03755, USA ting.yan.gr@dartmouth.edu 2nd Minghui Shang School of Information Science and Engineering University of Jinan Jinan 250022, China 2870062251@qq.com 3rd Haolang Sun School of Information Science and Engineering University of Jinan Jinan 250022, China lannistersun@126.com 4th Xu Wang School of Information Science and Engineering University of Jinan Jinan 250022, China ise wangx@ujn.edu.cn 5th Yamin Han* Quancheng Laboratory Jinan 250100, China hr-hanym@qcl.edu.cn 6th Mingze He Department of Computer Science and Technology Sichuan Police College Luzhou, 646000, China mingzebox@163.com Abstract—Imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems increasingly raises privacy concerns, as UAV aerial surveillance routinely captures sensitive objects such as pedes- trians and vehicles alongside ordinary scene content. Existing privacy-preserving approaches typically employ class-agnostic saliency detection to indiscriminately obfuscate all visually salient regions, leading to unnecessary information loss and hindering downstream scene analysis. This paper proposes a category-selective encryption framework for privacy-preserving UAV surveillance. The core advance over prior class-agnostic ap- proaches is semantic-level selectivity: the system first recognizes what is present in the scene via an 80-class detector, then encrypts only user-specified sensitive categories while leaving non-sensitive objects and background intact for downstream analytics. The framework supports two complementary encryption schemes: Thumbnail-Preserving Encryption (TPE), which applies adaptive pixelation with a learnable blend parameter and recovers content through a jointly trained Enhanced U-Net, and XOR stream cipher encryption, which offers parameter-free, mathematically exact reversibility. The architectural design, composite loss for- mulation, and joint training methodology are presented in detail, establishing a foundation for practical privacy-preserving UAV surveillance that balances protection strength and scene utility. Index Terms—Category-selective Encryption, Privacy Protec- tion for UAV Images, Object Detection, TPE, XOR Stream Cipher I. INTRODUCTION With the rapid development of the low-altitude economy, UAV aerial photography, as a high-efficiency data acquisition technology with high-resolution imaging capability, has been widely used in agricultural monitoring [1], urban planning [2], and environmental inspection [3]. However, such aerial images usually contain sensitive private information including human faces, pedestrians, and vehicle license plates. If these unprocessed images are leaked during air-to-ground wireless transmission or cloud storage, personal privacy will be ex- posed, which will lead to privacy breaches [4]. Moreover, with the continuous advancement of computer vision technologies, deep learning algorithms can accurately identify human con- tours and behavioral activities in aerial images [5]. To mitigate the privacy risks of aerial images, researchers have put forward a variety of image privacy protection schemes [6]. In recent years, a growing number of dedicated encryption algorithms have been developed specifically for UAV images. Shafique et al. [7] proposed an encryption scheme combining DNA encoding and bit-plane extraction to secure high-resolution UAV-captured images during transmis- sion. Zhou et al. [8] designed an encryption and compression algorithm based on two-dimensional hyperchaos for aerial images collected by agricultural UAVs. For smart agriculture scenarios, Zhou et al. [9] constructed an image protection scheme that optimizes chaotic S-boxes via simulated annealing and affine transformation. Aiming at facial privacy protection in UAV remote sensing images, Wen et al. [10] built a hybrid encryption framework integrating chaotic systems and DNA cryptography. Nevertheless, nearly all of the above schemes adopt a single fixed encryption mode. They fail to achieve discriminative selective encryption for semantic targets such as pedestrians, vehicles and public background areas, so they can- not adapt to diverse UAV patrol scenarios. Other mainstream privacy protection schemes rely on universal visual saliency detection, which applies blurring and encryption uniformly to all salient regions in an image [11]. These schemes cause massive loss of valid scene information and severely interfere with subsequent data analysis. To meet the requirements of personal information protection laws and low-altitude data security regulations, there is an urgent need to develop a UAV aerial image privacy protection scheme that supports category-selective processing while bal- ancing privacy protection and scene usability. To this end, this paper proposes a category-selective encryption framework for UAV images. It constructs a complete closed-loop processing pipeline of object detection, category-selective encryption, de- cryption and restoration, while maximizing the preservation of complete scene information under privacy security guarantees. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 1) The proposed framework employs a YOLO11 multi- category object detector to identify all 80 classes of targets in the image and applies encryption only to user- defined sensitive categories. 2) The system integrates two pluggable and complemen- tary encryption schemes, TPE and XOR stream cipher encryption. This design effectively accommodates the varying privacy protection requirements across different UAV aerial photography scenarios. 3) A collaborative optimization mechanism covering de- tection, encryption, and restoration is established with a multi-dimensional composite loss function to sig- nificantly improve the decryption quality of the TPE scheme. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews relevant studies. Section III elaborates on the spe- cific implementation of the encryption framework we design. Section IV presents experimental results and analysis. Finally, Section V concludes this paper and outlines future research directions. II. RELATED WORKS With the increasing popularity of UAV aerial photography applications, privacy security issues arising from aerial images have attracted widespread attention. This section introduces the TPE algorithm and XOR stream cipher encryption tech- nology. A. TPE To reduce the risk of image data leakage in cloud envi- ronments, traditional schemes encrypt images into visually meaningless noise. However, this approach renders ciphertext images completely unreadable and fails to support cloud- side tasks such as image retrieval, management and analysis. To address this limitation, Wright et al. [12] proposed a novel encryption paradigm that balances privacy protection and image usability, namely TPE. A standard TPE scheme generally divides the original image into multiple sub-blocks and encrypts each sub-block independently while retaining the pixel average of each block to preserve the overall visual outline of the image. The trade-off between encryption security and image usability can be flexibly adjusted by modifying the block size. With the advancement of relevant research, existing TPE techniques are categorized into exact TPE [13], [14] and approximate TPE [15], [16] according to whether the ciphertext thumbnail is strictly consistent with the original thumbnail. Early studies mostly adopted traditional signal pro- cessing and cryptographic operations, maintaining thumbnail structures via block permutation, pixel replacement and mean value preservation to strike a balance between security and usability. In recent years, deep learning has achieved remark- able progress in image modeling and generation, motivating researchers to adopt learnable models to fit the complex map- ping between privacy protection effects and visual usability of images. Following this research line, Chai et al. [17] designed a GAN-based TPE-GAN scheme that greatly improves the usability of ciphertext images, yet there remains room for further optimization in the visual reconstruction quality of encrypted and decrypted images. B. XOR Stream Cipher Fundamentals XOR stream cipher implements encryption and decryption by performing bitwise XOR operations between the pseudo- random key stream and the binary sequences of image pixels. It relies on the inherent symmetric and reversible property of the bitwise XOR operation: for any pixel data d and key stream k, the equation d ⊕k ⊕k = d (1) always holds. The original image can be losslessly restored using the identical seed key [18]. With low computational overhead, this algorithm is well suited for lightweight terminal devices. However, traditional XOR stream ciphers only support full-image or fixed-region encryption and lack the capability of semantic target screening. After encryption, the overall visual information of the image is completely lost, making it difficult to balance privacy security and image usability. III. PROPOSED SCHEME This section proposes a category-selective encryption frame- work oriented to object detection, which forms a closed- loop pipeline of object detection, category-selective encryp- tion, decryption/image restoration as shown in Fig. 1. The framework consists of three core modules: a multi-class object detection module based on YOLO11, a TPE module, and an XOR stream cipher encryption module. An independent decryption and restoration module is matched to the above encryption branches, and a multi-stage joint training strategy is specially designed only for the TPE branch. The detailed implementation schemes of each module are elaborated as follows. A. Object Detection Module This module adopts the lightweight multi-class detector YOLO11n to identify and categorize all objects within aerial scenes, which is fine-tuned on the VisDrone2019 dataset [19]. The detector outputs bounding boxes for all detected targets. Users can customize a set of sensitive semantic categories to be encrypted at runtime; only objects falling into the designated sensitive classes are processed with encryption. Bounding boxes screened by the category filter are normalized to a unified coordinate range for subsequent mask generation, enabling semantic-aware selective encryption.

Overall Flowchart of the Proposed Scheme. B. Selective Encryption Schemes The proposed framework integrates two interchangeable encryption schemes with fundamentally different mechanisms, namely TPE and XOR stream cipher encryption. The two schemes share a unified input interface. Only sensitive pixel regions covered by detection boxes are modified, while all non- sensitive background pixels remain identical to the original image. 1) TPE Encryption: TPE performs pixelation transforma- tion on sensitive target regions, and the original visual content can be restored by a well-trained Enhanced U-Net decoder. The encryption generates mosaic blur via average pooling and nearest-neighbor upsampling. A learnable blending coefficient α is introduced to adjust the weight ratio between pixelated patches and original patches, which automatically balances privacy protection strength and image restoration quality dur- ing joint training. For each bounding box containing sensitive regions, the encryption pipeline consists of three steps: a) Adaptive Block Size Calculation: The kernel size of each block is dynamically calculated according to the width and height of the target box: k = max  kmin, min(h, w) d  (2) where the minimum block size kmin = 6 and the scaling factor d = 8. Larger blocks are used for larger targets to achieve stronger mosaic blur, while distant small targets use finer blocks, ensuring consistent visual encryption effects for objects of all scales. b) Pixelation Processing: The image patch Ptarget inside the bounding box is processed by average pooling with identi- cal kernel size and stride k, then upsampled back to the origi- nal patch resolution (h, w) via nearest-neighbor interpolation. Average pooling compresses each k × k pixel block into a single average color value, and the subsequent upsampling recovers the spatial size of the region to form standard mosaic texture. c) Learnable Blending Fusion: The encrypted patch is obtained by linear weighted fusion of the pixelated patch and the original patch, where the weight is controlled by the learnable parameter α: Penc = α · Ppix + (1 −α) · Ptarget (3) α is constrained within the range [0, 1] in the forward prop- agation. When α = 1, the region is fully pixelated with the strongest privacy protection; when α = 0, the patch is identical to the original image without any encryption effect. 2) XOR Stream Cipher Encryption: The XOR stream ci- pher realizes encryption relying on the involution property of the bitwise XOR operation. Deterministic pseudo-random noise is generated from the user-specified secret key to ob- fuscate pixels in sensitive regions, which achieves mathemat- ically lossless reversibility without any neural network for restoration. The user-defined key string is mapped to a fixed- length seed through SHA-256 hashing. The seed initializes the PCG-64 pseudo-random number generator to produce a three-channel uniform noise map with the same resolution as the input image. The whole noise map is generated at one time rather than box by box, which guarantees consistent encryption results even when target boxes overlap. A binary mask M ∈{0, 255}H×W is constructed, where pixels inside sensitive boxes are set to 255 and background pixels are set to 0. Bitwise XOR operation is only conducted on pixels marked by the mask: Y[i, M = 255] = X[i, M = 255] ⊕N[M = 255] (4) where X and Y denote the original uint8-format image and encrypted image respectively. Background pixels uncovered by the mask retain their original values. C. Decryption and Restoration Module This paper designs supporting decryption pipelines for TPE and XOR encryption branches to restore original content from encrypted images. 1) TPE Decryption: The learnable mosaic blur of the TPE module lacks a straightforward mathematical inverse transformation. An enhanced U-Net decoder is thus utilized to recover texture information from masked sensitive regions. The network receives the encrypted image Ienc as input. Its multi-scale skip connections suppress mosaic artifacts and re- store target details without altering background pixels, yielding the restored output Irest. Joint training is performed on the U- Net decoder and TPE module to maintain reliable restoration quality for targets of diverse scales and different encryption intensity α. 2) XOR Stream Cipher Decryption: Relying on the invo- lution property of bitwise XOR, decryption follows the same workflow as encryption. The original secret key regenerates PCG-64 pseudo-random noise, and the encryption mask serves to localize sensitive pixels. Performing XOR once more over masked regions recovers lossless uint8 pixel values without neural network computation, which enables lightweight de- cryption.

Joint Training Strategy A modular joint training scheme is adopted for the detec- tion, encryption and decryption modules. Gradient backpropa- gation optimization is only performed on the TPE encryption branch to balance detection accuracy, privacy protection per- formance and image restoration quality. 1) Parameter Freezing and Update Rules: The weights of the pre-trained YOLO11n detection network are fully frozen throughout joint training, so that the target local- ization and classification performance will not be disturbed by the encryption and restoration task. Only two types of parameters are updated during training: the learnable blending coefficient α of TPE and all weights of the Enhanced U- Net restoration network. This strategy drastically reduces the number of parameters to be optimized and cuts down GPU memory consumption during training. The binary mask M generated in the encryption stage is reused for loss calculation. Only sensitive pixels covered by the mask participate in loss computation and gradient backpropagation, while background pixels are excluded from optimization to guarantee consistency between the background area and the original image. 2) Loss Function Design: The overall joint loss is com- posed of a weighted sum of reconstruction loss and encryption regularization loss: Ltotal = Lrec + λαLα (5) where λα denotes the regularization weight, which is set to 0.6 in the experiments. a) Mask-Constrained Reconstruction Loss Lrec: L1 loss is utilized to optimize the restoration quality of sensitive regions, and pixel-wise error is only calculated within the masked encryption area: Lrec = (Irest −Igt) ⊙M

Comparative Analysis Existing saliency-driven privacy schemes, traditional region- selective encryption and basic object anonymization share two inherent limitations. Category-customized encryption for designated semantic targets cannot be realized, and most alternatives only support irreversible visual masking without complete high-fidelity recovery pipelines. Two classic full-image TPE algorithms, HF-TPE [15] and TPE-GAN [17], are taken as baselines for fair performance benchmarking of the proposed TPE and XOR encryption modules. As illustrated in Fig. 3, both baselines implement full-image encryption that triggers visual distortion on non- sensitive regions such as roads and buildings. Such distortion destroys inherent aerial scene features, impairs the perfor- mance of subsequent scene recognition tasks, and introduces substantial computational overhead. A favorable balance be- tween privacy preservation and image utility is attained by the presented framework through encryption limited to predefined sensitive objects only. Reconstruction quality of all algorithms is quantified in Table II with SSIM and PSNR metrics, where all approaches are categorized into cryptographic and deep learning-based groups. Satisfactory reconstruction perfor- mance is obtained by HF-TPE among cryptographic schemes. Benefiting from invertible XOR operations, the propsed XOR scheme branch delivers perfect lossless pixel reconstruction with an SSIM value of 1 and infinite PSNR. For deep learning- based TPE-GAN, its GAN encoder-decoder architecture gener- ates severe reconstruction artifacts and deteriorates the quality of decrypted outputs. By contrast, the proposed TPE scheme achieves outstanding reconstruction fidelity and effectively alleviates such severe distortion. Overall, redundant encryption over background regions is eliminated by both presented schemes. Furthermore, superior reconstruction performance against corresponding baselines within each technical category is achieved by the two proposed encryption branches. Detection Performance and Privacy Implications Quantitative reliability tests on the VisDrone test set [19] show that the pre-trained model achieves mAP@0.5 = 27.6% and mAP@0.5:0.95 = 15.5%, which is standard for lightweight detectors in complex UAV scenes with dense small objects and varying altitudes. Although distant tiny targets have limited recognizable details due to low resolution, privacy leakage may still occur through cross-frame contextual reasoning and temporal correlation analysis. Future research will mitigate these risks through more robust detection pipelines or unified joint optimization of detection and encryption.

The XOR pipeline is a handcrafted lightweight bitwise operation without neural network components, achieving only 0.5 ms latency for both encryption and decryption under the unified experimental environment. In the TPE branch, encryption and decryption show a clear latency gap: encryption uses only a manually defined hyperparameter α to control adaptive blurring intensity in sensitive areas, resulting in a low latency of approximately 1 ms. In contrast, TPE decryption employs a deep convolutional reconstruction network with 50.29 million trainable parameters to recover distorted texture details, incurring substantial matrix computation and memory access overhead and a latency of around 30 ms. Benefit- ing from target-selective encryption, both modules restrict computation to YOLO11n sensitive bounding boxes, thereby reducing the number of processed pixels. CONCLUSION This paper designs a dual-mode category-selective image encryption framework integrated with object detection. YOLO is utilized to locate sensitive targets, and TPE adaptive pix- elation encryption and XOR stream cipher encryption are separately adopted to realize regional privacy protection. The TPE scheme leverages a learnable blending coefficient to balance the masking effect and image readability, and relies on an enhanced U-Net for texture restoration; the XOR scheme achieves lightweight lossless encryption and decryption. Ex- perimental results demonstrate that the proposed scheme only encrypts targets of designated categories, which drastically reduces redundant computation. It simultaneously delivers visual privacy protection while preserving basic image content, making it suitable for real-time image transmission scenarios of UAVs. Future work will further optimize the network inference speed and encryption security strength, expand the applicable scope of the algorithm, and adopt more robust detection and joint detection-encryption optimization strategies to mitigate privacy leakage risks caused by undetected small, occluded or poorly illuminated sensitive objects. title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
section: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
content: Root cause analysis (RCA) of microservice failures has attracted many LLM agents whose investigation is hand-crafted, through standard operating procedures, fixed stages and role agents. Each is evaluated on its own data against few baselines, so it is unknown whether this design beats letting a capable model investigate on its own. We compare three simple harnesses that prescribe none of the model’s calls (one call over an evidence package, a SQL agent and the Codex coding agent) with five published LLM RCA agents and with statistical and causal methods on RCAtlas, 90 validated cases from eight public datasets, across six models and three reasoning efforts. The simple harnesses are the most accurate (PR@1 65–77% on three mid-tier models), ahead of the published agents (16–53%) and the non-LLM methods (6–39%), on every model on which both families were run. The published agents fix from a tenth to all of their model calls in the program, and a case study shows how these prescriptions skip the decisive evidence. A stronger model mainly improves reliability, a multi-turn harness mainly improves aptitude, and more reasoning effort changes accuracy by a few points at most while multiplying the time by up to seven. Among runs more accurate than the best non-LLM method, every Pareto-optimal run in cost or time uses a simple harness.

content: Failures in the microservices behind web services cascade across components, and operators must find the root cause among hundreds of services, pods and nodes from metrics, traces, logs and events ( Beyer et al., 2016 ; Zhou et al., 2021 ; Dang et al., 2019 ) . Three lines of work improve this task: RCA methods, from statistical and causal ranking ( Lin et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Ma et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Pham et al., 2024a ) to LLM agents; the LLMs underneath them; and general-purpose agent harnesses. A harness is the program around a model that feeds it data and carries out its actions. The simplest harness only feeds data, in a single call; richer ones let the model query the data, or write and run code as Codex ( OpenAI, 2026 ) does.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Published LLM RCA agents hand-craft the investigation with standard operating procedures, fixed stages, expert or role sub-agents and votes, so the program decides much of what is read and when ( Pei et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Muhammad et al., 2026 ) . Each is evaluated against a few baselines on one to three systems, often collected by its own authors, and benchmarks run one reference agent or none ( Fang et al., 2026a ; Cai et al., 2026 ) . Whether hand-crafting still pays off as models and harnesses improve is therefore unknown.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: We compare the three lines on the same cases. RCAtlas pools eight public RCA datasets into one format, screens 542 cases for validity and samples 90 across 23 scenarios. On it we run three simple harnesses that prescribe none of the model’s calls (one call over an evidence package, a SQL agent over the raw telemetry, and Codex), five published LLM agents, and statistical and causal methods, with six models, three reasoning efforts and one scorer. We change a method only where it cannot run on our data or has an implementation error.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Harnesses that leave the model free to choose what to look at and how to reason win (Figure 1 ). The simple harnesses reach PR@1 65–77% on three mid-tier models, ahead of the published agents (16–53%), which are mostly ahead of the non-LLM methods (6–39%). The trajectories show why: when the program decides what to read, it can skip the decisive evidence, such as a log line or a service that stops receiving calls. A stronger model mainly improves reliability, a multi-turn harness mainly improves aptitude, and more reasoning effort changes little. Among runs more accurate than the best non-LLM method, every Pareto-optimal run in cost or time uses a simple harness.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Classical RCA for microservices ranks components from telemetry by statistical deviation (NSigma, BARO ( Pham et al., 2024a ) , ϵ \epsilon -Diagnosis ( Shan et al., 2019 ) ), causal discovery and inference (CIRCA ( Li et al., 2022 ) , RCD ( Ikram et al., 2022 ) , DyCause ( Pan et al., 2021 ) , FaultInsight ( Bi et al., 2024 ) ), propagation on dependency graphs (MicroRCA ( Wu et al., 2020 ) , MicroRank ( Yu et al., 2021 ) ), or multi-source fusion (TORAI ( Pham et al., 2026 ) ). LLM-based methods mostly fix the investigation in the program: standard operating procedures the agent must follow (FoA ( Pei et al., 2025 ) ), a controller that never sees data and an executor that writes code (RCA-Agent ( Xu et al., 2025 ) ), observation management with expert sub-agents (RCAgent ( Wang et al., 2024 ) ), voting among role agents (mABC ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) ), one agent per trace span (RCLAgent-V2 ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) ), tree search with self-reflection (LATS-RCA ( Naakka et al., 2027 ) ), or program-side retrieval followed by one LLM reranking call (DecompRCA ( Muhammad et al., 2026 ) ). Failure studies trace recurrent errors to the shared agent architecture rather than the model ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , catalogue reasoning failures across agentic and non-agentic prompting ( Riddell et al., 2026 ) , and contrast successful and failed trajectories ( Lu et al., 2026 ) .

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Coding agents have grown into general harnesses such as Codex ( OpenAI, 2026 ) and Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2026 ) : the model decides what to do next and acts by writing and running code, with no task-specific procedure. For RCA, such a harness without any RCA design already outperforms purpose-built agents on OpenRCA and RCAEval ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . OpsHarness ( Huang et al., 2026 ) then adds a self-evolving layer that learns from labelled past incidents of the same system. We take the complementary view: we test simple harnesses without such a layer (Codex, a SQL agent and a single call) against prescribed pipelines and non-LLM methods on the same cases.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Model-wide evaluations rank models on many tasks and sub-capabilities; the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index ( Artificial Analysis, 2026 ) has recently added an RCA-style task suite, ITBench-AA ( Sebin et al., 2026 ) , built from ITBench ( Jha et al., 2025 ) . RCA-specific datasets include RCAEval ( Pham et al., 2025 ) , OpenRCA ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026a ) , LEMMA-RCA ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , the AIOps challenge data and RCA-100 ( Cai et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2026 ) , and a fault-propagation-aware TrainTicket benchmark ( Fang et al., 2026b ) . Each covers one to three systems, and each evaluates a narrow slice of methods: OpenRCA 2.0 runs one reference agent across models, AgenticOpsEval ( Cai et al., 2026 ) releases data and a scoring protocol without method results, and new methods are often evaluated mainly on data collected by their own authors ( Pham et al., 2024a ; Pham et al., 2026 ) . Audits show that simple rules or telemetry-free priors reach high scores on some of them ( Fang et al., 2026b ; Buljić, 2026 ) . RCAtlas pools eight of these sources, screens every case for validity, and evaluates simple harnesses, published LLM agents and non-LLM methods on the same cases with one scorer.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Evidence from other domains questions elaborate agent pipelines. A fixed localise–repair–validate pipeline competed with software-engineering agents at a fraction of the cost ( Xia et al., 2025 ) ; splitting a task across conversational turns degrades LLMs mainly through lower reliability ( Laban et al., 2026 ) ; and input length alone can hurt even when retrieval is perfect ( Du et al., 2025 ) . More broadly, general methods that scale with computation tend to overtake hand-engineered knowledge ( Sutton, 2019 ) . We test this question directly on RCA.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The systems under test are microservice applications on Kubernetes. Their entities are services, the pods and containers that run them, the nodes (hosts) that run the pods, databases and middleware, and the operations a service exposes. Four kinds of telemetry are recorded: metrics , time series per entity such as CPU and memory use, request counts, error rates and latency (timestamp, entity, metric name, value); traces , one span per call between operations (trace and span identifiers, parent span, operation, duration, status), which reveal who calls whom and where errors and delays arise; logs , timestamped lines per pod with a level and a free-text message; and events , Kubernetes records such as restarts, evictions or scheduling failures. Each case also carries an inventory of entities and their relations (calls, deployment, placement).

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: A case gives an incident’s flagged period, a period known to precede it, the candidate inventory and the telemetry of both periods. The method returns a ranked list of root-cause entities; we score the first five. Labels name one root-cause entity per case (three cases have two), at the level its dataset annotates: service, pod or node (we count databases as services and hosts as nodes).

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Datasets label at different levels, and an answer may be finer than the label, such as a pod of the faulty service. Before matching, we therefore map each answered entity upward: it is replaced by itself and those of its parents in the inventory (container, pod, service) that lie at the levels the dataset annotates. Duplicates are then dropped, the first five distinct entities form the answer list, and they are compared with the labels by name. For example, when a dataset labels services, an answer naming a pod of cart counts as cart, and a second pod of cart further down the list adds nothing. Methods that rank metric columns, as most non-LLM methods do, are mapped the same way through the entity that owns each column. Each answer can match at most one root cause.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The sources span nine systems, from Online Boutique, Sock Shop and TrainTicket to a bank, a telecom system and a cloud platform, with faults injected by chaos tools, by challenge organisers, or in drills on a managed Kubernetes service. Each case is converted to the same tables: an entity inventory with call, deployment and placement relations, and the metrics, traces, logs and Kubernetes events of a window around the fault, all in UTC. The conversion removes traces of the injection tools (for example their pods and log lines) so that no case reveals its answer.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The sources have released 2,359 cases; we screened 542 of them, and 348 pass eight exclusion rules. Among others, a case is excluded if its labels contradict each other, if it contains several faults, if the culprit is missing from the data, if neither a judge model nor an automatic check finds evidence of the fault in the telemetry, if data are incomplete, if the period before the fault is not clean, or if the fault starts late in the flagged window. The most frequent reasons are an unclean before-period (69 cases) and no evidence (56).

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: From the 348 eligible cases we draw the 90-case core set (RCAtlas-Core): a minimum per scenario, then cases that diversify fault class, root-cause level, data kinds and telemetry volume. The core set spans 23 scenarios and ten fault classes; the root cause is a service in 59 cases, a pod in 20 and a node in 11. Cases range from 37k to 5.6M telemetry rows, and the exact random-guess hit rate under our scoring rule ranges from 0.25% to 16.7% (median 3.45%). All experiments in this paper use the core set.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: We provide the core-set case list and our code at ( https://ufile.io/5ww9iyfb ). The file cases/core90_cases.csv gives, for each case, its identifier in the source dataset, the time window, the data kinds and the answer template, so that every case can be rebuilt from its public source; cases/core90_labels.json gives the root-cause labels and their levels (59 services, 20 pods and 11 nodes). The folder methods/ holds the three simple harnesses (the one-shot method, the SQL agent and the Codex run settings) and our reimplementations of FoA (with its SOP files), RCAgent, DecompRCA and SimpleRCA. Shared code in rcatlas/ covers path configuration, an OpenAI-compatible model client, answer parsing and the data tools shared by FoA and RCAgent; prompts/ holds the one-shot prompt templates and background notes, and answer_templates/ the answer templates of the 23 scenarios in the version used in the paper, without hints on the root-cause level. We plan to release the converted core-set data (about 11 GB) and an extended set of about 500 cases built with the same rules.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: One-shot sends the whole case to the model in a single call: an evidence package with the system inventory, the metric series that moved (as raw samples), per-minute trace statistics, log templates and events; the model answers with up to five candidates and no tools (Appendix C.2 ). The SQL agent is a single ReAct loop over the raw files with DuckDB, modelled on the reference agent of OpenRCA 2.0 ( Fang et al., 2026a ) : tools to list files, read a schema, run SQL and submit, at most 100 calls. Codex runs the Codex CLI ( OpenAI, 2026 ) in the case folder with a task statement and six rules (read only this folder; no network or installs; do not modify the data; do not try to identify the source dataset; always write a final report; one hour at most); the model writes its own shell and Python.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: We run RCA-Agent ( Xu et al., 2025 ) and mABC ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) from their released code, and reimplement FoA ( Pei et al., 2025 ) , RCAgent ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and DecompRCA ( Muhammad et al., 2026 ) , which have no released code, from their papers; our DecompRCA reproduces the paper’s numbers on RCAEval RE1. The reimplemented agents share one set of data tools over the raw files. We follow one rule for fairness: fix only what prevents a method from running on our data or what is an implementation error, and add no capability. Examples are converting time zones for RCA-Agent, restoring modules missing from mABC’s release, and completing tool descriptions in FoA’s code agent; the appendix summarises the changes. We exclude RCLAgent-V2 ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) (about USD 0.9 and up to an hour per case), LATS-RCA ( Naakka et al., 2027 ) (its released search strips the agents’ tools), EviRCA ( Wang et al., 2026 ) and MicroRCA-Agent ( Tang et al., 2025 ) (each needs a hand-written adapter per system or is built around one benchmark’s data layout), and supervised methods, which need a labelled training split.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: We answer five research questions. RQ1 (effectiveness): how do simple harnesses, published LLM agents and non-LLM methods compare on the same cases? RQ2 (mechanism): why do the simple harnesses win, and how much of each method’s investigation is prescribed by its program? RQ3 (capability and effort): how do a stronger model and more reasoning effort change how agents investigate and how accurate they are? RQ4 (aptitude and stability): how much accuracy is reproducible across passes, and how much appears only in some? RQ5 (cost-effectiveness): which model and method combinations are Pareto-optimal in accuracy against cost and time?

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Table 3 shows three layers. Averaged over the three mid-tier models, the simple harnesses reach PR@1 65–77%, the published LLM agents 16–53%, and the non-LLM methods 6–39%, against 5.5% for a random ranking. Codex is best overall, and even the weakest simple harness (one-shot) leads the best published agent (FoA) by 12 points. The lower two layers overlap: NSigma (38.9%) beats DecompRCA and mABC. Every LLM method is less accurate on pod- and node-level root causes than on service-level ones, and the published agents lose the most: from service to pod, Codex drops 9 points, FoA and RCAgent 31–38. NSigma is the only method more accurate on pods than on services (55.0% vs. 33.9%), since resource faults show on the culprit’s own metrics. Appendix C analyses the hardest groups. More kinds of data do not make a case easier. The 17 cases with all four kinds, which come from RCA-100 and ITBench-SRE, are the hardest for the simple harnesses (52–71%), and they form the only column in which a published agent matches the best simple harness: FoA reaches 70.6%, as Codex does. Conversely, the ten cases with metrics only are the easiest for the SQL agent (95.6%). The ordering does not depend on the model (Tables 5 and 5 ). On each of Luna, Haiku and Flash, every simple harness is ahead of every published agent (one-shot’s 5.9-point lead on Luna is not significant), and Codex is best or tied on every model it ran on. Across models, the simple harnesses fall into two tiers at the jump of the AA index from 34.5 to 45.1: 60–71% on Luna and Haiku, 74–87% on Flash, Sol and Astra. Leaving out MiMo (see below), 12 of the 13 cross-tier model pairs differ significantly, but only one of the nine within-tier pairs (Appendix B ). MiMo is the exception: its AA index (46.3) places it in the upper tier, but its accuracy (58–74%) matches the lower one, partly because it finished only 69–86 of the 90 cases.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
section: 6.2. Why simple harnesses win: a case study (RQ2)
content: The difference between the families is who decides what to look at and how to compute on it, which is what the prescribed-call ratio (Section 6.3 ) measures. The SQL agent writes its own queries and Codex writes its own analysis code, so the model chooses both what to read and how to compare it, and none of their calls is prescribed. The published agents fix part of this in the program. FoA can only choose among the steps of its built-in procedures, so when the matched procedure has no log step, it never sees the logs. RCA-Agent’s controller never touches the data and learns about the case only from its executor’s summaries, and mABC starts from an alert its program computes and walks the call chain from there. In the terms of our title, the SQL agent and Codex are free to look and free to reason; one-shot is free to reason over evidence that rules select.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
section: 6.2. Why simple harnesses win: a case study (RQ2)
content: We follow one case through the methods, rca100-main-0104 from RCA-100 (Figure 2 ). The inventory Service selects no pods, so cart’s calls to it are refused. The root cause raises no errors of its own: its request count collapses, while cart’s error rate rises and cart logs “Connection refused (inventory:9090)”. All runs below use Luna.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The program decides what the model reads (the evidence-package rules), and the model does the reasoning. The package holds a log template from the cart pod (E27.2) whose refusal line grows from 43 lines before the fault to 609 during it. All three passes cite this item and rank inventory first (Figure 3 ).

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The SQL agent starts from the symptom and follows “who cannot reach whom” to the root cause (Figure 4 , left). Its 31 queries reduce to six steps: it reads which tables exist (steps 1–7); counts failing calls by service and finds cart failing (step 12); searches the logs for error keywords and finds 1,291 lines in which cart’s connections to inventory are refused (step 14); queries inventory’s requests per minute and confirms that they fall from about 1,450 to 109 in the first 30 seconds of the fault and then to none; checks inventory’s pod logs and its place in the topology (steps 18–30, including an SQL error at step 17 that it fixes itself); and submits inventory (step 31).

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Codex casts a wide net first and then narrows down, in seven commands. After listing and loading the files, its third command runs comparison code it wrote itself over every entity and metric before and during the fault, together with events, spans and error logs; cart’s error rate (0.017 to 0.325) ranks first, and the refusal line is already in the output. It then pulls the events and the metrics and logs of inventory, cart and frontend side by side (commands 4–6), reads the logs of the two minutes around the onset (command 7), which show inventory serving until 01:59:22 and cart refused from 01:59:23, and writes its report naming inventory.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The SOP chosen by the program decides what is read. FoA fills in the fault description itself as “microservice incident”, which matches a generic SOP whose fixed steps never read logs; its judge declares the root cause found, cart, in the first round, after four calls of the controller (11 model calls in all). In the original paper the alert carries the fault type (“Network Issue” in its Figure 4), from which the SOP is chosen; we give every method only the anomalous period, because the fault type would reveal the answer. Four of our 12 SOPs, written after the paper’s examples, read logs, but none matched this case (the SOP files are in the released code; Appendix A ).

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The framework walks down the call chain from the alert: the frontend-proxy ingress at 02:03, frontend’s POST, and its four callees. In that minute only cart’s AddItem still receives a call (one, failing); the other three receive none. Inventory, three hops down, is never compared at the interface level; it served 109 calls with no errors at 01:59 and none afterwards. mABC stops at cart. A method that walks the call chain and inspects only the calls a service receives cannot see a service that stops receiving them.

authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: NSigma and BARO score each metric by its largest standardised deviation, keeping the sign, so only metrics that rise score high. Inventory’s request count falls sharply; its z-score is large and negative, and the metric ranks second to last among the 373 columns.

content: Three points qualify these numbers. First, the one call of one-shot counts as a main call, because the model receives the whole task, whereas DecompRCA’s single call counts as prescribed, because the model only reranks a list the program has already narrowed. One-shot’s evidence package is still selected by rules (it keeps only metric series that moved), which is why the case study says the program decides what one-shot reads. Second, mABC’s records do not say which role made each call, so its ratio is a lower bound. Third, simply counting calls does not separate the families: the SQL agent makes 27 calls per case, the same order as the multi-step published agents (35–50), while one-shot and DecompRCA both make one.

content: Because the simple harnesses leave the investigation to the model, their accuracy rests on the model: it rises with the model’s tier (Section 6.1 ). We now ask how a stronger model and more reasoning effort change the investigation itself. Figure 5 compares three pairs of runs. A stronger model investigates less and finds more (contrast A): from Luna to Sol, both agents make fewer calls and query fewer entities (Codex 16% → \rightarrow 12%, SQL agent 21% → \rightarrow 12%), yet reach the root cause in more cases and gain 14–18 points of PR@1. More reasoning effort does the opposite (contrasts B and C, Luna medium to max and Sol medium to xhigh): agents make more calls and query more entities, but gain only 2–4 points of PR@1 (first pass of the SQL agent and Codex), at 1.5 to 4 times the wall time. Appendix B covers every effort level (Figure 8 ). In all three contrasts the runs query the root cause in two to five more cases out of a hundred (RC visited); the difference is what the model makes of it. Sol turns what it sees into a correct first answer, while a larger budget mostly adds queries that the model then does not use to change its answer. A larger budget buys exploration; a stronger model buys direction.
