content: In operations, accuracy is not the only concern: an incident needs an answer quickly and at a sustainable cost. Figure 1 plots PR@1 against time and against cost per case. We count a run as usable only if it is more accurate than the best non-LLM method (NSigma, PR@1 38.9%), a threshold fixed before drawing the frontier, and draw the Pareto lines through all usable runs. Seven runs of published agents qualify (FoA, RCAgent and RCA-Agent, 43–63%), yet every run on either line uses a simple harness: each published agent is beaten in accuracy by a simple harness that is no more costly, and by one that is no slower. The DecompRCA runs, the cheapest and fastest of all, fall below the threshold (24–29%). The frontier gives three practical choices. When cost matters most, Luna with Codex reaches 68.9% for under one cent per case. When accuracy per dollar matters, Flash with Codex reaches 85.6% for about five cents. When the answer is needed quickly, Sol with the SQL agent answers in 45 s at 85.6%. The most accurate run, Sol at xhigh with Codex (88.9%), costs about 26 cents and takes 277 s per case, so the last few points of accuracy cost roughly five times as much as the cheapest strong setup.

content: Our study has five limitations. First, Codex is the only general-purpose coding harness we test; others, such as Claude Code, may behave differently. Second, all models are from 2026, so we cannot say whether the ordering holds for the weaker models for which many prescribed workflows were designed. Third, budget kept us from current frontier models such as Fable, Opus or Argon. Fourth, despite careful conversion and reimplementation, our datasets and methods may still differ from their originals; the appendix summarises the changes. Fifth, the case study follows a single case. The prescribed-call ratio extends its mechanism to all 90 cases, but it measures how much of an investigation is fixed, not that this fixing causes the lower accuracy; an ablation that lifts the prescriptions from one agent would test that directly.

authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: For microservice root cause analysis, a capable model that is given the data and left to decide what to look at and how to reason outdiagnoses agents whose investigation is hand-crafted, and both mostly outperform statistical and causal methods. A stronger model improves accuracy and reliability; more reasoning effort adds little. Practitioners can start from a simple harness and pick the model and harness on the cost–accuracy frontier. Designers of RCA agents should compare against such harnesses on shared, validated cases, which RCAtlas provides.

content: Our results do not show that domain knowledge is useless. They show that fixing it into the control flow hurts when a procedure does not fit the case, as in our case study, where the procedure that FoA matched never read the logs. Offering procedures to the model as optional guidance, rather than prescribing them, is a natural next step.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: FoA (54.4 / 58.9 / 46.7) runs one of twelve SOPs written before any run after the examples in ( Pei et al., 2025 ) . In FoA the alert names the fault type, which selects the SOP; our setting withholds it, since it would reveal the answer, so FoA describes the incident itself. Luna then matches the generic Microservice Issue SOP (abnormal metrics → \rightarrow entry requests → \rightarrow traces) in 69 of the 90 cases; Flash, which more often guesses a fault type, does so in 33. Only four SOPs contain a log step (Memory, Network Loss or Partition, Code or Configuration Error, Database or Cache). FoA’s accuracy varies widely by fault group: on Luna 93% on application-code faults but 41% on resource saturation. RCAgent (54.4 / 50.0 / 43.3) prescribes 35% of its calls and, with FoA, comes closest to the simple harnesses on Luna; Luna leaves 7 cases and Flash 19 cases unanswered within its 30 steps. RCA-Agent (32.2 / 63.3 / 34.4): its released executor discards outputs above 16,384 tokens after two tries, which costs Luna, which prints whole tables, 16% of its executor steps (Haiku 3%, yet Haiku scores as low). DecompRCA (24.4 / 32.2 / 28.9): the program’s at most 15 candidates contain the root cause in only 57.8% of the cases, which bounds the model’s rerank. mABC (11.1 / – / 20.0) walks down the call chain from the alert, so a service that receives no requests is never reached. Luna also declares the cause undetermined in 42 of 89 cases, concentrated in sources with few or no traces (LEMMA 5 of 5, RCAEval RE1 8 of 9); Haiku answers 85 of 90.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The gap lies in where the evidence is. On resource saturation (34 cases) NSigma reaches 62%, close to one-shot on Luna (65%); on errors, outages, configuration faults and network breaks (33 cases), whose evidence is in logs, traces and events, NSigma and BARO reach 15% and 6% against 67% for the SQL agent and Codex on Luna. Three causes add to this. Many sources have thousands of series with about 15 pre-fault samples, half of them constant, so normal jumps outrank the root cause. NSigma and BARO score the largest signed deviation, so a drop ranks last (inventory’s request drop in the case study: 372nd of 373). Causal-graph methods cannot learn dependencies from tens of samples: RCD misses the root cause entirely in 71 of 89 cases.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: A paired bootstrap over the 90 cases (10,000 resamples, 95%) confirms the main gaps: the SQL agent and Codex beat the best published agent on every model they ran on, by 14 to 24 points (one-shot on Flash and Haiku only), and, with MiMo left out of the tiers as in Section 6.1 , 12 of 13 cross-tier model pairs differ against 1 of 9 within-tier pairs (with MiMo grouped with the lower tier by its accuracy: 20 of 21 and 1 of 14). The best published agent beats NSigma on Luna and Flash, but mABC falls significantly below it, so the family order holds for the strongest members.

authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Cases are converted to one format (entity and relation tables, metrics, traces, logs, events; UTC), with traces of the injection tooling removed. Of 542 screened cases, 348 pass the exclusion rules; the most frequent reasons are an unclean pre-fault period (69), no evidence (56), incomplete data (38) and a fault late in the window (37). LEMMA has no traces and hundreds of pods per scenario. RCAEval injects faults into only five services per system, so guessing among the injected services hits 20%; against the full inventory our random-guess rate is far lower (Section 4 ).

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: Cases share entity and relation tables and UTC telemetry; labels and answer material are kept separate. Duplicate metric observations are collapsed, source attributes distinguish otherwise duplicate rows, and injection-tool entities, spans, logs and events are removed. Source fault windows are retained where available; RCA-100 adds 20 minutes before the alert, and sources giving only an injection time use an initial before-period and flag the remainder without exposing the onset. Automatic checks cover label consistency, culprit coverage, fault timing, completeness, shortcuts and observable evidence. Claude Sonnet 5.5 reviews labels, check results, row counts and the twelve most-changed series; ITBench-SRE uses automatic checks only. Exclusions are contradictory labels (8), multiple faults outside the multi-fault scenario (20), a missing culprit or its data (14), no evidence (56), incomplete data (38), failure of the multi-fault pre-filter (5), an unclean before-period or nearby fault (69), and less than a third of the window remaining after the fault (37); rules overlap. Of 542 screened cases, 348 remain. RCAEval supplies three cases per sub-suite (27); other scenarios supply at least three where eligible. Remaining places diversify scenario, fault class, root-cause level, data kinds, volume and clue coverage, with fixed tie-breaking and seed, before method runs.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: The prompt includes instructions, the question, recorded and flagged periods, all selected evidence and the scenario’s answer template, with neutral item titles. S1 gives the incident record, inventory, topology, placement and coverage. S2 supplies moved metrics as raw samples: using the before-period median and robust spread (MAD × 1.4826 \times 1.4826 ), a series needs a change score max ⁡ ( median shift , 0.6 × largest departure ) ≥ 4 \max(\text{median shift},0.6\times\text{largest departure})\geq 4 spreads, plus a median shift of at least 10% or a departure of at least 20% of the baseline level. Identical series are collapsed; unlabelled duplicate-row series are omitted. At most 120 series are selected in turns across moving entities and rendered on the source time grid, with missing samples marked. S3 gives per-minute entry requests, errors, duration quantiles and caller–callee statistics, including missing downstream spans. S4 groups logs into masked templates: the 30 most-changed entities receive separate items, with up to eight templates and twelve raw lines per entity, prioritising errors, warnings and new templates. S5 groups Kubernetes events by object and reason (at most 60 groups). Constant series are counted only; series beyond the cap, full raw traces and logs, injection traces and answer material are omitted. The case study contains 136 items (about 75k tokens); no one-shot prompt was truncated.

title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
authors: Tingzhu Bi, Xun Zhang, Jinglin Li, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
content: LLM methods run without generation parameters (except effort in Setting 3), one hour per case, first five answers scored. Interface fixes: shared raw-data tools for FoA, RCAgent and mABC; complete tool descriptions for FoA’s code agent; UTC+8 times for RCA-Agent; modules missing from mABC’s release, a loop limit, a cut at “Observation” and a format hint; resampling for TORAI; missing functions for FaultInsight. Setting differences: no temperatures; RCAgent’s expert also reads metrics and traces (at most 30 steps); mABC’s alert on the entry service’s requests. The SQL agent differs from the reference agent of ( Fang et al., 2026a ) in temperature, an optional think tool, its answer format, and the topology files that every case folder carries.

Three AIOps 2022 cases fail for reasons in the data: no clear metric on the faulty node, a fault that leaves almost no trace, and an unlabelled burst on another node. No one-shot prompt was truncated; cases with all four data kinds have a median of 115k tokens.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
section: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
content: Continuous Integration and Delivery (CI/CD) are fundamental to modern software development, yet configuring pipelines such as GitHub Actions (GHA) workflows remains complex and error-prone. Recent work has explored Transformer-based models for GHA workflow recommendation, but existing approaches typically model workflow steps as a single homogeneous generation task. This formulation overlooks a key distinction: reusable Actions are structured, ecosystem-level components, whereas project-specific Scripts encode local build, test, and deployment semantics. Consequently, current models struggle to capture the different forms of knowledge required for accurate workflow completion. In this work, we present FLOWSTEP , a framework for GHA workflow step completion that explicitly distinguishes between Action and Script generation. FLOWSTEP combines large language models (LLMs) with contrastive learning to better capture semantic relationships among workflow contexts, Actions, and Scripts. Evaluated on established benchmarks, FLOWSTEP improves end-to-end workflow step prediction accuracy from 38.23% to 51.09%. Beyond prediction accuracy, we further study whether LLM-as-a-judge can provide a more semantic evaluation of generated workflow steps. By comparing LLM-based assessments with human annotations, we find that the best-performing model configuration reaches substantial agreement with human ground truth (Krippendorff’s α = 0.701 \alpha=0.701 ), suggesting that LLM-as-a-judge can serve as a scalable complement to manual evaluation.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: GitHub has become the largest collaborative software ecosystem, connecting more than 180 million developers and hosting over 630 million repositories as of 2025 [ 1 ] . As projects grow, Continuous Integration and Delivery (CI/CD) has become essential for automating building, testing, and deployment [ 2 ] . To natively support these activities, GitHub launched GitHub Actions (GHA) [ 3 ] in November 2019, offering an integrated CI/CD environment directly within the platform. Within only 18 months, GHA surpassed Travis CI to become the most widely used automation framework on GitHub [ 4 ] . Its convenience and ecosystem of reusable components ( Actions ) have made workflow automation more accessible than ever.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: Despite these advantages, configuring CI/CD pipelines remains challenging. Prior studies have repeatedly shown that developers struggle with pipeline setup, maintenance, and debugging [ 5 , 6 ] . In a survey by Saroar et al. [ 7 ] , about 60% of 90 participants reported difficulties when automating workflows using GHA, underscoring an urgent need for intelligent authoring support. While automated code assistance has seen breakthroughs in general programming tasks ( e.g., code completion [ 8 ] , assertion generation [ 9 ] , automated repair of vulnerabilities and bugs [ 10 , 11 ] ), workflow authoring introduces unique challenges. A CI/CD pipeline interleaves reusable Actions with free-form scripting and natural-language documentation, while embedding highly context-specific details such as directory paths or download URLs. These characteristics make workflow recommendation significantly harder than traditional code completion.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: The rapid adoption of GHA has motivated learning-based workflow generation. Transformer models and LLMs have been used to synthesize or recommend workflow steps [ 12 , 13 ] , but existing approaches often treat steps as homogeneous generation targets. This overlooks the different prediction strategies required by Actions and shell Scripts : Actions require selecting a reusable identifier from the GHA ecosystem, whereas Scripts require generating project-specific shell commands from workflow context. Our analysis shows that this mismatch contributes to prediction errors and reduces robustness across heterogeneous workflow steps.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: In this work, we address the problem of recommending the next step in GHA workflows, accounting for the heterogeneous nature of workflow steps. To this end, we propose FLOWSTEP , a multi-step prediction framework comprising (i) a binary classifier that predicts whether the next step is an Action or a Script , (ii) a RoBERTa model with contrastive learning that predicts the specific Action , and (iii) an LLM that generates the step when it is a Script . For comparability with prior work, we use the GHA workflow corpus by Decan et al. [ 14 ] , further processed by Mastropaolo et al. [ 12 ] into two variants: a raw version preserving original content and an abstracted version replacing project-specific tokens (e.g., paths) with placeholders while retaining commands and tool options. We evaluate FLOWSTEP on both variants to assess robustness across data granularities. The next step is predicted from the preceding workflow context concatenated with the step’s descriptive name, reflecting real workflow authoring scenarios.

content: Each workflow contains one or more jobs , representing independent execution units that run on GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runners . Jobs may run concurrently or sequentially, and they remain isolated unless they explicitly share artifacts or caches. Each job consists of a series of steps , the smallest executable elements in a workflow. Steps can be defined either with the run keyword to execute shell commands ( Scripts ) directly within the runner (e.g., gradle build ) or with the uses keyword to invoke reusable Actions [ 16 ] . Script -based steps are preferred for simple or project-specific tasks, whereas Actions encapsulate recurring operations and can be versioned for reproducibility (e.g., actions/checkout@v3 ). Through this declarative structure, GHA provides a unified mechanism to automate CI/CD pipelines directly within GitHub repositories.

authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: The evolution of Transformer architectures [ 17 ] and encoders like BERT [ 18 ] has enabled models to learn deep contextual representations of text and code. RoBERTa [ 19 ] , a refinement of BERT, employs dynamic masking and achieves more stable and robust performance across various Natural Language Processing tasks. Contrastive learning [ 20 ] further improves representation learning by introducing pairwise comparison, encouraging similar examples (positive pairs) to align closely in the embedding space while separating dissimilar ones (negative pairs). Given a batch of samples, an encoder transforms each input into a latent vector, and a similarity function ( e.g., cosine similarity) quantifies pairwise closeness. The resulting contrastive loss enhances semantic discrimination, which we leverage to fine-tune RoBERTa for more context-aware and task-specific representations in workflow step generation.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: In recent years, LLMs have emerged as powerful tools capable of understanding and generating human-like text through extensive pre-training. Their versatility stems from the ability to generalize across diverse tasks using only textual instructions, without additional parameter updates. To further improve performance, researchers have proposed prompt engineering techniques [ 21 , 22 ] that carefully design input prompts to guide model behavior. Depending on the amount of task-specific context provided, LLM usage can be categorized into three settings [ 23 ] : (i) zero-shot , relying solely on pre-trained knowledge; (ii) one-shot , where a single example is provided; and (iii) few-shot , where multiple examples are given to refine responses. LLMs have transformed how developers interact with code, enabling natural-language-driven programming and automation. Models such as GPT-4 [ 24 ] , Claude-Sonnet [ 25 ] , CodeT5 [ 26 ] , and CodeBERT [ 27 ] demonstrate strong performance in code completion and synthesis. However, prior work largely focuses on general-purpose languages, leaving configuration artifacts underexplored. GHA workflows, written in YAML to define CI/CD automation, represent a distinct form of infrastructure configuration. Prior attempts to generate such workflows using fine-tuned T5 and LLMs [ 12 , 13 ] only partially capture workflow semantics, leading to limited accuracy and generalization. In this work, we guide LLMs to generate accurate and context-aware workflow steps for GHA automation.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: Another emerging paradigm is LLM-as-a-Judge , which uses large language models as automatic evaluators of generated content instead of relying solely on human annotators. This idea builds on the observation that instruction-tuned models can reason about and compare outputs in a human-like manner [ 28 ] . Recent surveys [ 29 ] describe LLM-as-a-Judge as a scalable and cost-effective alternative to manual evaluation, although challenges such as bias, inconsistency, and over-alignment remain. In software engineering, recent studies [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] explore its use for automatically evaluating code and software artifacts, suggesting that with proper calibration, LLMs can complement human evaluators in domain-specific tasks.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: In this study, we propose FLOWSTEP ( F ramework for L earning t O predict Workflow STEP s), a step-type-aware approach designed to complete GHA workflow steps. Given the preceding workflow context together with the descriptive name of the target step (if applicable), FLOWSTEP recommends a workflow step that fulfills the intended functionality.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: In our study, we represent each workflow as a sequence of steps extracted from its execution context. Specifically, each instance in our dataset D is defined as a tuple (input_context, target_step, type_step) , where input_context denotes the preceding workflow context ( i.e., all workflow elements appearing before the target step concatenated with the descriptive step name), target_step the next step to be generated, and type_step its type ( Action or Script ). This formulation reflects the central modeling challenge of GHA step completion: a target step may require either selecting a reusable Action identifier from the ecosystem or generating a project-specific shell Script . We further derive two task-specific datasets from D D : D A ​ c ​ t ​ i ​ o ​ n D_{Action} and D S ​ c ​ r ​ i ​ p ​ t D_{Script} , which contain samples of type Action and Script , respectively.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: Building on this formulation, Fig. 1 presents the overall architecture of FLOWSTEP . The framework integrates two RoBERTa models with a state-of-the-art LLM in a unified pipeline, so that each subtask is handled by a model aligned with its output space. Given an input_context , a RoBERTa classifier first predicts the step type ( type_step ). If the predicted type is Action , a second RoBERTa model trained with contrastive learning recommends the most suitable Action . Otherwise, an LLM generates the corresponding Script to fulfill the intended functionality. Using the predicted scripts, we further investigate the feasibility of the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm in our evaluation setting. In the following subsections, we describe each component of FLOWSTEP in detail.

content: The design of FLOWSTEP is motivated by an empirical analysis of the limitations in prior GHA recommendation models. Mastropaolo et al. [ 12 ] analyzed 384 workflow steps incorrectly predicted by their step prediction model GH-WCOM, and found that 159 recommendations were genuinely incorrect, while the remaining errors involved only minor issues. In this study, we further inspected these 159 erroneous predictions and found that 33.3% (53/159) are mismatches between Actions and Scripts , i.e., cases where an expected Action was replaced with a Script , or vice versa. For example, the step was predicted to be a script execution “ run: pip install tox ” while the developers adopted an existing Action “ uses: actions/cache@v1 ”.

content: Based on this, we hypothesize that explicitly distinguishing between Action and Script steps can improve the recommendation accuracy by preventing a single model from conflating two different prediction spaces. Therefore, we implement a Step-Type Predictor based on a RoBERTa encoder, mapping a workflow context ( i.e., input_context ) to a contextualized representation. This representation is passed through a dropout layer and a fully connected layer to perform binary classification of step type ( 1 1 : Action , 0 0 : Script ). The RoBERTa model is initialized with pre-trained weights from Hugging Face and fine-tuned using Binary Cross-Entropy with Logits Loss.

content: During FLOWSTEP inference, the Step-Type Predictor acts as a router: it determines the step type for a given context and forwards the input to the corresponding downstream component: either the Action Predictor or the Script Generator .

section: III-B Action Predictor with Contrastive Learning
content: The Action Predictor in FLOWSTEP consists of two primary components: (i) a RoBERTa-based context encoder that employs contrastive learning to align workflow contexts referring to the same Actions while pushing apart those referring to distinct Actions ; and (ii) a classification head that maps these high-dimensional embeddings into specific Action categories. During model development, the context encoder and classification head are trained in two distinct phases:

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
section: III-B Action Predictor with Contrastive Learning
content: Phase 1: Contrastive training of the context encoder. We fine-tune RoBERTa using a contrastive objective that combines N-pair Loss and Soft-Nearest Neighbor Loss [ 33 ] . For each Action instance, we pair its workflow context with another context using the same Action as a positive example, while contexts using different Actions in the same batch serve as negative examples. This encourages contexts that require the same reusable Action to be close in the embedding space and separates contexts associated with different Actions ; implementation details and the full loss formulation are provided in our replication package.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs

section: III-B Action Predictor with Contrastive Learning
content: Phase 2: Training the classification head. We freeze the encoder to preserve the learned semantic space, and attach a classification head consisting of a feed-forward network with ReLU activation and dropout ( p = 0.2 p=0.2 ). The model is then fine-tuned on D A ​ c ​ t ​ i ​ o ​ n D_{Action} using Cross-Entropy loss to map context representations to Action identifiers.

content: As shown in Table IV , over 28% of GH-WCOM’s errors are due to step-type mismatches, with 2,336 (28.25%) and 2,415 (28.69%) cases in the abstracted and raw datasets, respectively. In particular, GH-WCOM misclassifies 1,105 (abstracted) and 1,143 (raw) Actions as Scripts , while misidentifying 1,231 (abstracted) and 1,272 (raw) Scripts as Actions . In contrast, FLOWSTEP , equipped with an explicit Step-Type Predictor M T M_{T} , substantially reduces these errors by nearly half. On the abstracted dataset, it records only 603 Action → \rightarrow Script mismatches (9.23%) and 345 Script → \rightarrow Action mismatches (5.28%), totaling 948 errors (14.51%) using the final 6,534 incorrect predictions as the denominator. On the raw dataset, these numbers are 644 Action → \rightarrow Script mismatches (9.86%) and 430 Script → \rightarrow Action mismatches (6.58%), totaling 1,074 errors (16.45%) using the final 6,530 incorrect predictions as the denominator.

section: Contribution of Contrastive Learning & Classification Head to M A M_{A} (RQ 2.2 )
content: We conduct an ablation study comparing M A M_{A} with its two variants ( No-classification head and No-contrastive ), evaluated using Top- K K accuracy on D A ​ c ​ t ​ i ​ o ​ n D_{Action} . Table V reports the results of the M A M_{A} variants on both abstracted and raw datasets, using GH-WCOM as the baseline. Without contrastive learning, the model yields poor performance (Top-1: 21.51%/23.37%, Top-5: 50.30%/52.49%), showing that standard fine-tuning alone is insufficient for accurate Action prediction. Introducing contrastive learning leads to substantial improvements, increasing Top-1 performance to 80.05%/83.57% and Top-5 to 89.11%/91.26%. Adding the classification head further improves Top-1 by 7.18%/4.51% and Top-5 by 5.52%/2.91%, with diminishing gains as K K increases. This trend is consistent across both abstracted and raw datasets, and the full model substantially outperforms GH-WCOM. Overall, contrastive learning accounts for most of the performance gain, while the classification head provides additional improvements, particularly for Top-1 accuracy. The high Top-5 accuracy of the full model (94.63%/94.17%) further shows that M A M_{A} can provide a compact ranked set of plausible reusable Actions , which is useful when the top-ranked prediction is not correct but the correct Action remains among the leading candidates.

content: Table VI and Table VII present the performance of different models for Script generation on D C ​ a ​ l ​ i D_{Cali} using both abstracted and raw data, evaluated with accuracy (Acc), BLEU, and ROUGE metrics, with GH-WCOM serving as the baseline. Under zero-shot prompting, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 achieves the best overall performance across most metrics, reaching 24.4% and 27.4% accuracy on abstracted and raw data, respectively, together with strong BLEU (31.03%/36.86%) and ROUGE (57.68%/60.54%) scores. Claude-Haiku-4.5 and DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp also perform competitively, while GPT-4.1 achieves comparable accuracy but lower BLEU on abstracted data. In contrast, GPT-3.5-turbo performs notably worse across all metrics, with accuracy (7.2%/11.5%) that remains below or only slightly above the baseline.

section: Impact of Model Choice on M S M_{S} (RQ 2.3 )
content: One-shot prompting leads to improvements for several models, although the effect is not uniform across all systems. In particular, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 further increases its accuracy to 27.5% and 29.6% on abstracted and raw data, respectively, while also achieving the highest BLEU (37.79%/42.81%) and ROUGE (61.57%/63.44%) scores among all models. DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp and GPT-4.1 also show moderate gains in both accuracy and lexical similarity metrics. However, the impact of one-shot prompting is less consistent for smaller or weaker models, such as GPT-3.5-turbo, where performance does not improve and in some cases slightly decreases. Overall, these results indicate that providing a single demonstration example can help guide stronger models toward better Script generation, although the benefit depends on the model capacity.

content: The T5-small model, trained solely for the Script generation task, while behind most LLMs except GPT-3.5-turbo, performs competitively (18.8%/14.7% accuracy) and serves as a practical offline alternative that does not require API access, making it a suitable backup model for M S M_{S} . Together with the API prices in Table I , these results illustrate a quality–deployment-cost tradeoff: Claude-Sonnet-4.5 offers the best generation quality, whereas T5-small serves as a lightweight local baseline. Open-weight LLMs also provide a viable self-hosted alternative and will be investigated in future work.

content: Using the manually labeled dataset, we then ask the LLMs to provide their judgments. To align LLM judgments with human assessments, we design structured prompts that present the workflow context along with the ground-truth and generated steps, following the same guidelines used for human annotation. As in RQ2, we evaluate zero-shot and one-shot prompting, with both prompts available in our replication package. As observed in prior studies [ 37 ] , LLMs may produce verbose or inconsistent output formats, so we explicitly instruct them to return only a decision number ( i.e., 0, 1 or 2). All judgments were then manually verified by the first author to ensure their validity.

content: Recall that the two human annotators achieved α = 0.82 \alpha=0.82 , serving as a practical benchmark for alignment with human judgment. DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp achieves the highest agreement in the zero-shot setting ( α = 0.701 \alpha=0.701 ), whereas GPT-4.1 performs best in the one-shot setting ( α = 0.687 \alpha=0.687 ). Claude-Sonnet-4.5 ( 0.648 0.648 zero-shot; 0.656 0.656 one-shot) and Claude-Haiku-4.5 ( 0.631 0.631 ; 0.612 0.612 ) also show substantial agreement. GPT-4.1 improves from 0.604 0.604 to 0.687 0.687 with one-shot prompting, while GPT-3.5-turbo exhibits fair-to-moderate agreement ( 0.490 0.490 ; 0.285 0.285 ). Overall, one-shot prompting provides no consistent benefit across models: it improves agreement for Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-4.1 but reduces it for the other judges. Moreover, even the best LLM remains about 0.12 below human–human agreement ( 0.70 0.70 vs. 0.82 0.82 ), indicating that although modern LLMs can approximate human evaluation reasonably well, they still fall short of human reliability and cannot yet fully replace human annotators in high-fidelity evaluation settings.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: We further compare LLM-based judges with traditional automatic metrics ( i.e., BLEU and ROUGE). Since all 350 samples in this experiment correspond to incorrect script snippets, the accuracy is always zero and therefore not meaningful for comparison. To examine how well different evaluation approaches reflect human judgment, we compute the Spearman correlation ρ \rho between each metric and the human ground-truth. As shown in Table VIII , BLEU achieves a moderate correlation with human labels ( ρ = 0.514 \rho=0.514 ), while ROUGE reaches a stronger correlation ( ρ = 0.692 \rho=0.692 ). The five LLM judges achieve correlations ranging from 0.382 0.382 to 0.703 0.703 across zero-shot and one-shot settings. In the zero-shot setting, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp achieves the highest correlation ( ρ = 0.703 \rho=0.703 ), while in the one-shot setting GPT-4.1 performs best ( ρ = 0.695 \rho=0.695 ). These results suggest that the best-performing LLM-judge configurations match or slightly exceed widely used lexical-overlap metrics in their alignment with human judgment, while additionally assessing the functional correctness of generated scripts.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: From a cost-efficiency perspective, the LLM judges also provide a practical advantage: in our experiment, judging all 350 samples cost only $0.07–$1.41 depending on the model, whereas expert annotation required substantial manual effort from multiple authors. This suggests that LLM-as-a-Judge can serve as an affordable first-pass evaluation mechanism, while human judgment remains necessary for calibration and adjudication.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: To investigate why LLM judges diverge from human consensus and exhibit inconsistent alignment across models, we analyze their prediction behavior using confusion matrices (Fig. 2 ), using the zero-shot setting as an example. The results show that most disagreements occur in the Functionally Almost Correct category, where borderline cases are frequently misclassified as either correct or incorrect, suggesting that LLM judges lack the sensitivity needed to reliably evaluate borderline functional equivalence. The matrices also reveal different evaluation tendencies across models. DeepSeek exhibits the most balanced predictions with most mass on the diagonal, which explains its highest correlation with human annotations. In contrast, Claude models and GPT-4.1 tend to be stricter by downgrading correct Scripts to almost correct, while GPT-3.5 shows a strong conservative bias by rarely predicting correct samples. This suggests that LLM judges differ in both accuracy and strictness, meaning that model selection plays a critical role depending on whether conservative or balanced evaluation is desired.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: Traditional lexical metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE, while useful for source code, often fail to capture the functional equivalence of generated scripts. Our findings indicate that LLM-based judges can bridge this “semantic gap” by evaluating the intent and logic of a generated Script rather than its character-level overlap. While human expert annotation remains the “gold standard” for reliability, it is unscalable and expensive. Although LLM judges do not yet match human reliability, their substantial alignment with human annotations suggests they can serve as a scalable and cost-effective evaluation method for workflow automation tasks.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: Threats to internal validity concern whether the study accurately reflects cause–effect relationships. Since FLOWSTEP consists of multiple models trained on large datasets, bias may arise from data preprocessing or training configurations ( e.g., random initialization, batch composition, and optimizer choice). To mitigate this, we fixed random seeds across experiments, used consistent data splits to support reproducibility. Another threat concerns the manual annotation in the LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation; to reduce subjective bias, two annotators independently labeled the samples, with disagreements resolved by a third annotator, and inter-rater agreement was measured before aggregating results.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: Threats to external validity concern the generalizability of our findings beyond the studied dataset and setup. FLOWSTEP was evaluated on a large-scale dataset of GHA workflows from prior studies [ 14 , 12 ] . Although we refined this dataset ( e.g., separating Action and Script samples, filtering malformed workflows, and aligning context–step pairs), it still represents only open-source GitHub projects and may not reflect private or industrial workflows. Moreover, LLM-based evaluation depends on prompt design and model versions, which may yield different behaviors over time. To mitigate this, we used uniform prompting templates and documented all configurations to support replication.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: Threats to construct validity concern whether our evaluation truly measures the intended concepts. Automatic metrics such as Top-K accuracy, BLEU-4, and ROUGE-L capture syntactic similarity but may overlook semantic equivalence. To address this, we adopted the LLM-as-a-Judge framework to evaluate correctness and contextual relevance, and analyzed inter-rater agreement among humans and between humans and LLMs to assess consistency. Another threat lies in the binary Action – Script distinction: some functionalities can be implemented either way, making the separation occasionally simplistic, which is a limitation to be explored in future work.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
section: VII-A GitHub Actions and CI/CD Automation
content: GHA has rapidly become a dominant CI/CD service on GitHub [ 4 ] , with studies showing broad developer adoption and generally positive perceptions [ 38 ] . Prior empirical work has characterized Action reuse [ 14 ] , resource consumption [ 39 ] , dependency and input-validation vulnerabilities [ 40 ] , workflow failures [ 41 ] , and longitudinal security risks [ 42 ] . These studies establish the practical importance of GHA and motivate better authoring support for reliable workflow construction.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
section: VII-B Learning-based Program and Workflow Generation
content: Learning-based techniques have also been applied to workflow-related prediction tasks. CIGAR [ 43 ] uses contrastive learning for Action recommendation, while GH-WCOM [ 12 ] applies T5 to workflow-step completion. Zhang et al. [ 13 ] evaluated LLMs for workflow generation, defect detection, and repair, finding improvements in validity but remaining challenges in security and logical consistency. Gavel [ 44 ] addresses a different task, categorizing reusable Actions from README files to improve Marketplace visibility.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
section: VII-C LLMs for Software Engineering Tasks
content: LLMs now support many SE tasks, including code generation, completion, summarization, bug localization, test generation, and automated repair [ 45 , 46 , 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 ] . Related work also studies requirements engineering [ 52 , 53 ] , prompt-engineering strategies [ 54 ] , and practical developer use of tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot [ 55 ] . More recently, Crupi et al. [ 37 ] evaluated LLM-as-a-Judge for code generation and summarization, showing promise but also imperfect alignment with human judgment.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
section: VII-D Distinction and Contribution of FLOWSTEP
content: Together, prior studies show the promise of learning-based workflow automation but leave two gaps. First, GH-WCOM [ 12 ] treats workflow steps as monolithic outputs, while CIGAR [ 43 ] focuses only on Action recommendation. Second, LLM-based workflow studies [ 13 ] emphasize generation validity but provide limited treatment of contextual correctness and semantic evaluation. FLOWSTEP addresses these gaps by explicitly modeling step type, predicting reusable Actions , generating project-specific Scripts , and evaluating generated scripts through human-calibrated LLM judges.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: In this work, we introduced FLOWSTEP , a framework designed to improve the recommendation of GitHub Actions workflow steps by explicitly modeling the heterogeneity between Actions and Scripts . By leveraging a “divide-and-conquer” architecture, we integrated a RoBERTa-based classifier for step-type prediction, contrastive learning for reusable Action selection, and Large Language Models for project-specific Script generation. Our evaluation demonstrates that this step-type-aware formulation substantially outperforms existing baselines. As commonly used metrics do not fully capture the correctness of generated scripts, we further validated whether LLMs can serve as reliable evaluators. Our results show that there is substantial alignment between human annotations and LLMs’ evaluations, indicating a promising path in this direction.

title: FLOWSTEP: A Framework for Learning to Predict GitHub Actions Workflow STEPs
authors: Jiangnan Huang, Bin Lin, Yutaro Kashiwa
content: Although FLOWSTEP improves workflow step generation accuracy, it relies solely on the workflow specification and does not exploit repository-specific information. As future work, we plan to investigate an agentic CI system that actively explores the target repository to leverage project-specific context for more accurate workflow generation and correction. We also plan to integrate vulnerability detection and security analysis to generate CI/CD workflows that are both functionally correct and secure by design.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
section: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
content: Engineering Multi-Agent System (MAS) requires choosing agents, orchestration strategies, communication mechanisms, reasoning approaches, and memory configurations. These choices depend on framework-specific capabilities and abstractions, requiring developers to learn different APIs when exploring alternative implementations. We present GEAR , an open-source tool for configuring MASs and generating framework-specific implementations from a common specification. GEAR uses a feature-based representation to make configuration options and their constraints explicit, enabling users to validate specifications before code generation. Through connectors for ten agentic frameworks, users generate projects from the same specification and can then inspect reports describing framework-specific adaptations. A preliminary assessment of mapping feasibility identifies translation strategies for 271 of 320 evaluated feature–framework pairs (84.69%). GEAR supports developers prototyping agentic systems and researchers exploring MAS configurations across frameworks. GEAR is available as open-source software at https://github.com/brellsanwouo/gear-framework and a video demo is available at https://youtu.be/iwNi-oC2tCw .

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Nowadays, developers and researchers increasingly build multi-agent applications using frameworks such as CrewAI [ 1 ] , Google ADK [ 2 ] , and AutoGen [ 3 ] . Although these frameworks provide similar capabilities (like definition of agents, memory, reasoning, or orchestration), they expose them through different abstractions, terminology, and APIs [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . As a result, developers and researchers must both navigate a large configuration space and continuously learn framework-specific concepts and implementation choices making the design process time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to reason about.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Software engineering has addressed similar problems in highly configurable systems through variability modeling [ 7 ] . In particular, Feature Models (FMs) provide explicit representations of configuration spaces and their constraints, together with automated reasoning capabilities for validating configurations [ 8 , 9 ] . However, to the best of our knowledge, no existing tool has leveraged FMs to explicitly design and manage the variability of Multi-Agent System s (MASs) .

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: In this paper, we present GEAR , an open-source tool that provides a common, framework-independent language for describing configurable MASs . Users specify their agents, modules, workflows, and configuration choices once, and GEAR validates this specification and generates executable implementations for selected target frameworks. This allows developers to reuse the same MAS specification when exploring different target frameworks. GEAR connector-based architecture also separates the common specification from the implementation logic, enabling the integration of emerging frameworks and capabilities. A preliminary assessment across the 10 10 supported frameworks identifies translation strategies for 271 271 of 320 320 evaluated feature–framework pairs ( 84.69 84.69 %).

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Envisioned users : GEAR targets both developers building or prototyping LLM-based MASs and researchers studying agentic system designs. Developers can use GEAR to explore configuration choices, detect invalid configurations before implementation, and generate executable implementations for different frameworks from the same specification. Researchers can use the common representation to systematically vary MAS designs, compare their implementations across frameworks, and reproduce experimental setups without manually reimplementing each system.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Specification of MAS . Recent LLM-based multi-agent frameworks, such as CAMEL-AI [ 10 ] , AutoGen [ 3 ] , MetaGPT [ 11 ] , CrewAI [ 1 ] , and Google ADK [ 2 ] , provide abstractions for orchestrating agents through prompts, tools, and communication protocols. However, these frameworks primarily rely on code-level definitions, embedding system design decisions into implementation artifacts and offering limited support for reuse or systematic exploration of alternative configurations. More recently, specification-oriented efforts, including Open Agent Specification [ 12 ] , Agent Definition Language (ADL) [ 13 ] , AgentSPEX [ 14 ] , and Härer [ 15 ] , have introduced more declarative representations of agents and workflows. While these approaches contribute toward separating design from execution, they primarily describe individual system configurations or execution flows, with limited support for explicitly modeling variability across alternative MAS designs.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Variability Modeling. Variability modeling has been widely used to capture and manage configuration choices in software systems, and has also been applied to machine learning systems [ 16 ] . More recently, it has been also used to study the configuration of Large Language Models (LLMs) [ 17 ] . Yoshimura et al. study variability in industrial AI agents for root-cause analysis, illustrating the value of explicitly managing variations across equipment, models, data, and operational contexts [ 18 ] . While their work focuses on adapting a domain-specific agent to different operational contexts, GEAR addresses variability at the MAS level through a common, framework-independent representation that supports configuration, validation, and generation across heterogeneous agentic frameworks.

content: GEAR provides a five-step workflow from MAS configuration to execution across different target frameworks, as shown in Fig. 1 . We illustrate this workflow with a log-analysis system comprising two agents: LogParser , which parses logs, and LogAnalyzer , which analyzes them to identify potential causes.

authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
section: III-A GEAR Core Features and Workflow
content: Configure. Users define a framework-independent specification through GEAR Studio. The specification comprises three main elements: (i) agents , with properties such as their model, task, tools, memory, and execution controls; (ii) modules , which define reusable orchestration structures such as parallel or iterative execution; and (iii) workflows , which connect agents and modules and define their execution flow. In our example, the user configures the two agents and groups them into a DiagnosisLoop module used in the workflow.

authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
section: III-A GEAR Core Features and Workflow
content: Validate. GEAR automatically validates agents, modules, and workflows, reporting errors such as references to undefined agents or incompatible configuration options. Users can then correct these errors before proceeding to framework selection. In our example, the user selects both parallel and loop execution for DiagnosisLoop . Because these strategies are mutually exclusive, GEAR reports the conflict and asks the user to select a single strategy.

The same specification can then be reused to generate implementations for other frameworks. In our example, the user first selects CrewAI and then repeats the generation with Google ADK, obtaining two implementations from the same log-analysis specification.

Each project contains source code, a configuration file and an execution entry point. title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Fig. 2 presents the architecture and processing pipeline supporting the workflow described above. GEAR separates the common specification of a MAS from the mechanisms required to transform it into framework-specific implementations.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Specification Layer. The specification layer (highlighted in blue in Fig. 2 ) relies on feature modeling to represent the configurable properties of agents, modules, and workflows. A feature model organizes these properties hierarchically and specifies whether they are mandatory, optional, or alternative, together with dependencies and constraints governing their combinations [ 8 ] . Fig. 3 illustrates an excerpt of GEAR ’s common variability representation. In particular, 32 32 features encode MAS concepts identified through a review of the literature and an analysis of ten agentic frameworks, selected based on their availability, documentation, active maintenance, Python support, and ability to compose agents into workflows [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . In addition, the feature model covers agent identity, model and task configuration, tools, memory, reasoning, execution controls, and orchestration. Overall, it exhibits 53 53 features and encodes approximately 2.4 × 10 8 2.4\times 10^{8} valid configurations.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Processing Layer. The processing layer (highlighted in brown in Fig. 2 ) transforms this specification into framework-specific implementations. During the validation phase, GEAR checks the specification structure, feature-model constraints, and workflow consistency, and normalizes valid configurations into a common intermediate representation. During the translation phase, a connector for each target framework applies explicit feature mappings and provides the manifest, templates, and assembly logic required by that framework. The Assembly engine then deterministically generates the executable artifacts, including source code, configuration files, and execution entry points. A conversion report records how selected features were mapped, adapted or unresolved, preserving traceability between the common specification and each generated implementation.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: We conducted a preliminary mapping assessment across the ten frameworks, listed in Figure 4 . For each of the 32 evaluated GEAR features, we examined whether a framework-specific implementation was feasible, yielding 320 feature–framework pairs. We considered a mapping as identified when we could determine how the feature could be implemented in the target framework, using a native mechanism, an adaptation, or synthesized code. Otherwise, we marked the mapping as unresolved, particularly when the feature was not exposed by the framework or remained implicit in its internal mechanisms. The identified mappings were then used to define and extend the framework-specific connectors of GEAR .

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Figure 4 presents the mapping results for 320 feature–framework pairs, obtained by evaluating each of the 32 GEAR features against the ten selected frameworks. Overall, mappings were identified for 271 pairs (84.69%), while 49 (15.31%) remained unresolved. CrewAI achieved the highest coverage, with mappings identified for 31 GEAR features (96.88%) and one unresolved, followed by Google ADK with 30 (93.75%) and two, respectively. At the other end, Microsoft Agent Framework had 24 identified mappings (75.00%) and eight unresolved, while PydanticAI had 23 (71.88%) and nine. A given GEAR feature may be mapped to some frameworks while remaining unresolved in others.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: To further assess GEAR , we are conducting an ongoing user study in which participants use the tool to specify and generate MASs . We evaluate usability, effort, and the difficulties they encounter.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: While GEAR demonstrates its ability to facilitate the configuration, validation, translation, generation, and execution of MAS across different frameworks, several limitations remain. First, the current implementation focuses on the core abstractions and functionalities shared by the considered frameworks. More advanced capabilities, such as multimodal inputs and streaming are currently out of scope. Many of these capabilities are highly framework-specific and were intentionally excluded to preserve a common abstraction level and enable a controlled comparison across frameworks.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: Second, support for a new target framework currently requires manually defining the corresponding connectors and mappings between GEAR ’s framework-independent specification and framework-specific concepts. Although these mappings are reusable once implemented, their initial development requires both engineering effort and knowledge of the target framework. Reducing this effort, for instance through partially automated connector generation or mapping inference, is therefore an important direction for future work.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: GEAR validates specifications against encoded constraints and reports target-specific translation limitations. Unresolved properties are omitted, so generated projects may differ from the requested specification. Future work should therefore investigate these behavioral differences more systematically, extend the range of supported features, and evaluate GEAR on larger and more representative real-world multi-agent applications.

title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
authors: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
content: In this paper, we presented GEAR , an open-source tool for configuring and generating MASs across heterogeneous agentic frameworks. By separating the specification of a MAS from its framework-specific implementation, GEAR allows users to reuse the same MAS specification across different frameworks through framework-specific connectors. It also makes configuration choices explicit through its feature-based model and makes the support of new frameworks easier through its connector-based design. Overall, GEAR contributes to bridging variability modeling with MAS , and opens new directions for their study and evaluation. Data Availability GEAR is open-source and available at https://github.com/brellsanwouo/gear-framework . A demonstration video presenting an end-to-end case study is also available at https://youtu.be/iwNi-oC2tCw .

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
section: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
content: Edge-centric IoT systems are increasingly evaluated through sensor values or platform features, yet the telemetry pipeline itself, the sequence of sensing, serialization, message mediation, ingestion, and persistence, is rarely released as a measurable object. This limits reproducible benchmarking of timeliness, provenance, and operational cost, especially in early-stage IoT design where real deployments and high-quality open data are often unavailable. I present a measurement-first edge IoT testbed and dataset that elevate timeliness, provenance, and energy to first-class telemetry dimensions. The testbed operationalizes a role-based event-driven architecture with explicit Source–Broker–Aggregator responsibilities and a schema-governed TelemetryMessage envelope (Avro) that embeds correlation identifiers and a uniform, cross-role vocabulary of stage-level timestamps. To trace mediation effects, I extend an MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto) with a plugin that annotates messages with high-precision ingress/egress timestamps. I release the dataset in a dual representation: (i) replayable raw events as compressed Avro streams and (ii) analysis-ready long-format Parquet tables partitioned for efficient query and benchmarking, generated by a deterministic raw-to-tabular transformation pipeline. The contribution is an integrated engineering artifact and dataset built from established components. The demonstration describes one deployment through latency summaries, measurement-context distributions, and energy aggregates; it does not establish a new attribution method or a controlled performance benchmark. By co-releasing heterogeneous telemetry with pipeline timing and energy signals in both replayable and queryable forms, the artifact provides a basis for reproducible exploratory analysis and subsequent benchmarking studies.

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: The Internet of Things (IoT) is an increasingly pervasive paradigm in which intelligent things, humans, and software systems are interconnected and interact through sensing, actuation, and networked communication [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . The defining capability of these things is not only that they observe and influence the physical world, but also that they continuously transform physical phenomena into digital information that can inform human decision-making or automated control [ 3 , 1 , 5 , 7 ] . As IoT technologies mature, they underpin solutions with substantial technical, social, and economic impact across domains such as environmental monitoring [ 8 ] , smart buildings and urban infrastructure [ 9 , 10 ] , transportation [ 2 ] , healthcare [ 11 ] , and precision agriculture [ 12 ] . Beyond domain impacts, IoT is also associated with broader economic and productivity effects [ 13 ] and sustainability-oriented innovation agendas [ 9 ] . Yet this growth intensifies long-standing engineering challenges rooted in heterogeneity and scale: devices differ in capabilities and protocols; deployments evolve over time; and system-level properties such as robustness, Quality of Service (QoS), interoperability, and openness become decisive for user-centric IoT applications [ 6 , 3 , 5 , 4 , 14 ] .

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: A persistent practical difficulty is that IoT systems are fundamentally data-driven [ 1 , 5 , 7 ] , while data is often the very resource that is missing at the earliest stages of design and evaluation [ 6 ] . When practitioners begin with limited resources, potentially without access to “things,” they still need to prototype quickly, understand the physical environment, and validate end-to-end behavior before committing to costly deployments [ 2 , 3 ] . In such settings, relying on open real-world data is frequently impractical due to quality issues, availability constraints, licensing restrictions, and incompleteness [ 4 , 7 ] . Purely synthetic or simulated data can reduce friction and enable early experimentation, especially for time-series workloads [ 15 ] ; however, synthetic traces rarely capture the operational realities that govern whether an IoT system is usable in practice: the timing behavior of the data-production pipeline, the effects of event mediation, and the energy footprint of continuously running edge nodes [ 6 , 3 , 5 ] . Consequently, many evaluations remain either value-centric (focused on sensor readings) or infrastructure-centric (focused on platforms), while the data pipeline itself is treated as an opaque conduit rather than a measurable object [ 3 , 5 ] .

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: This paper argues that, for edge-centric IoT systems, the telemetry pipeline should be treated as a first-class measurement target [ 3 , 6 ] . Contemporary IoT deployments are commonly organized around event-driven communication, where edge nodes publish observations and downstream components consume, transform, and persist them for analytics and actuation [ 3 , 14 , 5 ] . In such architectures, timeliness is not a secondary attribute but a functional requirement: delays, jitter, and tail latencies can directly affect alerting, automation, and decision quality [ 5 , 16 , 7 ] . At the same time, practical edge operation is constrained by energy [ 6 , 3 , 9 ] . Even when the sensing problem appears simple, the continuous cost of compute, networking, and serialization on small devices determines feasibility and longevity [ 6 , 5 ] . Despite these realities, datasets and testbed artifacts often under-specify the provenance of telemetry events, omit stage-level timing that enables end-to-end auditing, and report energy separately from the telemetry produced during the same observation windows [ 6 , 3 ] .

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
authors: Dimitris Gkoulis
content: I address this gap by presenting an edge-focused IoT testbed and a dataset that jointly capture heterogeneous telemetry and the behavior of the telemetry pipeline that produced it, motivated by telemetry requirements found in environmental, agricultural, and health-oriented IoT deployments [ 8 , 12 , 11 ] . The core idea is measurement discipline at the edge , expressed through three consistent differentiating axes that structure the paper: (i) pipeline observability , by systematically recording role-spanning, stage-level timeliness signals across Source, Broker, and Aggregator; (ii) energy alignment , by co-measuring plug-level energy in a way that can be associated with telemetry production and cadence; and (iii) dual representation , by releasing the artifact as both replayable raw events (Avro) and analysis-ready tabular views (partitioned Parquet). Timeliness metadata is embedded directly into a schema-governed telemetry envelope, enabling message correlation and inspection of recorded provenance within the telemetry envelope [ 14 , 5 ] . To support both systems-level replay and data-centric analytics, the dataset is released in a dual representation generated by a deterministic transformation pipeline. This combination yields an artifact that is simultaneously interpretable as an event stream and structured for exploratory analysis and subsequent reproducible evaluation [ 4 , 2 ] .

title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking

content: The contribution is an integrated testbed and dataset, rather than a new messaging protocol, latency attribution method, energy attribution model, or provenance mechanism. Its practical value lies in making the following established instrumentation and publication choices available together in a documented artifact. The present deployment measures indoor environmental conditions; it does not validate an agricultural, healthcare, or industrial application.
