title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: To isolate the agent, we hold the workflow-oriented design fixed and run tasks with Claude Code, Codex, and Grok Build (Figure 4 a,c). All share a C1 baseline, so a C1-realizable case that an agent fails to reach across its attempts is lost at the agent layer. We label each such loss from its traces as a refusal, an input normalization that removes the attack, or a malformed or abandoned call, and read retention beside benign task completion, since lower attack rates matter only if the agent completes legitimate tasks.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: The three agents retain 86-91% of consequences (38–40 of 44) while completing 76-83% of benign task attempts. The choice of agent moves retention by at most 4.5 percentage points (two cases), no agent neutralizes a class, and each loses at most 2 of the 40 realizable cases (Table 2 ). Across the tested requests, all three largely carry the attacks through to backend execution. Claude Code and Codex lose no realizable case to refusal, input normalization, or execution failure. Each leaves 10% of its retained cases transformed, including changes to a non-essential outer file name on a package-import attack. Grok Build loses 5% of the realizable cases to malformed or abandoned calls in multi-step resource-handling workflows and leaves 8% of its retained cases transformed. Similar execution errors occur in its benign runs, whose completion rate is 76%. Doubling the caps recovers one of its two lost cases (Appendix C ), showing budget sensitivity in one observed loss. Its lower retention accompanies lower benign completion, with no case-level losses attributed to selective refusal. Claude Code and Codex tie on retention and differ by one percentage point in completion. Because the underlying models are opaque and the losses are few, these observations do not establish a specific internal cause or a reliable security ranking.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: We then hold Claude Code fixed and vary only the capability design (Figure 4 b,c), reading retention beside benign coverage and task completion. The query-oriented design uses a fixed planner and snapshot index, and any contrast holds for our implementations rather than for the standards themselves.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: The endpoint-oriented design retains 95% of consequences (42/44) at 92% benign coverage (46/50), the workflow-oriented reference 91% (40/44) at 84% (42/50), and the query-oriented design 39% (17/44) at 46% (23/50); task completion is 89%, 82%, and 41%, respectively. The design thus moves retention by 56.8 percentage points, against at most 4.5 across agents, but narrowing the surface removes exploit paths and useful operations together. The one-factor sweeps do not measure agent-by-design interactions, and another agent may behave differently under the query-oriented design.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Most of the difference occurs at the interface stage. The endpoint-oriented design makes 98% of cases expressible with almost no subsequent loss. For the query-oriented design, 24 of its 27 losses (55% of all cases) occur at the interface stage, where no intent reaches the required operation or slot filling fails to transmit the required argument; the other 3 are C1-realizable cases that Claude Code fails to exploit. To control for workflow coverage, we examine the 21 workflows (42%) that all three designs support, fixed before any attack result, which correspond to 17 cases. The ordering holds: the designs retain 16, 15, and 9 cases (94%, 88%, and 53%). The two workflow-oriented losses here have a supported workflow but an unexposed operation or argument. Of the 8 query-oriented losses, 6 reach the relevant intent but lose the attack argument in slot filling, and 2 are Claude Code failures. The gap therefore reflects argument delivery through typed slots rather than natural-language access as such, conditional on our slot schema, planner, and request set.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Preserving Legitimate Functionality. As agents become a primary entry point to Web services, interface restrictions determine which tasks users can delegate. Our results show that lower exploitability can accompany the removal of legitimate workflows. The comparison on shared workflows shows that an operation can remain available while attack inputs fail to reach the backend. In the query-oriented design, these losses reflect both slot constraints and planner execution. This distinction motivates interface designs that preserve required business functions and constrain inputs according to their intended use. Agent safeguards require a similar distinction between rejecting harmful actions and failing to execute tasks. The execution failures observed in RQ2 affected both attacks and legitimate tasks, providing little basis for treating lower attack success alone as stronger protection.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Authorization Granularity. Exposing a capability for a legitimate business task leaves open which users may apply it to which objects and under what conditions. A capability for retrieving orders, for example, still requires checks on the caller’s access to the requested order. Binding calls to a user identity establishes who acts; object-level authorization and business rules determine what that user may do. Agent-facing interfaces can support these checks by binding identity-dependent arguments and limiting unnecessary input control. The backend must enforce the corresponding policy on each request, including requests expressed through valid business arguments. As services move beyond website navigation, these rules must remain effective across every interface exposing the operation.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Agent-Generated Call Sequences. The single step-completion case shows that an agent can supply prerequisite calls omitted from a user’s request and thereby complete an attack. The security implications of delegation thus extend to the sequence the agent constructs during execution. Each call may invoke an ordinary business operation, while the resulting sequence violates a rule governing eligibility, ordering, or repeated execution. This motivates enforcing workflow rules against the current application state throughout execution. Checks on the initial instruction or the availability of individual tools alone cannot establish whether the completed workflow is authorized.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Evaluating an agent-facing service requires explaining why an attack fails and what legitimate functionality remains available. An unavailable operation, an unsuccessful agent run, and an enforced authorization check have different implications for service design. Aggregate attack success can obscure these differences. The comparisons in this study show the value of testing what an interface permits independently of agent execution and verifying the resulting effects on the application. Reading these outcomes alongside benign coverage and completion helps distinguish reduced exposure through functionality removal from restrictions that preserve the intended task.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Future evaluations should also examine the call sequences agents generate and repeat measurements as models and interfaces evolve. An agent update may recover an execution failure that previously prevented an attack, while an interface update may expose a missing operation or argument. Broader comparisons across agent–interface combinations would clarify whether the effects observed in our separate sweeps persist when both layers change.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Representativeness. The benchmark covers 44 documented vulnerabilities across twelve application families, with cases drawn from production applications and deliberately vulnerable environments. It supports controlled comparisons of known defects, but does not estimate their prevalence across deployed Web services.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Interface Construction. Retention depends on how much an interface exposes, and we built the interfaces ourselves, so the 91% reference figure is not an estimate for deployed services. We derive them blind from benign workflows, freeze them before any security test (Section 3.2 ), report benign coverage beside retention, and give a range across three designs (39% to 95%) rather than a single point. The query-oriented results additionally depend on our planner and slot constraints, and other implementations may expose different operations or preserve different attack inputs.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Execution and Measurement. Observed exploitability depends on the tested requests, agent versions, and execution budgets. A security-oriented system prompt or approval by a party other than the user may change agent-layer outcomes and is not tested. Case-level retention records success in at least one repetition and does not imply consistent success across attempts. Failures remain specific to the tested conditions, as illustrated by the case recovered with a larger budget. Independent oracles verify predefined security consequences; they do not enumerate every possible harm. Our one-factor comparisons identify differences around the reference configuration, while interactions between agents and interface designs remain to be evaluated. The results apply to capability-based access under the stated threat model; browser-driven access and attacks that compromise the agent require separate investigation.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Agents as Web Attackers. A growing body of work measures whether LLM agents can exploit Web vulnerabilities on their own. Benchmarks such as WebExploitBench ( Liu et al., 2026a ) , CVE-Bench ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and PACEbench ( Liu et al., 2026b ) deploy vulnerable applications as isolated targets, and studies show that agents can hack live websites and exploit disclosed one-day vulnerabilities from their descriptions ( Fang et al., 2024b ; Fang et al., 2024a ) . Related systems configure models for penetration testing and exploit construction ( Deng et al., 2024 ; Happe and Cito, 2023 ) . These studies examine agents’ vulnerability-discovery and exploitation capabilities under different levels of prior knowledge and access. We reuse such environments as a source of validated cases but study a different setting, in which a human attacker who already knows the attack reaches the same backend through a default-configured agent and an agent-facing interface. The question is not whether the agent can find or build an exploit but whether this mediation carries a known one through.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Attacks on LLM Agents. A parallel line treats the agent itself as the target. Direct and indirect prompt injection can override an LLM-integrated application ( Greshake et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , benchmarks measure how often tool-using agents follow injected instructions ( Zhan et al., 2024 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ) , and emulated sandboxes expose unsafe agent behavior at scale ( Ruan et al., 2024 ) . Agent-in-the-middle attacks intercept messages between cooperating agents ( he2025aitm ) , whereas our agent in the middle sits between a user and a backend. AgentHarm evaluates harmful-task execution ( Andriushchenko et al., 2025 ) , while ST-WebAgentBench evaluates safety and policy adherence during business tasks ( Levy et al., 2026 ) . BrowserART studies whether refusal training transfers to browser agents ( Kumar et al., 2024 ) , and the Cybersecurity Refusal Framework examines refusals in cyber tasks in relation to operational context ( Jones et al., 2026 ) . Our study complements these evaluations by comparing access paths to the same vulnerable backend, separating interface effects from the external agent’s execution, and measuring the accompanying loss of legitimate functionality. We submit requests that preserve the attack objective and exploit-relevant inputs to a task assistant and verify the resulting backend consequences with independent oracles.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: Agent-Facing Web Access. Agents increasingly act over real Web interfaces, from grounded interaction environments ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) to generalist agents on live sites ( Deng et al., 2023 ) , built on reasoning-and-acting and tool-use methods ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) . Access schemes such as OpenAPI descriptions, MCP ( Anthropic, 2024 ) , and NLWeb ( Microsoft, 2025 ) , together with commerce protocols such as UCP ( Shopify and Google, 2026 ) , define how services expose functionality to these agents. Security analyses of MCP catalog threats such as malicious tool descriptions ( hou2025mcp ) , and prompt-to-SQL injection shows that an LLM-integrated Web application can relay attacker input into database queries ( pedro2025p2sql ) . This literature describes how agent-mediated access works and the risks it adds, whereas we measure its security consequence for existing vulnerabilities through matched access paths and oracle-verified effects.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: We presented Vela , a benchmark that compares native access, direct capability invocation, and agent-mediated execution on the same vulnerable backends under independent oracles, separating the effect of the agent-facing interface from that of the agent. Across 44 cases, the agent removed none of the attacks the reference interface let through, and 91% of the vulnerabilities retained their native consequence. The capability design shifted retention far more than the choice of agent, from 95% under an endpoint-oriented design to 39% under a query-oriented one, though the latter also lowered benign coverage to 46%. As agent-facing interfaces become a common path to the Web, what each capability exposes, rather than the agent, is the main lever on exposure in our implementation, with the admissible argument domain of each capability as the most promising refinement to test.

title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie
content: We exercise vulnerabilities only in applications that we deploy and control, inside isolated environments with synthetic accounts and synthetic data, and we test no live service and no third party. The work involves no human subjects or personal data, and the vulnerabilities come from existing public benchmarks and disclosed advisories, so we report no new vulnerabilities and make no disclosure claims. Our findings concern how agents and interfaces handle known exploits rather than a flaw in a specific product. A characterization of which attacks survive agent mediation could inform misuse, but we judge its defensive value to outweigh this risk, since it helps interface designers and testers close exposed paths. The released artifact reproduces only these public cases in isolated deployments and contains no new exploit.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
section: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
content: Statistical procedures often control expected loss at a prescribed level while leaving part of their risk budget unused. Building on the e-value representation of risk-controlled decisions and the e-closure principle for multiple testing, we formulate recertification , a general paradigm for improving procedures by exploiting computable slack in their validity certificates. In particular, a valid procedure’s losses normalized by their risk budgets form a state-indexed e-value collection; conversely, decisions whose normalized losses are bounded by this collection inherit its risk guarantees. Recertification uses distributional structure to quantify slack, enlarge the certifying e-values while preserving validity, and construct less conservative decisions.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
section: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
content: We develop two applications. For conformal risk control (CRC) with a known loss family, recertification redistributes unused risk budget among the held-out points of each hypothetical augmented sample. The resulting controller is valid under every finite exchangeable law and is no more conservative than CRC on any calibration sample. For convex losses on an interval of actions, repeated recertification converges geometrically to an admissible controller. For false discovery rate control with arbitrarily dependent e-values, recertification exploits unused conditional budgets in randomized e-BH. It yields a closed-form randomized procedure whose rejection set contains that of randomized e-BH for every realization of the shared randomization and whose expected number of rejections is maximal among randomized procedures satisfying the same conditional e-value budget constraints. Recertifying instead with the larger e-collection of closed e-BH gives a second closed-form procedure, whose rejection set contains that of the first. Experiments on CIFAR-100 hierarchical classification and multiple testing simulations demonstrate improved budget utilization and gains in informativeness and power over the corresponding baselines.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: Many statistical procedures turn data into an informed action, while guaranteeing that some expected loss stays below a prescribed level. Statistical decision theory formalizes this task through a decision rule mapping data to actions, a loss depending on the action and an unknown state of nature, and the resulting statewise expected loss, or risk ( Wald, 1950 ; Berger, 1985 ) . The bound imposes a risk budget that must hold in every state. Among rules satisfying this constraint, one seeks the most useful decisions, as in the constrained problems of Hodges and Lehmann (1952) .

The false discovery rate is therefore controlled even when the analyst chooses among the certified rejection sets after seeing the data. Conversely, Xu et al. The principle applies equally to other error rates that are expected losses, and it contains the classical closed testing principle for the familywise error rate ( Marcus et al., 1976 ) as the case of e-values taking only the values 0 0 and 1 / α 1/\alpha .

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: Nothing in this argument depends on the actions being rejection sets. In a general decision problem, a state s s specifies a class of distributions for the data X X , an action a a is chosen from an arbitrary set, and each of several losses L t ​ ( s , a , X ) L_{t}(s,a;X) , indexed by t t , carries its own budget α t ​ ( s ) \alpha_{t}(s) . A family of e-values, one for each state and risk, certifies the actions whose losses fit within all the budgets it allows. Every data-dependent choice among the certified actions then controls every risk, and every procedure with this guarantee is certified by some such family ( Grünwald, 2023 ; Grünwald, 2024 ; Andrews and Chen, 2025 ) . In Section 2 we review the e-closure principle at this level of generality, with menus of arbitrary actions, possibly continuously indexed states and risks, and losses that may depend on the data.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: The correspondence can be read in both directions, and the direction from procedures to e-values suggests how to improve a procedure. Improving a decision rule directly is difficult: a more liberal rule may have higher power or utility, but it is rarely clear how far a given rule can be pushed before its guarantee fails. By contrast, improving an e-value is easier. If an e-value has expectation strictly below one, and the shortfall can be computed, for instance conditionally on a statistic whose conditional law is known under the null, then adding the shortfall back yields a larger e-value. Through the e-closure correspondence, larger e-values translate back into decisions. Starting from a valid procedure, we apply this construction to its canonical e-values: its losses divided by their risk budgets. Inverting the enlarged certificate yields a menu containing the original actions and potentially more liberal ones, all with the same guarantee. We call this step recertification . It generalizes the anchoring idea of Ramdas (2026) , which keeps an existing false discovery rate procedure and spends the slack in its validity proof, and it can be repeated.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: We apply recertification to two problems. The first is conformal risk control (CRC) ( Angelopoulos et al., 2024 ) , which extends conformal prediction from coverage to general monotone losses. Given n n exchangeable calibration points and a known family of losses indexed by a conservativeness parameter λ \lambda , CRC selects the least conservative λ \lambda for which the calibration losses, together with a bound on the loss of the unseen test point, fit within the budget ( n + 1 ) ​ α (n+1)\alpha . The selected controller typically leaves part of this budget unused. Recertification computes this unused budget on every such sample, redistributes it among the n + 1 n+1 held-out positions, and inverts the resulting e-values. The new controller is valid under every finite exchangeable law, and for every calibration sample it is no more conservative than CRC. In this sense, for a fixed loss family and observation domain, it improves CRC uniformly. This recertification step can be repeated, with diminishing returns. For convex losses, the iterates converge geometrically to a controller that admits no further pointwise improvement, and on finite outcome spaces a coordinatewise sweep reaches such a controller without convexity (Section 3 ).

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: The second application returns to multiple testing. The e-BH procedure is valid under arbitrary dependence but can be conservative, and Xu and Ramdas (2023) showed that external randomization recovers part of the lost power. Their U-eBH procedure boosts the e-values by dividing them by a single uniform random variable and then applies e-BH. In this setting, we treat the conditional law of the rejection set given the e-values as a randomized action. In these terms, U-eBH is certified by the family of e-values behind e-BH, through a version of the self-consistency condition of Blanchard and Roquain (2008) that holds on average over the randomization, and it typically leaves part of the budget allowed by this family unused. Recertification spends this budget and yields a closed-form randomized rule, recertified U-eBH (RU-eBH), which rejects at least as many hypotheses as U-eBH for every realization of the randomization and has the largest expected number of rejections among all randomized procedures certified by the same family.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: The same principle applies to closed e-BH, the improvement of e-BH by e-closure ( Xu et al., 2026b ) , whose family of e-values is larger because it adapts to the number of true nulls. Recertifying with this family gives a second closed-form rule, recertified closed e-BH (RC-eBH), whose rejection set contains that of RU-eBH and which has the largest expected number of rejections among all randomized procedures certified by this family, closed e-BH included (Section 4 ). In simulations, both rules are more powerful than e-BH and U-eBH in every setting, and RC-eBH is the most powerful of the eight procedures we compare in nearly every setting.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: E-values have become a standard tool for testing and multiple testing ( Vovk and Wang, 2021 ; Ramdas and Wang, 2025 ) . Their link to decision making is developed by Grünwald (2024) , who allows the significance level and the loss to be chosen after seeing the data, and by Koning (2023) and Chugg et al. (2026) , who study post hoc testing and its admissible procedures. For a single risk, our certified menu is the set of actions whose e-posterior risk bound ( Grünwald, 2023 ) , with each state’s loss divided by its budget, is at most one. Andrews and Chen (2025) study decisions reported together with certificates of their loss, and Koning and van Meer (2026) give evidence-weighted loss bounds for decisions based on conformal e-prediction sets. Decision-theoretic views of conformal prediction also study how prediction sets should inform downstream actions ( Lekeufack et al., 2024 ; Kiyani et al., 2025 ) . These works allow general states and actions; our focus is the constructive use of the correspondence, which keeps the error budget fixed and recertifies an existing procedure.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: Closed testing ( Marcus et al., 1976 ) controls the familywise error rate, and every coherent procedure for that error rate is a closed testing procedure ( Sonnemann, 2008 ) . Closed testing also yields simultaneous bounds on the false discovery proportion of every rejection set ( Goeman and Solari, 2011 ) , and only closed testing procedures are admissible for that purpose ( Goeman et al., 2021 ) . E-closure ( Xu et al., 2026b ) extends the closure principle to error rates defined by expected losses. Its follow-ups include the uniform improvement of the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure ( Goeman, 2026 ) , anchoring ( Ramdas, 2026 ) , online versions ( Xu et al., 2026a ) , and complete-class and admissibility results for e-value procedures ( Sun and Wang, 2026 ) . We note that representation and admissibility are separate questions. Every valid procedure is certified by some family of e-values, while admissibility requires further conditions, and our admissibility results for CRC rely on the structure of that problem.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: Randomization is classical in testing, where it makes tests based on discrete statistics exact ( Lehmann and Romano, 2022 ) . For false discovery rate control with e-values under arbitrary dependence, Xu and Ramdas (2023) showed that stochastic rounding of the e-values and U-eBH increase the power of e-BH, and Xu et al. (2026b) combine stochastic rounding with e-closure. These methods randomize the e-values. Our procedures instead choose the distribution of the rejection set directly, subject either to per-hypothesis budgets that form a randomized version of the self-consistency condition of Blanchard and Roquain (2008) or to the constraints that certify closed e-BH. Other uniform improvements of e-BH include its minimally adaptive version ( Ignatiadis et al., 2024 ) , closed e-BH ( Xu et al., 2026b ) , and conditional calibration ( Fithian and Lei, 2022 ; Lee and Ren, 2024 ) , which recalibrates the e-values given a sufficient statistic.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: CRC already handles several, even infinitely many, risks that share a monotone action parameter ( Angelopoulos et al., 2024 , Section 4.3) . Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets (RCPS) and Learn then Test (LTT) instead provide high-probability statements about population risks ( Bates et al., 2021 ; Angelopoulos et al., 2025 ) . Extensions of CRC treat non-exchangeable data ( Farinhas et al., 2024 ) , cross-validation ( Cohen et al., 2024 ) , non-monotonic losses ( Angelopoulos, 2026 ) , and end-to-end training ( Yeh et al., 2025 ) . The leave-one-out characterization of validity that we use (Lemma 3.1 ) is the risk-control counterpart of the universality of conformal prediction ( Vovk et al., 2022 , Proposition 2.9) ; see also Tibshirani et al. (2026) , and Angelopoulos (2026) for its sufficiency direction. Conformal prediction with e-values is developed by Vovk (2025) , Koning (2026) , Gauthier et al. (2025) , and Koning and van Meer (2026) . Apart from the sharper bound on the unseen test loss in envelope CRC ( Yeh et al., 2025 ) , which serves as our starting point, we are not aware of work on improving CRC controllers pointwise or on their admissibility. We use CRC to show concretely how large such improvements can be and what they cost in computation.

authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: Section 2 formulates e-closure for general decision problems, including randomized actions, and introduces recertification. Section 3 develops the improvement of CRC, including its admissibility theory, worked examples and a real-data study. Section 4 returns to multiple testing, recertifies randomized e-BH with the e-collections of e-BH and closed e-BH, and reports simulations on Gaussian mean testing. Section 5 comments on the choice among certified actions and concludes.

content: The e-closure principle for multiple testing is recovered as follows. Take both the state space and the action space to be 2 [ K ] 2^{[K]} , let 𝒫 T \mathcal{P}_{T} contain the distributions under which T T is the set of true null hypotheses, and use the loss L ⁡ ( T , R ) = | T ∩ R | / ( | R | ∨ 1 ) L(T,R)=|T\cap R|/(|R|\vee 1) . The certified menu ( 2.3 ) then consists of the rejection sets certified by ( 1.1 ), which is the e-closure principle for the false discovery rate ( Xu et al., 2026b ) , and the loss L ( T , R ) = 𝟙 { T ∩ R ≠ ∅ } L(T,R)=\ind\{T\cap R\neq\varnothing\} gives its familywise error rate version. E-values for intersection hypotheses, which are valid whenever T T is contained in the set of true nulls, are in particular valid for the exact-state classes 𝒫 T \mathcal{P}_{T} used here. Section 4 reviews this setting in more detail. The general framework requires no structure on the actions, such as unions or an ordering, and no monotonicity of the losses. For instance, the false discovery proportion can decrease when a rejection is added.

content: A valid menu can be enlarged in two ways, and the distinction between them is central to our approach. The first is closing , which adds every action whose losses lie beneath the current envelopes of the menu. By Theorem 2.1 , closing preserves every envelope: the closed menu offers more choice, which in multiple testing is the simultaneity gain described by Xu et al. (2026b) , but it uses exactly the budget that the original menu uses. Any budget that the original procedure leaves unused therefore remains unused after closing. The second way, which we call recertifying , first replaces the envelopes by larger ones that still respect the budgets and then closes with respect to the new envelopes. The recertified menu can therefore contain actions whose losses exceed those of every action in the original menu, and this is how recertification spends the unused budget.

First, the iterates decrease and the losses are non-increasing, so stopping at a data-dependent round no later than a fixed maximum incurs at most the loss of the maximal round and preserves validity. Exact recertification thus trades computation for a uniform improvement.

content: In both applications, recertification enlarges the menu of certified actions, and we selected its most liberal element – the least conservative controller in CRC, and the boosting rule that rejects the most hypotheses in multiple testing. Nothing in the framework requires this choice. By Theorem 2.1 , every data-dependent selection from a certified menu is valid, so one may instead select the action that maximizes a utility, for instance a posterior expected utility under a prior. Such a selection is Bayes optimal among selections from the menu, and its validity does not depend on the prior. This differs from the constrained problems of Wald (1950) and Hodges and Lehmann (1952) , which optimize a single rule subject to the risk constraints and, by Theorem 2.1 , amount to optimizing the e-collection and the selection jointly. Similarly, our admissibility results compare procedures on every calibration sample or conditionally on the e-values; they do not address classical risk admissibility, which allows a rule to trade larger losses at some observations for smaller losses at others.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: In summary, this paper formulates the e-closure principle for general decision problems and uses the resulting correspondence constructively. Recertification starts by measuring the budget that a valid procedure leaves unused, spends it through larger e-values, and inverts them into an improved procedure with the same guarantee. The source of this budget differs between our two applications. In conformal risk control, exchangeability makes the budget computable on every hypothetical augmented sample, and recertification yields pointwise improvements of CRC and an admissible limit. In multiple testing, the e-values themselves supply the budget once randomized procedures are treated as randomized actions, and recertifying U-eBH yields two closed-form procedures, RU-eBH and RC-eBH, each optimal among the procedures certified by its e-collection.

title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
authors: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas
content: The two applications also differ in cost. RU-eBH and RC-eBH require only sorting the e-values and, for RC-eBH, a convex minorant, whereas repeated recertification of CRC trades computation for a uniform improvement, with diminishing returns, and can be expensive when the controller depends on individual scores. Exploiting the structure of the loss and the data to compute stronger certificates economically remains an important practical question, and whether RC-eBH is admissible among all FDR procedures is open. More broadly, any procedure whose validity proof leaves an identifiable budget unused is a candidate for recertification, and we expect further applications of this kind, especially those with more complex states, actions or loss structures.

section: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
content: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because the estimation errors of fitted Q Q -functions and occupancy-ratio estimates cannot be directly evaluated from held-out transitions. Bellman-residual and minimax validation methods often require auxiliary regressions or optimization over separate critic classes, adding computational and tuning costs. We introduce pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a tuning-free minimax procedure for selecting among finite classes of fitted Q Q -functions and occupancy-ratio estimators using held-out transitions. PBV constructs critics from pairwise differences between candidates, reducing validation to computing a finite collection of penalized empirical moments, without fitting auxiliary validation models or optimizing over a separate critic class. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. Our key insight is that Q Q -function errors and log ratios between candidate and true occupancy ratios provide oracle critics whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. These unknown critics can be approximated using pairwise differences between candidates, while penalties account for comparator approximation error. For Q Q -function selection, we first develop unweighted PBV, which evaluates pairwise Bellman moments under the offline distribution and admits oracle guarantees under a pairwise coercivity condition relating the offline distribution to the target-policy dynamics. We then develop target-aligned PBV (TA-PBV), which uses marginalized importance weighting to provide error control without pairwise coercivity. For occupancy-ratio selection, we develop adjoint PBV (A-PBV), which evaluates adjoint Bellman moments against log-ratio critics. On Hopper and Deep OPE, unweighted PBV performs competitively, while target-occupancy weighting can improve performance in settings with controlled overlap.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: The goal of off-policy evaluation (OPE) is to estimate the value of a target policy using data collected under a different policy in a Markov decision process (MDP). In offline reinforcement learning, two central objects are the target-policy action-value function, or Q Q -function, and the discounted occupancy ratio ( Uehara et al., 2026 ) . These functions underlie direct, importance-weighted, and doubly robust OPE, as well as semiparametrically efficient inference ( Jiang and Li, 2016 ; Xie et al., 2019 ; Kallus and Uehara, 2020 ; Kallus and Uehara, 2022 ; van der Laan et al., 2025 ) . They are characterized, respectively, as fixed points of the Bellman and adjoint Bellman operators ( Uehara et al., 2021 ) . Leveraging this structure, the Q Q -function and occupancy ratio can be learned using fitted-iteration methods, such as FQE, or minimax methods that test Bellman residuals against a class of critic functions, such as DualDICE and minimax Q Q -learning ( Munos and Szepesvári, 2008 ; Nachum et al., 2019 ; Uehara et al., 2020 ; Uehara et al., 2021 ; van der Laan and Kallus, 2026 ) .

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: A central challenge in OPE is model selection and hyperparameter tuning. Different choices of algorithms, function classes, regularization, and hyperparameters produce competing Q Q -function and occupancy-ratio estimates, but neither admits a supervised validation loss that can be directly evaluated from logged data. For Q Q -functions, squared temporal-difference error is generally unsuitable for comparing candidates under stochastic transitions because it includes a candidate-dependent conditional-variance term ( Baird III, 1995 ) . Bellman-residual validation instead estimates the Bellman residual Q − ℬ π ​ Q Q-\mathcal{B}_{\pi}Q , where ℬ π \mathcal{B}_{\pi} denotes the target-policy Bellman operator, and selects the candidate with the smallest estimated mean-squared residual. This typically requires fitting a separate regression for each candidate ( Zitovsky et al., 2023 ) , which can be computationally prohibitive and introduces an additional tuning problem. An alternative is minimax moment validation, which avoids regression by evaluating moments of the Bellman residual against a class of critic functions and selecting the candidate that minimizes the largest absolute empirical moment over that class ( Uehara et al., 2021 ; Miyaguchi, 2026 ) . This approach requires specifying and potentially tuning a critic class and can involve computationally demanding and numerically delicate optimization, particularly with flexible critics. More recently, LSTD-Tournament ( Liu et al., 2025 ) avoids specifying a separate critic class by comparing candidates pairwise using least-squares temporal-difference Q Q -learning (LSTDQ). However, its theoretical guarantees require the true Q Q -function to belong to the finite candidate class, a strong realizability assumption, as well as matrix-conditioning assumptions linking the offline distribution to the target-policy dynamics.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: We introduce pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a tuning-free minimax procedure for selecting among finite classes of fitted Q Q -functions and occupancy-ratio estimators using held-out transitions. PBV provides oracle selection guarantees without requiring realizability. Operationally, PBV constructs a finite class of critics from pairwise comparisons between candidates and evaluates each candidate using empirical moments of its Bellman or adjoint Bellman residual against these critics. For Q Q -function selection, each moment is the held-out average of a one-step temporal-difference residual multiplied by a critic. PBV subtracts a penalty for critic size from each empirical moment and selects the candidate with the smallest maximum score over its pairwise critics. Validation therefore reduces to computing a finite collection of sample averages, without fitting auxiliary validation models or separately optimizing critic functions.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation

content: Our key observation is that estimation errors provide oracle critics whose corresponding moments control estimation error. Under suitable conditions, we show that evaluating the Bellman residual of Q i Q_{i} against Q i − Q π Q_{i}-Q^{\pi} controls its squared L 2 L^{2} error, while evaluating the adjoint Bellman residual of w i w_{i} against log ⁡ ( w i / w π ) \log(w_{i}/w^{\pi}) controls its generalized-KL error. Since these oracle critics depend on unknown targets, we approximate them using pairwise differences: Q i − Q j Q_{i}-Q_{j} for Q Q -function selection and log ⁡ ( w i / w j ) \log(w_{i}/w_{j}) for occupancy-ratio selection. These pairwise critics recover the oracle critics when the comparator equals the truth and approximate them when it is close. Together with a penalty for critic size, this construction yields oracle guarantees relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation

content: For Q Q -function selection, we first develop unweighted PBV, which evaluates these moments under the offline distribution with a quadratic critic penalty. Because the target-policy Bellman operator need not be contractive in the corresponding L 2 L^{2} norm, our guarantees require a pairwise coercivity condition analogous to matrix-conditioning assumptions in LSTD-Tournament and linear TD learning ( Bradtke and Barto, 1996 ; Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, 1997 ; Lagoudakis and Parr, 2003 ; Amortila et al., 2026 ) . We then develop target-aligned PBV (TA-PBV), which uses marginalized importance weighting to evaluate the same moments under the discounted target-occupancy distribution, where contraction provides error control without pairwise coercivity. Thus, unweighted PBV avoids occupancy-ratio estimation, whereas TA-PBV removes the coercivity requirement at the cost of importance weighting.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: For occupancy-ratio selection, we develop adjoint PBV (A-PBV), which evaluates adjoint Bellman residuals against log-ratio critics with a penalty proportional to the squared Hellinger distance between candidate ratios. A-PBV requires neither importance weighting nor a coercivity condition because the adjoint Bellman operator is already contractive in KL divergence under the offline distribution ( van der Laan and Kallus, 2026 ) .

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation

content: To our knowledge, unweighted PBV and TA-PBV are the first tuning-free procedures for selecting among fitted Q Q -functions with finite-sample oracle guarantees under candidate-class misspecification. A-PBV provides an analogous first result for selecting among fitted occupancy-ratio estimators, without auxiliary estimation or additional tuning.

content: Model selection for Q Q -functions and occupancy ratios. Existing OPE model-selection methods have focused primarily on Q Q -functions, using Bellman residuals, candidate-dependent projections, nested classes, or auxiliary regressions and critics in place of the unavailable supervised loss ( Farahmand and Szepesvári, 2011 ; Xie and Jiang, 2021 ; Zhang and Jiang, 2021 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Zitovsky et al., 2023 ; Miyaguchi, 2026 ) . These approaches generally introduce additional estimation or structural requirements beyond the candidate class itself; LSTD-Tournament is an important exception and is discussed separately below. By contrast, model selection among already-fitted occupancy-ratio estimators has received substantially less attention, despite extensive work on occupancy-ratio estimation ( Nachum et al., 2019 ; Uehara et al., 2020 ; Uehara et al., 2021 ; van der Laan and Kallus, 2026 ) . Extended discussion appears in Appendix E .

For each pair ( Q i , Q j ) (Q_{i},Q_{j}) , it constructs a two-dimensional feature map from the candidates and evaluates the corresponding LSTDQ normal-equation residuals ( Lagoudakis and Parr, 2003 ) . Its selection criterion (Equation 10 in their work) can equivalently be viewed as a minimax procedure that evaluates the Bellman residual of each candidate Q i Q_{i} against the candidate Q Q -functions themselves as critics. Its theoretical guarantees assume candidate-class realizability and depend on the conditioning of pair-specific LSTD matrices.

content: We evaluate PBV on Hopper ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and Deep OPE/D4RL ( Fu et al., 2021 ; Fu et al., 2020 ) . We compare unweighted PBV, its variant without the quadratic penalty, TA-PBV, squared temporal-difference (TD) error, and LSTD-Tournament using the normalized-difference implementation of Liu et al. (2025) . We consider both the original benchmarks and controlled-overlap benchmarks constructed to examine target-occupancy weighting when overlap is favorable. In the controlled-overlap benchmarks, the logging policy samples one benchmark policy uniformly for each trajectory, and each component policy is treated in turn as the target. Thus, the expected on-policy fraction is 1 / 10 1/10 for Hopper and 1 / 11 1/11 for Deep OPE, and the corresponding trajectory and discounted occupancy ratios are bounded by 10 and 11, respectively.

The selected ratio is then used to select a Q Q -function on an independent validation sample of n Q = 3,200 n_{Q}=3{,}200 transitions. Following Sinha et al. content: On the original benchmarks, unweighted PBV has the lowest mean value error on Hopper, while LSTD-Tournament performs best on Deep OPE (Table 1 ). Relative to unweighted PBV, the corresponding differences for TA-PBV are 1.07 1.07 ( [ 0.14 , 2.43 ] [0.14,2.43] ) on Hopper and − 3.55 -3.55 ( [ − 9.98 , 2.88 ] [-9.98,2.88] ) on Deep OPE (Table S2 ). authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: On the controlled-overlap benchmarks, TA-PBV achieves the lowest mean value error on both Hopper and Deep OPE (Table 1 ). Relative to unweighted PBV, its paired mean differences are − 1.20 -1.20 (90% bootstrap interval [ − 5.83 , 2.69 ] [-5.83,2.69] ) on Hopper and − 4.95 -4.95 ( [ − 14.40 , 1.54 ] [-14.40,1.54] ) on Deep OPE. Its mean errors are also lower than those of LSTD-Tournament, although all four bootstrap intervals for comparisons involving TA-PBV include zero (Table S2 ). The policy-level differences vary across settings (Figures S1 and S2 ). TA-PBV has the lowest mean initial-state value RMSE on both benchmarks.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: The competitive performance of PBV and LSTD-Tournament ( Liu et al., 2025 ) suggests that candidate-induced critics provide an effective approach to offline model selection. We recommend unweighted PBV and TA-PBV with tempered ratios as practical choices. Unweighted PBV requires no occupancy-ratio estimation. Its oracle inequality allows candidate-class misspecification but requires pairwise coercivity under the offline distribution. TA-PBV avoids this requirement through target-occupancy weighting, at the cost of occupancy-ratio estimation, and can provide additional gains when overlap is favorable.

Each π j \pi_{j} is evaluated in turn as the target under the same logging distribution. Since ℙ log = L − 1 ​ ∑ j = 1 L ℙ π j \mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{log}}=L^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{j}} , the target-to-logging trajectory density ratio is bounded by L L , as is the corresponding discounted occupancy ratio.

For Deep OPE, L = 11 L=11 , and all eleven targets are evaluated in each of four environments, giving 44 combinations. We use five independent occupancy-ratio data replicates per combination. The occupancy-ratio training and validation samples are independent of the samples used to fit and select the Q Q -function. Within each environment–target combination, the Q Q -candidate class and its validation sample are held fixed across the five occupancy-ratio replicates. Each occupancy-ratio training or validation sample contains at least 51,200 51{,}200 transitions. title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: The original Hopper benchmark uses the 15 candidate Q Q -functions from Liu et al. (2025) . These candidates are induced by a grid of perturbed Hopper simulators, with either gravity or transition-noise level varied across the grid. For each target policy, candidate Q Q -values are computed by Monte Carlo rollouts in the corresponding simulator rather than by fitting FQE. For Deep OPE and controlled-overlap Hopper, we fit a 15-candidate neural FQE grid on an independent sample containing at least 51,200 51{,}200 transitions. 1 1 1 The HalfCheetah and Walker2d medium-replay datasets contain fewer than 102,400 102{,}400 usable transitions. For these original Deep OPE settings, we form disjoint trajectory pools and complete each nominal block by sampling complete trajectories within its pool; at least 90% of each block consists of distinct source rows. Each Q Q -network is a multilayer perceptron with two SiLU hidden layers of width 64, 128, or 256. For each width, checkpoints are saved after 50, 100, 200, 400, and 800 fitted-Q iterations, giving 15 candidates in total. Each iteration comprises 20 AdamW updates with minibatches of size 512, learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and Huber loss. Inputs are standardized, the target network is updated after each fitted-Q iteration, and no early stopping is used. All fits use γ = 0.99 \gamma=0.99 . Deep OPE splits preserve complete trajectories. For stochastic target policies, conditional action expectations are approximated using eight draws per transition and 32 draws per reset state.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: TA-PBV uses neural FORE estimators of the discounted target-to-logging occupancy ratio. The log ratio is represented by a ReLU network with either one or two 64-unit hidden layers. Each architecture is trained full-batch with AdamW at learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} or 10 − 3 10^{-3} and weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Snapshots after 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, and 1,600 updates give 28 FORE candidates. A-PBV selects among these candidates on an independent occupancy-ratio validation sample. Before validation, fitted ratios are floored at 10 − 6 10^{-6} and rescaled on the training sample to satisfy the empirical constant adjoint moment. The selected ratio estimator is then held fixed when TA-PBV selects the Q Q -function. For the primary analysis, we temper the selected ratio as w T = w 1 / T / ℙ n , w ​ [ w 1 / T ] w_{T}=w^{1/T}/\mathbb{P}_{n,w}[w^{1/T}] with T = 5 T=5 , where the normalizing constant is computed on the ratio-training sample and then held fixed. Target-policy returns and selected Q Q -function performance are not used in occupancy-ratio selection. For the original Hopper benchmark, the ratio-training and ratio-validation samples each contain 3,200 3{,}200 transitions; for the original Deep OPE benchmark, each contains 25,600 25{,}600 transitions. The controlled-overlap comparisons use 51,200 51{,}200 transitions in each sample.

authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: Section 1.3 compares PBV with existing Bellman validation methods and LSTD-Tournament. Here we place the problem in the broader literatures on OPE model selection, occupancy-ratio estimation, supervised aggregation, and statistical inverse problems.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: Model selection for Q Q -functions and occupancy ratios. Existing OPE model-selection methods have focused primarily on Q Q -functions, replacing the unavailable supervised loss with structured Bellman criteria. BErMin estimates Bellman error with complexity penalties; BVFT and BVFT-PE use projected Bellman errors over candidate-dependent state aggregations; and ModBE uses relative square-loss tests for nested model classes ( Farahmand and Szepesvári, 2011 ; Xie and Jiang, 2021 ; Zhang and Jiang, 2021 ; Lee et al., 2022 ) . Supervised Bellman validation instead regresses the one-step TD target on the current state and action separately for each candidate. Duality-based Residual Estimation learns residual critics and selects among critic configurations on an additional split ( Zitovsky et al., 2023 ; Miyaguchi, 2026 ) . PBV instead uses candidate-induced critics directly, avoiding candidate-dependent projection, nestedness, and auxiliary critic fitting.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: Model selection arises at several levels in off-policy evaluation. One line of work selects or combines scalar value estimates, including MAGIC, SWITCH, shrinkage estimators, SLOPE, proxy-task and cross-validation methods, and OPERA ( Thomas and Brunskill, 2016 ; Wang et al., 2017 ; Su et al., 2020a ; Su et al., 2020b ; Udagawa et al., 2023 ; Cief et al., 2025 ; Nie et al., 2024 ) . A second line uses OPE to rank policies or tune complete offline-RL pipelines ( Irpan et al., 2019 ; Paine et al., 2020 ; Tang and Wiens, 2021 ; Yang et al., 2022 ; Nie et al., 2022 ) . Zhang and Jiang (2021) primarily study offline policy selection but also use BVFT-PE to select among candidate Q π Q^{\pi} estimates for a fixed policy. We instead study nuisance selection for a fixed target policy. From finite classes of candidates fitted independently of the validation data, we select the Q Q -function or occupancy-ratio estimate used for OPE. This differs from selecting scalar value estimates or policies because neither nuisance is observed, so their target losses are not directly available.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: Marginalized importance sampling, DICE methods, and minimax weight learning estimate discounted occupancy ratios from adjoint Bellman equations, typically using prescribed ratio and critic classes ( Xie et al., 2019 ; Nachum et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ; Uehara et al., 2020 ; Uehara et al., 2021 ) . FORE is an occupancy-ratio analogue of FQE that estimates the ratio through fitted adjoint Bellman recursion without requiring Bellman completeness ( van der Laan and Kallus, 2026 ) , while FORC is a related finite-horizon method that does require Bellman completeness ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Huang and Jiang, 2024 ) . These methods construct an occupancy-ratio estimate within a specified function class. A-PBV instead selects post hoc among already-fitted candidates using pairwise log-ratio critics and Hellinger-penalized adjoint Bellman scores.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
content: In supervised prediction, held-out outcomes make the risk of a fixed candidate directly estimable. Cross-validation uses this risk to select algorithms or tuning parameters, while stacking and Super Learner combine candidates using cross-validated predictions ( Stone, 1974 ; Wolpert, 1992 ; van der Laan and Dudoit, 2003 ; van der Laan et al., 2007 ) . Model-selection aggregation instead seeks to match the best element of a finite dictionary; under squared loss, Q-aggregation attains sharp oracle inequalities with logarithmic remainders ( Dai et al., 2012 ; Lan and Syrgkanis, 2024 ) . These supervised criteria are unavailable here because neither Q π Q^{\pi} nor w π w^{\pi} is observed, squared temporal-difference error is not a valid target loss, and offline-distribution Bellman moments need not control target-policy error. PBV instead constructs directly estimable pairwise criteria and selects a supplied candidate rather than forming an aggregate.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
authors: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus
section: Model selection in linear inverse problems.
content: Related model-selection challenges arise in statistical linear inverse problems, where instability of the inverse operator motivates operator-dependent risk estimates and penalties ( Cavalier et al., 2002 ; Abramovich et al., 2018 ) . For example, Regularized DeepIV uses an out-of-sample Tikhonov criterion to obtain oracle guarantees under misspecification in nonparametric instrumental-variable regression ( Li et al., 2024 ) . In general, small forward error need not control structural error without regularization and source or link conditions. Here, the Bellman evaluation operator is a γ \sqrt{\gamma} -contraction in L 2 ​ ( d π , γ ) L^{2}(d_{\pi,\gamma}) , while the adjoint Bellman update contracts generalized KL divergence by a factor of γ \gamma . These contractions convert pairwise Bellman moments into target-error bounds without a Tikhonov bias–variance choice or generic inverse-problem source conditions. This does not eliminate structural assumptions: TA-PBV requires coverage and occupancy-ratio accuracy, A-PBV requires an upper envelope and bounded pairwise log ratios for the fitted candidates, and unweighted PBV requires pairwise coercivity under the offline distribution.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
section: L U C I D : L ocal U nderstanding of C ovariate I mportance with Conditional D ensity Estimation
content: Computing local-level variable importance (VI) is critical for understanding machine learning models. Local permutation-based VI metrics offer a simple yet powerful approach, measuring how much a model’s output changes when perturbing its inputs. However, existing perturbation strategies often ignore feature dependence or account for it only through restricted approximations. Perturbing a feature without fully respecting this dependence can generate unrealistic counterfactuals, thereby evaluating the model in regions unsupported by the observed data distribution. We address this gap by introducing a new model-agnostic local VI metric and estimator, Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with conditional Density estimation (LUCID). LUCID perturbs features of interest using plausible values drawn from the full conditional distribution given the remaining observed features. We establish theoretical connections between LUCID and existing VI measures, and provide an estimator with convergence guarantees and uncertainty quantification. Finally, we demonstrate LUCID’s stable performance and practical utility across simulated and real-world examples.

authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: Variable importance (VI) is a fundamental tool for interpreting machine learning models, enabling the characterization of features’ usage and their effects on the model’s predictions. VI is particularly useful for probing the otherwise opaque behavior of black-box machine learning systems ( Guidotti et al., 2018 ; Casalicchio et al., 2019 ; Fisher et al., 2019 ) . Most established VI methods summarize each feature with a single population-level score or ranking ( Breiman, 2001 ; Gregorutti et al., 2015 ) . However, a feature may strongly influence the model in one region of the covariate space while being irrelevant in another, so averaging importance across the population can obscure when, where, and for which observations a feature matters. For example, in the Bike Sharing dataset ( Fanaee-T and Gama, 2014 ) , the importance of temperature and humidity changes substantially over the course of a day, while their global VI scores, shown as dashed lines, collapse this variation into single values and obscure the underlying heterogeneity (Figure 1 (a)). More fundamentally, distinct local importance patterns can share the same population average, meaning that global importance alone cannot identify how importance is distributed across observations. This motivates local VI and its accurate estimation, which makes observation-level feature usage accessible and characterizes heterogeneous feature usage across individual predictions.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: A central challenge for local VI is determining how to perturb the feature. Existing local perturbation-based approaches typically sample counterfactuals from the marginal distribution of the feature of interest ( Casalicchio et al., 2019 ; Bladen et al., 2026 ) , which can break feature dependence and generate implausible counterfactuals. For example, in the Bike Sharing data, plausible temperature values vary across seasons, whereas marginal permutation draws replacements from the same pool regardless of the remaining covariates (Fig. 1 (b)). Although global conditional importance methods provide dependence-aware alternatives, their perturbation schemes often rely on restricted approximations whose validity requires additional assumptions ( Fisher et al., 2019 ; Chamma et al., 2023 ; Borgonovo et al., 2026 ; Strobl et al., 2008 ; Debeer and Strobl, 2020 ; Molnar et al., 2024 ; Blesch et al., 2025 ) . Such schemes can recover population-average importance while producing systematically biased local scores, because errors across observations may cancel after averaging ( Section 5.1 DGP 3). Accurate local estimation therefore requires capturing the observation-specific conditional structure. This motivates flexible estimation of the full conditional distribution, which existing perturbation schemes may struggle to capture, particularly under heteroskedasticity, multimodality, high dimensionality, or complex interactions.

content: We organize subsequent contents around four questions motivating our framework: “why local importance?” (DGP 1); “why conditional perturbations?” (DGP 2); “why density estimation?” (DGP 3); and “why estimate the conditional density directly?” (irrelevant-feature robustness test). We also consider DGP 4 to show why subgroup-based methods can struggle to recover interaction structure, and DGP 5 to further explore the relationship between LUCID and local LOCO; we defer these two experiments, along with analytical LUCID calculations and additional experimental details and results, to Appendix E .

content: LUCID handles feature heterogeneity, unlike global VI measures. This case study uses three independent standard Gaussian features, X 1 , X 2 , X 3 ∼ iid 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,1) , and a simple tree predictor g ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = x 1 ​ 𝟏 x 3 > 0 + x 2 ​ 𝟏 x 3 ≤ 0 g(\bm{x})=x_{1}\mathbf{1}_{x_{3}>0}+x_{2}\mathbf{1}_{x_{3}\leq 0} , so that X 1 X_{1} is active only when X 3 > 0 X_{3}>0 , whereas X 2 X_{2} is active only when X 3 ≤ 0 X_{3}\leq 0 ( Bladen et al., 2026 , a setup similar to the one considered in) . As shown in the DR-BART panel in Figure 3 , because X 1 X_{1} and X 2 X_{2} play symmetric roles across the discontinuity, their global importance (dashed line) is identical, masking the fact that only one of them matters at any given observation. In contrast, LUCID captures this heterogeneity exactly, with the yellow and purple points representing observations on the two sides of the discontinuity.

content: LUCID correctly identifies locally irrelevant features. When a feature is locally inactive, perturbing it leaves the prediction unchanged, so LUCID is zero by Equation 5 . In contrast, LIME, SHAP, conditional SHAP, and local LOCO assign nonzero scores to X 1 X_{1} at every inactive instance ( x 3 ≤ 0 x_{3}\leq 0 ); a representative point is highlighted by the red box in Figure 3 . This results in importance leakage for different reasons: LIME fits a locally linear model that does not recognize boundaries, while SHAP and conditional SHAP average over subsets that omit X 3 X_{3} , mixing contributions across the discontinuity. Moreover, finite-sample errors in model refitting can lead to local LOCO producing nonzero scores. Section E.4 contains detailed comparisons and experiment results.

content: Conditioning in LUCID accounts for correlated features. When features are dependent, marginal permutation breaks the observed dependence structure and may evaluate the fitted model on unrealistic feature combinations ( Strobl et al., 2008 ; Hooker et al., 2021 ) . We isolate this effect using two jointly Gaussian features, ( X 1 , X 2 ) ⊤ ∼ 𝒩 2 ​ ( 0 , Σ ρ ) (X_{1},X_{2})^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}_{2}(0,\Sigma_{\rho}) with unit variances and correlation ρ \rho , and the predictor g ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = x 1 g(\bm{x})=x_{1} . In contrast to marginal permutation, conditional perturbations preserve features’ dependency and therefore measure the additional information in X 1 X_{1} beyond X 2 X_{2} . Accordingly, in this DGP, the analytical-average LUCID equals 2 ​ ( 1 − ρ 2 ) 2(1-\rho^{2}) (where ρ \rho denotes the correlation between features), whereas global marginal permutation importance remains equal to 2 2 . Thus, as ρ → 1 \rho\to 1 (i.e., as features become increasingly correlated), conditional importance reflects the increasing redundancy, whereas permutation-based methods fail to respect the feature dependence structure, leading to poor performance in the MSE comparison in Table 2 ; see Section E.5 for experiment results.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: Residual-based conditional permutation importance fail to capture heteroskedasticity. We isolate heteroskedastic dependence by letting X 2 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) X_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) and X 1 | X 2 = x 2 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , x 2 2 ) X_{1}\mid X_{2}=x_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,x_{2}^{2}) , with predictor g ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = x 1 g(\bm{x})=x_{1} . Thus, the conditional mean 𝔼 ⁡ [ X 1 ∣ X 2 ] = 0 \mathbb{E}[X_{1}\mid X_{2}]=0 is constant, while the conditional variance Var ⁡ ( X 1 ∣ X 2 = x 2 ) = x 2 2 \operatorname{Var}(X_{1}\mid X_{2}=x_{2})=x_{2}^{2} varies with x 2 x_{2} . Even with the correct conditional mean, methods based on globally permuted residuals ( Fisher et al., 2019 ; Borgonovo et al., 2026 , e.g.,) draw perturbations with the pooled residual variance 𝔼 ⁡ [ X 2 2 ] = 1 \mathbb{E}[X_{2}^{2}]=1 , failing to preserve this heteroskedasticity. As a result, while the analytical LUCID is x 1 2 + x 2 2 x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2} , these methods asymptotically yield x 1 2 + 1 x_{1}^{2}+1 . Importantly, this local misspecification is invisible after global averaging because 𝔼 ⁡ [ X 2 2 ] = 1 \mathbb{E}[X_{2}^{2}]=1 : the incorrect local scores recover the correct global average importance despite systematically misrepresenting where the feature matters. Moreover, Section E.6 shows that any common replacement distribution incurs a population local MSE of at least 2 2 in this DGP, further demonstrating why accurate conditional density estimation is essential for local variable importance. In Figure 4 , we show the resampling distributions induced by each method. Only CDE-based approaches capture the changing conditional spread, with DR-BART most closely matching the analytical CDE.

content: Conditional density estimation is more robust to high-dimensional covariate spaces than joint density estimation. Similar to our DR-BART estimator of LUCID, cARFi also generates perturbations by sampling from a learned density ( Blesch et al., 2025 ) . cARFi obtains conditional replacements from the joint distribution using Adversarial Random Forest ( Watson et al., 2023 , ARF;) , whereas we instead fit the conditional density directly. Because joint distribution estimation generally becomes more difficult as the ambient dimension grows ( Izbicki and Lee, 2016 ) , we consider a naive stress test: we augment each of the five DGPs with 0 0 , 5 5 , 10 10 , or 20 20 independent standard Gaussian noise features and compare ARF with DR-BART. These additions increase the ambient dimension without changing the true conditional distribution of X 1 X_{1} or its analytical LUCID. As shown in Figure 5 , the LUCID estimation MSE increases sharply for ARF as irrelevant features are added, whereas DR-BART’s estimated conditional density is far more stable. In Section E.12 , we further consider more challenging high-dimensional settings with additional relevant features, where the degradation of joint-density-based estimation is even more pronounced.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
section: LUCID reveals local heterogeneity across real covariate contexts.
content: Figure 1 (a) shows that temperature LUCID varies substantially over the day, so its global importance masks when temperature matters most. As shown in Figure 1 (b), its conditional replacement distribution also shifts across seasons, whereas marginal permutation fails to capture this heterogeneity by drawing replacements from the same marginal distribution throughout. Figure 6 shows a complementary pattern for hour: on working days, importance peaks sharply during the morning and evening commuting periods, whereas this structure is largely absent on non-working days. Unlike temperature, however, hour is only weakly predictable from the remaining features, so its local importance is less constrained by information already captured by those covariates. The observed heterogeneity therefore mainly reflects changes in the model’s sensitivity to hour. Together, these results show that LUCID identifies when a learned model relies on a feature and how its plausible perturbations vary given the remaining covariates. In the next paragraph, we show how group LUCID complements this individual-level view by capturing shared information among related features, as motivated in Section 3.4 .

authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
section: Group LUCID complements individual local importance.
content: Figure 7 (a) compares the joint LUCID of the weather group (temperature, humidity, and season) with the sum of their individual LUCIDs. Both are small overnight, whereas the group LUCID substantially exceeds the individual sum during the day, particularly during evening rush hours. Thus, assessing the weather features individually does not fully capture their joint local predictive importance in these periods.

content: Figure 7 (b) shows that the temperature–season pair exhibits a gap similar to that of the full weather group. Its pattern closely tracks that of the full weather group, while the temperature–humidity and humidity–season pairs contribute much smaller gaps. This might be because, for the other two pairs, season or temperature remains in the conditioning set, respectively, and can constrain the joint replacements through its dependence on the selected features. Thus, evaluating these features separately can understate their collective local importance when they share information.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: We present LUCID, a model-agnostic framework for local variable importance based on the full conditional feature distribution. LUCID characterizes where and how strongly a fixed model responds to conditionally plausible feature changes, with an interpretable decomposition, convergence guarantees, and Bayesian uncertainty quantification. Its flexible estimation framework accommodates modern conditional density estimators and feature groups. Future work could extend LUCID to outcome-reference importance and model class reliance ( Fisher et al., 2019 ) , moving from explaining a fixed model toward assessing importance for the prediction problem. Also, since global conditional permutation importance is the expectation of LUCID, accurate local estimation also supports accurate global conditional importance.
