title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: Breiman (2001) introduced permutation-based VI in his seminal work on Random Forests, recognizing that if predictions change when shuffling the inputs to the forest (i.e., resampling them from their respective marginal distributions), then the forest likely depends on the feature. This core principle has inspired subsequent approaches to global perturbation-based variable importance that go beyond sampling from marginal distributions, but the sampling distribution in these methods is often restricted and its validity requires additional assumptions. Residual-based approaches ( Fisher et al., 2019 ; Chamma et al., 2023 ; Borgonovo et al., 2026 ) estimate the conditional mean of the feature of interest and use the residual distribution to generate counterfactuals, which can yield biased importance estimates when the residual distribution varies with the conditioning covariates, such as under heteroskedasticity or other changes in the conditional residual distribution. Tree- or subgroup-based approaches ( Strobl et al., 2008 ; Debeer and Strobl, 2020 ; Molnar et al., 2024 ; Chamma et al., 2023 ) permute or resample feature values within regions defined by tree-based partitions, which may overlook local variation in the conditional distribution, while overly fine partitions leave too few observations for resampling. Approaches based on joint-distribution estimation ( Blesch et al., 2025 ) instead require modeling the full joint distribution, which can become increasingly challenging as the ambient dimension grows ( Izbicki and Lee, 2016 ) . There are several recent methods that extend permutation-based importance to the local level, including Individual Conditional Importance ( Casalicchio et al., 2019 , ICI;) and Conditional Local Importance by Quantile Expectations ( Bladen et al., 2026 , CLIQUE;) . However, these existing local perturbation-based methods ignore dependence between the perturbed feature and the remaining covariates. In contrast, LUCID defines observation-level importance with respect to the full conditional feature distribution. Accurate estimation of this distribution yields replacements that preserve dependence between the feature of interest and the remaining covariates.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: Several related methods target different notions of feature importance. (i) Local explanation methods also explain individual predictions by assigning contributions to features. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based methods ( Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ; Aas et al., 2021 ) evaluate changes in model outputs as features are added or marginalized over, with conditional SHAP using conditional feature densities to account for dependencies between features ( Aas et al., 2021 ; Jullum et al., 2025 ) . However, their estimand differs from LUCID, as SHAP allocates the deviation of an individual prediction from a baseline across feature coalitions, whereas LUCID measures the change in model behavior induced by conditionally plausible replacements of a specified feature while holding the remaining context fixed. LIME ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ) , by contrast, constructs a locally linear surrogate approximation of the prediction function, using the local linear regression’s parameters as explanations for the black box. Both of these methods can unfaithfully capture nonzero variable attribution to features that are inactive at the observation being explained, especially when the data exhibits discontinuities. As we show in Figure 3 , LIME, SHAP, and SHAPr (a SHAP variant) all yield non-zero feature attribution even when the feature is completely unused by some specific regions of the known outcome generating function. (ii) Feature-removal methods such as leave-one-covariate-out ( Lei et al., 2018 , LOCO;) importance measure how much predictive information is lost by retraining the predictive model with all-but-one of the original features. In practice, this change can arise from both information loss due to feature removal and errors introduced by model refitting, making it difficult to disentangle these effects. Moreover, because LOCO compares two different models, it does not directly quantify how the original fitted model relies on the omitted feature. Instead, it describes how much the algorithm that discovered the model relies on the feature ( Fisher et al., 2019 ) . At the population level and under squared loss, however, LOCO with optimal reduced predictor is proportional to and closely related to conditional permutation feature importance ( Reyero-Lobo et al., 2025 ) . We further explore this relationship at the observation level in Section 3.3 . (iii) Grouped VI methods measure the importance of sets of related features jointly to account for shared or redundant information ( Gregorutti et al., 2015 ; Au et al., 2022 ; Chamma et al., 2024 ; Little et al., 2026 ) . Our framework naturally extends this idea but to the local level, quantifying conditional importance for feature groups at the observation level.

We therefore use classification BART ( Chipman et al., 2010 ; Quiroga et al., 2022 ) to estimate these probabilities directly. For a binary feature, we estimate P ⁡ ( Z = 1 ∣ 𝑿 = 𝒙 ) P(Z=1\mid\bm{X}=\bm{x}) and draw replacements from the corresponding Bernoulli distribution. For a feature with multiple categories, we estimate a vector of conditional category probabilities that sum to one and draw replacements from the resulting categorical distribution. Each posterior draw of these probabilities specifies a complete conditional distribution, which can be used in the same LUCID estimation and posterior summarization procedures described below.

content: The repeated experiments confirm that the qualitative conclusions of the main experiments are stable across random seeds. DR-BART achieves the lowest mean MSE in DGPs 2–4 and remains highly competitive in DGP 5. In DGP 1, where the relevant features are independent and no conditional density estimation is required, simpler permutation-based approaches attain smaller errors. DGP 5 is similarly favorable to cs-PFI, although DR-BART remains close and exhibits low variability across repetitions. content: What happens to local VI when the covariate dependence involves interactions? This case examines dependence driven by an XOR-type interaction between X 2 X_{2} and X 3 X_{3} in the conditional distribution of X 1 X_{1} . Such interactions can be difficult for recursive tree methods based on univariate split selection, because their joint signal is not apparent from individual univariate splits ( Hornung and Boulesteix, 2022 ) . We use this setting to assess how this difficulty affects local importance estimation. As shown in the results for DGP 4 in Table 2 , DR-BART (which explores ensembles of tree structures through Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations ( Orlandi et al., 2021 ) ) yields estimates closest to the analytical LUCID. The cs-PFI estimates closely resemble marginal permutation, consistent with its transformation-tree partition failing to recover the pure interaction. ARF substantially improves on marginal permutation, but its MSE is still approximately 3 × \times higher than our DR-BART implementation. These results highlight the importance of recovering interaction structure in the conditional distribution when estimating LUCID. Additional results are provided in Figures 12 and 17 .

content: How does LUCID differ from local LOCO? LOCO provides a natural comparison for LUCID because both assess a feature’s contribution given the information available in the remaining features. Although global LOCO and global conditional permutation importance differ only by a factor of two under squared loss and an oracle regression predictor ( Reyero-Lobo et al., 2025 ) , this proportionality does not generally hold locally, as established in Section 3.3 . Compared to local LOCO, LUCID additionally accounts for prediction variability under conditional feature replacement, reflecting how important it is to know the exact feature value; omitting this component can substantially alter local feature rankings. We construct a heteroskedastic DGP with an extreme-tail component in the prediction function to examine the consequences of this distinction. Analytical local LOCO and analytical LUCID yield different feature rankings with an analytical probability of 67.4 % 67.4\% (Analytical local LOCO and LUCID assign different feature rankings to 68.6% of the evaluated observations.). Consistent with this theoretical discrepancy, estimated local LOCO disagrees with estimated LUCID on 69.6 % 69.6\% of the evaluated instances, as shown in Figure 8 . The disagreement between the analytical rankings demonstrates that this discrepancy is intrinsic to the two importance measures and cannot be eliminated by improving LOCO estimation alone. This example shows that LUCID provides fuller local feature information about dispersion, leading to substantially different feature rankings from local LOCO despite their proportionality at the global level. Additional results are provided in Figures 13 and 18 .

content: Across all 16 settings, DR-BART achieves the best overall mean rank of 2.31 2.31 , followed by cs-PFI with a mean rank of 2.81 2.81 . The relative performance varies substantially with the structure of the conditional distribution. In the linear setting, DR-BART is highly competitive and attains the lowest MSE in three of the four configurations. Its advantage is particularly pronounced in the multiple linear dependencies setting, where X 1 X_{1} depends jointly on nine covariates and DR-BART attains the lowest MSE in all four configurations. This setting is challenging for subgroup-based permutation methods because a tree must approximate several simultaneous linear dependencies through repeated partitioning; indeed, Molnar et al. (2024) similarly identify this setting as particularly difficult for cs-PFI.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: The independent setting represents a different edge case. Because X 1 ⟂ 𝑿 − 1 X_{1}\perp\bm{X}_{-1} , the correct conditional distribution is simply the marginal distribution of X 1 X_{1} , so no conditional density estimation is required. Methods that estimate a conditional distribution can therefore incur additional finite-sample estimation error without gaining information, whereas marginal or near-marginal perturbation schemes can perform particularly well. This explains why the simplest methods obtain very small errors in this setting and why the independent case should not be interpreted as favoring a more flexible conditional estimator.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: In the non-linear setting, cs-PFI performs best in all four configurations, while DR-BART ranks second in three of the four configurations. This DGP is particularly favorable to the subgroup construction used by cs-PFI: both the conditional mean and variance of X 1 X_{1} change across only a small number of axis-aligned regions defined by the signs of X 2 X_{2} and X 3 X_{3} . A transformation tree can therefore represent the relevant conditional structure using only a few splits. In contrast, DR-BART estimates the full conditional density through a flexible mixture representation, which is substantially more general than is required for this piecewise structure and consequently pays a larger finite-sample estimation cost. Nevertheless, its error decreases sharply as the sample size increases. For example, when p = 10 p=10 , the MSE decreases from 41.87 41.87 at n = 300 n=300 to 3.86 3.86 at n = 3000 n=3000 , while for p = 90 p=90 it decreases from 101.58 101.58 to 3.97 3.97 . Thus, although the finite-sample problem is substantially harder for DR-BART in this setting, the improvement with increasing sample size indicates that it is able to recover the underlying conditional structure with sufficient data.

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: Another notable result is the poor performance of ARF in these higher-dimensional settings, where it is consistently among the worst-performing methods and often deteriorates markedly as the ambient dimension increases. This provides further empirical support for our motivation to estimate the conditional density directly: approaches such as ARF recover the conditional distribution through an estimated joint distribution of all covariates, a task that becomes increasingly challenging as the feature dimension grows ( Izbicki and Lee, 2016 ) .

title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia Rudin
content: Overall, these experiments emphasize that no conditional sampler uniformly dominates across all dependence structures. Subgroup permutation is particularly effective when the conditional distribution admits a simple tree partition, whereas direct conditional density estimation is substantially more competitive when dependence is smooth or distributed across many covariates. Importantly, LUCID itself is agnostic to this choice of conditional density estimator; these results therefore characterize the statistical trade-offs of the sampling mechanism rather than a restriction of the LUCID framework.

The results reveal substantial heterogeneity for temperature, humidity, and season: their plausible replacement values shift across different covariate contexts, and their local importance varies accordingly. content: High predictability indicates that conditional resampling permits less variation on average relative to marginal resampling because information in this feature is already captured by the remaining features. Consequently, a small individual LUCID may reflect either limited model sensitivity to the feature or limited variation under conditional replacement. If the remaining features completely determine the feature of interest, then conditional replacement introduces no variation and LUCID is zero. Conversely, low predictability alone does not imply large LUCID, because the effect of replacement also depends on the model’s response: if the model does not use the feature of interest, its LUCID remains zero. content: We further examine the squared-loss decomposition of LUCID into its dispersion and displacement components in practice. In Figure 25 , V V denotes the dispersion term and D D denotes the displacement term; observations with similar contributions from the two components appear near the balanced region. Averaged over all observations, the decomposition is nearly even, with V = 51.3 % V=51.3\% and D = 48.7 % D=48.7\% , consistent with Corollary C.2 . Importantly, this near equality in the global average masks substantial observation-level heterogeneity in the mechanism driving local importance.

content: We use the hour feature as an example to show how to interpret the decomposition locally. For hour, which is only weakly predictable from the remaining features, conditional replacement leaves a relatively broad range of plausible hour values. The labeled examples in Figure 25 illustrate several qualitatively different regimes. At late-night observations such as example (1), the observed prediction can be far below the conditional replacement mean, producing a substantial displacement contribution. During the morning and evening commuting peaks on working days, as in example (2), the original model prediction is substantially higher than the conditional mean of the replacement predictions, so local importance is strongly displacement-driven. At similar hours on non-working days, the observed prediction is often closer to the conditional replacement mean, consistent with the less pronounced commuting pattern on non-working days and the remaining importance is driven more by dispersion across plausible replacements. Around midday, as illustrated by example (3), displacement is smaller, and variation across replacements contributes a larger share of the total LUCID. Thus, even for the same feature, a large LUCID can arise through different local mechanisms.

content: Finally, Figures 26 – 30 compare the conditional replacement distributions produced by the different sampling methods across season, working-day status, and hour periods. The goal here is not to identify a ground-truth conditional distribution, which is unavailable in the real data, but to illustrate how the different estimators behave under the same observed covariate contexts. DR-BART, ARF, cs-PFI, and GCMR generally preserve the support and qualitative structure of the observed features, whereas CMR can generate values outside the natural feature range because its residual-based construction is not intrinsically support-preserving; GCMR was designed in part to address this limitation for continuous features. Marginal permutation, by construction, does not adapt its replacement distribution to the conditioning context and therefore misses context-dependent distributional shifts. Differences among the conditional methods are most visible for features such as temperature and humidity, whose replacement distributions vary appreciably across season or hour period.

While training DR-BART itself requires expensive Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) iterations, the DR-BART model is fixed at prediction time and runtime for explanations depends only on time to sample posterior draws, counterfactuals for each posterior, and fitting/comparing the fixed predictive models. In contrast, other local explanation methods like LIME can require refitting new surrogate models for each new test observation, increasing explanation-inference time.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
section: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
content: Multi-objective reinforcement learning is a fundamental problem for modern AI, with applications spanning post-training, reasoning models, and robotic control. A central challenge is to learn policies that balance competing objectives, such as helpfulness versus honesty in safety and alignment, or speed versus energy in robotics. The optimal policy can vary sharply with objective-weighting combinations, and the extent of this variation depends crucially on the degree of conflict among objectives, making per-preference policy learning sample-inefficient. In this paper, we introduce objective-conflict coefficients and derive near-optimal regret bounds for online settings using this measure, thereby quantifying the impact of misalignment on learning efficiency. Then, we design routed ensemble policy learning, an algorithm that maintains a small set of basis policies and dynamically routes trajectories to the policy with the highest potential reward. Finally, we consider trajectory selection as another approach to mitigate objective conflict, and design a kernel surrogate trajectory attribution algorithm that estimates how feedback signals from a set of trajectories influence policy learning on other trajectories. The kernel can capture nonlinear interactions such as synergy and antagonism between trajectories. We evaluate our approach across diverse environments and benchmarks: routed ensembles improve average performance by 4.3% over baselines for online environments from Meta-World and MO-Gymnasium, and kernel surrogate attribution improves correlation with leave-one-out analysis over existing baselines by 50%. When applied to trajectory selection, kernel-based attribution yields a 27% improvement in reward over baseline attribution methods.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
content: Given m m potentially competing objectives in a reinforcement learning (RL) environment, how can we learn a small set of policies that maximizes expected reward under any specified preference weighting? This problem is fundamental in multi-agent systems [ 29 ] , and is ubiquitous in modern AI systems. In robotics, agents often need to balance speed and energy efficiency. In reinforcement learning with human feedback, reasoning models, and post-training, models are often evaluated under competing criteria such as helpfulness, safety, and honesty [ 20 , 37 ] .

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
content: A core challenge in multi-objective RL (MORL) is that the optimal policy can vary drastically with objective weight combinations. For example, even small changes in preference can lead to qualitatively different optimal policies [ 34 , 55 ] . Prior work has focused on approximating the Pareto frontier of the optimal reward trade-offs [ 42 , 52 , 55 ] , or learning one policy for each objective [ 44 , 53 ] , and it remains unclear whether or when transferring trajectories across objectives is effective.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
content: A key yet underexplored question is that the difficulty of learning across preferences is fundamentally tied to the degree of misalignment among objectives. When objective weightings are well aligned (e.g., rewarding both final and intermediate progress), additional objectives can facilitate learning, and data collected under one preference can benefit policy learning for others. When objectives are misaligned or adversarially-injected (e.g., RLHF with corrupted reward components), naive transfer can become inefficient or even harmful [ 20 , 27 ] . This problem is especially acute in high-dimensional settings, making it a critical open challenge to identify objective alignment [ 21 ] .

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
content: To address this challenge, we introduce a new theoretical framework based on measuring objective conflict coefficients that quantify the degree of misalignment among objectives through the χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence. Our analysis shows that this coefficient interacts with the coverability coefficient [ 46 ] —which captures how well a single exploration policy can cover the preference space—to determine the sample complexity of online MORL. Our regret bound generalizes single-objective results [ 1 , 19 , 46 , 9 , 7 ] and is the first to formalize how objective misalignment affects learning efficiency across preferences. Our theoretical framework builds on recent advances in transfer learning under distribution shifts [ 50 ] . However, the technical challenge in MORL lies in quantifying the discrepancy in policy learning. Our main result, Theorem 3.6 , relies on a low-rank basis assumption, along with a coverability condition that ensures sufficient exploration of the basis.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
content: Motivated by our theoretical framework, we propose routed ensemble policy learning , an online algorithm for learning a small set of basis policies, which can be applied to a real-world RL environment. This algorithm alternates between two steps: (i) routing each trajectory to the basis policy with the highest expected return under the corresponding preference weight, and (ii) partitioning trajectories into disjoint clusters and updating each basis policy using its assigned trajectories with a standard policy learning algorithm such as proximal policy optimization.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
content: Next, we consider an alternative perspective for tackling objective conflicts, based on selecting trajectories. This motivates the problem of quantifying the influence of individual trajectories upon the learned optimal policy, a problem for which we term trajectory attribution . We design a scalable kernel-based trajectory attribution procedure that estimates how trajectories help or hinder policy learning. Our procedure fits a kernel ridge regression surrogate to approximate policy performance across trajectory subsets. This can capture both individual contributions and higher-order interactions between trajectories. These interactions are common in high-dimensional settings and often underlie unexpected transfer behavior [ 21 ] . However, they are not captured by first-order influence approximations such as influence functions [ 36 ] , linear surrogate models [ 26 , 56 ] , or gradient-similarity-based analysis [ 45 , 17 ] . Our approach goes beyond prior work by leveraging efficient approximations grounded in policy gradients and random projections [ 55 ] . The results from more accurate trajectory attribution can guide trajectory selection in downstream policy learning.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
content: Lastly, we empirically validate our approach on the Meta-World robotics benchmark and high-dimensional MO-Gymnasium tasks. Our algorithm consistently outperforms multi-objective baselines, achieving a significant reduction in cumulative regret in environments with structured objective conflicts. Specifically, routed ensemble learning outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.3 % 4.3\% on the Meta-World benchmark and achieves an 8 % 8\% average improvement in hypervolume on MO-Gymnasium tasks. Similar results are also observed in reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) settings. Additionally, kernel-based attribution provides a 50 % 50\% improvement in terms of the Spearman correlations with ground-truth leave-one-out influence scores. When applied to downstream task selection, kernel-based selection yields a 27 % 27\% higher reward than existing attribution baselines. We present detailed ablation studies to validate the theoretical insights from our proposed framework. For instance, after the routed ensemble procedure, the coverability metric drops from 1.3 1.3 for a single policy to 0.2 0.2 for the ensemble policies, indicating that routing mitigates the exploration bottleneck caused by objective conflicts. We also conduct a detailed analysis on the number of basis policies in the ensemble, as well as validate a low-rank basis assumption in our theoretical setup.

content: We highlight three findings. First, routing mitigates negative transfer and reduces cumulative regret in synthetic environments. Second, routed ensembles outperform baselines by a 4.3% relative margin in multi-task RL, up to 48% in multi-objective RL, and 17% in large language model benchmarks. Third, our kernel surrogates improve correlation with ground-truth marginal gains by 50% for trajectory attribution and improve downstream task-selection reward by 27%. Our code repository can be found at https://github.com/VirtuosoResearch/Multi-objective-reinforcement-learning-code/ .

In Table 2 , we compare Algorithm 1 , uniform assignment, and learning a single policy for each objective. Our algorithm consistently increases hypervolume on the induced frontier. In the synthetic environment, our method improves hypervolume by 17 % 17\% over the single-policy baseline and 14 % 14\% over the uniform ensemble. Averaged across the two models, the corresponding improvements are 5.0 % 5.0\% and 8.2 % 8.2\% on HelpSteer2, and 6.2 % 6.2\% and 3.0 % 3.0\% on UltraFeedback.

These results suggest that routing trajectories across basis policies helps distinguish aligned from conflicting data and approximates the Pareto frontier more efficiently than uniform assignment.

content: A reinforcement learning environment is typically formalized by means of a Markov decision process [ 40 , 2 ] . Existing approaches in the literature on multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) generally fall into two categories. The first reduces MORL to single-objective RL through scalarization, optimizing a fixed or sampled preference vector to learn a single policy [ 14 , 33 , 32 , 38 ] . The second, which includes our work, examines the multi-objective nature of the problem by learning multiple policies (e.g., to approximate the Pareto frontier) to address sharp variation in optimal policies across preferences [ 42 , 44 , 30 ] . Recent work [ 55 ] proposes a convex relaxation algorithm for partitioning multiple objectives into disjoint, related groups. We build on this line of work by providing a theoretical characterization of objective conflicts in MORL, introducing a routed ensemble algorithm, and developing trajectory-level attribution to interpret model behavior . One interesting future direction is to examine the policy learning dynamics in multi-objective Markov decision processes [ 22 , 24 ] . Lastly, sequential decision-making problems also occur in experimental design, where one often needs to roll out an experiment through staggered adoption [ 47 , 48 ] .

content: Influence estimation techniques [ 23 , 35 ] have recently been extended from supervised learning to reinforcement learning to trace model behaviors. In the context of offline RL, [ 11 ] proposes a framework to attribute specific policy decisions to past trajectories. A fundamental challenge in the online RL setting is the circular dependency where current policy updates influence future data distribution. Recent work [ 17 ] addresses this by employing local data attribution via gradient similarity to identify and filter harmful transitions.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
authors: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang
content: In this paper, we study how to learn policies that balance competing objectives in multi-objective reinforcement learning. We first analyze the theoretical limits of transfer learning across preferences, highlighting that structural misalignment between objectives is the primary cause of negative transfer. To overcome this challenge, we propose a routed ensemble algorithm guided by a new measure, the objective conflict coefficient. Furthermore, we introduce a kernel-based trajectory-attribution method that captures widespread nonlinear interactions among trajectories and can improve subsequent policy learning. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior sample efficiency and attribution accuracy compared to state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks.

content: Our work connects to the literature on influence estimation and mechanistic interpretability, which aims to trace model behavior back to influential training data. Prior work include influence functions [ 23 ] , TracIn [ 35 ] and linear surrogate models [ 26 ] . In reinforcement learning, recent efforts have adapted these techniques to explain policy decisions, including trajectory-level attribution in offline RL [ 11 ] and snapshot influence functions for filtering harmful data in online RL [ 17 ] . One of the open questions in this area is to develop better theoretical characterizations of attribution methods. Our kernel-based objective attribution thus offers a principled approach and accurately estimates second-order interactions across preferences. This connection seems particularly relevant in light of recent advances in RL reasoning [ 4 ] .

content: In the following proof, we prove the lower bound by embedding a standard Bernoulli two-armed bandit problem into a simple subclass of MOMDPs. This is sufficient because a lower bound for one valid MOMDP family is automatically a lower bound for the larger MOMDP class. The constructed family has K K pairwise-disjoint sub-chains, one per objective, each containing one Bernoulli two-armed bandit. Here, a sub-chain means a branch of the environment state space, not a policy: the k k -th optimal basis policy is the policy that routes into sub-chain 𝒮 k \mathcal{S}_{k} and then plays the better binary action.

content: Standard reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms based on Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps. To address this issue, distributionally robust RL algorithms based on robust MDPs (RMDPs) have been proposed, for ensuring that agents can perform reliably to unpredictable conditions in real-world environments. Despite of the rich literature, an efficient model-free method is still lacking for robust RL, particularly for Markovian data, which is more relevant in practical applications. In this work, we take a step towards settling this problem by proposing a sample efficient (asynchronous Q-learning) algorithm for robust RL. content: As a fast-growing subfield of artificial intelligence, reinforcement learning (RL) demonstrated impressive success across various domains, including networked systems ( Qu et al., 2022 ) , trading ( Park and Van Roy, 2015 ) , operations research ( de Castro Silva et al., 2003 ; Pan et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2021 ) , large language model alignment ( Ziegler et al., 2019 ) , healthcare ( Fatemi et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2019 ) , and robotics and control ( Kober et al., 2013 ; Mnih, 2013 ) . Due to the unprecedented dimensionality of the state-action space, enhancing sample, space and computational efficiency has become a central challenge in contemporary RL applications. As a result, significant research efforts have been devoted to developing sample-efficient and memory-efficient algorithms and to characterizing the sample complexity and space complexity ( Li et al., 2021b ; Li et al., 2024c ; Li et al., 2022 ) across diverse RL settings, including different algorithm paradigms (model-based ( Li et al., 2024c ) ; model-free ( Li et al., 2021a ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) ) and different data-access regimes (online ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2020 ) ; offline ( Li et al., 2024b ; Rashidinejad et al., 2022 ) ).

content: Despite this progress, practical applications of standard RL techniques can still be greatly affected by the sim-to-real gap or environmental uncertainty ( Bertsimas et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ) . For instance, a standard RL agent trained in an ideal environment might fail dramatically when the real-world environment is subject to small adversarial disruptions ( Klopp et al., 2017 ; Mahmood et al., 2018 ) . Consequently, in addition to maximizing the expected total reward, robustness has emerged as an important goal for an RL agent, especially in high-stakes applications like robotics, autonomous driving, clinical trials, and financial investments. To address these challenges, distributionally robust RL ( Bäuerle and Glauner, 2022 ; Cai et al., 2016 ; Iyengar, 2005 ; Nilim and El Ghaoui, 2005 ; Xu and Mannor, 2010 ; Shi et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2024b ; Jiao and Li, 2024 ) , offers a flexible framework by drawing on principles from distributionally robust optimization and supervised learning ( Bertsimas et al., 2018 ; Blanchet and Murthy, 2019 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Duchi and Namkoong, 2021 ; Gao, 2023 ; Lam, 2019 ; Rahimian and Mehrotra, 2019 ) . This approach aims to develop policies capable of maintaining high performance even when the deployed environment deviates from the nominal model due to environmental uncertainty.

content: • We design an efficient Q-learning algorithm for RMDPs that operates on a single trajectory and achieves O ⁡ ( S ​ A ) O(SA) space complexity. Moreover, the algorithm processes samples as they arrive along a single trajectory generated by a fixed behavior policy. content: Robust MDPs have been extensively studied, both empirically and theoretically, under various forms of uncertainty sets ( Panaganti and Kalathil, 2021 ; Ding et al., 2024 ; Goyal and Grand-Clement, 2023 ; Ho et al., 2018 ; Ho et al., 2021 ; Iyengar, 2005 ; Xu and Mannor, 2010 ; Tamar et al., 2014 ) . However, most existing theoretical studies either focus on planning algorithms ( Tamar et al., 2014 ; Xu and Mannor, 2010 ; Iyengar, 2005 ) or adopt an asymptotic perspective ( Roy et al., 2017 ) .

authors: Yuchen Jiao, Gen Li
content: Recently, several robust RL algorithms have been developed, focusing on finite-sample performance guarantees under various sampling mechanisms, as show in Table 1 . A line of work focuses on model-based algorithms. In particular, Yang et al. (2022) ; Panaganti and Kalathil (2022) studied model-based robust RL algorithms with an ( s , a ) (s,a) -rectangular uncertainty set specified by the TV distance, which matches our uncertainty-set specification, and used data collected from a generative model, corresponding to the synchronous setting in this work. They also considered other uncertainty sets, including those specified by the χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence or the KL divergence, and Yang et al. (2022) additionally considered the s s -rectangular case under these measures. Zhou et al. (2021) assumed that the reward follows a certain distribution on a bounded set and conducted an offline analysis where states are uniformly sampled by a known policy, focusing on uncertainty sets defined by the KL divergence. Panaganti and Kalathil (2021) proposed a policy iteration algorithm based on linear function approximation and analyzed its convergence asymptotically under certain dedicated assumptions on the iterative policy and the induced stationary distribution. Though an asynchronous setting is considered, its space complexity in the tabular case is O ⁡ ( S 2 ​ A 2 ) O(S^{2}A^{2}) to store the feature matrix. Moreover, Shi et al. (2024a) provided the near-optimal sample complexity bounds for model-based robust RL algorithms with access to a generative model when the uncertainty set is measured by the TV distance or the χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence. Specifically, for a TV-based uncertainty set, the minimax-optimal sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( S ​ A ε 2 ​ ( 1 − γ ) 2 ​ max ⁡ { 1 − γ , σ } ) \widetilde{O}\left(\frac{SA}{\varepsilon^{2}(1-\gamma)^{2}\max\{1-\gamma,\sigma\}}\right) is achieved by robust value iteration. However, these algorithms require at least O ⁡ ( S 2 ​ A ) O(S^{2}A) space complexity to store the transition probability kernel, which is prohibitive for large-scale problems.

title: Provably Efficient Q-learning for Robust Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yuchen Jiao, Gen Li
content: Another line of research focuses on memory-efficient algorithms with a reduced space complexity of O ⁡ ( S ​ A ) O(SA) and their finite-sample performance analysis. Wang et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2024) considered a randomized reward function and an ( s , a ) (s,a) -rectangular uncertainty set under the KL divergence with a sufficiently small uncertainty level σ ≲ p min \sigma\lesssim p_{\min} , where p min p_{\min} denotes the minimum nominal transition probability. They reduced the space complexity by collecting a large batch of samples and using them to update the Q-function for one state-action pair ( s , a ) (s,a) at a time, then discarding the data before moving on to the next one. This design achieves O ⁡ ( S ​ A ) O(SA) space complexity; however, it implicitly assumes that the learner can query any state-action pair on demand, an assumption that holds under a generative model (synchronous setting) but fails in the asynchronous setting, where samples arrive sequentially along a single trajectory induced by the behavior policy. In addition, the restriction σ ≲ p min \sigma\lesssim p_{\min} on the uncertainty level limits its applicability. In contrast, Yang et al. (2023) proposed an algorithm for the asynchronous setting that performs Q-learning-style stochastic approximation updates on the penalized dual formulation of the RMDP. Their analysis relies on two key assumptions: that the Markov chain induced by the behavior policy is uniformly ergodic, which is also assumed in our work, and that the objective in the Bellman operator is strongly convex at its optimum. Under these conditions, they derived sample complexity bounds for various uncertainty sets, with an explicit bound of O ~ ​ ( 1 μ 𝗆𝗂𝗇 9 ​ ε 3 ​ ( 1 − γ ) 9 ​ ( 1 ( 1 − γ ) 6 + t 𝗆𝗂𝗑 3 ) ) \widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{\mathsf{min}}^{9}\varepsilon^{3}(1-\gamma)^{9}}\left(\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^{6}}+t_{\mathsf{mix}}^{3}\right)\right) for the χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence. This bound has worse dependence on the accuracy and mixing parameters than ours, although the two results concern different uncertainty sets.

content: Our algorithm differs from that of Yang et al. (2023) in the Bellman formulation, the update mechanism, and the scope of uncertainty sets. First, our Bellman operator minimizes the expected next-state value over an uncertainty set, whereas theirs penalizes the divergence from the nominal transition kernel. They show that, for a given initial-state distribution, a suitable penalty coefficient yields the same optimal objective value as the constrained formulation. The two formulations nevertheless lead to different update mechanisms. Second, their method uses stochastic gradient ascent to update the dual variable alongside Q-function updates. These dual-variable updates slow the overall convergence because the dual variable must converge faster than the Q-function to control the overall error. In the generative-model setting, this requirement is reflected in an additional inner optimization loop. Our method instead approximates the robust Bellman update using a single resampled next state and online estimates of the resampling parameters. This avoids dual optimization and achieves a smaller sample complexity bound (Table 1 ). Third, their framework accommodates general divergences under regularity conditions, whereas our resampling scheme is tailored to TV-based uncertainty sets. Table 1 compares their χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence formulation with our TV-based formulation. We use their χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence result because their paper explicitly provides a convergence rate for this case, but not for the others.

section: Comparison with analysis of standard Q-learning.
content: Compared with the standard Q-learning analysis of Li et al. (2024a) , our analysis addresses two additional challenges. First, errors in the estimated resampling parameters cause the distribution of the surrogate state s t + 1 ′ s_{t+1}^{\prime} to deviate from the target worst-case kernel P V k − 2 P^{V_{k-2}} . This introduces resampling bias into the Bellman update, which we isolate in ( 50 ) and bound in Lemma 5 . Second, the worst-case kernel depends on the value function and changes across stages. The resulting error propagation requires bounds on accumulated variance terms under these changing kernels, developed in Lemmas 7 – 9 .

authors: Yuchen Jiao, Gen Li
content: In this paper, we present a model-free algorithm designed for RMDPs, and provide a sharp analysis for its sample complexity under uncertainty sets defined by the Total Variation (TV) distance, assuming access of a single sample trajectory. Our algorithm achieves an optimal space complexity of O ⁡ ( S ​ A ) O(SA) , which is significantly more efficient compared to the O ⁡ ( S 2 ​ A ) O(S^{2}A) space requirement of existing model-based approaches. Compared with other memory-efficient algorithms, our algorithm operates in a more realistic asynchronous setting. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algorithm reliably produces an ε \varepsilon -approximate Q-function estimate using O ~ ​ ( 1 μ 𝗆𝗂𝗇 ​ ε 2 ​ ( 1 − γ ) 3 ​ max ⁡ { 1 − γ , σ } + t 𝗆𝗂𝗑 μ 𝗆𝗂𝗇 ​ ( 1 − γ ) ) \widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{\mathsf{min}}\varepsilon^{2}(1-\gamma)^{3}\max\{1-\gamma,\sigma\}}+\frac{t_{\mathsf{mix}}}{\mu_{\mathsf{min}}(1-\gamma)}\right) samples. This bound is nearly minimax optimal with an additional factor of O ~ ​ ( 1 1 − γ ) \tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\right) , and significantly outperforms sample complexity of existing asynchronous Q-learning algorithms for RMDPs. Finally, we extend both the algorithm and its analysis to the synchronous setting, achieving a sample complexity of O ~ ​ ( S ​ A ε 2 ​ ( 1 − γ ) 3 ​ max ⁡ { 1 − γ , σ } ) \widetilde{O}\left(\frac{SA}{\varepsilon^{2}(1-\gamma)^{3}\max\{1-\gamma,\sigma\}}\right) . These results highlight the effectiveness and efficiency of our model-free method in addressing RMDPs.

title: Provably Efficient Q-learning for Robust Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yuchen Jiao, Gen Li
content: Our work paves the way for numerous future research directions. One direction for future research is to develop model-free algorithms with minimax-optimal sample complexity for robust MDPs. For standard MDPs, Li et al. (2024a) establish that vanilla Q-learning incurs an additional factor of ( 1 − γ ) − 1 (1-\gamma)^{-1} relative to the minimax lower bound. This limitation does not rule out improvements through algorithmic modifications: variance reduction improves the effective-horizon dependence of asynchronous Q-learning to ( 1 − γ ) − 3 (1-\gamma)^{-3} , matching the minimax dependence on this parameter ( Li et al., 2021b ) . Our robust Q-learning upper bound contains the same additional factor. It is therefore of interest to investigate whether variance reduction can close this gap in the robust setting. Another direction is to explore alternative distance measures, such as χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence. While we have established a model-free algorithm and its sample complexity for RMDPs under the TV distance, our approach relies heavily on the specific structure of the TV uncertainty set and can not be extended trivially to more general uncertainty sets. Extending our resampling construction and its guarantees to other uncertainty sets is left for future work.

title: Complete entropy contraction from conditional hyperboundedness
authors: Li Gao, Lijun Wang
content: Relative entropy is a fundamental information measure of distinguishability between two quantum states [ 30 , 19 ] . A key property of quantum relative entropy is the data-processing inequality, which states that any quantum information processing modeled by quantum channels cannot increase this distinguishability [ 24 , 11 ] . It is then natural to quantify the loss of information via a strong data-processing inequality that asks for a contraction coefficient strictly below one [ 20 ] . For quantum Markov semigroups, the corresponding exponential entropy decay is characterized by a modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality (MLSI), which is a powerful tool for obtaining quantitative bounds on mixing time to equilibrium [ 23 , 3 ] . When considering the correlated initial states with an external reference system, the complete versions of entropy contraction were studied for the same contraction rate after adjoining any idle auxiliary system, uniformly in its dimension [ 11 , 17 , 16 ] .

title: Complete entropy contraction from conditional hyperboundedness
authors: Li Gao, Lijun Wang
content: In the classical framework of Markov chains, detailed balance is a standard condition to ensure the equilibrium state. In the quantum setting, the detailed balance condition admits different generalizations. Under Gelfand–Naimark–Segal (GNS) detailed balance, the strongest among the quantum detailed balance conditions, a general route from spectral estimates to complete entropy decay is available. Gao and Rouzé [ 17 ] established finite-dimensional complete MLSI bounds in terms of the spectral gap and the complete index of the equilibrium expectation. Gao, Junge, LaRacuente, and Li [ 15 ] later obtained logarithmic index dependence through mixing in complete positivity order. More recently, Gao and Guo [ 14 , 13 ] obtained channel contraction and complete entropy-decay criteria without detailed balance, using GNS contraction or coercivity. These results motivate a natural question: whether the index assumption, which can be seen as an ultracontractive estimate, can be replaced by a weaker regularity estimate in terms of hyperboundedness.

title: Complete entropy contraction from conditional hyperboundedness
authors: Li Gao, Lijun Wang
content: A further motivation comes from the recent breakthrough of Chen, Kastoryano, and Gilyén [ 7 ] , who constructed an efficiently implementable Gibbs sampler satisfying exact Kubo–Martin–Schwinger (KMS) detailed balance for noncommuting Hamiltonians. Their construction, and its extensions [ 10 ] , make KMS-symmetric Lindbladians central to quantum thermal state preparation. KMS symmetry is weaker than GNS symmetry, so the GNS-symmetric entropy bounds do not apply directly. Subsequent work proved high-temperature rapid mixing [ 27 ] , size-uniform KMS spectral gaps for one-dimensional spin chains at every fixed finite temperature [ 5 ] , and further mixing and entropy-decay estimates for one-dimensional noncommuting systems [ 28 , 6 , 9 , 12 ] as well as at high temperature in general spatial dimensions [ 8 ] . Liu, Wan, and Wu [ 25 ] proved MLSI for every finite-dimensional primitive KMS-symmetric quantum Markov semigroup and gave a primitive KMS-symmetric example without CMLSI. These developments call for entropy estimates that can use the available norm and gap information beyond GNS detailed balance.

title: Complete entropy contraction from conditional hyperboundedness
authors: Li Gao, Lijun Wang
content: In the primitive KMS-symmetric setting, hyperboundedness offers such a connection. A single finite-time L 2 L_{2} -to- L q L_{q} estimate, together with a spectral gap, gives quantitative hypercontractive and L 2 L_{2} -logarithmic Sobolev bounds [ 29 ] . Wan and Wu [ 31 ] established a quantum Cheeger inequality for finite-dimensional primitive KMS-symmetric semigroups and obtained quantitative logarithmic Sobolev and hypercontractivity bounds. In our previous work [ 18 ] , we obtained a direct passage from hyperboundedness and centered L 2 L_{2} contraction to entropy contraction for a single channel, and derived MLSI bounds for primitive KMS-symmetric semigroups without assuming L p L_{p} -regularity. Becker, Rouzé, and Salzmann [ 4 ] extended the positive-time criterion to an infinite-dimensional primitive KMS setting. For finite-dimensional primitive KMS-symmetric semigroups, Wu [ 33 ] proved reverse hypercontractivity for 1 / 2 < p ≤ q < 1 1/2<p\leq q<1 and showed that the p = 1 / 2 p=1/2 logarithmic Sobolev constant can vanish.

title: Complete entropy contraction from conditional hyperboundedness
authors: Li Gao, Lijun Wang
content: The non-primitive case presents an additional obstruction. The limiting state is E ∗ ​ ρ E_{*}\rho , where E E is the equilibrium conditional expectation, and therefore depends on the input. Bardet [ 3 ] developed the corresponding MLSI framework, and Bardet and Rouzé [ 2 ] formulated hypercontractivity and weak logarithmic Sobolev inequalities using amalgamated L p L_{p} norms. In this setting the defect-free L 2 L_{2} -logarithmic Sobolev inequality often fails [ 2 , Theorem 5.1] , even though entropy decay can hold. This is related to the fact that the Rothaus lemma used to remove a logarithmic Sobolev defect in the primitive case has no direct non-primitive extension [ 16 ] : the obstruction also occurs for matrix amplifications of symmetric classical semigroups [ 15 , Proposition 1.5] . Thus the primitive route through defect removal to defect-free hypercontractivity or L 2 L_{2} -LSI does not extend to the conditional and complete setting for quantum systems.

content: Inspired by our primitive results, we study a direct passage from conditional hyperboundedness to entropy contraction with the help of a gap condition. The defect is removed at the entropy level. The resulting rates depend only on the hyperboundedness data and gap, which replaces the order control used in [ 14 ] .

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
section: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
content: Quantum networks are built from independent sources, and their nonlocality has mostly been studied with sources that emit bipartite entangled states. A source of three entangled qubits is richer, since its nonlocality can be tested by the Mermin or the more demanding Svetlichny inequality. We ask how network nonlocality relates to these two single-source notions, and find that the answer depends on the wiring. When two central nodes without inputs share every source, Bell-state measurements turn every Svetlichny violation into a network violation, and even all entangled generalized Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states violate the network inequality. When a single central node is shared, the relation reverses, and a network violation requires a Mermin violation of the source. With more sources, the maximal violation depends on whether their number is even or odd, and we give tight bounds for both cases. These results show that the way multipartite sources are wired decides which kind of nonlocality a network inherits.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: Violation of Bell’s inequality implies that the correlations of a single entangled state cannot be explained by a local hidden variable shared among the observers [ 5 , 13 , 9 ] , giving rise to the concept of nonlocality. Beyond its foundational significance, Bell nonlocality also enables practical tasks such as device-independent protocols [ 29 , 30 , 44 ] , quantum cryptography [ 1 , 17 , 38 , 22 ] , communication complexity [ 10 ] , and certification of randomness [ 37 , 2 ] , and thus lies at the heart of quantum information science [ 9 ] . A quantum network changes the central structure of the scenario. Here several independent sources distribute particles to different nodes and edges of the network. In the nodes the experimentalist can do joint measurement on particles produced by different independent sources. The natural local model assigns one hidden variable to each source and keeps these variables independent [ 7 , 8 , 18 ] . Correlations that escape every such network local model are called network nonlocal. Since the sources are independent, the local correlations form a nonconvex set, the inequalities that bound them are nonlinear. A node can reveal nonlocality even if it always performs the same joint measurement [ 8 , 18 , 39 ] . The bilocal scenario of entanglement swapping [ 51 , 7 ] , its extensions to star and other topologies [ 48 , 34 , 40 , 12 , 47 , 3 , 26 , 15 , 11 , 36 ] and the first experiments [ 41 ] have made network nonlocality a central part of the theory of the quantum internet [ 49 , 46 ] , which is one of the central goals of recent quantum technologies.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: However, almost all of the existing works on network nonlocality assume that every source emits a pair of particles. For two qubits there is a single notion of nonlocality, and the bilocality inequality is tied to it in a simple way. Two identical copies of a two-qubit state violate the bilocality inequality exactly when one copy violates the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality [ 21 , 3 ] . A source that emits three particles is different. Three-qubit entanglement comes in the inequivalent GHZ and W W classes [ 23 , 16 ] , and nonlocality itself splits into several notions. The Mermin inequality [ 31 ] excludes fully local models. The Svetlichny inequality [ 45 , 43 , 14 ] also excludes models in which two of the three parties share arbitrary resources, so its violation certifies genuine tripartite nonlocality [ 19 , 4 ] . A state may violate the first and satisfy the second.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: Network nonlocality with multipartite sources have been studied in a very limited number of works before. Trilocal inequalities for three tripartite sources were derived in Ref. [ 35 ] , where it was also noticed that genuine tripartite entanglement is not needed for a violation. General nonlinear inequalities that cover GHZ sources were given in Ref. [ 28 ] . Closest to the present work, Ref. [ 33 ] considered three tripartite sources whose particles are measured by two intermediate parties with a fixed GHZ-basis measurement. These works show that such networks can be nonlocal and that their violation can signal entanglement. See Table 1 for a more detailed comparison with these related works. However, nonlocality in multipartite systems have different notions, making it distinct from the ususal Bell-CHSH scenario. All the mentioned related works do not tell us how the network nonlocality compares with the nonlocality of a single tripartite source.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: This leads to the question we address in this work. When independent sources emit three-qubit states, how is a violation of the network inequality related to the Mermin and Svetlichny nonlocality of a single source, and does this relation depend on how the sources are wired? The answer is not obvious. A network test uses several copies of the source and joint measurements, so it might be stronger or weaker than either single-copy test. We study the two simplest ways of wiring tripartite sources, shown in Fig. 1 . In the closed network, two central nodes, Alice and Charlie, each receive one particle from every source and always perform the same measurement. The third particle of each source goes to an end node with two measurement settings. In the open network, a single central node receives one particle from every source, and the other two particles of each source go to two end nodes.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: Our main result is that the two wirings are bounded by the two single-copy inequalities from opposite sides. In the closed network with Bell-state measurements, the two-copy value of the network inequality is never smaller than the normalized Svetlichny value of one copy ( Theorem 2 ). Svetlichny nonlocality of the source is therefore sufficient for network nonlocality, and it is not necessary. All entangled generalized GHZ states, noisy W W states that satisfy the Svetlichny inequality and even biseparable states violate the network inequality. In the open network the relation is reversed. With a Bell-state measurement at the central node, a violation implies that one copy of the source violates the Mermin inequality ( Theorem 3 ).

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: Two further results follow from this analysis. First, for GHZ sources the entanglement that the closed network swaps to its end nodes is heralded only by the joint outcome of the two central nodes. Given the outcome of one central node alone, the end nodes share a separable state ( Proposition 2 ). Second, we ask what happens with more sources. Because the central nodes have no input, the two correlators of the network inequality must be read from one fixed measurement. For an odd number of sources they involve anticommuting observables, and the maximal violation of the inequalities drops below its value for an even number of sources. We derive tight bounds for both cases ( Theorem 4 ).

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: The paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the Mermin and Svetlichny inequalities and the network model, and fixes the measurement classes used throughout. Section III treats the closed network and its relation to the Svetlichny inequality. Section IV looks at the state that the closed network prepares at its end nodes. Section V treats the open network and its relation to the Mermin inequality. Section VI turns to many sources and the parity effect. Section VII discusses what the results mean and concludes. Proofs are given in Appendix Appendices A , B , C , D , E and F , and the numerical methods in Appendix G .

First, any inequality that holds for the star also holds for the closed network, and inequalities for the star are well known [ 48 ] . Sorted by the two perpendicular directions of the end node, the Svetlichny expression contains four three-body correlators X , Y , Z , W X,Y,Z,W , two for each direction. Alice and Charlie must switch between two settings, and as a result the correlators enter with weights whose absolute values add up to at most one. section: VI Many sources and the parity effect
content: So far we have used two sources. In both networks the central nodes have no input, and this has a consequence that becomes visible once more sources are added. A central node must provide the signs for both correlators, I I and J J , from the same measurement in every run. We now show that this is possible without loss for an even number of sources, but not for an odd number.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
section: VI Many sources and the parity effect
content: Intuition. Consider the closed network with n n sources, as in Fig. 1 (b), and qubit end nodes. The sum and the difference of the two observables of the i i th end node are proportional to Pauli operators along perpendicular directions 𝒏 i {\bm{n}}_{i} and 𝒏 i ′ {\bm{n}}_{i}^{\prime} , and two such operators anticommute. The correlator I I probes the product P P of the n n operators 𝒏 i ⋅ 𝝈 {\bm{n}}_{i}\cdot{\bm{\sigma}} , and J J probes the product Q Q of the n n operators 𝒏 i ′ ⋅ 𝝈 {\bm{n}}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot{\bm{\sigma}} . Moving Q Q past P P produces one minus sign per factor, so P ​ Q = ( − 1 ) n ​ Q ​ P PQ=(-1)^{n}QP . For even n n the two products commute, and the central nodes can herald states in which both have definite values. For odd n n they anticommute, and no state of the end nodes can have large expectation values of both [ 27 ] . A central node with a binary input could measure in a basis adapted to P P for one input and to Q Q for the other, and the star inequality with such a node is violated up to 2 \sqrt{2} for every n n [ 48 , 3 ] . A central node without input has to compromise, as long as the inequality contains only these two correlators.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: In this work, we studied how the nonlocality of a network whose sources emit three-qubit states is related to the Mermin and Svetlichny nonlocality of a single source. For the inequalities and measurements studied here, the answer depends on the wiring. In the closed network, where two central nodes without input share every source, the two-copy value with Bell-state measurements is bounded from below by the normalized Svetlichny value. Svetlichny nonlocality is thus sufficient for a violation, while all entangled generalized GHZ states, noisy W W states and even biseparable states show that it is not necessary. In the open network, where one central node is shared, the two-copy value with a Bell-state measurement is bounded from above by the normalized Mermin value, and GHZ sources reach the algebraic maximum.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: Both bounds have a simple operational origin. A central node without input does not switch settings. In the closed network this is an advantage, because the central nodes read all parities of their Bell-state measurements in every run, whereas the parties of a Svetlichny test must switch. In the open network it is a limitation, because the two parities that the central node uses belong to perpendicular directions, whereas the third party of a Mermin test may choose any two directions. With many sources the same feature produces the parity effect. A central node without input cannot decide in each run which of two anticommuting observables to herald, and for an odd number of sources this lowers the maximal violation from 2 \sqrt{2} to 2 1 / 2 − 1 / ( 2 ​ n ) 2^{1/2-1/(2n)} in the closed network and from 2 2 to 2 1 − 1 / ( 2 ​ n ) 2^{1-1/(2n)} in the open network.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: For entanglement distribution the closed network has a further feature. With GHZ sources, the entanglement swapped to the end nodes is heralded only by the joint outcome of the two central nodes, while the outcome of one central node leaves the end nodes in a separable state. In the presence of noise, the network inequality is violated at visibilities where the heralded state does not violate the CHSH inequality for two sources, or the Svetlichny inequality for three. These statements concern the specific tests named here, and we do not claim that the network offers a practical advantage for a particular task.

title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty, Amit Kundu
content: Several directions remain open. The values 𝒩 c \mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{c}} and 𝒩 o \mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{o}} refer to Bell-state measurements. Our numerics indicate that product projective measurements at the central nodes do not help for GHZ sources but do help for W W sources, and a closed form for the optimal measurement of a general state would be valuable. It would also be interesting to know whether the parity bound of the closed network holds for end nodes of higher dimension, and whether inequalities with many correlators, like the one of Ref. [ 48 ] , can be built for the closed network and related to the Mermin and Svetlichny values of a single source. Since biseparable sources already violate the inequalities used here, a further task is to find network tests with tripartite sources that certify the genuine multipartite character of the sources.

title: Interference-induced dynamical crossovers in quantum walks on disordered square lattices
authors: Ramnarayan Bera, Arijit Roy, Soumyadip Ghosh, Soumen Roy
section: Interference-induced dynamical crossovers in quantum walks on disordered square lattices
content: We study discrete-time quantum walks with Fourier, Grover, and Hadamard coin operators on disordered square lattices, alongside classical random walks. Edges in the lattice are absent with a probability, p p . In this case, both classical and quantum walks exhibit an essentially identical degradation of transport. We then study a general version of this model, in which the existing edges are retained. However, the absent edges are no longer absent, but become partially transmitting, with a transmission coefficient f f . We find that the response is now quite sensitive to the walk protocol and coin symmetry. The classical walk exhibits asymptotic stability of the anomalous diffusion exponent, β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) . In comparison, quantum walks exhibit a monotonically decaying β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) beyond the initial transient regime, leading to the absence of quantum diffusion in two dimensions. We map the transport regimes in the ( f , p ) (f,p) plane and identify the contour for β = 1 \beta=1 , which separates the subdiffusive and superdiffusive regimes. We also examine the effective diffusion coefficient, the inverse participation ratio, and the first two moments of edge transmission. We restrict ourselves to analyzing bulk propagation prior to finite-size boundary reflections. The results indicate that quantum transport depends significantly on coin-specific interference and cannot be fully described by transmission statistics alone.

title: Interference-induced dynamical crossovers in quantum walks on disordered square lattices
authors: Ramnarayan Bera, Arijit Roy, Soumyadip Ghosh, Soumen Roy
content: Quantum walks are the quantum-mechanical analogues of classical random walks and represent a foundational basis in quantum information science and quantum simulation [ 2 , 6 ] . On translationally invariant lattices, DTQWs spread ballistically because of unitary evolution and quantum interference. Their mean-squared displacement scales as σ 2 ​ ( t ) ∼ t β \sigma^{2}(t)\sim t^{\beta} , with β = 2 \beta=2 . By contrast, a CRW shows diffusive scaling with β = 1 \beta=1 . Quantum walks also provide a framework for studying quantum search, spatial exploration on complex networks, and state-transfer protocols [ 5 , 9 ] .

title: Interference-induced dynamical crossovers in quantum walks on disordered square lattices
authors: Ramnarayan Bera, Arijit Roy, Soumyadip Ghosh, Soumen Roy
content: Disorder can disrupt coherent quantum transport in crystalline and networked systems. Impurities, broken links, and phase fluctuations alter propagation. The scaling theory of localization predicts Anderson localization for non-interacting particles in two dimensions with static disorder [ 1 , 3 ] . This prediction concerns the infinite-system limit and the assumptions of the scaling theory. In a bond-percolation model, each edge is removed with probability p p . Edge removal can break network connectivity and create bottlenecks. These geometric effects may dominate transport and obscure differences between quantum interference and classical diffusion.

title: Interference-induced dynamical crossovers in quantum walks on disordered square lattices
authors: Ramnarayan Bera, Arijit Roy, Soumyadip Ghosh, Soumen Roy
content: To separate geometric disconnection from coherent scattering, we also study a beam-splitter disorder model. In this model, defects have transmission coefficient 0 ≤ f ≤ 1 0\leq f\leq 1 and occur with probability p p . Unlike bond removal, partial transmission preserves the links while allowing reflection and scattering. The transport therefore depends on both the disorder parameters and the coin operator. We compare the time dependence of β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) for classical and quantum walks to test whether the quantum walk shows a sustained diffusive regime within the simulated time window.

title: Interference-induced dynamical crossovers in quantum walks on disordered square lattices
authors: Ramnarayan Bera, Arijit Roy, Soumyadip Ghosh, Soumen Roy
content: We compare DTQWs and CRWs on disordered two-dimensional square lattices. We consider Fourier, Grover, and Hadamard coin operators. First, we examine transport under binary bond percolation. In this model, edges are either present or absent. We then study the beam-splitter model, which allows partial transmission and reflection. We compare the transport response across the walk protocols and coin operators.Our main findings are as follows: ∙ \bullet Absence of stable quantum diffusion: We find that the classical exponent β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) approaches a plateau, whereas the quantum exponent decreases over the analysed time window. This behaviour is consistent with localization, but the finite-time data alone do not prove asymptotic localization. ∙ \bullet Non-equilibrium phase diagrams: We map the measured transport regimes in the ( f , p ) (f,p) plane. The contour β = 1 \beta=1 separates superdiffusive spreading ( β > 1 \beta>1 ) from subdiffusive spreading ( β < 1 \beta<1 ). These labels describe the observed scaling and do not, by themselves, identify a unique microscopic interference mechanism. ∙ \bullet Effect of heterogeneity or percolation: The extracted threshold f c ​ ( p ) f_{c}(p) reaches a maximum near p c ≈ 0.50 p_{c}\approx 0.50 in our data. We examine whether this feature coincides with the bond-percolation threshold. A claim that it results from maximal destructive interference requires additional evidence. ∙ \bullet Statistical transport diagnostics: We analyse the early-time effective diffusion coefficient D eff D_{\mathrm{eff}} , the inverse participation ratio (IPR), and the first two moments of link transmission. We compare these observables for classical and quantum walks. The results test whether transmission statistics describe the classical response and whether additional coin-dependent effects are needed to describe quantum transport.

content: In this work, we presented a comprehensive numerical and comparative investigation of transport dynamics and localization phenomena in DTQWs and CRWs across disordered two-dimensional square lattices. By contrasting the Fourier, Grover, and Hadamard coin operators against classical diffusion, our show the fundamental differences between classical stochastic transport and coherent wave propagation in disordered low-dimensional media.

content: A central insight guiding our framework is the methodological motivation for transitioning from strong bond percolation to partial transmission edge disorder. Under standard binary bond percolation, where lattice edges are completely removed with probability 1 − p 1-p , structural link absences create severe topological ruptures that dominate the transport degradation. In this strong-disorder regime, both classical diffusion and quantum walks experience an essentially identical collapse in transport efficiency.So, this case completely erase the distinct signatures of coin operator symmetries. To circumvent this topological obliteration and investigate how intrinsic coin symmetries and coherent phase interference govern transport resilience, we implemented the partially transmitting edge lattice model. This model preserves underlying lattice connectivity while introducing controlled local phase shifts and scattering, thereby uncovering sharp, coin-dependent transport regimes that remain entirely obscured in conventional percolation models.

content: Our dynamical diagnostics provide direct numerical evidence for the absence of sustained quantum diffusion in two-dimensional non-interacting lattices subject to weak static disorder. By isolating early-time bulk propagation within the causal light-cone window prior to boundary reflections, we revealed contrasting dynamical scaling between classical and quantum walks. Whil CRWs asymptotically settle into a stabilized diffusion exponent ( β ≈ 1 \beta\approx 1 or fixed subdiffusive values), quantum walks exhibit a persistent, monotonic decrease in β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) past the microscopic transient regime. This decaying scaling exponent, coupled with the asymptotic saturation of the inverse participation ratio ( IPR \mathrm{IPR} ), demonstrates that coherent wave packets do not support an intermediate, stable quantum-diffusive phase; rather, cumulative destructive interference drives the system toward Anderson localization, aligning with the one-parameter scaling theory in two dimensions.

content: Furthermore, mapping the non-equilibrium phase diagrams across the ( f , p ) (f,p) parameter space established the critical dynamical interface at β = 1 \beta=1 , which separates domains of transient super-diffusive mobility from destructive sub-diffusive arrest. We demonstrated that the position and peak of this interface depend strongly on the spatial heterogeneity of the disorder and the specific coin symmetry. The Grover coin operator, while sustaining higher early-time effective diffusion coefficients D eff D_{\mathrm{eff}} due to preferential diagonal transmission, ultimately localizes into a more spatially confined volume than the Hadamard or Fourier coins. Statistical analysis against network transmission moments highlighted that while classical transport correlates monotonically with transmission variance σ T 2 \sigma_{T}^{2} , quantum propagation decouples from simple disorder moments, governed instead by multi-path interference pathways.
